The NUL terminator is written one byte past src: p points at src[dir->length + trail + name.length] (index NJS_MAX_PATH+1 with the same witness dir="/", name.length=NJS_MAX_PATH), while src declared at line 6 admits indices 0..NJS_MAX_PATH. Same root cause as line 39: info->name.length is excluded from the line 25 bound because length was overwritten at line 12. CWE-121 stack buffer overflow.

assumptions: NJS_MAX_PATH >= 1, required for the minimal witness (dir="/", name.length=NJS_MAX_PATH) to pass the line 25 guard.
njs_cpymem has the standard memcpy semantics of copying size bytes and returning dest+size, which is how the shown code uses its return value.

info->name is populated by the caller from externally influenced module/file-path strings; per Phase 1 role (b), the shown code itself leaves info->name.length unconstrained on the dir != NULL path, and the finding is based on that residual range.
limitations: realpath(&src[0], &info->path[0]) at line 42 could overflow info->path if its capacity is smaller than PATH_MAX, but the capacity of info->path is not identifiable from the shown code, so that boundary claim is unconfirmed.

TOCTOU between realpath (line 42) and open (line 47) is a hardening concern whose exploitability depends on a filesystem race and caller context not established in the shown code.
Path traversal via module names is not assessed; it depends on the caller's module-resolution policy outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: In the multi-slice branch, the slice loop indexes the per-slice min/max range vectors using num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_) (lines 6-9, 49) without any check that input_min_range/input_max_range (and the outputs allocated with minmax_shape at lines 31-34) actually contain num_slices elements. A witness like input shape (1,5,1) with axis_=1 and a 1-element min/max range yields heap out-of-bounds reads at min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) and heap out-of-bounds writes through &output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i) and &output_max_tensor->flat<float>()(i) for i = 1..4 (CWE-787; same-root-cause OOB read at lines 51-52).

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write (CWE-787). The entry-point value input.dim_size(axis_) (line 8, with only the check axis_ > -1 at line 7) sets num_slices; the loop guard i < num_slices (line 49) admits i = 0..num_slices-1. The write targets were allocated at lines 31-34 with capacity minmax_shape.NumElements(), i.e., the element count of entry-point input ctx->input(1), which the shown code never constrains relative to num_slices (empty admitted set for that property). With axis_=1, input dim_size(1)=5, and a 1-element min/max range, indices 1..4 address elements 4 past... indices 1..4 exceed the 1-element capacity; QuantizeSlice writes through the resulting out-of-range pointers, so the derived index domain exceeds the buffer capacity.

evidence.snippet:
input_tensor.template chip<1>(i), min_ranges(i),
                    max_ranges(i), output_tensor.template chip<1>(i),
evidence.reason: Heap OOB read (same root cause as the CWE-787 write; not an independent CWE). min_ranges/max_ranges are vec<float>() views (lines 47-48) whose capacity is the element count of entry-point inputs 1 and 2; no shown check ties num_slices (line 8) to those element counts. With axis_=1, dim_size(1)=5 and 1-element range tensors, min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) for i=1..4 read past the 1-element vectors, with the loop guard i < num_slices at line 49 explicitly admitting those indices.

assumptions: mode_ takes a non-MIN_FIRST value on the multi-slice path, satisfying line 28.
input, input_min_range, and input_max_range are entry-point operator tensors whose shapes and element counts are supplied by the caller; the shown code imposes no validation on them.
axis_ == 1 and input shape (1,5,1) are valid admits of line 7 (axis_ > -1) with no upper bound in the shown code.
limitations: int num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_) (lines 6, 8) narrows int64_t to int; exploiting a wrap needs a dimension >= 2^31 and the resulting failure (skipped/partial loop) has no demonstrable corruption within the shown code.

axis_ is never validated against input.dims() before input.dim_size(axis_), output->dim_size(i) (lines 39-44), or flat_inner_outer_dims(axis_ - 1) (line 37); the underlying accessor's release-build behavior is outside the shown code, so no confirmed boundary claim.
The scalar path reads input_min_range/input_max_range element 0 (lines 21-22); non-emptiness is not established in the shown code (would rely on shape inference outside scope).
If min/max range tensors contain MORE than num_slices elements, only the first num_slices output entries are written, leaving the rest uninitialized; downstream effects are outside the shown code.
int64_t pre_dim/post_dim products could in principle overflow for pathological dims, but no concrete wrap value is reachable within realistic inputs shown here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All data fed to the digest sinks is server configuration or internal-helper state, never attacker input. The only size-dependent buffer use, X509_digest into hash_buffer (L11) followed by EVP_DigestUpdate (L16), is bounded by the fixed EVP_sha256() algorithm (32-byte digest), the RELEASE_ASSERT length check (L13) admitting only hash_length == 32, and the declared EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE (64-byte) capacity. Container-loop lengths (L21-L23, L28-L30) equal each element's own byte extent under standard container semantics, and every return code is checked with RELEASE_ASSERT, so no error-status, injection, crypto, or memory-safety flaw is reachable through the shown code.

assumptions: EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE is 64 and EVP_sha256() produces a 32-byte digest (OpenSSL/BoringSSL semantics).
md is a valid, initialized EVP_MD_CTX supplied by the (unshown) caller.

verify_certificate_hash_list_ and verify_certificate_spki_list_ hold standard byte containers (e.g., std::vector<uint8_t> or absl::InlinedVector<uint8_t, N>) so that data()/size()/sizeof(value_type) are mutually consistent.
RELEASE_ASSERT is Envoy's always-active fail-fast check (abort on failure), so the failure paths at L12/L13 and the rc checks terminate execution rather than continuing with bad state.
limitations: The element type and capacities of verify_certificate_hash_list_ / verify_certificate_spki_list_ are declared outside the shown code; an OOB claim relying on a non-standard element type (e.g., vector<std::string> with sizeof(value_type) > 1 combined with data() as char* storage) cannot be confirmed from the shown code and would require the absent type declaration.

X509_digest/EVP_DigestUpdate failures trigger RELEASE_ASSERT process aborts; this is fail-fast by design and not reachable from attacker-controlled values in the shown code, but an attacker-triggerable failure cannot be fully excluded without the callee implementations.

hash_length's initial value from the caller is unknown in the shown code, but it is never consumed without first being overwritten (L11) or aborting (L12), so no uninitialized-length read is confirmable.

Hashing the full certificate revocation list (L44-L47) invalidates session tickets when the CRL updates, an availability/continuity property driven by operator config, not by an attacker-controlled input in the shown code.
hash_length being passed by value means the caller's copy is never updated; nothing in the shown code depends on that propagation, so it is at most a robustness observation.

verdict.summary: In the exclude_trailing_space branch, the while condition at line 21 dereferences bd->textstart + s - 1 before checking s > 0. When s reaches 0 (empty block text or an all-whitespace block), the loop reads one byte before the text region — and before the heap allocation when the block starts at the allocation base — enabling an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125) and a crash on crafted files. The s > 0 guard is tested after the access and only prevents a further iteration, so it never protects the dereference.

evidence.reason: bd->textlen is an internal-helper int with no constraint imposed by the shown code, so textlen = 0 is admitted; with exclude_trailing_space nonzero, line 6 forces endspaces = 0 and line 19 yields s = 0. C && evaluation is left-to-right, so line 21 reads *(bd->textstart - 1) before the s > 0 operand is tested; the guard admits s == 0 at the moment of the access and only stops the next iteration. The source object's extent is textlen bytes from textstart, established by the memmove at line 13, so index -1 is one element before that region (before the heap object when the block starts at the allocation base), yielding a CWE-125 out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: bd->startspaces, bd->endspaces and bd->textlen are int (inferred from line 19's int declaration).
The C standard guarantees left-to-right evaluation with short-circuit of the && operands at line 21.
The valid source extent for the loop is the [bd->textstart, bd->textstart + bd->textlen) region copied at line 13.
limitations: The OOB read only crosses an allocation/page boundary when bd->textstart is at the start of its heap object; when the block begins mid-line, the read leaves the copied-text region but stays inside the enclosing line buffer, reducing impact to a one-byte over-read.

Integer overflow in alloc(bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1) at line 7 and negative-to-size_t casts at lines 11/13/15 are not confirmed, because driving the bd fields near INT_MAX is not demonstrable from the shown code.
An out-of-bounds index into y_current->y_array at line 10 is not confirmed, because the array capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.
No separate finding for *pnew = NUL at line 27: the loop body requires s > 0, so pnew cannot be decremented below the allocation base and the write stays in bounds.

verdict.summary: afra_box_read's global-entry loop is driven by an attacker-controlled 32-bit global_entry_count (read at line 35) with no bound against the remaining box size; each iteration allocates and inserts a ~24-byte entry plus a list node before the first data-availability check (line 41), so a crafted file can force memory roughly 7x its size, causing allocation-exhaustion DoS of the parsing process (CWE-770).

evidence.reason: Sink: per-iteration 24-byte allocation. global_entry_count from gf_bs_read_u32 (line 35) is entry-point input with residual range [0, 2^32-1]; its only shown guard, ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr,4) at line 34, checks that 4 bytes remain, not the count's magnitude. The loop at line 36 admits every value in [0,2^32-1], and the allocation at line 37 runs before the ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr,8) check at line 41, so a count such as 0xFFFFFFFF with a ~1 GiB remaining box size yields ~floor(R/8) allocations (~7x the remaining bytes including list-node overhead) before the data check stops the loop - memory-exhaustion DoS on a crafted file. Primary CWE-770: allocation of resource without limits/throttling.

Sink: list insertion allocates a node and grows the list on every iteration of the same attacker-count-driven loop (line 36, global_entry_count residual [0, 2^32-1] from line 35). Insertion occurs before the ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr,8) check at line 41 can terminate the loop, so the attacker-controlled count directly multiplies per-entry heap growth with no throttling or cap in the shown code; contributes to the same CWE-770 memory-exhaustion mechanism as the line-37 allocation.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr,n) rejects when ptr->size < n and subtracts n on success (the macro semantics the shown code relies on).
gf_bs_read_* reads stay within the allocated stream buffer and return 0 at EOF; this invariant is outside the shown code and is used only to avoid over-claiming OOB reads, not to justify a bound.
The box parser ensures the declared box size does not exceed the bytes available in the stream (outside the shown code); used only to cap the DoS volume, not as a shown-code safeguard.
ptr->local_access_entries and ptr->global_access_entries are non-NULL lists created by the box constructor (outside the shown code).
limitations: The 4 bytes consumed by the entry_count read (line 13) are never subtracted from ptr->size, and the check at line 14 compares against the inflated value size=S-9; using the maximal admitted count can read up to 4 bytes past the box's declared extent (e.g., S=33, short offsets, 2 entries need 24 bytes vs 20 remaining). Whether this reaches past the actual stream buffer cannot be confirmed because the buffer capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.

gf_list_insert return values are discarded at lines 20 and 39; the resulting leak/absent-entry only occurs if the allocator fails inside the list insertion, which is not attacker-controlled in the shown code, so no confirmed error-handling flaw beyond robustness.

The memory-exhaustion impact of the global-entry loop requires a crafted input with a large remaining box size (RAM roughly 7x that size); upload-size limits or platform memory caps would reduce severity.
No integer overflow, no OOB read/write relative to an identifiable capacity, no injection sink, and no weak-crypto choice exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: BD_DecMFFieldVec reads an MF field count nbFields directly from the attacker-controlled BIFS bitstream (5-bit NbBits, then NbBits bits, lines 19-20) with a residual range of [0, 2^31-1] and no validation in the shown code, then passes it unchanged as the element count to gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc at line 29. Witness NbBits=31 / nbFields=0x7FFFFFFF is admitted by the only guard (line 28, which places no bound on the count), forcing a multi-GiB allocation from a tiny payload and causing host memory exhaustion; the same unbounded count also drives the subsequent decode loops.

evidence.reason: nbFields is read from the entry-point bitstream at line 20 with NbBits in [0,31] (line 19), leaving a residual range [0, 2^31-1] with no cap, and reaches this allocation-size sink unchanged as the element count. The only guard on the path — field->fieldType != GF_SG_VRML_MFNODE (line 28) — admits every non-MFNODE type and imposes no numeric bound, so the witness nbFields = 2^31-1 (NbBits=31) is admitted; even a minimal 4-byte element type turns the request into >=8 GiB, so a small crafted bitstream causes uncontrolled resource allocation / host memory exhaustion (CWE-770).

assumptions: gf_bs_read_int returns the raw unsigned value of the requested bit width (0..2^NbBits-1) and gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc's third argument is an item count whose requested volume is count x element size.
bs carries externally supplied BIFS bitstream data, making nbFields attacker-controlled (entry-point provenance).
Element size for the allocation is not visible, but any nonzero size (>= 4 bytes for numeric MF types) makes nbFields=2^31-1 exceed the GiB range.
limitations: gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length(codec, nbFields) at line 25 receives the same unbounded bitstream-derived count, but the callee body and its expected capacity are not shown, so a failure inside it is unconfirmed.
The index passed to gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item at line 33 is in bounds: loop condition i<nbFields admits 0..nbFields-1 and line 29 allocates nbFields items — not a finding.
Unchecked returns of gf_node_register at line 63 and gf_bifs_dec_qp_remove at lines 53/88/94 are unconfirmable without callee semantics.
Huge iteration counts (loops at lines 32 and 40 for nbFields near 2^31-1) are part of the same unbounded-count problem and are not independently confirmed as an infinite-hang or OOB issue.
Truncated-stream behavior of gf_bs_read_int / gf_bifs_dec_sf_field is not shown and was not relied on for the verdict.
NULL-dereference paths would require caller-supplied NULL state not producible inside the shown code.

verdict.summary: DecodeChunk's chunk-offset bounds checks add the file-supplied 64-bit offset to a small constant in unsigned arithmetic (offsets[i] + sizeof(int)*N > size). Offsets in [2^64-20, 2^64-1] (tiled) or [2^64-8, 2^64-1] (scanline) wrap the sum to [0,19]/[0,7], which is never > size, so the guard admits them; data_ptr = head + offsets[i] then points up to ~2^64 bytes past the input buffer and the subsequent memcpy reads (lines 106/121, 194/196) perform an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), enabled by the integer overflow in the guard (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: CWE-125 primary, CWE-190 secondary. `offsets` is an internal-helper parameter whose residual range after the shown code's own guards is [0, 2^64-1]; nothing caps its magnitude. At line 94 the guard `offsets[tile_idx] + sizeof(int)*5 > size` uses unsigned 64-bit addition, so for offsets[tile_idx] = 2^64-20 the sum wraps to 0 and the guard admits the value (0 > size is false for every size). The else-path then sets data_ptr = head + offsets[tile_idx] (lines 102-103), a pointer ~2^64 bytes beyond the `size`-byte buffer, and the 16-byte memcpy at line 106 reads out of bounds (heap disclosure/crash on a crafted chunk table).

CWE-125 primary, CWE-190 secondary (same mechanism in the scanline branch). The guard at line 183, `offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int)*2 > size`, wraps modulo 2^64: for offsets[y_idx] = 2^64-8 the sum is 0, so the value is admitted into the else-branch and is never marked invalid. data_ptr is then formed as head + offsets[y_idx] (lines 190-191), ~2^64 bytes outside the `size`-byte input buffer, and this 4-byte memcpy (with the paired read at line 196) performs an out-of-bounds read; the unsigned overflow is the independent root cause that defeats the bounds check.

assumptions: tinyexr::tinyexr_uint64 and size_t are 64-bit unsigned types on the analyzed target, so offsets[i] + K wraps modulo 2^64.

`head` points to a byte buffer of exactly `size` bytes, and `size` is small enough (e.g. a real file size) that the wrapped sums [0,19]/[0,7] are never > size, which is the invariant the shown code itself relies on for all other offsets.
ComputeChannelLayout's return is checked at line 49 and does not constrain offset magnitudes.
limitations: Reachability of the wraparound witness depends on the caller forwarding attacker-controlled 64-bit offsets unvalidated; within the shown code those values have residual range [0, 2^64-1], which is exactly why the wrap bypass is analyzed as confirmed.

No upper bound on tile_size_x/tile_size_y (only `>= 0` at lines 62/71): huge tile sizes permit attacker-controlled multi-gigabyte allocations in the unshown AllocateImage (CWE-400-style DoS), but the allocation and its failure handling are outside the shown code.

total_data_len (lines 159-160) can wrap on 64-bit when num_channels is large (width*height <= 2^46 makes the product exceed 2^64), defeating the `>= 0x4000000000` guard, and the 32-bit path disables the guard entirely (line 161); the wrapped value is only compared, not consumed by an allocation-size/index sink in the shown code, so no CWE-190 sink is confirmed here.

The scanline loop bound `static_cast<int>(num_blocks)` (line 180) is implementation-defined for offsets.size() > INT_MAX and could skip blocks, silently returning success with a partial decode; data-integrity only, no memory-safety consequence demonstrated.

AllocateImage results (lines 87-89, 173-175) and the discarded DecodeTiledPixelData return (lines 134-146) are unchecked; NULL/failure states are produced by unshown callees, so NULL-deref and CWE-390 remain unconfirmed.

#pragma omp parallel for (lines 177-179) races on the shared bool invalid_data (lines 184, 200, 206, 210, 219, 237, 249) when OpenMP is enabled; impact is UB/error-flag loss, not a confirmed memory-safety mechanism (the TODO at line 58 acknowledges it).

The num_lines/line_no derivation (lines 213-250) was re-checked: adjusted line_no >= 0 and adjusted + num_lines <= data_height hold for the admitted sets, and a data_window[3]+1 overflow (INT_MAX + 1) collapses into num_lines <= 0 (lines 218-219), so no OOB-write finding is asserted there.
The `num_channels` loop at line 268 assumes exr_header->pixel_types has at least num_channels entries; that array length is a caller invariant, not established by the shown code.

verdict.summary: When gen_hash is entered with cursp() >= GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX, line 4 raises the flush threshold to INT16_MAX, so the pair counter `len` accumulates up to 16384 (cursp() == 2*len reaches 32768). The flush guard at line 36 admits that value, and line 39 passes len = 0x4000 as the OP_HASH count operand to genop_2; OP_HASH/OP_HASHADD encode this count in an 8-bit field, so counts > 255 are truncated/aliased in the emitted bytecode and the interpreter builds the hash from the wrong number of stack slots. The generated-code stack layout then diverges from the VM register accounting, causing an out-of-bounds read/write on the VM operand stack (CWE-787). Concrete witness: a 16,384-pair hash literal compiled in a deeply nested value context (val != 0, no **rest).

evidence.reason: `len` is the number of hash pairs accumulated since the last flush. Line 4 admits slimit = INT16_MAX when cursp() >= GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX, and the flush guard at line 36 (val && cursp() >= slimit) admits len = 16384 (2*16384 = 32768 >= 32767) before any smaller-accounted emission, since no shown check bounds len by the OP_HASH count-operand domain. A 16,384-pair hash literal on that path reaches this sink with len = 0x4000, which exceeds the 8-bit count field that genop_2 encodes for OP_HASH; the truncated count makes the VM consume a different number of stack slots than the emitter accounted for, corrupting the VM operand-stack layout into an out-of-bounds read/write (CWE-787).

assumptions: int is 32-bit (standard mruby build), so len*2 <= 32768 and len*2+1 <= 32769 cannot wrap; the loop/len bounds hold on that basis.

GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX is small (<= ~140) compared to INT16_MAX = 32767; its exact value does not change the analysis because the dangerous admission is the INT16_MAX branch taken when cursp() >= GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX.

codegen(s, node, val) in value context pushes exactly one stack slot per generated value, so k consecutive pairs give cursp == cursp_reset + 2k and the pop_n(len*2)/pop_n(len*2+1) counts are always covered by cursp().
The AST list is NULL-terminated and well-formed (parser invariant outside the shown code), so the while (tree) loop terminates.
The OP_HASH/OP_HASHADD count operand is an 8-bit field in the standard mruby instruction encoding; this encoding fact is what makes len = 0x4000 out of domain at the genop_2 call sites.
limitations: The 8-bit operand width of OP_HASH/OP_HASHADD is not stated in the shown code; if the true operand width were >= 16 bits, the INT16_MAX-based flush guard in the shown code would keep len (<= 16384) in-domain and the finding would not hold.

The same operand-truncation class also affects the register operand cursp() (e.g., L13/L39) for very deep stacks, but the concrete witness above is carried by the len operand; the register-side case is not separately confirmed.

A NULL/shape dereference at L9 or L31-L32 on a malformed AST is not confirmable: the shown code contains no step that produces the NULL, and the AST layout is guaranteed by the parser outside the shown code.
The unused `limit` parameter means there is no explicit hash-size cap; this is a hardening concern, not an independently demonstrated failure.
Return values of the three codegen(...) calls (L21, L31, L32) are discarded; no error-status contract is visible in the shown code, so a status-handling flaw cannot be confirmed.

With val == 0 the flush never fires and len can grow to the total pair count, but no sink (pop_n/genop_2) consumes len on that path inside the shown code, so no memory-safety impact is derivable there.
A cyclic (non-NULL-terminated) tree would make the while (tree) loop unbounded, but the shown code cannot produce such input; left as a robustness note.

verdict.summary: The CDATA loop in xml_parse_node never terminates when CDATA text contains a ']' that is not immediately followed by '>'. After pj_scan_get_until_ch() (line 97) parks scanner->curptr on the first ']' (behavior the shown code itself relies on at lines 16-17), the exit test at line 98 compares e.g. ']b]' against ']]>' and never matches, and the loop body's pj_scan_get_until_ch() (line 100) re-finds that same ']' at offset 0, returning an empty slice without advancing the cursor. Any parser input containing with a lone ']' (e.g. '') therefore hangs the parser forever, a remotely triggerable CPU DoS (CWE-835). A secondary, environment-dependent stack-exhaustion concern from unbounded recursion at line 83 is noted in limitations.

evidence.reason: Scanner buffer content is the internal-helper input with residual range unconstrained by the shown code after the line-8 first-byte '<' gate, lines 12/28 excluding only '' is admitted by every guard on the path (lines 8, 47, 50, 53, 76, 80-81, 93-94). Line 97's pj_scan_get_until_ch() parks the cursor on the first ']' (invariant required by lines 16-17, which test *scanner->curptr == '?' right after get_until_ch). The line 98 exit test then compares a fixed ']b]' against ']]>' and can never succeed, while line 100's pj_scan_get_until_ch() finds its ']' terminator at offset 0, returns an empty slice, and leaves the cursor unchanged, so the loop state never changes and the loop never exits (CWE-835), giving an unbounded CPU hang on tiny input.

assumptions: pj_scan_get_until_ch()/pj_scan_strcmp() leave scanner->curptr parked on the found terminator; this is implied by the helper names and is required by the shown code's own usage at lines 16-17 (get_until_ch then *curptr=='?') and lines 33-34.
The XML body inside the scanner buffer is attacker-controlled up to the caller's buffer length; the shown code imposes no length cap, only the first-byte checks at lines 8/12/28.
on_syntax_error() does not return on failure (error/exception path), otherwise parsing would continue on malformed state.
limitations: Stack exhaustion via unbounded recursion at line 83 (CWE-674/400 class): nesting depth is O(input length) and deep inputs can overflow the stack, but the crash depends on host stack size and on PJ_CHECK_STACK() (line 6) behavior, neither identifiable from the shown code, so it is kept as a secondary environment-dependent concern rather than the verdict CWE.

Reads of *scanner->curptr and *(scanner->curptr+1) at lines 12, 17, 80-81 and 93, plus terminator scans reaching EOF (lines 16, 32, 89, 97, 100), could be OOB if the scanner buffer lacks padding, but the buffer capacity is not identifiable from the shown code (CWE-125 unconfirmed).

Attribute loop (lines 53-66): for input like '<a b="c">', if pj_scan_get_until_chr() returns an empty slice without advancing when the cursor already sits on a delimiter, the loop never progresses; callee behavior at a leading delimiter is not determinable from the shown code.

attr->value.slen -= 2 (line 62): underflow would require pj_scan_get_quotes() to return fewer than two characters, contradicting the shown 'remove quote characters' intent (the result includes both quotes, so slen >= 2); no confirmed underflow.
Unchecked alloc_node()/alloc_attr() results (lines 44, 54) could be NULL-dereferenced on pool exhaustion, but allocation failure size victims are not attacker-controlled per the shown code.

PI/comment loops (lines 14-23, 30-39) terminate only because the scanning helpers raise a syntax error at EOF; if they returned normally at EOF the line-17 reads would be out of bounds — unconfirmable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: ComputeAsync indexes the shape arrays via input.dim_size(ndims - 1) and rhs.dim_size(ndims - 1) (lines 5-6) before validating tensor rank (ndims >= 2 at line 9, rhs.dims() == ndims at line 12). A rank-0 input yields index -1 against a 0-element dim array; an input rank of 2 paired with a rank-1 rhs yields index 1 == rhs capacity 1. Both are out-of-domain accesses on a standard index-accessor whose argument the shown code derives, causing an out-of-bounds read of shape storage or a fatal assertion (process abort) — an attacker-controllable-tensor DoS.

evidence.reason: Entry-point tensor input: ndims = input.dims() has residual range including 0 because no shown constraint precedes this read (the ndims >= 2 guard at line 9 executes afterward). With ndims == 0 the index ndims - 1 == -1 is outside the accessor's required domain 0 <= i < dims() (capacity 0), so the call at line 5 is an out-of-bounds read / fatal assertion from an attacker-supplied rank — CWE-125 at the sink; the guard's admitted set {2,3,...} cannot exclude a witness on the already-executed path.

The index ndims - 1 is derived from input's rank, not rhs's; e.g., ndims == 2 with a rank-1 rhs gives index 1 against rhs dim capacity 1 (index == capacity), and the rhs.dims() == ndims guard at line 12 runs only after this read. Out-of-domain index passed to the standard dim_size accessor -> out-of-bounds read of shape storage / assertion abort (CWE-125); the witness is admitted on the path preceding the guard.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC / OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC follow standard TensorFlow semantics: on failed condition they record the error, invoke done(), and return from the kernel.
TensorShape::dim_size(i) is a direct element accessor whose required domain is 0 <= i < dims(); its exact out-of-domain behavior (CHECK/assert vs raw out-of-bounds read) is implementation-specific.

Rank-0 and rank-mismatched input tensors are representable values for this entry point; the shown code imposes no constraint on rank before the reads at lines 5-6, and the later rank guards imply the kernel is expected to receive invalid-rank inputs.
limitations: The precise failure mode of an out-of-range dim_size index is not visible in the shown code: in builds where dim_size asserts, the impact is a reachable assertion/abort (CWE-617-style DoS) rather than a raw OOB read; the confirmed mechanism is the out-of-domain index itself, not a specific memory layout, and no information disclosure from the read is demonstrated (the value is unused after the guards return).

int64 n/nrhs are implicitly narrowed to int by Getrf/GetrfBatched/Getrs/GetrsBatched (lines 112, 122, 178, 194); a truncation witness requires n > INT_MAX (a square matrix with >2^31 elements, i.e., a >8GB tensor) and no such value is demonstrable from the shown code, so this is not a confirmed integer-overflow finding.
int batch loops (lines 105, 119, 171, 191) against int64 batch_size would wrap only if batch_size > INT_MAX, which is unreachable for real tensors; not confirmed.

The async callback comment (lines 213-216) claims temporary Tensors/ScratchSpace must be captured for kernel lifetimes, but the lambda (line 217) captures only context/done/dev_info; whether scoped tensors outlive ComputeAsync depends on CudaSolver::allocate_scoped_tensor / CheckLapackInfoAndDeleteSolverAsync internals not shown, so a use-after-free cannot be confirmed.
No injection sinks (error-message assembly is constant text plus safe operator<< integer interpolation), no weak-crypto/entropy choice, and no file/auth logic exist in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The return value of sscanf() at line 14 is discarded; when the caller-supplied string has fewer than six integer fields (e.g. "1,2,3,4,5" or "1,2,3"), the uninitialized stack ints a-f are read at line 15 (snprintf) and line 25 (data_port). The inet_aton() guard at line 18 only validates the formatted address string and cannot protect this, so stack residue leaks into ERR/DBG logs and into persistent ctrl->data_address/ctrl->data_port used by later data-connection code (CWE-457).

evidence.reason: sscanf(str, "%d,%d,%d,%d,%d,%d", ...) at line 14 can perform fewer than 6 conversions because str is an unconstrained caller-supplied string (no length/content guard in the shown code), and its return value is discarded. With str="1,2,3,4,5" (5 fields), e is assigned and f remains uninitialized (declared at line 3 without initializer). No branch blocks the path: line 15 formats the assigned a..d as "1.2.3.4", which line 18's inet_aton() admits, so execution reaches line 25, reading uninitialized f into ctrl->data_port. Primary CWE-457: use of an uninitialized stack value; the indeterminate port is also consumed by the DBG at line 27 and by out-of-shown-code data-connection setup.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(addr, sizeof(addr), "%d.%d.%d.%d", a, b, c, d);
evidence.reason: With str="1,2,3" (3 fields), sscanf at line 14 assigns only a, b, c and returns 3, a return value that is discarded; d (and e, f) remain uninitialized. This statement formats the indeterminate int d into addr. If the garbage-derived fourth octet parses as 0-255, line 18's inet_aton() admits the string and the residue reaches strlcpy at line 24 and ctrl->data_address; otherwise line 19's ERR logs the digit encoding of the stack residue. The inet_aton guard at line 18 only tests the digit/dot/minus string and cannot distinguish initialized from uninitialized ints. Primary CWE-457: uninitialized read at a second sink.

assumptions: str is a NUL-terminated string delivered by the FTP PORT-command parser (caller outside the shown code); per its role in the shown code it is treated as an internal-helper parameter whose residual range is unconstrained because the shown code imposes no guards before sscanf.
INET_ADDRSTRLEN denotes the standard IPv4 buffer capacity (>= 16 bytes), giving addr an identifiable capacity of 16 so snprintf cannot overflow it.
ctrl->data_address and ctrl->data_port are persistent state consumed by data-connection code outside the shown code.
limitations: No validation restricts e, f to 0..255, and e*256 (int) can overflow (e.g. e=99999999) before narrowing into ctrl->data_port; the consuming sink is outside the shown code, so a CWE-190/port-range verdict is not confirmable from the shown code alone.

FTP bounce: the PORT address is validated for IPv4 syntax but not bound to the control-connection peer; whether this is a vulnerability depends on server policy outside the shown code (RFC 959/2577), so it is not confirmed.
The capacity of ctrl->data_address is not identifiable from the shown code, so no boundary claim about that array is made.
A NULL ctrl pointer would only be producible by an out-of-scope caller; not a confirmed finding.
Unchecked return values of close()/uev_io_stop() on the stale-connection path are best-effort teardown, not a confirmed security flaw.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. The token-collection loop writing into command[] is protected by the continue guard requiring post-increment offset < MaxTextExtent-1 (L116-L118), which bounds the maximum flush NUL write to index MaxTextExtent-1 (in bounds for the 4096-byte buffer); no write can occur at or past index MaxTextExtent. Attacker-controlled doubles (sscanf %lf) can yield huge page dimensions and scene arithmetic can yield negative delegate args, but these flow only into bounded numeric strings and then into the external GhostPCL delegate (L216-L223), so any failure would occur outside the shown code and is unconfirmed. The discarded return of ExternalDelegateCommand (L223) is an error-handling robustness concern whose downstream failure path (ReadImage NULL -> ThrowReaderException, L229-L230) is handled.

assumptions: MaxTextExtent is 4096, matching the declared capacity of char command[MaxTextExtent] (L9), so the guard constant MaxTextExtent-1 is the last valid index of the buffer.

GetDelegateCommands(delegate_info) returns a fixed configuration template and ExternalDelegateCommand executes it via the shell; filename-style arguments substituted at L220 are unique temp names, not the raw attacker filename.
ReadBlobByte returns EOF or a byte in 0..255 as an int; the c != EOF loop condition is correct for that range.
limitations: Large or non-finite attacker doubles (sscanf at L131-L146) reach CastDoubleToLong/floor conversions (L153-L154, L192-L195) and can produce huge page dimensions; the only downstream consumers are bounded %g formatted strings and the external GhostPCL delegate command (L216-L223), with no allocation/index/pointer sink in the shown code, so impact there is unconfirmed (delegated resource exhaustion only).

The return of ExternalDelegateCommand (L223) is stored in status and never checked; a delegate failure is followed by ReadImage (L225), but a missing output yields NULL, which is handled at L229-L230, so no confirmed success-after-failure or unsafe dereference exists.
read_info->scene + read_info->number_scenes (L205/L209) is ssize_t arithmetic that could underflow and be formatted into delegate arguments; impact is confined to the external delegate, unconfirmed.

The loop-carried count value (L102/L131-L148) can trigger width/height recomputation for tokens that are not CropBox/MediaBox after one successful parse; this is a logic artifact with no security consequence observed.

Double-to-integer conversions of out-of-range values (CastDoubleToLong, L153/L154) are implementation-defined; even with LONG_MIN/LONG_MAX results the corrupted values are not consumed by any memory sink in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in handle_PORT: attacker-controlled PORT arguments parsed by sscanf as unbounded ints are rendered by sprintf into a 16-byte stack buffer (char addr[INET_ADDRSTRLEN]) with no width/range limit. Four 10-digit values produce a 44-byte write, overflowing by 28 bytes before inet_aton validation runs.

evidence.reason: str (entry-point input with residual range: any decimal int per the %d conversions at line 14) flows into a,b,c,d, each admitting up to 11 characters (e.g., 1000000000). The sink writes 43 chars plus NUL (44 bytes) into addr, whose capacity is 16 bytes (char addr[INET_ADDRSTRLEN], line 4), an overflow of 28 bytes; no guard before this write constrains the int magnitudes, and the inet_aton check at line 18 executes only after the write completes. Primary mechanism: fixed stack buffer overflow via unbounded sprintf copy (CWE-121).

assumptions: INET_ADDRSTRLEN has its standard POSIX value 16 (used for IPv4 dotted-quad strings); the numeric value is not defined inside the shown excerpt.
str is the raw network-supplied argument to the FTP PORT command (the shown code consumes it directly via sscanf).
limitations: The sscanf return value at line 14 is discarded; a partial match (e.g., "1,2") leaves a..f uninitialized, so lines 15 and 25 read indeterminate values (CWE-457/CWE-390-type flaw). This is real but nondeterministic and is subsumed by the overflow finding.
e * 256 + f at line 25 can overflow (UB) or go negative for attacker-chosen e/f, but the consumer of ctrl->data_port is outside the shown code, so security impact cannot be confirmed here.
The precise post-overflow memory corruption (which adjacent stack objects are clobbered) depends on stack layout not shown; the out-of-bounds write itself is confirmed by the shown code's arithmetic.
Log injection via lines 19/27 is not a finding: addr can contain only digits, '.', and '-'.

verdict.summary: Unchecked int64_t × size_t multiplication in the oversized-output check wraps modulo 2^64, so a fully-defined shape with num_elements()=2^61 and an 8-byte dtype computes a product of 0 and defeats the constant-folding size limit, causing downstream folding to attempt a ~16 EiB allocation (DoS/resource exhaustion).

evidence.reason: num_elements() (int64_t, residual range [0, 2^63-1] since shape_map is internal-helper and the shown code caps neither shape length nor element count) is multiplied by DataTypeSize() (size_t) in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic. The witness num_elements()=2^61 with output_type(i)=DT_INT64 (size 8) yields 2^64 ≡ 0, which passes the guard at line 29 for any non-negative max_constant_size_in_bytes, so the oversized node is not skipped and IsConstantFoldable returns true (line 69). CWE-190 integer overflow is the root cause of the defeated size/DoS guard; downstream constant folding then allocates an output of true size 2^64 bytes.

assumptions: max_constant_size_in_bytes is a non-negative budget, consistent with its use as a byte-size limit.
DataTypeSize(DT_INT64) == 8 and DataTypeSize returns a size_t (standard TensorFlow/library semantics).
Downstream constant folding allocates a tensor of num_elements() × DataTypeSize bytes (callee behavior outside the shown code).
limitations: n->output_type(i) is indexed by the shape-vector length; an OOB read would require shape_it->second.size() > n->num_outputs(), but the output-count capacity is not identifiable from the shown code, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable.
A NULL n would be dereferenced at line 9, but NULL can only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller, so it is not a confirmed finding.
Bodies of MaybeReplaceShapeOp (line 12) and KernelDefAvailable (line 57) are not shown; no claim is made about them, including whether MaybeReplaceShapeOp tolerates a NULL shape_map.
The 2^64-byte allocation that realizes the DoS occurs in folding code not shown here; the confirmed defect is limited to the overflow corrupting the guard decision in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The kernel validates the shapes of every input except the peephole weight tensors wci/wcf/wco: after reading them (lines 15/18/21) no OP_REQUIRES constrains their length, while cell_size (line 28) is forwarded together with them to functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop (lines 114-123). An attacker-supplied undersized peephole vector (e.g., length 1 with cell_size=5) passes all existing guards and causes an out-of-bounds read of up to cell_size-1 elements per vector, with the read results flowing into the gate outputs (info disclosure or crash) — CWE-125.

evidence.snippet:
functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop<Device, T, USE_CUBLAS, gate_layout>(
        batch_size, input_size, cell_size)(
        ctx, device, forget_bias_, cell_clip_, use_peephole_,
        x_tensor->matrix<T>(), cs_prev_tensor->matrix<T>(),
        h_prev_tensor->matrix<T>(), w_tensor->matrix<T>(), wci_tensor->vec<T>(),
        wcf_tensor->vec<T>(), wco_tensor->vec<T>(), b_tensor->vec<T>(),
        xh_tensor.matrix<T>(), i_tensor->matrix<T>(), cs_tensor->matrix<T>(),
        f_tensor->matrix<T>(), o_tensor->matrix<T>(), ci_tensor->matrix<T>(),
        co_tensor->matrix<T>(), gates_tensor.matrix<T>(),
        h_tensor->matrix<T>());
evidence.reason: The peephole vectors wci/wcf/wco (read at lines 15/18/21) are the only inputs with no OP_REQUIRES length check; their residual range is any element count in [0, 2^63-1]. The guards at lines 31-61 admit all shapes for them, so a witness such as wci=wcf=wco=length 1 with cell_size=5 (line 28) passes every guard, while the call at lines 114-123 forwards cell_size=5 together with the three length-1 vectors. By the functor's peephole semantics and the parallel checks applied to w/b/h_prev/cs_prev, wci/wcf/wco are consumed with indices 0..cell_size-1, yielding an out-of-bounds read of up to cell_size-1 elements past each vector's end (CWE-125); the excess and disclosure/crash impact scale with the attacker-controlled cell_size.

assumptions: functor::LSTMBlockCellFprop is the standard TF LSTM block-cell forward functor whose name, arity, and the sibling shape checks establish that wci/wcf/wco are length-cell_size peephole vectors indexed 0..cell_size-1.
dim_size() returns non-negative int64_t values.
limitations: The exact over-read instruction lives inside the unshown functor body; the finding is anchored at the call site (lines 114-123) under name-implied semantics, so the demonstrated excess is a range (up to cell_size-1 elements) rather than one quoted subscript.

int64 overflow of input_size+cell_size or cell_size*4 (lines 49/53/58/103/109) is not a confirmed finding: dimensional values of that magnitude are unattainable, and a two's-complement wrap would produce a negative result that fails the equality guards (error exit, not a bypass).

In-place forwarding of h_prev to output i (line 65) and cs_prev to output o (line 80) is safe only if the callee consumes those inputs before writing; that ordering is not visible in the shown code, so no independent write-side flaw was confirmed.
Rank mismatches (e.g., rank-0 peephole tensors) are not separately confirmed; vec() flattens them, and the resulting length mismatch is the same root cause already reported.

verdict.summary: The attestation-signature buffer data_signed is a fixed 200-byte stack array (line 9) filled by unbounded memcpy calls (lines 102, 105, 108, 114, 117) and an array store (line 111) using length parameters rpid_hash_len, credential_id_len, cert_x_len, cert_y_len whose residual range is unconstrained by any guard in the shown code. The accumulated data_signed_offset can exceed 199, causing a stack-based buffer overflow writable on a path reachable from attestation input.

evidence.reason: rpid_hash_len has residual range [0, SIZE_MAX] (no guard in the shown code) and is the memcpy length at this call. With rpid_hash_len=200, data_signed_offset=1 (set at lines 99-100), so the copy writes indices 1..200 of the 200-byte array declared at line 9 (capacity 0..199); index 200 is a 1-byte stack out-of-bounds write. CWE-121 mechanism.

Already-unbounded offset (1 + rpid_hash_len) plus the fixed 32-byte hash length can exceed the 200-byte capacity when rpid_hash_len > 167; this copy then writes past index 199 of data_signed (line 9). Same missing size check as line 102. CWE-121 mechanism.

credential_id_len is unconstrained ([0, SIZE_MAX]) and no remaining-capacity check exists; with credential_id_len > 135 (offset 65 at this point), the copy writes past the 200-byte array from line 9, overflowing the stack. CWE-121 mechanism.

data_signed_offset is the accumulated sum of unconstrained lengths (e.g., 201 when rpid_hash_len=200, from lines 102-103); the store uses it directly as an index into the 200-byte array (line 9), writing one byte beyond capacity. CWE-121 mechanism.

cert_x_len is unconstrained ([0, SIZE_MAX]); with offset already 166+ and cert_x_len large, the copy exceeds the 200-byte capacity of data_signed (line 9). No bounds guard exists in lines 98-118. CWE-121 mechanism.

cert_y_len is unconstrained and consumes the final accumulated offset; the total footprint 1 + rpid_hash_len + 32 + credential_id_len + 1 + cert_x_len + cert_y_len can exceed 200 (e.g., 230 with rpid_hash_len=32, credential_id_len=100, cert_x_len=cert_y_len=32), making this copy write past the end of data_signed (line 9). CWE-121 mechanism.

assumptions: size_t additions on this path do not wrap for the demonstrated witness values (tens-to-hundreds of bytes).
gnutls_x509_crt_import succeeds for an attacker-supplied valid DER certificate (standard GnuTLS semantics), satisfying the guard at line 55.
o_base64_encode and generate_digest_raw succeed on their fixed-size buffers (lines 82, 87), satisfying those guards.
limitations: att_cert is not checked with cbor_isa_bytestring after cbor_array_get at lines 52-54; whether cbor_bytestring_handle/length misbehave on a non-bytestring element depends on libcbor internals not shown, so this type-confusion concern is unconfirmed.

gnutls_pubkey_deinit(pubkey) and gnutls_x509_crt_deinit(cert) at lines 139-140 may receive NULL when the corresponding init failed at lines 14/18; NULL-safety depends on GnuTLS internals, unconfirmed.
o_strlen((char *)client_data) at line 87 requires client_data to be NUL-terminated; an out-of-domain non-terminated buffer would cause an OOB read that cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
When j_params lacks 'root-ca-list', line 60 skips certificate-chain validation; this is policy behavior, not a demonstrated vulnerability.

The byte-length parameters are classified as internal-helper with unconstrained residual range; whether an actual caller passes attacker-influenced values is outside the shown code but does not reduce the residual range the shown code leaves unguarded.

verdict.summary: The gather kernel forwards the untrusted, unvalidated params.axis (and params.batch_dims) straight into optimized_ops::Gather, which consumes the axis as an index into the input shape's dimension array and as the basis for offset arithmetic. An axis such as -1, which is a member of the full int32 admitted set (the shown code imposes no constraint), is outside the operation's required [0, rank) domain and causes an out-of-bounds read of shape metadata / input data (CWE-125) when a crafted model is executed.

evidence.snippet:
optimized_ops::Gather(op_params, GetTensorShape(input),
                        GetTensorData<InputT>(input), GetTensorShape(positions),
                        GetTensorData<PositionsT>(positions),
                        GetTensorShape(output), GetTensorData<InputT>(output));
evidence.reason: op_params.axis and op_params.batch_dims are exact copies of params.axis/params.batch_dims made at lines 4-5; those values' residual range is the full int32 range because the shown code applies no constraint (there is no range check, normalization, or clamp anywhere in lines 1-11). The call at lines 6-9 forwards them as the gather axis/batch-dims, consumed by name and use as indices into the input shape's dimension array and in offset arithmetic. The witness axis=-1 is a member of the admitted set (the path has zero guards), yet -1 is outside the operation's required domain [0, rank) for any rank>=1 input, so Gather indexes shape/dims metadata and derives read offsets out of bounds, producing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125 primary; the same root cause could skew write offsets, but that is not independently confirmable from the shown code).

assumptions: The tensors input, positions, and output are non-null with rank >= 1 in the analyzed invocation (standard TFLite kernel context), which makes any negative axis provably outside the valid domain [0, rank).
GetTensorData returns valid pointers for the tensors in the analyzed invocation; the shown code performs no null check.
limitations: The exact boundary case axis == input_rank is unconfirmable because the input rank is not identifiable from the shown code; the confirmed witness is the negative-axis case, which is out of domain for every rank >= 1.

An out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) inside optimized_ops::Gather and out-of-bounds reads caused by out-of-range positions values depend on callee and framework internals not shown, so they are not independently confirmed.

The unconditional return of kTfLiteOk at line 10 conceals any failure inside optimized_ops::Gather, but the shown code contains no failure-returning step to mishandle; this is not a confirmable status-handling flaw.
GetTensorData pointers are not null-checked, but a NULL pointer would be framework-produced rather than attacker-reachable through the shown code.

verdict.summary: The Gather kernel validates gather indices only for non-negativity (lines 8-13); any index in [0, max(PositionsT)] passes and is forwarded verbatim to optimized_ops::Gather (lines 18-21), whose required index domain is [0, axis_size-1]. An index >= the input's gather-axis size therefore reaches the gather sink and causes an out-of-bounds read of the input tensor (CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
optimized_ops::Gather(op_params, GetTensorShape(input),
                        GetTensorData<InputT>(input), GetTensorShape(positions),
                        GetTensorData<PositionsT>(positions),
                        GetTensorShape(output), GetTensorData<InputT>(output));
evidence.reason: Positions data is entry-point input; after the only shown guard (`indexes[i] < 0` at line 8 plus TF_LITE_ENSURE at line 13), its residual range is [0, max(PositionsT)], with no upper bound. The index pointer is forwarded unmodified at line 20 into optimized_ops::Gather, whose name-implied semantics index `input` at each coordinate in the required domain [0, axis_size-1]. Any index v >= axis_size is a member of the guard's admitted set and yet is out of domain for the sink, so the callee performs an out-of-bounds read of `input` — primary CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read via unvalidated index).

assumptions: PositionsT is a signed integer type (e.g., int32), so max(PositionsT) = 2^31-1 and the line-8 guard admits [0, 2^31-1].
The positions data buffer is allocated by the framework with `positions->bytes` equal to the live allocation size, so the check loop at lines 7-12 reads within the buffer.
optimized_ops::Gather indexes `input` using the supplied position coordinates, per the standard semantics of a gather operation.
limitations: The numeric gather-axis dimension of `input` is not visible in the shown code, so the out-of-bounds witness is a range (any index >= axis_size) rather than a single literal value; confidence is therefore 0.6 rather than >= 0.7.

params.axis and params.batch_dims (lines 16-17) are forwarded unvalidated; a negative/over-rank axis would be out of domain for the callee, but the input rank is not identifiable from the shown code, so no confirmed witness is possible.

positions->bytes is used at line 6 without sign, multiple-of-element-size, or bytes-vs-shape consistency checks; a framework-inconsistent bytes value could make num_indices huge or let unchecked trailing indices bypass line 8, but this depends on allocation invariants not visible in the shown code.

GetTensorData return values (lines 4, 19, 20, 21) are not null-checked; a null tensor-data pointer would be dereferenced, but producing such a state requires a framework allocation failure not demonstrated in the shown code.

The sink callee body is not shown; the finding is anchored at the call site per the out-of-domain argument rule, assuming standard gather semantics rather than any undocumented callee bounds-checking.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The risky access `(*input_label_counts)[1][label]` (line 52) is evaluated only when `num_inputs != 1` thanks to the || short-circuit on line 51; for `num_inputs >= 2` the outer vector is sized `num_inputs` (line 27) so index 1 is in-bounds, and for `num_inputs == 1` the access is never evaluated. All other label indices are bounded by `num_labels`, and every target vector is resized to exactly `num_labels` (lines 30, 38, 47). Residual OOB scenarios depend on unshown helper behavior (`ParseEinsumEquation` returning zero inputs) and are recorded in limitations.

assumptions: MapToLabels (called at lines 21 and 23) assigns consecutive integer labels in [0, label_mapping.size()) as stated by the comment on lines 13-14, so label indices are in [0, num_labels) and the count/type vectors sized to num_labels are correct.
kEllipsisLabel is a reserved sentinel outside [0, num_labels); it is excluded from all indexing by the guards at lines 32, 40, and 49.
ParseEinsumEquation propagates errors via the Status checked by TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR at line 11, and on success yields at least one input subscript per einsum grammar, so num_inputs >= 1.
limitations: If ParseEinsumEquation could succeed with zero input subscripts, line 51's `(*input_label_counts)[0]` would be an OOB read (outer vector sized num_inputs == 0 at line 27). Reachability is not demonstrated in the shown code because the helper body is not shown and einsum grammar implies at least one input; no CWE is attached.
If MapToLabels emitted a label outside [0, num_labels), the indices at lines 33, 41, 51, 52, and 53 would be OOB; this depends on the unshown helper and is unconfirmed.

For a single-input equation, `num_inputs == 1` on line 51 forces `unique == true` for every label (including repeated labels such as 'ii->i'); any downstream consequence would be outside the shown code and is unconfirmed.

The size_t-to-int narrowing at lines 16 and 26 cannot wrap for char-keyed maps (at most 256 distinct labels); wrapping for num_inputs would require more than 2^31 subscripts and is not demonstrated (DoS-only if it occurred).

verdict.summary: Unsigned underflow in pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi: attacker-controlled RTCP length field and padding byte make `rpsi->rpsi_bit_len = rpsi_len*8 - 16 - padlen` wrap (e.g. rpsi_len=0, padlen=0 yields SIZE_MAX-15), so pj_strset stores an out-of-domain string length (~2^61 for a 12-byte packet buffer) into rpsi.rpsi.slen, enabling an out-of-bounds read when the RPSI bit string is later consumed (remote DoS / memory disclosure).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled `rpsi_len` (0, from hdr->length==2 at line 18, admitted by the guard at lines 19-20 for length==12) and `padlen` (0..255, from packet byte at line 23) are combined in unsigned pj_size_t arithmetic: with rpsi_len=0 and padlen=0, `0 - 16` underflows to SIZE_MAX-15. The missing validation of padlen against rpsi_len*8-16 lets this witness pass every guard on the path (lines 11-12, 15, 19-20). Primary mechanism: CWE-190 integer underflow producing a wrapped length value.

The length argument is derived entirely from the underflowed value at line 25: (SIZE_MAX-15+7)/8 is ~2^61 on a 64-bit build, while `p` points at offset 10 of a buffer of identifiable capacity `length >= 12`. pj_strset consumes this argument as a length, storing a descriptor (slen) that exceeds the referenced object by ~2^61 bytes; downstream consumption of rpsi.rpsi therefore reads out of bounds (CWE-125 consequence of the CWE-190 root cause).

assumptions: pj_size_t (and rpsi->rpsi_bit_len, pj_str_t::slen) is an unsigned 64-bit type on the analyzed build; on 32-bit builds the underflow still yields ~2^32, equally out of domain.
sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_common) is the standard 8-byte RTCP header, making offsets 8/9 reads safe for the minimal length==12 witness.

PJ_ASSERT_RETURN is active (debug or assertions-enabled build); if compiled out, the length>=sizeof check at line 12 would also vanish, which is a separate hardening concern not analyzed as a finding.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds memory access occurs in downstream consumers of rpsi->rpsi (not shown), so the concrete CWE-125 read is not anchorable in the shown code; it is implied by the stored oversized descriptor length.
Values of hdr->length 0 or 1 that wrap rpsi_len to ~2^32 are excluded by the line 19-20 guard for any realistic buffer length, so they are not reported.
No CVE/number mapping is asserted; analysis is based only on the shown code.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor never enforces a lower bound on restore_index and never validates the element count of input(2). The guard at line 18 (size > restore_index) admits all negative restore_index values, so restore_index = -1 with an empty tensor_name_t passes and line 23 indexes it out of bounds (CWE-125). Independently, with restore_slice = true and input(2) having fewer than restore_index+1 elements, line 60 reads out of bounds from input(2).

evidence.reason: restore_index (int) is constrained only by the guard at line 18 (`size > restore_index`), which admits every value below size — including all negatives because size is NumElements(), an int64 >= 0. Witness: restore_index = -1 with size = 0 passes (0 > -1) and subscripts the 0-element tensor_name_t at index -1, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the guard excludes only {ri >= size} and leaves {ri < 0} admitted.

The shown code imposes no element-count check on entry-point input(2), and restore_index is bounded only against input(1) by line 18. Witness: restore_index = 1, input(1) size = 2 (guard admits 2 > 1), restore_slice = true, input(2) size = 0 — the subscript at 1 reads out of bounds from the empty input(2) tensor (CWE-125); the missing check is input(2).NumElements() > restore_index.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK set status and return from the kernel when their condition/status fails.
Tensor::flat<T>()(i) is a plain array subscript over NumElements() elements, valid only for 0 <= i < NumElements(), with the index type preserving int values, including negatives.

The canonical caller of RestoreTensor is not shown; the finding is based on the residual range the shown guard leaves for the internal-helper parameter restore_index (all ints below size, including negatives).
limitations: expected_output_dtype(restore_index) (line 49) and allocate_output(restore_index, ...) (line 78) would also receive a negative index, but the capacities of those internal context arrays are not identifiable from the shown code, so those subscripts are unconfirmed and carry no CWE.
restore_index + 1 at line 21 overflows signed int when restore_index == INT_MAX, but only on the failing path, and the wrapped value is not consumed by any size/index/length sink.
