The early return on bs allocation failure (lines 9-11) returns a partial list; impact is OOM-only and not attacker-scaleable within the shown loop.
Unchecked r_str_newf at line 19 could leave bs->name NULL; no consumer of bs->name is shown, so no confirmed dereference.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one in the process-args copy loop: the guard `i < argc - first_arg` admits a final iteration with `i = argc - first_arg - 1`, making the argv index `first_arg + i + 1` equal to `argc`, i.e. the mandatory NULL terminator. The NULL pointer is passed to the strdup-family wrapper `xstrdup` at line 44, a NULL-pointer dereference / UB on every `crun exec` invocation without `--process` (availability-only crash, low). The write side stays in bounds (capacity argc+1, at most argc-first_arg+1 elements written), so no OOB class applies.

evidence.reason: Entry-point argv (residual: argv[0..argc-1] non-NULL, argv[argc] == NULL) and argp-derived first_arg (0..argc) reach the index expression first_arg + i + 1. The loop guard `i < argc - first_arg` (line 43) admits i = argc - first_arg - 1, which yields index argc — the C-standard NULL terminator — so the final iteration passes NULL to the strdup-family wrapper xstrdup. Witness: argv = {crun-exec, id, cmd}, argc = 3, first_arg = 1, i = 1 => argv[3] == NULL. There is no protective check that stops the copy before index argc; the only in-code bounds (allocation argc+1 at line 42 and the loop guard) protect the write side only. Mechanism: NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476) in the dup wrapper causing a crash of the runtime; if the wrapper tolerates NULL the only effect is a duplicated terminator, which has no confirmable security impact.

assumptions: argv is the standard main argv (C11 5.1.2.2.1): argv[0..argc-1] non-NULL and argv[argc] == NULL.
argp_parse sets first_arg to the index of the first unparsed argument (0..argc) and exits on parse errors (ARGP_NO_EXIT not set).
crun_assert_n_args is name-implied: it aborts/errors when argc - first_arg does not match the expected count (1 or 2), and its discarded return is therefore safe.
x-prefixed helpers (xmalloc0/xmalloc/xstrdup) abort on OOM, and xstrdup is a strdup-family wrapper.
Line numbers are relative to the provided snippet (no file on disk).
limitations: The NULL-deref crash depends on xstrdup's (not-shown) NULL handling; if it tolerates NULL, the remaining effect is an args array with a duplicated NULL terminator and args_len = argc overcount, whose downstream impact is not confirmable from the shown code.

LISTEN_FDS handling: strtoll output (negative values, ERANGE -> LLONG_MAX) is truncated into int preserve_fds at line 31 with no validation, but the consuming fd-passing logic is outside the shown code, so no security impact is confirmable.
dup_array(exec_options.cap, exec_options.cap_size) uses an unvalidated parser-supplied length; the backing array's capacity is not identifiable in the shown code, so OOB cannot be confirmed.

process->args_len = argc (line 41) while only argc-first_arg+1 entries are initialized; consumers iterating args_len entries read in-bounds NULLs (xmalloc0), so any downstream NULL misuse is outside the shown code.
The discarded returns of argp_parse and crun_assert_n_args would be a concern only if those helpers fail to exit on error, which contradicts their name-implied behavior.
The non-zeroed xmalloc at line 62 is not a finding: all capabilities fields are assigned (lines 64-77) before publication at line 79.
(argc + 1) overflow at line 42 is unreachable in practice (requires argc near INT_MAX).

verdict.summary: When axis_ == 0, the multi-slice path reaches input.flat_inner_outer_dims<float, 3>(axis_ - 1) with begin = -1, an out-of-domain dimension index, causing an out-of-bounds read of the tensor shape storage (CWE-125) and a corrupted 3-D view that is subsequently used for per-slice quantization.

evidence.reason: axis_ is an entry-point attribute whose residual range after the guards at lines 7 and 8-9 is [0, dims()-1]; axis_ == 0 is admitted (e.g., input shape [2], min/max shape [2], non-MIN_FIRST mode: lines 15-40, 61, 71 all pass), yet axis_ - 1 yields begin == -1 at this sink. flat_inner_outer_dims' begin parameter is a zero-based dimension index requiring [0, dims()), so -1 indexes the tensor-shape storage out of bounds (OOB read, CWE-125) and feeds a corrupted 3-D shape into the chip/QuantizeSlice calls at lines 93-97.

assumptions: flat_inner_outer_dims<T, 3>(begin) interprets begin as a zero-based dimension index whose required domain is [0, dims()); a negative begin is out of domain under that standard semantics.
Input tensor shapes, min/max tensor contents, and the axis_ attribute are externally supplied entry-point data as consumed by this kernel.
limitations: Whether the corrupted 3-D view causes an actual out-of-bounds write inside Eigen's chip<1>/QuantizeSlice (lines 93-97) depends on callee geometry not shown; only the negative-index derivation and its OOB read of shape storage are confirmed.
For axis_ >= 1, axis_ - 1 also shifts the slice dimension relative to num_slices; the exact callee semantics are not shown, so a mismatch claim is unconfirmed.
int num_slices (line 14) narrowing from int64 would require dim_size > INT_MAX, unrealistic under shown constraints.
int64 pre_dim/post_dim products (lines 82-87) would overflow only beyond 2^63 elements.
Return status of QuantizeSlice/QuantizeTensor (lines 66, 93-97) is discarded but their signatures are not shown, so an error-handling flaw is unconfirmable.

verdict.summary: simplifyBroadcast reads shapes[0] with no guard that the ValueRange is non-empty. When `shapes` is empty, loop 1 (lines 7-12) iterates zero times, maxRank remains 0, the `maxRank == 0` guard at line 13 admits the empty range, and line 15 indexes element 0 of the zero-length ValueRange (index == capacity), causing an out-of-bounds read/UB (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: shapes is an internal-helper ValueRange whose residual range (Phase 1) includes size()==0 because no in-code check requires size() >= 1. Path: the empty range makes loop 1 (lines 7-12) yield maxRank==0, and the guard at line 13 (admitted set: all-zero-rank shapes OR empty shapes) admits the empty case; ValueRange::operator[](0) then requires 0 < 0, which is false (index == capacity), so line 15 performs an out-of-bounds read on the ValueRange (CWE-125). The witness (empty shapes) is a member of the line-13 guard's admitted set, and no later check protects this use.

assumptions: ValueRange behaves as an ArrayRef<Value>: operator[] performs begin()[index] with only a debug assert, so indexing at index == size() is an out-of-bounds read.
ArrayRefs returned by analysis.GetValueInfo outlive this function so the pointers stored in joined_dimensions (line 29) remain valid.
limitations: The int-vs-size_t loop condition `for (int i = 0; i != maxRank; ++i)` (line 45) would misbehave for maxRank >= 2^31 (counter cannot reach the bound, signed overflow on ++i), but no concrete witness is producible from the shown code, which would require materializing a rank of that size.

The mixed signed/unsigned expression at line 56 (`i - maxRank + shape_and_rank_for_dim[i].second`) wraps modulo 2^64 in the intermediate `size_t` subtraction, but for every reachable contributing position the final value equals the intended index in [0, rank); no corrupted value reaches the ExtractOp sink.
Line 49 casts the shape element type via RankedTensorType without a check; safety rests on a caller/verifier invariant not visible in the shown code.
builder is dereferenced (lines 14, 48, 50, 55, 57, 60) without a null check; a null OpBuilder is outside the framework-provided semantics visible here.

Whether an external attacker can actually invoke simplifyBroadcast with an empty `shapes` depends on callers not shown; the shown code itself provides no guard, so the empty range remains in the analyzed residual range.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476) in gf_isom_parse_movie_boxes_internal: in the GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS branch of the MOOF case, mov->moof->mfhd is dereferenced at line 365 without any NULL check, even though the same function NULL-guards every other parsed child-box pointer (lines 76, 332, 344, 458). An attacker-supplied fragmented MP4 whose top-level 'moof' box omits its 'mfhd' child passes every guard on the path (parse success at line 32, case GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_MOOF at line 292, non-debug, openMode == GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS at line 364) and triggers a NULL read, crashing the parser (DoS).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled input: a top-level 'moof' box parsed at line 30 (e >= 0 admitted at line 32, dispatched by switch on a->type at lines 49/292) whose child list need not contain 'mfhd'. Reachability: with single_moof_mode unset (line 298), debug flag unset (lines 312/325), and openMode == GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS (line 364), the branch at line 364 is entered; mov->moof was just assigned (line 308) but nothing guards mov->moof->mfhd, and the shown code's own NULL-checks of sibling child pointers (if (!mov->moov->mvhd) line 76, 'traf->tfhd &&' line 332, 'traf->trex && traf->tfhd' line 344, '!mov->moov->mvhd' line 458) establish that absent child boxes leave those pointers NULL after parsing. A moof without mfhd is therefore a member of every guard's admitted set and the dereference of NULL at line 365 is a NULL-pointer read (primary CWE-476), producing a parser crash on the crafted file.

assumptions: Compilation defines GF_ENABLE_ISOM_FRAGMENTS (i.e., GPAC_DISABLE_ISOM_FRAGMENTS is undefined) so the #ifndef block containing the MOOF case is compiled.

gf_isom_parse_root_box returns e >= 0 only with a successfully parsed box, and — consistent with the shown code's own NULL checks at lines 76, 332, 344, and 458 — leaves an absent child box's struct pointer NULL.
GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS is a caller-selected open mode reached while parsing attacker-supplied fragmented MP4 files; the shown code imposes no further precondition to reach line 365.
limitations: trak->Media->information->sampleTable dereference at line 100 without NULL checks: NULL-producibility depends on parser invariants not visible in the shown code; unconfirmed.

mov->moov->mvhd->timeScale at line 474: within a single invocation the shown code guards mvhd at lines 76 and 458, so a NULL would require cross-call state not demonstrated by the shown code; unconfirmed.

u64 underflow at lines 15-16 if mov->bytes_removed > mov->current_top_box_start in an assert-disabled build: bytes_removed is internal bookkeeping, not attacker-derived in the shown code; impact limited to a misplaced bitstream seek.
GF_LOG at line 27 passes a u64 to a %d format: format/type mismatch only; the format string is constant, so no injection.
Unchecked gf_list_add returns at lines 153, 327, 423 and unchecked gf_list_new at line 422: allocation-failure dependent, with no attacker-controlled volume demonstrable in the shown code.
Lines 379-381 test mov->root_ssix but delete mov->seg_ssix: the shown code never assigns root_ssix, so no confirmed double-free/leak state is demonstrable.
If mfhd were present with sequence_number == 0xFFFFFFFF, line 365 would wrap NextMoofNumber to 0, altering later SIDX handling; logic quirk with no memory-safety impact in the shown code.
OTYP-before-FTYP with mov->brand == NULL (lines 212-216): depends on unshown gf_list_del_item/gf_isom_box_del NULL semantics; unconfirmable as a finding.

Termination of the while loop at line 23 depends on gf_isom_parse_root_box advancing the bitstream on each success; the shown code does not enforce per-iteration advancement, so a non-advancing success cannot be ruled in or out from the shown code (not reported as a hang finding).

verdict.summary: Heap-buffer-overflow in GetEXIFProperty: FormatLocaleString(key,MaxTextExtent,"%s",description) at lines 783-784 writes a full EXIF tag description into key, which is heap-allocated at line 761 with only strlen(property)+1 bytes. With the admitted property "exif:*" (7-byte key) and any parseable EXIF entry, 27-33 bytes are written past the end of the allocation (e.g., 20-byte overflow for "exif:InteroperabilityIndex").

evidence.reason: key is the heap buffer allocated at line 761 via AcquireString(property) with capacity strlen(property)+1; property="exif:*" is admitted by the shown guards (443-447 non-empty and strlen>5; 451 switch case '*' sets all=1), giving a 7-byte buffer. The EXIF profile then supplies a tag (e.g., tag 0x0001, format BYTE, components=1 passing 616-626, 646, 652, 753), and the case-1 branch (764) sets description to an EXIFTag table string such as "exif:InteroperabilityIndex" (26 chars + NUL = 27 bytes). FormatLocaleString is a vsnprintf-style sink whose size argument here is the constant MaxTextExtent, not key's capacity, so 27 bytes are written into the 7-byte allocation — a 20-byte heap-buffer overflow (CWE-122). The guard set (652 requires p to hold one element; 753 requires value non-NULL) does not constrain the write size to key's capacity, so no protective check exists between 761 and 783.

assumptions: FormatLocaleString is vsnprintf-family: it writes up to its size argument (here MaxTextExtent), independent of the destination allocation.
AcquireString duplicates property into a heap buffer of strlen(property)+1 bytes.
MaxTextExtent is the ImageMagick output-buffer constant; its precise value is not needed beyond it being >35.
ReadPropertyByte consumes one byte and decrements length, so the header-scan loop at 533-548 terminates.
The EXIF profile is file-derived (attacker-controlled) entry-point data; property is treated as an internal-helper parameter per its residual range.
limitations: Caller-side origin of property is not shown; the finding rests on the residual range admitted by the shown code (len>=6 with property[5]=='*'), not on a caller invariant.
32-bit size_t multiplication wrap of components*tag_bytes[format] (line 624) is only partially mitigated by line 625 and is not confirmed on 64-bit targets.
NewSplayTree return (576-577) is unchecked; dereference at 612/614 requires an OOM that is not attacker-scaled by input volume.
Unaligned float/double loads in EXIFMultipleValues (lines 720, 725) are undefined behavior but not treated as a security finding.
The all==2 ('!') key writes (#%04lx/@%04lx) fit exactly within a 7-byte key and are not reported.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in finderrfunc. All inputs are framework-provided VM-internal state (L->base, L->stack, L->cframe, frame/cframe headers); the walk is bounded by guards visible in the shown code: line 5 ('frame > bot && cf') excludes every dereference at or below the stack bottom and every dereference of a NULL cframe, lines 12-13 terminate the cframe unwind on NULL before any re-dereference, and line 7 uses the restorestack result only in a comparison. Frame and cframe pointers only move toward bot, so no index/capacity overflow is derivable inside the shown code. Suspected issues (corrupted frame chain, INT32_MIN negation of cframe_nres at line 7, early exit when the cframe chain ends) are either guarded against or depend on VM-internal corruption/state outside the shown code, with no memory, injection, or crypto sink reached.

assumptions: VM-internal invariants assumed from the role of the data: the Lua stack region starts at tvref(L->stack) and extends upward so that L->base-1 lies within it; the frame chain and cframe chain are singly linked, acyclic, and terminate.

frame_prevl/frame_prevd always move the frame pointer to an earlier slot (toward bot), so the walk is monotone-decreasing; the direction is implied by their names and their use in this traversal loop, since their bodies are not part of the shown code.
cframe_nres is not INT32_MIN in valid VM state; the negation at line 7 is analyzed on that residual range.
Callers interpret 0 as 'no error handler found' and positive returns as a saved-stack offset of the error function.
limitations: If the VM-internal frame/cframe structures were corrupted by an unrelated memory-safety bug outside this function (e.g., a corrupted frame size/type causing frame_prevl/frame_prevd to jump arbitrarily), the walk here could read out of bounds or fail to terminate; no such corruption is provable from the shown code.

-cframe_nres(cf) at line 7 overflows if nres == INT32_MIN (signed-overflow UB), but the resulting pointer is only compared at line 7 and never dereferenced, so no security impact is demonstrable within the shown code.

cf = cframe_prev(cf) at lines 21 and 29 is not immediately null-checked; the shown control flow never dereferences cf while NULL because line 5 ('&& cf') is re-evaluated before any subsequent cframe access.

Termination of the inner loop (line 6) relies on the cframe chain ending in NULL (checked at lines 12-13) or the line 7 break; a cyclic cframe chain would hang, but that requires VM-internal corruption not shown here.

If the cframe chain ends (cf == NULL at line 5) while Lua frames remain below, the search for an error handler stops early; this is behavioral only and matches the upstream implementation, with no memory-safety or injection impact.

verdict.summary: selinux_ptrace_traceme is a straight pass-through authorization check: it calls avc_has_perm with the tracer (parent) as subject and the tracee (current) as object for PROCESS__PTRACE, and returns the verdict unchanged. No sink, guard bypass, memory operation, injection point, or return-status mishandling exists in the shown code.

assumptions: avc_has_perm returns 0 on grant and a negative errno (e.g., -EACCES) on denial or error, and the shown code propagates it directly.
task_sid_subj/task_sid_obj return valid SIDs for their task arguments in the kernel's ptrace hook context; their bodies are not shown.
The SELinux hook context guarantees parent is a valid task pointer and that the shown code may rely on the standard LSM hook contract, though no guard is present in the shown code itself.
limitations: A NULL parent passed to task_sid_subj(parent) would be a NULL-dereference candidate only if that callee dereferences it, but the shown code neither produces NULL (the only NULL literal is the non-dereferenced auditdata argument) nor dereferences parent itself, so the claim is unconfirmable from the shown code and carries no CWE.
No authorization correctness claim is made beyond the shown orientation (parent as subject, current as object), which matches PTRACE_TRACEME semantics; any caller-side flaw is out of scope.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The probe performs only a constant-size kzalloc (checked for NULL), balanced usb_get_dev/usb_put_dev on the error path, checked return values from hid_parse and hid_hw_start that are returned verbatim via ret on error, and queues delayed work only on the success path, where no free occurs. No attacker-controlled value reaches a memory, injection, crypto, file, or auth sink in the shown code.

assumptions: hid_is_usb(hdev) == true implies hdev->dev.parent points to a valid usb_interface, so the container_of-based interface_to_usbdev/to_usb_interface at line 15 is valid; this invariant comes from the HID core, not the shown code.
hid_parse and hid_hw_start return 0 on success and a negative errno on failure, and hid_hw_start performs its own cleanup on failure.
wq and ELO_PERIODIC_READ_INTERVAL are module-level globals/constants initialized outside this excerpt.
The reference taken by usb_get_dev at line 16 that survives the success path is released later in elo_remove (not shown).
limitations: Attacker-controlled report descriptors are consumed inside hid_parse/hid_hw_start, whose bodies are not shown; any descriptor-parsing vulnerability is out of scope for this excerpt.
Whether hid_hw_start can leave the device partially started on failure and require a later hid_hw_stop is a HID-core contract not visible here; unconfirmed, no CWE assigned.

The discarded return of queue_delayed_work at line 34 could mean the broken-firmware workaround silently fails to install; impact is loss of device functionality, not a security-relevant state, and the failure is not attacker-triggerable from the shown code.
The NULL-safety of udev relies on the framework invariant in the first assumption; a NULL dereference cannot be produced by any path inside the shown code itself.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in njs_module_path: the size_t addition at line 12 (length += dir->length) wraps, so the guard at line 25 admits a wrapped length <= NJS_MAX_PATH while the copies at lines 32/39 and the NUL at line 40 write dir->length + info->name.length + 1 bytes into src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1], exceeding the declared capacity by a computable amount (e.g., dir->length = 2^64 - P + 1, name.length = P). Primary CWE-787 with CWE-190 as the enabling root cause.

evidence.reason: njs_cpymem copies dir->length bytes into src (capacity NJS_MAX_PATH + 1, declared line 6); dir->length has residual range [0, SIZE_MAX] since no shown check constrains it. Witness: info->name.length = P = NJS_MAX_PATH, dir->length = 2^64 - P + 1; line 12 wraps the sum to 1, which passes both guards (line 14: 1 != 0; line 25: 1 <= P), and this copy alone writes 2^64 - P + 1 bytes into a P + 1-byte buffer, plus the P-byte copy at line 39 and NUL at line 40 — stack OOB write exceeding capacity by 2^64 - P + 1 bytes (primary CWE-787, enabled by the size_t wrap, CWE-190).

Second contributing copy sink for the same overflow: info->name.length (residual [0, SIZE_MAX]) is written into src after the dir copy, contributing P bytes in the witness above; combined with line 32 and line 40 the total written is 2^64 + 2 bytes against the identifiable capacity P + 1, so the guard's admitted set (wrapped length <= P) does not protect this sink.

Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): with dir != NULL, dir->length == 0 and info->name.length >= 1, the line-14 guard `length == 0` does not fire (length = name.length >= 1 is admitted), and dir->length - 1 underflows to SIZE_MAX, so the subscript reads dir->start[SIZE_MAX] — an index of -1 derived from a zero count, out of the subscripting domain of any object; the read value only feeds the '/' comparison, limiting impact to a fault or 1-byte over-read.

assumptions: NJS_MAX_PATH is a positive named constant P >= 1, so src's capacity P + 1 is identifiable from the declaration at line 6; its numeric value is irrelevant to the boundary argument.
njs_cpymem has memcpy semantics (copies exactly the given size in bytes, returns the destination end pointer) per its name and use in the shown code.
dir->start and info->name.start are caller-supplied buffers readable for dir->length / info->name.length bytes; the shown code never verifies this and consumes exactly these lengths.
size_t is 64-bit on the target platform; on 32-bit the same overflow witness shape holds with 2^32.
On success realpath NUL-terminates info->path, making the njs_strlen at line 53 well-defined.
limitations: A second confirmed finding (CWE-125 1-byte OOB read at line 18, dir->start[SIZE_MAX]) is reported in evidence but kept out of the cwe array per the single-primary-plus-one-secondary rule; severity low.
realpath at line 42 writes up to PATH_MAX bytes into &info->path[0], but info->path's capacity is not identifiable from the shown code — a capacity overflow there cannot be confirmed.
TOCTOU between realpath (line 42) and open (line 47) is not confirmed from the shown code; it needs local filesystem races and an authorization boundary not visible here.

Whether an njs script can construct njs_str_t length fields near SIZE_MAX is outside the shown code; the finding stands on the residual range [0, SIZE_MAX] that the shown code's own guards leave unconstrained.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in call_qftf_func. The only allocation (dict_alloc_lock, line 18) is NULL-checked before every use; cb_name is guarded at lines 9/11 before the callback invocation; and no input-derived size, index, or length reaches a memory, injection, or crypto sink in the shown code. The discarded dict_add_number returns (lines 20-24), the potential NULL-list dereference (line 35), and a possible per-call residual dict reference cannot be anchored to an attacker-reachable failure path and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: dict_alloc_lock(VAR_FIXED) returns a validly initialized dict_T* on success and signals failure with NULL, which the check at lines 18-19 fully handles.

call_callback does not consume or unref args[0], which is why the shown code pairs ++d->dv_refcount (line 25) with dict_unref(d) (line 39); the one residual reference is not observably dropped to zero in the shown code.
clear_tv(&rettv) at line 37 releases the caller-side reference of the returned typval, which is why the +1 list refcount at line 35 is taken before the clear.
limitations: NULL dereference of qfl at lines 9 and 22 is unconfirmed: no caller is shown, so a NULL qfl cannot be traced to an attacker-controllable path inside the shown code.
Potential NULL dereference of rettv.vval.v_list at line 35 is unconfirmed: the shown code provides no path that produces a VAR_LIST-typed typval whose v_list is NULL.

The discarded return statuses of dict_add_number at lines 20-24 are not confirmed findings: failure depends on internal allocation failure with no attacker-controlled size or volume, and the failure state (a valid dict missing a key) has no memory-safety consequence.

The refcount pattern at lines 25/39 may leave one residual reference per call, but whether that is a real leak depends on call_callback internals not shown, and at most it is a single-shot leak that does not compound with attacker-controlled volume in the shown code.
No loop exists in the shown code, so loop-bound, parser-invariant, and sentinel-termination analysis is vacuous.

verdict.summary: OP_ARGARY and OP_BLKPUSH perform an out-of-bounds read of one mrb_value past the environment stack when the keyword flag kd=1: the guard `MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1` omits the +kd term, so for the admitted boundary m1+r+m2 = MRB_ENV_LEN(e)-2 the sink `stack[m1+r+m2+1]` / `stack[m1+r+m2+kd]` indexes e->stack[MRB_ENV_LEN(e)], i.e. index == capacity.

evidence.reason: With kd=1 this reads stack[m1+r+m2+1] = e->stack[m1+r+m2+2] (stack = e->stack+1 at line 641). The only guard (line 639) admits m1+r+m2+1 < MRB_ENV_LEN(e), i.e. m1+r+m2 <= MRB_ENV_LEN(e)-2; at the admitted boundary m1+r+m2 = MRB_ENV_LEN(e)-2 the read index equals the capacity MRB_ENV_LEN(e) of e->stack (capacity per the GETUPVAR guard at lines 253-255), an out-of-bounds read by exactly one element (CWE-125). The index derives from the untrusted bytecode operand b (uint16_t, bits 4..15 -> kd,m1,r,m2 with ranges kd in {0,1}, m1 in [0,63], m2 in [0,31], r in {0,1}); e.g. b=0x50B1 (m1=10, r=0, m2=4, kd=1, lv=1) with MRB_ENV_LEN(e)=16 passes guard 639 (16 <= 15 is false) and triggers the read at e->stack[16].

Same kd off-by-one: guard (line 1170) requires m1+r+m2+1 < MRB_ENV_LEN(e), but with kd=1 and stack = e->stack+1 (line 1174) the operand index m1+r+m2+kd maps to e->stack[m1+r+m2+2]; for the admitted boundary m1+r+m2 = MRB_ENV_LEN(e)-2 the read location is e->stack[MRB_ENV_LEN(e)], one element past the env stack (CWE-125). The index is derived from bytecode operand b (lines 1159-1163) with residual ranges m1 in [0,63], m2 in [0,31], r,kd in {0,1}, lv in [1,15] and no shown constraint excluding the boundary.

Second sink of the same kd off-by-one in OP_BLKPUSH: for kd=1 and the guard-admitted boundary m1+r+m2 = MRB_ENV_LEN(e)-2, stack[m1+r+m2+kd] indexes e->stack[MRB_ENV_LEN(e)], equal to the capacity of e->stack; the out-of-bounds value is then stored into a VM register and consumed as the block argument, enabling adjacent-heap disclosure or a GC/VM crash (CWE-125).

assumptions: The irep/bytecode executed here is attacker-controlled (standard mruby surface: loading a crafted .mrb irep, e.g. via mrb_load_irep); operand values and the enclosing environment length MRB_ENV_LEN(e) are therefore both chosen by the bytecode.
MRB_ENV_LEN(e) is the capacity of e->stack in the shown code's own semantics: OP_GETUPVAR/OP_SETUPVAR (lines 253-255, 261-263) guard e->stack[b] with b < MRB_ENV_LEN(e).
mrb_assert is assumed compiled out in release builds.
limitations: Register/stack accesses indexed directly by operands (OP_MOVE, OP_HASH, OP_HASHADD, OP_ARYPUSH, OP_ARRAY2, OP_ENTER blk_pos/kw_pos, OP_EXEC stack_clear(regs+1, irep->nregs-1)) can exceed the frame when a crafted irep uses operand indices larger than nregs; the current frame's stack capacity is not identifiable inside this snippet, so no OOB claim is confirmed for those.

OP_JMPUW bounds the target `a < irep->ilen` only via mrb_assert; pc = irep->iseq + a (with a = (uint32_t)((pc-iseq) + (int16_t)a)) can then leave the iseq. This shares the untrusted-bytecode premise but the outcome depends on the heap layout after the iseq allocation, so it is left unconfirmed.

If ireps are only ever produced by the mruby compiler (trusted-bytecode model), the kd boundary combinations cannot be emitted and the finding does not apply; it holds under the untrusted-bytecode model stated in assumptions.

No integer-overflow, injection, weak-crypto, or NULL-dereference candidates were confirmed in the shown code; OP_GETIDX uses the bounds-safe mrb_ary_entry, and array/hash reads at lines 651, 660, 666 are covered by the same guard's non-kd range.

verdict.summary: A puma_parser_execute can read out of bounds when the caller passes off > len: the only constraint is a debug-only assert (line 5), and the parser's sole pre-dereference guard (line 15) checks p == pe, which admits p > pe, so the first byte read at case 1 dereferences buffer+off beyond pe.

evidence.reason: off (entry-point input, residual range [0, SIZE_MAX] when assert is compiled out) flows via line 7 'p = buffer+off' into the dereference at line 20. The only in-code constraint is assert(off <= len) at line 5, which vanishes under NDEBUG; the guard at line 15 ('if (p == pe)') admits every p != pe, including p > pe. Witness off = len + 1 gives p = buffer+len+1 > pe, passes the line-15 guard, and causes a CWE-125 out-of-bounds read of attacker-influenced magnitude (unbounded for larger off), with subsequent cases (e.g. case 2) continuing to dereference past pe.

assumptions: assert is compiled out under standard NDEBUG release builds; when asserts are enabled, line 5 blocks the off > len path and the parser is memory-safe within the shown code.
Marks are stored as absolute offsets and the same buffer is reused across incremental execute calls, so LEN(mark, p) remains in [0, len].
limitations: Attacker control of off is only role-classified (entry-point input); the product caller's derivation of off (typically 0 or parser nread) is not shown.

snake_upcase_char((char *)p) mutates the caller's const buffer in place (tr21/tr23); in-bounds, and in the real product the buffer is a writable Ruby heap string, so no confirmed attacker-reachable failure.
Non-ASCII bytes are rejected by signed-char range tests in several states (character-set handling), which is a robustness limitation, not a confirmed vulnerability.
Boundary claims about objects consumed inside the callback functions (request_method, http_field, header_done, etc.) cannot be verified because their bodies are not shown.

verdict.summary: pj_scan_get_char advances scanner->curptr past the only validated byte (the line 5 guard admits any non-zero byte at the original position) and then dereferences the incremented pointer at line 12 with no end-of-buffer or terminator check, producing an out-of-bounds read for input whose final byte is non-zero; if the out-of-bounds byte is whitespace, line 13 continues reading past the buffer.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). scanner->curptr is unconditionally advanced at line 10 past the byte validated at line 5, whose guard admits any non-zero byte but constrains only the original position; the dereference at line 12 targets position P+1 with no length/terminator check. For entry-point input whose final byte is non-zero and whose allocation ends at that byte (e.g., one-byte buffer {'A'}), line 10 moves curptr one past the end and this dereference reads 1 byte out of bounds; the value read at line 12 is only inspected afterward, so no guard admits/excludes it.

Continues the same out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). When the byte read out of bounds at line 12 is whitespace and scanner->skip_ws is set, scanner->curptr is one-past-end and this call scans forward from that position until a non-space byte, extending the over-read beyond the single byte and removing any bounded termination.

assumptions: scanner is non-NULL and curptr initially points within an allocated buffer (caller precondition not shown).
PJ_SCAN_IS_PROBABLY_SPACE is a pure predicate over a byte value (space/tab/CR/LF comparison) with no side effects.
pj_scan_syntax_err and pj_scan_skip_whitespace behave per their names: error reporting and forward whitespace skipping, respectively.

Failure impact (crash vs. information disclosure) depends on the surrounding process and allocator, which are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code alone. The read at line 11 is bounded by the guard at line 6 (admitted: s < end and *s != 0; excluded: s >= end or NUL). The post-increment dereference *s at line 15 is reached only after PJ_SCAN_CHECK_EOF(s) short-circuits first; under its standard precondition semantics it admits only in-range positions, excluding s == end. The residual hypotheses (1-byte OOB read at line 15 if PJ_SCAN_CHECK_EOF admits s == end and the backing allocation has no slack; unchecked return of pj_scan_skip_whitespace at line 18) depend on macro expansions and callee semantics absent from the shown code and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: Valid scanner character positions are [scanner->begin, scanner->end), as implied by the strict `>=` guard at line 6, so positions below `scanner->end` are the admitted read range.

PJ_SCAN_CHECK_EOF(s) acts as a read precondition (evaluated before the dereference at line 15 via C's left-to-right `&&`), admitting only positions still inside the text; its body is not in the shown code, so this is treated as an assumption, not a demonstrated invariant.

If `char` is signed, bytes >= 0x80 propagate negative values through `int chr` at lines 11/20; no sink in the shown code consumes the value, so no impact is traceable.
An interior NUL terminator is treated as EOF by line 6, silently truncating the scan; this is a robustness concern with no memory-safety impact visible in this function.

verdict.summary: elo_probe leaks a usb_device reference on every error path: usb_get_dev() at line 16 is never balanced by usb_put_dev() when hid_parse() or hid_hw_start() fails, so the kref is never decremented and the usb_device is not freed after disconnect. Repeated enumeration of devices that fail probe accumulates unreleased device objects (resource exhaustion, CWE-772).

evidence.reason: usb_get_dev(udev) at line 16 increments the usb_device refcount on every probe that passes the kzalloc check (line 11 admits only non-NULL priv). Both failure branches (line 23 from a nonzero hid_parse return and line 29 from a nonzero hid_hw_start return, admitted sets = any nonzero int) reach this block, which frees priv and returns ret without a matching usb_put_dev(priv->usbdev), permanently leaking the reference. A malformed USB HID report descriptor makes hid_parse return nonzero (attacker-controlled at the USB level), and each re-enumeration leaks another reference, so unreleased usb_device objects accumulate -> CWE-772 missing release of resource.

assumptions: hid_is_usb(hdev) (line 7) admits only devices with hdev->bus == BUS_USB, and for such devices the USB-HID transport sets hdev->dev.parent to the usb_interface, so the framework-derived pointers at line 15 are non-NULL.
hid_parse() and hid_hw_start() return 0 on success and nonzero on failure, as their names and standard kernel semantics imply.
The global workqueue wq and the constants ELO_PERIODIC_READ_INTERVAL are valid; probe failure never leaves the embedded delayed work pending because it is queued only on the success path (line 34).
limitations: After the error path, hdev->driver_data dangles (hid_set_drvdata at line 18, kfree at line 39), but no code in the shown function re-reads it, so no use-after-free is confirmable from the shown code.

Line 15 derives udev from hdev->dev.parent without a NULL check; the protection is the hid_is_usb guard plus the USB-HID transport invariant established outside the shown code, so a NULL-deref claim is a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

queue_delayed_work's return at line 34 is discarded while line 33 logs 'installing workaround'; a queueing failure would silently skip the workaround, but queueing failure is not attacker-controlled and impact is limited to a missing workaround.
On the success path the line-16 reference is released only in elo_remove (not shown), so a leak on the success path and any compounding there cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
The confirmed leak is low-severity resource exhaustion (CWE-772) requiring physical USB access and a probe that fails; it carries no memory-safety or injection impact.

verdict.summary: The shown code is a single authorization check: it calls avc_has_perm (lines 3-5) with the SIDs of parent and current for PROCESS__PTRACE and returns the verdict directly. No memory ops, arithmetic, casts, injection sinks, crypto, file operations, branches, or loops exist, so no memory-safety, injection, or logic flaw is confirmable within the shown code. The only reachable security sink is the avc_has_perm call, whose arguments are identity-derived SIDs with no out-of-domain derivation at the call site.

assumptions: task_sid_obj() returns the per-task SELinux SID and avc_has_perm() returns a permission verdict whose 0=allow/non-zero=deny semantics are honored by the not-shown hook caller.

The callers outside the shown code invoke this hook in the PTRACE_TRACEME path with parent as the tracing parent, matching the (parent -> current) parameterization.
limitations: A NULL parent would be dereferenced inside task_sid_obj(parent) at line 4, but NULL cannot be produced anywhere within the shown code; it would have to come from an out-of-scope caller, so this is not a confirmed NULL-dereference finding.

Correctness of the permission direction (source=parent, target=current) and the handling of SECSID_NULL/denial by avc_has_perm depend on callee and caller code not shown; no contradiction is visible in the shown code.
The control-flow surface is one linear return statement with no branches or loops, so no boundary, off-by-one, or iteration-bound claims are applicable.

verdict.summary: afra_box_read validates entry_count against the remaining box size (line 14) but never validates global_entry_count (line 36) before the allocation loop at lines 37-38. An attacker-controlled count (0..2^32-1) drives up to ~remaining_size/20 per-entry heap allocations and list insertions, bounded only by the per-field ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE read guards — an allocation-without-limits loop enabling resource exhaustion (CWE-770) from crafted MP4 input.

evidence.reason: global_entry_count is read from the attacker-controlled bitstream at line 36 with residual range 0..2^32-1 and, unlike entry_count, is never validated against the remaining box size before this loop (the line 14 check that caps the local loop has no global counterpart). Every admitted iteration unconditionally heap-allocates sizeof(GF_GlobalAfraEntry) at line 38 and inserts it at line 61 before any byte-budget guard runs. Witness: global_entries=1, long_ids=0, long_offsets=0, entry_count=0 (passes line 14), global_entry_count=0xFFFFFFFF, declared size=2^30 (passes line 35); the short-offset branch consumes 20 bytes/entry (lines 41,47-49,56-58), so ~53.7M allocations (~1.7 GiB plus list growth) occur before the per-field ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE guard aborts. The per-read guards bound the reads, not the allocations; primary mechanism is CWE-770 (allocation of resources without limits) with attacker-controlled volume in a reachable loop.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE has the standard GPAC semantics used by the shown code: it fails the function with GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE when ptr->size < n, otherwise subtracts n from ptr->size.

ptr->size is an unsigned remaining-byte budget whose initial value and the initialization of local_access_entries/global_access_entries are provided by the caller (not shown); the shown code never sets ptr->size past the box header.
The bitstream reads (gf_bs_read_u32/u64/u16/int) return attacker-controlled values in their declared unsigned ranges.
limitations: No out-of-bounds read or write is confirmed: every bitstream read is preceded by an ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE guard (lines 21,24,27,40,43,47,52,56), and the out-of-range-index behavior of gf_list_insert is not visible in the shown code, so an OOB write via index i cannot be anchored.
NULL dereference on an uninitialized local_access_entries/global_access_entries list cannot be confirmed because list initialization is outside the shown code.

The discarded return values of gf_list_insert (lines 31,61) could silently drop entries while the function still returns GF_OK (line 65); this is a status-handling concern with no confirmed attacker-visible memory-safety impact (malloc failures are checked).

The resource-exhaustion magnitude scales with the declared box size (~2x heap amplification in the shortest branch); amplification across multiple boxes depends on the caller's parse loop, which is not shown.
The local-entry loop (line 17) is bounded by the line 14 check (admitted set entry_count <= size/12 or size/16, exactly matching per-entry consumption), so it is not reported as a separate finding.

verdict.summary: The shown code performs only constant-size allocations (sizeof(*rsi_dev), kmalloc(2048)), checks every allocation and every non-void callee return value, contains no loop, no input-derived index/size/length, and no injection or crypto sink. All failure paths assign an error code before returning, and the only kfree frees a buffer the shown code still owns. No attacker-controlled value reaches any security-relevant sink within the shown code.

assumptions: adapter and pfunction are non-NULL pointers supplied by a valid caller; the shown code never derives NULL from internal computation.
rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints and rsi_usb_init_rx follow the convention the shown code assumes: non-zero return means failure (lines 15, 29).
rsi_usb_init_rx does not take ownership of or free rsi_dev->tx_buffer before returning failure; only the shown code's kfree at line 53 is considered.
limitations: If rsi_usb_init_rx (body not shown) freed rsi_dev->tx_buffer before failing, kfree at line 53 would be a double free; this depends entirely on non-shown callee behavior and is unconfirmed.

On the -EINVAL and -ENOMEM paths (lines 15-18, 24-27), adapter->rsi_dev was already assigned at line 11; whether the caller leaks rsi_dev or leaves a dangling pointer is not determinable from the shown code.
A NULL adapter or pfunction would crash at line 11, but NULL cannot be produced by the shown code; it requires an out-of-scope caller.

verdict.summary: Input tensor shapes are consumed before validation: `input.dim_size(ndims - 1)` (line 5) and `rhs.dim_size(ndims - 1)` (line 6) index the dims arrays before `ndims >= 2` (line 9) and `rhs.dims() == ndims` (line 12) are enforced, so a rank-0 tensor produces index -1 and an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) that feeds `n`/`nrhs` into allocations, memcpy sizes, and GPU size arguments. Additionally, the batch loops use `int batch` against int64 `batch_size` (lines 98-100, 112-118, 164-167, 184-193); for `batch_size >= 2^31` the counter wraps, the loops never terminate, and the pointer-scratch writes go out of bounds (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Rank-0 input yields ndims == 0, so the index ndims-1 == -1 is passed to input.dim_size before the guard ndims >= 2 at line 9 is evaluated (the guard admits this path because it runs after the read). The dims array has 0 entries, so dims_[-1] is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); the garbage value is then used as n in the pivots allocation (line 80), memcpy sizes (69/140/203) and GPU size arguments (105/115/171/187).

rhs is indexed with input's rank before the rhs.dims() == ndims check at line 12 (admitted only afterwards). With input rank 3 and rhs rank 1, index ndims-1 == 2 exceeds the 1-entry dims array, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose value flows into nrhs and the transposed_rhs shape (lines 124-127) and GPU size arguments (171/187).

batch_size is int64 and unbounded (line 73, from attacker-chosen shape). For batch_size == 2^31+1 (e.g., n == 1 over a tensor with >= 2^31 elements), the int counter reaches INT_MAX and wraps to INT_MIN, the guard batch < batch_size still admits the wrapped value, and input_copy_ptrs_base[batch] writes outside the scratch buffer of batch_size entries allocated at lines 87-89 (CWE-787), also reading input_copy_reshaped at a negative batch; the loop never terminates. Same pattern at lines 112-118, 164-167, 184-193.

Same int-vs-int64 loop flaw for the second pointer-scratch pair (allocated at lines 150-155): for batch_size >= 2^31 the wrapped negative batch writes input_copy_ptrs_base[batch] and transposed_rhs_ptrs_base[batch] out of bounds (CWE-787) and dereferences the reshaped tensors at a negative batch index, with no terminating bound reached.

assumptions: input and rhs are entry-point tensors whose shapes (rank and dims) are supplied by the graph/model, i.e. attacker-controlled.
TensorShape::dim_size(d) indexes the rank-sized dims array; Tensor::dims() returns the rank (>= 0).
batch_size (line 73) equals the product of the outer dims of the reshaped input, i.e. NumElements / (n*n).
limitations: The line 5/6 dims over-read is unreachable in the shipped product if MatrixSolve's graph-construction shape function rejects ranks < 2 and mismatched rhs ranks before ComputeAsync runs; that invariant is not present in the shown code, which performs the check only after the reads (lines 8-12 vs 5-6).

The batch-loop OOB write (CWE-787) requires a successfully allocated tensor with >= 2^31 elements (~8.6 GiB for float32; ~17 GiB for double), so it is resource-intensive; no shown code caps batch_size.

Narrowing int64 n / batch_size to the int parameters of Getrf/GetrfBatched/Getrs/GetrsBatched (Calls at 105-106, 115-116, 171-174, 187-191) would need n > 2^31, i.e. ~2^62 matrix elements, which is physically unreachable.
sizeof(Scalar*) * batch_size (lines 87-89, 150-155) could overflow only for batch_size > 2^61, physically unreachable.

The singular-matrix check in info_checker (lines 213-220) executes only when the status is an InvalidArgument error; with an OK status and info > 0 the CPU-style singular check is skipped (error-reporting / correctness behavior depending on CheckLapackInfoAndDeleteSolverAsync semantics, not shown), so it is not confirmed as a security finding.
The 128 * batch_size computation (line 91-92) cannot overflow in practice for any allocatable tensor.

verdict.summary: In both blocklist loops, the return status of seccomp_rule_add is checked with 'r < 0 && r == -EFAULT' (lines 212 and 230), which is logically equivalent to 'r == -EFAULT'. Any other negative errno (e.g. -EINVAL, -ENOMEM) — which means the deny rule was NOT installed — is silently treated as success: the loop continues, the BPF filter is exported (line 261) and setup_seccomp returns TRUE (line 269). The resulting seccomp filter is missing the deny rule for that syscall (e.g. unshare/mount/clone3), failing open and weakening the sandbox while reporting success. This is an improper check for the exceptional failure condition (CWE-754); no memory-safety or injection issue is present in the shown code.

evidence.snippet:
if (r < 0 && r == -EFAULT /* unknown syscall */)
        return flatpak_fail_error (error, FLATPAK_ERROR_SETUP_FAILED, _("Failed to block syscall %d"), scall);
evidence.reason: r is the status of seccomp_rule_add (lines 209/211), whose residual range is 0 on success or any negative errno (-EINVAL, -ENOMEM, -EFAULT, ...). The guard only routes the error path for r == -EFAULT; every other negative value (rule NOT installed) is in the admitted-as-success set, so e.g. r = -ENOMEM passes, the loop at line 201 continues, the incomplete filter is exported at line 261, and TRUE is returned at line 269. A missing deny rule fails the seccomp blocklist open — CWE-754 (improper check of the unusual/exceptional failure condition).

evidence.snippet:
if (r < 0 && r == -EFAULT /* unknown syscall */)
            return flatpak_fail_error (error, FLATPAK_ERROR_SETUP_FAILED, _("Failed to block syscall %d"), scall);
evidence.reason: Identical flaw in the non-devel blocklist loop: r from seccomp_rule_add (lines 226/228) is only checked for -EFAULT; any other negative errno (e.g. -EINVAL, -ENOMEM) still means the deny rule for perf_event_open/personality/ptrace was not installed, yet the loop continues and the filter is exported (line 261) and setup_seccomp returns TRUE (line 269) — CWE-754 fail-open handling of the rule-add error status.

assumptions: seccomp_x86_64_extra_arches and seccomp_aarch64_extra_arches are 0-terminated, as the sentinel loop at line 186 requires (the invariant is not visible in the shown code).
socket_family_allowlist entries remain in numerical order as required by the comment at line 128 for the gap-blocking logic at lines 248-256 to cover every non-allowed family.
bwrap is non-NULL and arch is NUL-terminated when the caller invokes setup_seccomp; the shown code does not itself establish these.
limitations: The CWE-754 finding triggers only when libseccomp returns a negative errno other than -EFAULT (e.g. -ENOMEM); that trigger is not attacker-controlled through any value in the shown code, so confidence is moderate and the impact is silent filter weakening rather than immediate attacker-driven corruption.

Return values of seccomp_rule_add_exact at lines 251 and 256 are discarded; the shown code explicitly documents this as intentional ('ignore failures here', lines 235-237) and the failure is library/architecture-dependent — treated as a documented tradeoff, not a confirmed vulnerability.
bwrap NULL dereference at lines 266-267 would require a caller-supplied NULL; NULL is not produced on any path inside the shown code.
If the extra_arches arrays were not 0-terminated, line 186 could read out of bounds; the array capacity/termination invariant is not identifiable from the shown code, so this is unconfirmable.
If socket_family_allowlist ordering were violated, families in the gap would not be blocked; the ordering is a hardcoded compile-time table and not attacker-controlled in the shown code.
g_return_val_if_fail at lines 206 and 223 would return FALSE without setting *error for an invalid table entry; unreachable with the shown static tables.
The discarded lseek return at line 264 has no security impact.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All return values that gate dangerous follow-on operations are checked (dict_alloc_lock at line 23, call_callback at line 38), the reentrancy guard is reset on every non-nested path (lines 25, 50), and the only list-member write (qftf_list->lv_refcount++ at line 43) is guarded by the v_type == VAR_LIST check at line 40. Remaining concerns (NULL qfl, uninitialized qftf_cb, caller handling of a NULL return) depend on invariants outside the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

qftf_cb and qfl->qf_qftf_cb are initialized members; cb_name is NULL when the option is unset, and a global is zero-initialized.

If the global qftf_cb were left uninitialized, a garbage cb_name could spuriously enter the callback block; initialization is not visible in the shown code.
The recursion guard (lines 7-8) returns NULL to a nested caller; whether each nested caller tolerates a NULL list is a contract outside the shown code.
