verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in pcx_write_rle at the `*from` dereference in `data != *from || from == end` (line 14). The left operand of `||` is evaluated first, so when the loop's final iteration advances `from += step` (line 13) to `from == end` (step=1, witness: 1-byte buffer), `*from` reads one byte past the end of the input buffer before the `from == end` guard can act. The intended guard is present but evaluated after the dereference, so it cannot prevent the read.

evidence.reason: The `*from` dereference in the left operand of `||` is evaluated before the `from == end` check on the right. The outer-loop guard at line 10 (`from < end`) admits the final element (witness: 1-byte buffer B, end = B+1, step = 1), then line 13 (`from += step`) makes from == end, and line 14 reads `*end` at index == capacity of the half-open byte range [B, end) that the code's own comparisons establish — excess exactly 1 byte (CWE-125). The `from == end` clause was intended as the guard but is positioned after the dereference, so its excluded set is empty at the moment of the read; for step >= 1 this path is taken whenever the final byte is consumed as an outer-loop data byte.

assumptions: `from`/`end` delineate a half-open byte buffer [from0, end); the object's capacity for the witness (1 byte) is identified from the code's own comparisons at lines 10 and 20.
The confirmed witness uses step = 1; the shown code imposes no constraint on step, but the finding requires only step >= 1.
`gp_fputc` is a byte-output helper; its internal behavior does not affect the finding.
limitations: For step >= 2 the pointer can overshoot to from > end and line 14 reads further past the buffer; the excess is not computed here, and oversized/negative strides are caller-dependent since step is an internal-helper parameter with no guard in the shown code.

step == 0 causes a non-terminating loop at line 20 (`from += 0` never advances) rather than reaching the division at line 29; a hang finding is not confirmed because attacker control of step is not established in the shown code.
`max_run = step * MAX_RUN_COUNT` (line 8) can overflow int for |step| > INT_MAX/15, and the chunk loop at line 23 can become unbounded if max_run <= 0 — unconfirmed, caller-dependent.

All gp_fputc return values (lines 16, 24, 25, 29, 31) are discarded; this is an error-handling robustness concern (silent partial output) with no security mechanism visibly violated in the shown code.
The absolute allocation size of the input buffer is not declared in the shown code; the capacity used for the finding is derived from the function's own `from < end` invariant.

Division `(from - start) / step` at line 29 is not reachable with step == 0 (the hang at line 20 occurs first), and for step >= 1 the dividend is a non-negative multiple of step, so the division is well-defined on the confirmed path.

verdict.summary: SVDF Prepare reads dims->data[1] of input, weights_feature, and weights_time before any check that dims->size >= 2 (no NumDimensions guard in the shown code; line 47 only protects state). A crafted model with a rank-1 (or scalar) tensor makes dims->data[1] read one int past the TfLiteIntArray allocation — a heap OOB read (CWE-125) on every Prepare call for the admitted float32/int8 input types.

evidence.reason: weights_time is returned by GetInputSafe (lines 16-17), so weights_time->dims is model-supplied and its size is unconstrained by the shown code: lines 7-8 only fix the input/output counts and lines 19-20 only the input type. By TfLiteIntArray semantics data holds exactly dims->size ints, so index 1 requires dims->size >= 2; a crafted rank-1 weights_time (dims->size == 1) makes this read access element [1], one int (4 bytes) past the allocation — heap OOB read, primary CWE-125. No NumDimensions/dims->size guard precedes this read.

input and weights_feature come from GetInputSafe (lines 11, 13-14) with the same missing rank guard: neither dims array is checked for dims->size >= 2 before data[1] is read. A crafted rank-1 input or weights_feature tensor makes either read exceed the dims->data allocation by one int (heap OOB read, CWE-125); the equality check constrains values only after the out-of-bounds reads occur.

assumptions: int is 32-bit (standard TFLite build), so dims->data values and the products/quotients derived from them are 32-bit signed.
TfLiteIntArray::data holds exactly dims->size elements, so accessing data[1] with dims->size == 1 is out of bounds by one element.

Tensor dims, builtin params, and quantization metadata originate from the parsed flatbuffer model (entry-point input); GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe return the model's tensors unchanged, and dims pointers themselves are non-null for every tensor.
TF_LITE_ENSURE* macro semantics: a failing check returns an error from Prepare, so all statuses checked with them are treated as consumed.
limitations: memory_size * num_filters (lines 49-50) can overflow signed 32-bit int (e.g., memory_size = num_filters = 65536 wraps to 0), allowing the state-size check (lines 48-50) to accept a {batch, 0} state; the resulting undersized-state corruption would occur in Eval, which is not part of the shown code, so CWE-190/CWE-787 is not confirmed here.

Scale reads on the full-integer path (lines 194-199) dereference quantization params and scale->data[0] with no null or scale->size >= 1 check; a crafted int8 model can omit affine quantization, but the null/empty data production happens in flatbuffer parsing outside the shown code (robustness concern, no CWE).

Unchecked TfLiteIntArrayCreate results (lines 53, 66-70, 74, 104, 118, 134, 149, 163, 171) are dereferenced immediately; these are constant-size allocations without attacker-controlled volume, so the NULL-deref is not confirmed.

Crafted negative dims values would flow into batch_size/num_units/num_filters and then into ResizeTensor sizes (lines 56-57, 90-91, 180-181); whether that is memory-unsafe depends on framework handling not shown here.

verdict.summary: Reachable kernel assertion in rsi_send_beacon: skb_pull(skb, 64 - dword_align_bytes) is called on a freshly allocated skb whose skb->len is 0, for every guard-admitted dword_align_bytes in [1,63] (skb->data & 0x3f, no constraint forces 0). Standard skb_pull semantics require len <= skb->len and otherwise trigger skb_under_panic()/BUG(), a kernel panic (availability DoS). The failing value is OS/allocator-provided rather than attacker-controlled in the shown code, so this is a low-severity driver-internal crash on the AP beacon path.

evidence.reason: dword_align_bytes (line 12) has residual range [0,63]; the guard at line 13 admits {1..63}, so the pull length 64 - dword_align_bytes is in [1,63] on every taken branch. skb->len is exactly 0 at this point: dev_alloc_skb (line 6) yields a fresh skb with len == 0 and memset (line 10) does not modify skb->len; no shown code changes it. Standard skb_pull semantics require len <= skb->len and otherwise invoke skb_under_panic() -> BUG(), so every admitted value (witness 32 -> pull 32 > 0) triggers a kernel panic at this call site; no shown check bounds dword_align_bytes to 0 or skb->len. Primary CWE-617 (reachable assertion), availability impact.

assumptions: MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE is a positive compile-time constant; its exact value is not needed for the analysis.
Standard kernel semantics: dev_alloc_skb() returns a fresh skb with skb->len == 0 and memset() does not modify skb->len.
Standard kernel semantics: skb_pull() requires len <= skb->len and otherwise invokes skb_under_panic() (BUG(), kernel oops/panic).
rsi_prepare_beacon() is outside the shown code; only its call-site argument flow is analyzed.
limitations: The value reaching the pull-length sink is the skb->data alignment (OS/allocator-provided), not attacker-controlled in the shown code; the crash is a driver-internal robustness failure (fires for any unaligned allocation on the beacon path) rather than an attacker-driven taint flow, which caps severity at low despite near-deterministic kernel-panic behavior.

Any out-of-bounds write that might occur inside the unshown rsi_prepare_beacon() (e.g., writing up to MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE after the pull reduced tailroom) cannot be confirmed: the callee body and its write/put pattern are not part of the shown code, and no size/index argument is derived here.
A NULL common supplied by an out-of-scope caller would be dereferenced at the skb_queue_tail() call (line 20); NULL is not producible within the shown code, so this is not a reported finding.

If a particular kernel's skb_pull() were non-conforming and did not check len <= skb->len, the failure would instead be an unsigned underflow of skb->len; the downstream effect would depend on the unshown callee and is not separately confirmed.
No attacker-controlled index, size, format string, path, or crypto material exists in the shown code; the only anomalous behavior is the skb_pull domain violation.

verdict.summary: BD_DecMFFieldVec reads nbFields straight from the untrusted bitstream (line 20) with at most 31 bits and no upper-bound check, then forwards it as the allocation length to gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc (line 29) and as the QP14 length to gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length (line 25), and as loop bounds (lines 32, 43). A witness value of NbBits=31 / nbFields=0x7FFFFFFF passes every guard and forces a multi-GiB allocation request or up to 2^31-1 decode iterations from a few input bits, enabling memory-exhaustion/CPU denial of service (CWE-770).

evidence.reason: Entry-point bitstream input: line 19 reads a 5-bit NbBits in [0,31] and line 20 reads nbFields with NbBits bits, so the residual range is [0, 2^31-1] on u32; the line 28 guard (fieldType != GF_SG_VRML_MFNODE) only selects this branch and admits every value in that range, and no other check bounds nbFields. Witness NbBits=31, nbFields=0x7FFFFFFF (2147483647) reaches this allocation-size sink, requesting 2147483647 * element-size bytes (>= 4 GiB for any element >= 2 bytes), causing allocation failure or memory exhaustion on untrusted input. Primary mechanism: CWE-770 uncontrolled allocation of resources driven by an unbounded attacker-controlled count.

The same entry-point-derived nbFields (residual range [0, 2^31-1] from lines 19-20, no cap) is forwarded as the QP14 length/allocation count when codec->ActiveQP is set (line 22 admits the path with no constraint visible in the shown code). Witness nbFields=0x7FFFFFFF is a member of the admitted set of every guard on this path, so the QP14 setup consumes the same unbounded attacker-controlled count as an allocation length (CWE-770).

assumptions: gf_bs_read_int returns the unsigned value of the requested nBits (0..2^nBits-1), which is the standard bit-read semantics of the API used at lines 19-20.
nbFields is consumed at lines 25 and 29 as a length/count by functions whose names and argument use indicate allocation-size semantics.
limitations: A heap-overflow variant (count * element_size wrapping in gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc on 32-bit size_t, then OOB writes via the line 33/35 loop, CWE-190/CWE-787) is not confirmed: the callee's item sizes and the build width are not identifiable from the shown code.

In the MFNODE branch, when node==NULL and codec->pCurrentProto==NULL, a successfully decoded node is registered (line 46) but never attached (lines 49-79), leaking one node per iteration; provenance of node/pCurrentProto is internal-helper state, so the leak is not confirmable from the shown code alone.
Early error returns at lines 30/34/36 abandon a partially-filled MF without rollback; this is robustness/leak concern with no demonstrated security impact.

CPU-exhaustion via the loop bounds (lines 32, 43) only compounds with matching input volume or a successful huge allocation, so it is folded into the allocation-size DoS rather than reported separately.

verdict.summary: SVDF Prepare forwards model-controlled tensor dimensions to ResizeTensor without any positivity/bound check: batch_size (line 25), num_filters (line 26) and num_units = num_filters / rank (line 29) keep their full int32 residual range after the guards at lines 27-33 (rank != 0 and equality checks only). A witness such as batch_size = -1, rank = 1, num_filters = 1 passes every guard and produces negative dims in output_size_array (line 54) and scratch_size_array (line 75), which ResizeTensor (lines 57, 91) consumes as allocation sizes; the negative size converts to a huge size_t / wraps the byte-size product (CWE-195), yielding a mis-sized buffer and subsequent out-of-bounds access by this kernel.

evidence.reason: output_size_array->data[0] = batch_size (line 54) and data[1] = num_units (line 55), where batch_size = input->dims->data[0] (line 25) and num_units = num_filters / rank (line 29) are int32 model dims whose residual range after the shown guards (lines 27-33: only rank != 0, num_filters % rank == 0, and equality checks) includes negatives; witness batch_size = -1, rank = 1, num_filters = 1 passes all guards and reaches this ResizeTensor call as a -1 dimension, an out-of-domain allocation size whose conversion to size_t yields a huge/wrapped size (CWE-195) and a mis-sized output buffer.

scratch_size_array->data[0] = batch_size (line 75) and data[1] = num_filters (line 76) are unvalidated int32 model dims (num_filters negative is admitted: -1 % 1 == 0 at line 28); the same witness path delivers negative dims to this ResizeTensor call, consumed as allocation sizes (CWE-195), producing a mis-sized scratch buffer that this kernel later indexes by batch_size/num_filters elements.

On the full-integer path, output_temp_size_array is [num_units, batch_size] (lines 172-173); num_units = num_filters / rank (line 29) and batch_size (line 25) are negative-capable int32 values admitted by the guards at lines 27-33, so a repeated witness (e.g., batch_size = -1, rank = 1, num_filters = -1, int8 path) supplies negative allocation sizes to this ResizeTensor call (CWE-195), the same mis-sized-allocation mechanism as the output and scratch resizes.

assumptions: GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe/GetTemporarySafe error returns are fully handled by the TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK macro family, so those paths do not continue on failure.
IsHybridOp has its standard TFLite semantics: an all-float32 pair yields is_hybrid_op = false, so the float32/float32 witness executes only the output and scratch resize sinks.
Tensor dims and quantization metadata come from the interpreted model file and are therefore attacker-controlled entry-point data reaching Prepare without prior validation.
limitations: The signed int product memory_size * num_filters (line 50) can overflow for dims around 65536 x 65536, admitting an undersized state tensor, but the wrapped value is consumed only by the comparison guard, not by an allocation-size/index/length/pointer sink in the shown code; the dangerous downstream use is in Eval which is outside the shown code, so no CWE-190 finding is confirmed here.

The scale->data[0] reads (lines 201-206) are guarded only by quantization.type != kTfLiteNoQuantization; an empty scale array could admit an OOB read, but the scale array capacity (scale->size) is not identifiable from the shown code, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable.

Reads of dims->data[1] on rank-1 input/weights tensors (lines 30-33, 37) lack NumDimensions guards in the shown code, but the dims array capacity is not established by the shown code, so the OOB-read claim is unconfirmable here.

NULL dereferences after TfLiteIntArrayCreate/TfLiteIntArrayCopy (e.g., lines 53, 104) require an unchecked allocation to fail on fixed-size or single-call allocations with no attacker-volume scaling loop, which is out of scope per the confirmation rules.
scratch_tensor_index + 1..5 overflow (lines 97, 110, 126, 141, 155, 174) would require a framework-provided tensor index near INT_MAX; no attacker path to that magnitude is visible in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) into ADTSContext.pce_data: ff_copy_pce_data at line 43 copies an attacker-controlled PCE into a bit writer initialized at line 40 with a fixed MAX_PCE_SIZE-bit capacity, and the shown code never bounds the copied length or checks the returned count. A crafted ASC with object_type 2, sampling_index 4, chan_config 0, zero GASpecific flag bits, and a PCE header claiming 15 front/side/back, 3 LFE, 7 assoc and 15 CC elements passes every guard (lines 19, 23, 27, 31, 35, 39) and makes the copy exceed the 320-bit capacity, writing past pce_data.

evidence.reason: Entry-point input buf/size (residual range: unrestricted, no constraint in the shown code) reaches this sink via init_get_bits8 (line 8) and is copied into the bit writer pb that line 40 bound to adts->pce_data with the named capacity MAX_PCE_SIZE. The copy length is determined by element-count fields inside the attacker-controlled PCE; the shown code imposes no bound on it and uses the returned count only for pce_size arithmetic. A witness passing every admitted set (object_type 2 -> objecttype 1 admitted by line 19, sampling_index 4 admitted by line 23, flag bits 0 admitted by lines 27/31/35, chan_config 0 admitted by line 39) with a PCE header claiming the maximum element counts makes the copied bit count exceed MAX_PCE_SIZE, so the writer's advancing-pointer stores land past pce_data: out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: MAX_PCE_SIZE is a named constant giving the writer capacity and, per the conventional ADTSContext layout, the bit size of pce_data (the struct definition itself is not in the shown code).

ff_copy_pce_data copies a PCE whose length follows the PCE header's element-count fields in the input bitstream (standard ISO 14496-3 PCE semantics implied by the helper name and its bit-context parameters).
FFmpeg's get_bits/init_get_bits semantics zero-fill reads beyond the bitstream end, so skip_bits_long/get_bits past the end (line 14 and lines 27/31/35) do not constitute an out-of-bounds read.
limitations: The exact overflow byte excess depends on ff_copy_pce_data's per-element copy widths and loop bounds, whose body is not shown; the claim that the length can exceed MAX_PCE_SIZE is anchored in the standard PCE structure and the unbounded source size.
ADTSContext.pce_data's own byte size is not visible in the shown code; capacity is identified from the named constant MAX_PCE_SIZE used at line 40.

The return value of ff_copy_pce_data is unchecked, so a negative return would produce a negative pce_size, but the callee's error contract and downstream consumers are not visible, so this is not reported as a separate confirmed finding.
Non-NULL adts/s is a caller-side invariant not verifiable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. All attacker-relevant size arguments (hash_size at line 61; signature and private_key buffer capacities at lines 12/27/48/52/54/68/70; num_words vs num_n_words at line 58; scalar bit count num_n_bits+1 at line 27) are either forwarded unchanged to helpers whose bodies are not shown, bounded by external API contracts, or bounded by curve constants; the guards visible in the shown code (0<k<n at line 22, r==0 retry at line 28, RNG failure at line 37, s bit-length at line 64) are correctly placed and their return statuses are used. Residual concerns are recorded in notes.limitations.

assumptions: Curve fields (num_words, num_n_bits, num_bytes, G, n, p) are trusted framework/compile-time data with num_n_bits >= 1 and BITS_TO_BYTES(num_n_bits) <= num_bytes.

The two bcopy call sites (lines 52 and 68) are mutually consistent only under destination-first (memcpy-order) semantics, which the author evidently intended; the definition is not part of the shown code.
uECC_MAX_WORDS is assumed to be at least any supported curve's num_words, which is the purpose implied by its name and by its use as the stack-array size at lines 8-9 and 14.

Standard uECC helper APIs (EccPoint_mult, uECC_vli_modMult/modInv/modAdd, uECC_vli_set, bits2int, uECC_vli_bytesToNative/nativeToBytes) return void or their results are consumed where used; no discarded failure status is visible in the shown code.
limitations: hash_size (residual range 0..UINT_MAX, unconstrained in the shown code) is forwarded unchanged to bits2int at line 61; an over-read or under-read within bits2int cannot be confirmed because bits2int's body and message_hash's buffer capacity are not shown.

The signature write of 2*curve->num_bytes (lines 12/27 plus 68/70) and the private_key read of BITS_TO_BYTES(num_n_bits) bytes (lines 52/54) rely on external caller contracts (signature buffer of 2*num_bytes, key buffer of num_bytes) that are not identifiable from the shown code.

Line 58 copies num_words words into s while all later uses treat s as num_n_words words; this is only a hazard if num_words > num_n_words, an invariant that is external to the shown code, and s's declared capacity uECC_MAX_WORDS is not numerically defined here.

Line 27 passes num_n_bits+1 as the scalar bit count to EccPoint_mult; if the callee tests bit index num_n_bits (word index num_n_words for word-aligned curves such as secp256r1 and secp256k1), it would read one word past the scalar's extent, but the callee's loop bounds and the values of uECC_MAX_WORDS/WORD_BITS are not shown, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable.

If bcopy follows POSIX source-first semantics (definition not shown), line 52 writes into the const private_key buffer and line 68 copies in the wrong direction; impact would be key-buffer corruption and invalid signatures rather than an identifiable out-of-bounds access, and the internal consistency of both call sites favors the destination-first reading.

The signature s is not normalized to low-S and there is no explicit s != 0 check; the line 64 check is effectively a tautology for standard curves and does not enforce either property. These are signature-malleability/robustness concerns, not confirmable memory-safety or logic flaws in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The kernel consumes op inputs through typed Tensor accessors without ever validating dtype or rank. An attacker-controllable tensor of mismatched dtype for "stamp_token" (L5, scalar<int64>()) or "tree_ensemble_serialized" (L14, scalar<tstring>()) triggers TensorFlow's internal CHECK in Tensor::scalar<T>() and aborts the process: a crash-only denial of service. The suspicious Unref/release dance on the parse-failure path (L15-16) is actually safe because release() prevents a second delete, and the ALREADY_EXISTS resource leak is unconfirmable from the shown code.

evidence.reason: Entry-point input stamp_token_t has residual range 'any Tensor' because the only guard on the path (L4 OP_REQUIRES_OK on context->input) checks lookup success/non-null, not dtype or rank. A DT_FLOAT (non-int64) or non-scalar tensor admitted by that guard reaches the typed accessor, whose standard TensorFlow semantics is a CHECK abort (LOG(FATAL)), terminating the process: reachable-assertion DoS (CWE-617).

Entry-point input tree_ensemble_serialized_t is only constrained to be non-null by OP_REQUIRES_OK (L9-10); no dtype/rank check exists before scalar<tstring>()() is invoked. A non-DT_STRING tensor admitted by that guard reaches the typed accessor and, per standard Tensor::scalar<T>() semantics, fails an internal dtype CHECK that aborts the process: reachable-assertion DoS (CWE-617).

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES_OK at L4 and L9-10 guarantees the input tensor pointers are non-null when used at L5/L14.
Tensor::scalar<T>() with a mismatched dtype terminates the process via an internal CHECK; this is treated as the standard semantics of the accessed API.
Op input tensors are treated as attacker-controllable entry-point data because the kernel consumes them directly and the shown code imposes no further constraint.
limitations: The L15-16 Unref()/release() sequence on the parse-failure path is not a use-after-free or double-free in the shown code: L15 drops the sole reference (refcount 1->0, object deleted) and L16 release() nulls the unique_ptr so its destructor cannot delete the freed object; `result` is not dereferenced later on that branch (L25 is unreachable after the L19 return).
A double-Unref UAF at L15 would require InitFromSerialized itself to have released the reference before returning false; its body is not shown, so this is unconfirmed.

On the ALREADY_EXISTS path (L26) the ownership of the resource released at L25 is governed by CreateResource/ResourceMgr semantics not visible in the shown code; a per-call resource leak is unconfirmed.

Whether Tensor::scalar<T>() aborts or performs an out-of-bounds element-0 read for a zero-length or non-scalar tensor of the correct dtype cannot be determined from the shown code; only the dtype-mismatch CHECK abort is relied upon.
Graph-level dtype validation performed outside this kernel could prevent some mismatched-dtype graphs from executing; the shown code itself provides no such protection.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read of spans[1] in _inplace_src_spans when num_spans == 1: the guard at line 9 only excludes 0, so a count of 1 enters the do-loop, whose body unconditionally dereferences spans[1] (one past the end of the num_spans-element array), with the garbage value then flowing into len comparisons and possibly the memset length.

evidence.reason: num_spans is an internal-helper parameter whose only shown constraint is the line-9 guard `if (num_spans == 0) return`, leaving the residual range [1, UINT_MAX] which admits 1. The do-loop at line 14 executes its body once for num_spans == 1, and this line unconditionally dereferences spans[1] of a 1-element array (index == capacity), an out-of-bounds heap read by exactly one cairo_half_open_span_t (CWE-125). The OOB value is subsequently used in the len >= run_length comparison (line 16) and, on the partial-coverage path, as the source of `--len` for memset (line 85), so the read directly feeds downstream size logic.

assumptions: spans points to a contiguous array of exactly num_spans cairo_half_open_span_t elements, per its parameter declaration and all uses in the shown code.
cairo_half_open_span_t.coverage is a uint8-compatible value (compared against 0xff/0x0 and stored to uint8_t).
pixman_image_composite32 returns void, so no return status exists to mishandle.
limitations: The mask buffer (base) capacity is not identifiable from the shown code, so the writes at lines 83 and 85-86 (whose sizes derive from span x differences) cannot be confirmed as an out-of-bounds write.

A wrapped/hugely negative `len` from `spans[1].x - spans[0].x` (line 15) would require undefined signed overflow with extreme caller-supplied x values, and the corruption would need to exceed an unidentifiable mask capacity; unconfirmed.
Whether pixman_image_composite32 mishandles negative widths such as `spans[0].x - x0` or `spans[1].x - spans[0].x` cannot be determined from the shown code (span ordering is not enforced here).
No claim is made about whether any real caller passes num_spans == 1; the finding rests only on the residual range the shown code's own guard leaves unconstrained.

verdict.summary: rsi_send_beacon calls skb_pull(skb, 64 - dword_align_bytes) with a length of 1..63 on a freshly allocated skb whose skb->len is 0, and discards the return value. The pull length is out of the operation's domain, and under the in-tree subtract-first skb_pull_inline the u32 skb->len underflows to ~2^32 while skb->data/tail are still advanced; the resulting skb (len ~4 GiB over ~1 KB of data) is passed to rsi_prepare_beacon and queued on MGMT_BEACON_Q, where length-driven transmit processing can over-read far beyond the allocation (DoS/corruption).

evidence.reason: dword_align_bytes has residual range [0,63] from line 12's mask; the guard at line 13 admits {1..63}, so the pull length 64 - dword_align_bytes is 1..63 on an skb whose len is 0 (fresh dev_alloc_skb invariant; nothing here changes it). The length exceeds the operation's domain (len <= skb->len), the return is discarded, and with the in-tree subtract-first skb_pull_inline the u32 skb->len underflows to 2^32 - L while data/tail are advanced, corrupting the skb state forwarded to lines 15 and 19. Primary mechanism: CWE-190 unsigned length underflow rooted at this call site.

The over-pulled skb with the underflowed (~2^32) len and advanced data/tail is consumed here by a helper that sizes its frame construction against this skb state; both outcomes (error path lines 16-17 and success path line 19) operate on the corrupted skb.

The skb whose len underflowed to ~4 GiB (with roughly 1 KB of real data) is enqueued for transmission; tx-path consumers that derive transfer/DMA lengths from skb->len will read far beyond the allocation, completing the confirmed impact chain that begins with the out-of-domain skb_pull length at line 14 (CWE-190).

assumptions: dev_alloc_skb returns a fresh skb with skb->len == 0, skb->data == skb->head, skb->data_len == 0, and tailroom == MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE, and nothing in the shown code modifies skb->len before line 14.

The in-tree skb_pull_inline implementation subtracts before validating (skb->len -= len; then checks skb->len < skb->data_len), so an over-pull underflows skb->len and still advances the data pointer.
limitations: If the kernel build uses the older strict skb_pull variant that returns NULL when len > skb->len without mutating the skb, line 14 becomes a harmless no-op (alignment silently skipped) and the finding downgrades to a robustness/functional issue with no memory-safety impact.

The final length-driven over-read happens in transmit-path consumers whose bodies are not in the shown code; the shown code only demonstrates the corrupted skb being produced (line 14) and propagated (lines 15, 19).

The skb leak on the rsi_prepare_beacon failure path (lines 16-17 return -EINVAL without kfree_skb(skb)) is a single-shot resource leak with no attacker-scaled volume in the shown code, so it is recorded here rather than as a confirmed finding.
No loop structures exist in the shown code, so memory-safe reasoning applies only to its linear sequence.

Whether skb->data's low 6 bits are ever non-zero depends on heap/slab placement, so the exact triggering alignment value (e.g., 0x20 -> pull of 32) is framework-observable rather than attacker-chosen.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The NULL guard (line 7) and the tag guard (line 16) protect all subsequent node dereferences and the M_QuantizationParameter-typed write (lines 22-23), and the reference bookkeeping is internally consistent: line 27 sets num_instances to exactly 2, matching the two references created in the shown code (line 24 and line 31), while each early-exit path releases exactly one reference (lines 17, 11). The plausible use-after-free/double-unregister scenarios and unchecked-allocation NULL dereferences all depend on callee semantics or allocation failure not established in the shown code, and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: gf_bifs_dec_node returns a freshly created node not otherwise referenced, with node->sgprivate->num_instances == 1 (creator ownership transferred to the caller), and never returns a node already live in the scene graph.
gf_node_unregister decrements num_instances and frees the node when the count reaches 0.
gf_node_get_tag returns the concrete node type tag.
gf_sg_command_new and gf_sg_command_field_new return non-NULL (allocation succeeds); gf_list_add succeeds.
The teardown paths external to this function unregister the global_qp reference and the command field's new_node reference exactly once each.
limitations: Use-after-free/double-unregister of the previous global_qp (or of node) requires gf_bifs_dec_node to return a node already referenced in the scene (e.g., a USE of the existing global QP) so that the unregisters at lines 11 and 17 (or a premature free at line 11 while a prior command still stores the node at line 31) hit the same live object; this callee behavior is not visible in the shown code, whose own count of 2 at line 27 matches its two stores at lines 24 and 31.

inf->new_node = node (line 31) would NULL-dereference if gf_sg_command_new (line 29) or gf_sg_command_field_new (line 30) failed, but that requires a fixed-size allocation to fail with no attacker-controlled size, and the discarded gf_list_add status (line 34) followed by return GF_OK (line 35) is likewise OOM-driven with only attacker-volume DoS impact.

The reset of ActiveQP and global_qp (lines 13-14) occurs before the new node's tag is validated (line 16); a caller that ignores the GF_NON_COMPLIANT_BITSTREAM error and resumes decoding could later dereference the cleared ActiveQP/global_qp, but that propagation is outside the shown code.

The unconditional overwrite node->sgprivate->num_instances = 2 (line 27) assumes the decode-time reference count is exactly 1; if the decoder left a different count, later unregisters could prematurely free the node, but the count-at-decode invariant is established only outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: pcx_write_rle never validates the 'step' parameter (line 1); for step <= 0 the pointer increments at lines 13 and 21 cannot move 'from' toward 'end', so the guards at lines 10 and 20 can never become false and the function loops forever (hang/DoS). Negative step additionally walks 'from' below the buffer start (OOB read at line 11), unconfirmable because the buffer's lower bound is not shown. For step >= 1 the encoding is correct and all reads are guarded (lines 10, 14 short-circuit, 20).

evidence.reason: step (int, residual range unconstrained by any guard in the shown code, admitting 0 and negatives) flows to the increment 'from += step' at line 13. Witness: step == 0 with any from < end. The outer guard 'from < end' at line 10 admits this state, and because the increment adds 0 the condition is invariant and the exit is unreachable; with step < 0, 'from' strictly decreases so 'from < end' stays true forever. Unbounded execution = hang/DoS (CWE-835, loop with unreachable exit).

Same unconstrained step input reaches this scan loop. With step == 0 both operands '(from < end)' and '(*from == data)' are invariant (line 21 adds 0), so the loop never terminates; with step < 0, 'from' decreases and the first operand never fails. This is the immediate unbounded loop for the step == 0 witness (CWE-835); the division at line 29 is only unreachable because of this hang.

assumptions: byte is an unsigned 8-bit type (values 0..255), so 'data >= 0xc0' comparisons are meaningful.
int is 32-bit two's complement (relevant only to the overflow discussion in limitations).
from/end delimit a valid input range with from < end for any work to be performed; the shown code imposes no other invariant.
gp_fputc writes one byte and returns a status; the shown code never reads that status.
limitations: OOB read below the buffer start with negative step (line 11 after line 13) is unconfirmed: the buffer's lower bound/capacity is not identifiable from the shown code (only 'from' and 'end' are visible).
Division by zero at line 29 for step == 0 is unreachable because the inner loop (lines 20-21) hangs first; not reported as CWE-369.

Integer overflow of 'step * MAX_RUN_COUNT' (line 8) for |step| > INT_MAX/15 could corrupt max_run and drive the chunk loop (lines 23-27) into unbounded/UB behavior, but a single concrete witness (step >= 143165578 plus an in-buffer run long enough to enter the else branch) is not derivable entirely from the shown code.
All gp_fputc return values (lines 16, 24, 25, 29, 31) are discarded, so a write failure silently truncates output (CWE-252-style), but no security mechanism is identifiable from the shown code.

If callers guarantee step >= 1 (contract not present in the shown code), the hang is unreachable; because step's provenance is an internal-helper parameter, severity is low and the confidence is capped at 0.7.

verdict.summary: Bytecode operands are never validated against the register-frame capacity: OP_MOVE writes regs[a] with a decoded operand of up to 16/24 bits while the frame guarantees only max(4, irep->nregs) slots (mrb_stack_extend at OP_SEND/OP_CALL), giving a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787, e.g. a=0xFFFF vs capacity 4). Independently, the local mrb_value 'blk' declared in the OP_SEND/OP_SENDB path is never initialized in the shown code and is read (mrb_proc_p/mrb_proc_ptr) and dereferenced on the C-method-call path, an uninitialized-use flaw (CWE-457) with type-confusion/write potential.

evidence.reason: OP_MOVE writes regs[a] where a is a decoded bytecode operand with residual range up to 0xFFFF (16-bit via OP_EXT1/EXT2; up to 24-bit in wider formats) and the shown code imposes no constraint linking a to irep->nregs. The frame capacity identifiable in the shown code is max(4, irep->nregs) via mrb_stack_extend (line 474 OP_SEND, line 515 OP_CALL), so with crafted irep->nregs=1 the guaranteed bound is 4 slots; witness a=0xFFFF (first invalid index 4, excess 65531 elements) reaches line 48 as a member of every admitted set because no guard checks a against nregs. Writes an attacker-controlled mrb_value out of bounds of the heap-allocated VM stack: CWE-787.

'blk' is declared at line 413 (mrb_value recv, blk;) and never assigned anywhere in the shown function, yet it is consumed here (and at line 421 by prepare_missing, and in OP_SUPER at lines 532/569). verdict.summary: Signed underflow in ex_copy: count = line2 - line1 + 1 (line 6) is computed from entry-point line addresses that the shown code never constrains; for a reversed range (line2 < line1, e.g., line1=5, line2=3) count becomes negative (-1), and that negative value reaches appended_lines_mark(n, count) (line 50) and b_op_end.lnum = n + count (line 10), where it is consumed as a line count/position that is out of the domain implied by the loop (which appended zero lines). This corrupts undo/change-mark state from attacker-influenced input.

evidence.reason: count is derived at line 6 as `count = line2 - line1 + 1` from unconstrained entry-point inputs; for line1=5, line2=3 the signed subtraction yields -1, which is a member of every guard's admitted set (no input guard exists; the loop guard `while (line1 <= line2)` at line 29 excludes the loop body so zero lines are appended, but line 50 still runs). A negative 'number of appended lines' is out of the domain of this undo/change-mark helper per its name and use, so the shown code forwards an underflowed magnitude to a consuming call (CWE-191).

assumptions: linenr_T is a signed long (Vim type), so `line2 - line1 + 1` is signed arithmetic; for line2 < line1 the result is negative without any wrap.
cmdmod.cmod_flags does not have CMOD_LOCKMARKS set by default, so the change-mark branch at lines 7-12 executes.
limitations: Out-of-buffer ml_get(line1) OOB reads are unconfirmed: the line-table capacity is not identifiable from the shown code, ml_get's defensive behavior for invalid lnum is not shown, and real callers clamp addresses outside the shown code.
Extreme-value overflow variants (e.g., n+1 at line 25, n+count at line 10 for huge/reversed magnitudes) share the same root cause as the confirmed underflow and cannot be separately substantiated.
A negative or oversized destination n reaching ml_append (line 36) and u_save (line 25) depends on callee defensive handling not shown in this code.
If vim_strsave returns NULL (line 34) the copy is skipped yet count is still reported to appended_lines_mark; this requires an unchecked allocation failure and has no demonstrated security impact.
The b_op_end.lnum = n + count assignment (line 10) manifests the same negative count (inverted marks) but is cosmetic on its own and is not a second CWE.

verdict.summary: int64 tensor dims (a.dim_size/b.dim_size) are truncated into 32-bit ints at lines 9-12 with no magnitude bound; an entry-point tensor with a dim >= 2^31 (e.g., a=(1,2^31), transpose_a_=true, b=(1,1)) makes m wrap to -2^31, and the negative value is consumed by TensorShape({m,n}) in allocate_output at line 19, producing an invalid output shape that fails/aborts (DoS). The same truncation feeds the k==k2 validation at line 14, so the shown guard cannot enforce the int64 size compatibility it appears to.

evidence.snippet: const int m = transpose_a_ ? a.dim_size(1) : a.dim_size(0);
evidence.reason: Entry-point tensor dim a.dim_size(1) (residual range int64 [0, 2^63), no magnitude constraint in the shown code) is narrowed to a 32-bit int. Witness: transpose_a_=true, a.shape()=(1, 2^31) -> a.dim_size(1)=2^31 truncates to -2147483648. The wrapped value flows to TensorShape({m,n}) at line 19. Primary mechanism: CWE-681 incorrect numeric conversion (int64->int narrowing) as the root cause of the invalid out-of-domain shape argument.

Sink consuming the truncated values from lines 9-12. With the witness a=(1,2^31), b=(1,1), transpose_a_=true: m=-2147483648, n=1; guards k==k2 (line 14, 1==1) and k==0 (line 21, false) both admit the path. TensorShape with a negative dim is outside the domain of allocate_output/ TensorShape (non-negative dims), causing an invalid-shape failure/CHECK abort (DoS). CWE-681 confirmed at this consumption point.

assumptions: Tensor::dim_size() returns int64 and int is 32-bit on TF-supported targets (standard TF ABI)
TensorShape requires non-negative dims as its standard semantics; a negative-dim shape is invalid and fails/aborts
Tensor shapes and transpose/sparse attributes are attacker-controlled graph inputs (entry-point input role)
TensorShape dims are non-negative int64 (no negative dims at input), so the sign flip comes only from the narrowing
limitations: Exploiting the negative-dim sink requires the framework to have successfully materialized an input tensor with a single dim >= 2^31 (>= ~4 GB for bfloat16); allocation feasibility is not visible in the shown code and gates real-world reachability, hence confidence 0.6

k==k2 truncation bypass (dims differing by 2^32 pass the check, leading to Eigen contract of mismatched sizes at lines 53-54) needs tensors of ~2^31 and ~2^31+2^32 elements - unconfirmable from the shown code
Zero-dimension guards exist only inside if (transpose_b) (lines 77-80); when transpose_b is false a zero-dim right reaches DoMatMul (lines 96-106), but the impact depends on the unshown DoMatMul body
The show code has no loops; all iteration is in unshown callees (Eigen contract/shuffle, BFloat16ToFloat, DoMatMul), so no loop-bound or capacity claims are confirmable
Unchecked new Tensor allocations (lines 38, 44, 81-83) mirror sizes of already-live tensors; NULL deref only under unrelated memory pressure, not attacker-scaled volume

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code alone. The loop driver i < bin->ne_header->SegCount (line 7) feeds the sink &bin->segment_entries[i] (line 12) with no bound relating SegCount to the array's actual capacity, but that capacity is established entirely outside the snippet, so the exact OOB excess cannot be computed and the claim fails the OOB confirmation standard. Remaining candidates (NULL bin->ne_header at line 7, unchecked r_list_newf at lines 6/21) have no NULL-production path in the shown code or require OOM of a fixed-size allocation.

assumptions: bin, bin->ne_header, bin->segment_entries and the size of the segment_entries array are produced by a parse step outside this function; the shown code implicitly relies on SegCount <= capacity(segment_entries) without stating it.
Field widths and signedness (SegCount, length, minAllocSz, flags, offset, alignment) are not declared in the snippet; NE-format 16-bit widths are assumed for the arithmetic discussion only.

A fuller codebase view would be required to confirm this candidate (CWE-125 hypothesis only).
NULL dereference of bin->ne_header at line 7 is not confirmable: the shown guard at line 3 checks bin and segment_entries but not ne_header, yet no shown path produces NULL ne_header.

Unchecked r_list_newf result (line 6) reaching r_list_append (line 21) would require OOM of a fixed-size allocation (not attacker-controlled), and the callee may self-check; treated as robustness, not a finding.
Discarded r_list_append return (line 21): a failed append drops the entry and leaks bs, but no security mechanism (e.g., volume compounding) is derivable in the shown code.

(ut64)se->offset * bin->alignment (line 18): no wrap for ≤32-bit unsigned operands; negative signed operands would require field signedness not shown in the snippet, and paddr has no security-relevant sink in the shown code.
If SegCount were a wide unsigned type, int i would overflow in the loop; the declaration is not in the shown code, and this is not reachable under the assumed 16-bit NE field semantics.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Every index/size the shown code derives is clamped: start to [0, length] (line 26), deleteCount to [0, length-start] (lines 32/42), final length capped by NJS_MAX_LENGTH (line 47), loops bounded by delete with max index length-1 (lines 61, 68), inserted-item write span start..start+items-1 inside the derived new length length+delta (line 116), and the memcpy source args[3..nargs-1] within the nargs-sized call frame. Remaining boundary claims depend on callee capacity contracts (njs_array_alloc/njs_array_expand, fast-array size>=length, njs_object_length status protocol) that are not visible in the shown code, and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: arg frame invariant: for a native njs call, args[0..nargs-1] are valid njs_value_t slots, so args[3..nargs-1] exist whenever items = nargs-3 > 0.

fast-array invariant (callee-side, not in shown code): njs_array_alloc and njs_array_expand guarantee array->start has capacity >= array->length, and njs_object_length returns array->length for array objects; if these engine invariants are violated the line 62/116 accesses could go OOB, but that is outside the shown code's domain.
njs_value_to_integer maps every JS number to a valid int64_t (ToInteger), so no UB on NaN/Infinity is assumed to produce a dangerous value.
NJS_MAX_LENGTH is the engine's maximum legal array length; the line 47 check bounds the final length.
limitations: C1 (possible uninitialized length): line 16 checks only ret == NJS_ERROR for njs_object_length. If that helper can return NJS_DECLINED without setting *length (its protocol is not shown; the shown code itself treats NJS_DECLINED as a real outcome at line 74), length would be used uninitialized at lines 26/32/42/47/104/123/146, potentially driving indices at lines 62 and 116 out of bounds. Unconfirmable from the shown code, so no CWE is attached.

C2 (algorithmic DoS): Array.prototype.splice.call(obj, 0, huge) with an object whose reported length and deleteCount are near 2^53 would iterate up to ~2^53 times through the line 68/129 loops. This requires njs_object_length to expose such lengths, is finite and terminating, and is DoS-only; treated as a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

C3 (capacity-dependent OOB): bounds for array->start and deleted->start (lines 62, 116) are guaranteed only by callee allocation/growth contracts (njs_array_alloc, njs_array_expand) not identifiable from the shown code, so per the capacity rule these boundary claims are unconfirmable.

C4 (int64->uint32 truncation of delete at line 54) is only reachable for lengths > UINT32_MAX, which excludes the raw-buffer fast branch; the slow path never indexes deleted->start, so no memory impact is demonstrated.

C6: line 104 passes constant 0 as the copy direction flag while line 123 passes (delta < 0); if that flag controls overlap ordering in njs_array_copy_within, the fast path could mis-relocate elements for delta<0. That would corrupt values, not index memory out of domain, and the callee semantics are not shown.
No other vulnerability classes are present: the code contains no format strings, command/SQL/path construction, crypto/entropy choices, file/access-control logic, or authn/authz decisions.

verdict.summary: On little-endian builds (uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN == 1), the copy at line 61 has reversed source/destination under standard bcopy(src, dst, n) semantics: it writes BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) bytes of tmp into the caller's private_key buffer instead of loading the private key into tmp (the intent pinned by the else-branch comment '/* tmp = d */' at line 63 and the s = r*d computation at line 68). This unconditional write corrupts the ECDSA private-key storage (a const-qualified input region; a fault when const/ROM-backed), and because tmp never receives d and the paired bcopy at line 77 is likewise reversed, the s half of the signature is never written and emitted signatures do not verify, breaking signing/authentication. Primary CWE-787: write into a memory region other than the intended destination buffer.

evidence.reason: Standard bcopy(const void *src, void *dst, size_t n) copies from the first argument to the second, so this statement writes BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) bytes (== curve->num_bytes, derived from curve fields read at lines 18-20) from tmp (declared at line 8; contents 1 followed by zeros after lines 44-45 on the no-RNG path) into private_key — the entry-point input at line 1 — rather than loading d into tmp as the else-branch comment '/* tmp = d */' at line 63 and the s = r*d multiplication at line 68 require. The sink is guarded only by the compile-time macro at line 60 and executes unconditionally for every call that passes the guards at lines 23 and 37 (witness: k=1, g_rng_function==NULL, secp256r1 — line 23 admits 1 since 1 < n, line 37 passes because p = x(G) is nonzero); there is no runtime guard restricting the destination. Confirmed failure: the caller's private-key storage is overwritten in place (key corruption; fault if const/ROM-backed), tmp never holds d so line 68 multiplies r by the wrong scalar, and the reversed copy at line 77 never stores s into the signature. Primary CWE-787 mechanism: writing data into a memory region outside the function's intended destination buffer (tmp) — the write lands in the caller's key input region.

assumptions: bcopy follows the standard POSIX/BSD declaration void bcopy(const void *src, void *dst, size_t n) — source first, destination second — as documented by glibc and macOS libc.
uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN is 1 on affected little-endian builds; when it is 0, the bcopy bodies are not compiled and the non-LE branches are used.

curve is one of the library's own constant curve objects with num_words == num_n_words <= uECC_MAX_WORDS and num_bytes == BITS_TO_BYTES(num_n_bits), keeping the stack arrays at lines 8-9 large enough for all uECC_vli_* calls.
The caller supplies private_key with at least curve->num_bytes bytes and signature with at least 2 * curve->num_bytes bytes per the uECC API contract.
limitations: Line 77's bcopy is the same reversed-direction defect: with standard semantics it copies curve->num_bytes bytes from signature + curve->num_bytes into the local s buffer instead of storing s into the signature; both accesses are in-bounds, so this is a correctness defect (the signature's s half is never written) without independent memory-safety impact and is not reported as a separate CWE.

If a platform provides bcopy with destination-first argument order (a nonstandard definition used by some embedded SDKs), the two LE copies behave as the surrounding comments intend and the defect does not manifest; the shown code contains no cast or comment pinning the argument order, which caps confidence below 1.0.

The curve fields num_words/num_n_words are never validated against uECC_MAX_WORDS in the shown code; a malformed curve with num_n_words > uECC_MAX_WORDS would make line 66 (s[num_n_words - 1] = 0) and line 44 (uECC_vli_clear(tmp, num_n_words)) exceed the stack arrays, but curve is trusted library data, not attacker-derived in the shown code, so this is unconfirmed as attacker-triggerable.
Signature and private-key buffer capacities cannot be identified from the shown code (pointer parameters), so boundary claims about them are unconfirmable here.
message_hash/hash_size are passed to bits2int at line 70 without a length check in the shown code; safety relies on bits2int clamping to the curve size, and its body is not shown.

A signature with s == 0 (line 72) is not rejected by the shown code — the check at line 73 only rejects s wider than num_bytes — but s == 0 is probabilistic (~1/n) and not attacker-triggerable in the shown code.
regularize_k's return value is used as an index into k2[2] at lines 31/34/36; it is assumed to be 0 or 1 by contract, and its body is not shown.

verdict.summary: 32-bit int overflow in `size * 8` at L8: `size` is an unconstrained int (residual range [INT_MIN, INT_MAX]; no bound check in the shown code). With size = 268435456 (2^28) the product wraps to -2147483648 and is passed to init_get_bits as the GetBitContext bit length; every later gb operation (skip_bits_long L12, get_bits L25/L29/L33, ff_copy_pce_data L41) then runs against a corrupted size_in_bits, the validation reads clamp to 0, and the function returns success (write_adts = 1) on data it should reject.

evidence.reason: size is an int with no guard in the shown code (Phase 1 residual range [INT_MIN, INT_MAX]); `size * 8` is computed in 32-bit int and wraps for size >= 2^28 — witness size = 268435456 yields -2147483648, a member of the admitted set since no constraint exists. The wrapped value is consumed by init_get_bits as the GetBitContext bit length (a length sink), so all later gb reads (L12, L25, L29, L33, L41) see a corrupted size_in_bits, the one-bit validation reads clamp to 0 and pass, and ADTS metadata is recorded for a stream that should be rejected. Primary mechanism: integer overflow (CWE-190) corrupting a length consumed by a bounds-defining API.

assumptions: 32-bit two's-complement int arithmetic behaves as wrap (C signed-overflow UB treated as wrap) for `size * 8`.
avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2 returns a bit offset bounded by its own size-limited parse, so `off` is assumed <= size*8.
GetBitContext/PutBitContext are standard FFmpeg readers whose get_bits/put_bits clamp to initialized sizes and rely on caller-side padding for small overreads.
limitations: PCE copy into adts->pce_data (L38 init_put_bits(&pb, adts->pce_data, MAX_PCE_SIZE); L41 ff_copy_pce_data(&pb, &gb)) is not bounded by the shown code: the copied length is chosen inside ff_copy_pce_data from attacker bitstream data, so an exact excess over MAX_PCE_SIZE cannot be derived from the shown code alone; unconfirmed (historically hardened inside the callee).

`off` from L9 is only checked for negativity (L10); no upper-bound check against `size * 8` exists before skip_bits_long (L12), but off > size*8 would require the parser to violate its own size-bounded parse, so it is unconfirmed from the shown code.

The 1-bit validation reads (L25/L29/L33) and the PCE reads (L41) have no explicit remaining-bit precondition; safety depends on GetBitContext clamping and caller-side padding, which are outside the shown code.
pce_size arithmetic (L41) truncates when (ret+3) is not a multiple of 8; impact is limited to a shorter ADTS PCE length field with no security consequence.

verdict.summary: OP_JMPUW computes the jump target a = (uint32_t)((pc - irep->iseq) + (int16_t)a) with no bounds check against irep->ilen on the main path, then executes pc = irep->iseq + a (line 330); a crafted instruction stream (e.g. a == irep->ilen, or a wrapped negative) makes the next instruction fetch read past the bytecode array (CWE-125). Separately, blk is declared at line 421 but never initialized in the OP_SEND/OP_SUPER paths, and is read by mrb_proc_p(blk) (line 452) and prepare_missing (lines 429/574); every send of a C-implemented method performs an indeterminate tag test that can escalate to a garbage-pointer write at line 455 (CWE-457).

evidence.reason: The jump target a is derived at line 310 from the decoded int16 operand and the current pc offset, then cast to uint32_t. No guard on the main path restricts a to [0, irep->ilen): the catch-handler test at line 322 only fires inside the (ch != NULL) branch and merely decides whether to THROW_TAGGED_BREAK; the only in-bounds assertion (line 316) is a debug-only mrb_assert on the restore path. Since the operand's residual range is the full int16 range, a witness such as a == irep->ilen (e.g. ilen=16, JMPUW placed so (pc-iseq)=14, operand +2) or a wrapped negative causes the fetch after JUMP to read iseq beyond its ilen entries — OOB read (CWE-125), index equal to capacity.

blk is declared at line 421 and never assigned in the OP_SEND/OP_SSEND/OP_SENDB path (only recv is assigned, at line 425); it is also passed uninitialized to prepare_missing at line 429. The branch at line 436 (MRB_METHOD_CFUNC_P) admits every C-implemented method, so ordinary sends reach this read of indeterminate stack memory with no guard — use of uninitialized value (CWE-457).

When the indeterminate tag read at line 452 equals MRB_TT_PROC, mrb_proc_ptr(blk) at line 453 turns the garbage bits into a struct RProc* and this statement writes through that garbage pointer, producing a nondeterministic type-confusion write (CWE-457 consequence); the same uninitialized blk is passed to prepare_missing at lines 429 and 574.

evidence.snippet: m = prepare_missing(mrb, recv, mid, &cls, a, &c, blk, 0);
evidence.reason: The uninitialized blk (declared line 421, never assigned before this point on the reachable missing-method path) is passed by value into the method_missing dispatch machinery whenever MRB_METHOD_UNDEF_P(m) admits the call; no shown guard initializes or validates blk, so indeterminate data flows into the callee (CWE-457, part of the same uninitialized-use root cause).

assumptions: irep->iseq is an array of irep->ilen entries; the only place the shown code states that bound is the debug assertion at line 316 (mrb_assert is treated as an NDEBUG/compile-time no-op).

The bytecode stream and its decoded operands (a/b/c) are treated by the shown code as given, unvalidated data: the function contains no opcode-level validity check for register, pool, sym, or jump operands.

mruby allocation helpers (mrb_ary_new_from_values, mrb_ary_new_capa, mrb_hash_new_capa) never return NULL; the code consistently dereferences their results without NULL checks, consistent with longjmp-based OOM signaling.
The uninitialized blk scenario assumes a build without MRB_NAN_BOXING tag-value coincidence; the C-level uninitialized read itself is unconditional.
limitations: OP_ARGARY (line 640) and OP_BLKPUSH (line 828) read stack[m1+r+m2(+1)] with offsets up to 96 relative to regs+1 when lv==0, with no guard in the shown code; the bounds checks at lines 644 and 831-832 apply only to the lv!=0 env branch. The capacity of regs (ci->stack) is not identifiable from the shown code (mrb_stack_extend/irep->nregs appear at 482/523/618 without stating a size), so this is unconfirmable, not a finding.

OP_ENTER narrows ARY_LEN to int at line 739 and uses it as copy counts at lines 766-777; a length >= 2^31 would wrap, but the only in-function producer of the argc==15 packed array (line 722) creates exactly 15 elements, so such a value cannot be produced inside the shown code.

Pool and symbol indices (e.g. lines 53, 74, 128, 415) are never compared against irep->plen/irep->slen, which never appear in the shown code; capacities are not identifiable, and OP_LOADL's bigint path (line 74) passes the signed char s[1] as a length whose callee semantics (mrb_bint_new_str) are outside the shown code.
OP_JMP, OP_JMPIF, OP_JMPNOT, OP_JMPNIL (lines 283-307) also lack an irep->ilen bound and share OP_JMPUW's out-of-bounds fetch property for malformed operands; this is reported once via OP_JMPUW.

The uninitialized-blk impact is nondeterministic: it becomes a memory-safety failure only when the indeterminate tag coincides with MRB_TT_PROC, so the garbage-pointer write has no single deterministic value witness.
If the not-shown fetch macros or a not-shown irep loader validate operand ranges, some residual ranges above would shrink; those validations are not part of the analyzed code.

verdict.summary: Unchecked 32-bit signed arithmetic on the Ex-range parameters: `count = line2 - line1 + 1` (line 6) and `n + count` / `n + 1` (lines 9-10, 25) wrap for admitted line numbers, writing an inverted/negative range into `b_op_start`/`b_op_end` and passing a wrapped negative count to `appended_lines_mark()` (line 50), corrupting op-range and undo/mark bookkeeping. The same unvalidated values are forwarded unchanged as buffer indices to `ml_get(line1)` (line 33) and `ml_append(curwin->w_cursor.lnum, ...)` (line 36), whose return status is discarded; the shown code imposes no bound on any of these values. Primary confirmed mechanism: integer overflow (CWE-190); downstream OOB depends on unshown callees and is therefore recorded as a limitation.

evidence.reason: line1/line2 are internal-helper parameters with zero value constraints in the shown code, so their residual range is the full signed 32-bit linenr_T domain. Witness: line1=0, line2=2147483647 are both members of the admitted set (no guard tests either), yet line2-line1+1 = 2147483648 wraps to -2147483648, and this wrapped count then flows to line 10 and line 50. Primary CWE-190 mechanism: the wrap is the root cause of the corrupted range/undo state.

Both n and count are unconstrained (admitted set = full parameter domain). Witness: n=2000000000 and count=2000000000 are admitted, yet n+count = 4000000000 wraps to -294967296 in the declared signed type, so b_op_end.lnum stores a negative end while b_op_start.lnum = n+1 stays positive - an inverted op-range pair consumed by later buffer-range logic. No check between the Phase-1 inputs and this sink exists in the shown code.

count arriving here is the value derived at line 6, which can be the wrapped LONG_MIN (e.g., from line1=0, line2=2147483647). The negative appended-count is passed into appended-line/mark and undo bookkeeping, propagating the CWE-190 wrap into state that downstream code consumes as line numbers/counts. The guard set on the path (p != NULL, u_save == FAIL) constrains unrelated data and does not restrict count.

assumptions: linenr_T is a 32-bit signed long in the target build (Vim's standard definition); its width is not visible in the shown code, and all wrap witnesses depend on it.
The default path is assumed: CMOD_LOCKMARKS bit clear, so lines 9-11 execute; when the bit is set those assignments are skipped.
ml_get's valid input domain is 1..ml_line_count and ml_append's is 0..ml_line_count (callee contracts, not visible in the snippet).
limitations: Out-of-bounds read/write inside ml_get/ml_append is not confirmed: those callee bodies and the buffer capacity (ml_line_count) are not identifiable from the shown code; only the out-of-domain index derivation at lines 33/36 is visible.

Real Vim callers (Ex-range parsing in ex_copymove, address clamping, MAXLNUM limits) may in practice bound line1/line2/n and make the overflow unreachable end-to-end; those constraints are outside the shown code and per the task rules cannot be used to exonerate or convict.

Unbounded-resource concern: for admitted ranges near LONG_MAX the loop iterates ~2^31 times with one vim_strsave + ml_append per iteration (lines 33/36); termination itself is guaranteed for all inputs (line1-line2 gap never decreases, line1 strictly increases), so no hang is claimed; the volume scales with caller-supplied magnitudes, which are not visible here.
The discarded ml_append return (line 36) becomes exploitable only on an allocation failure that is not attacker-controlled directly.
No injection, crypto, file, or authz surface exists in this snippet; only range-arithmetic and buffer-index concerns apply.

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable vulnerability is confirmable in the shown code. Every state-machine read and in-place write is bounded by the top-level EOF guard (if (p == pe) goto _test_eof) and per-state guards (if (++p == pe) goto _test_eofN) that precede every case-N read, so all accesses stay inside [buffer+off, buffer+len] whenever the asserted contract off <= len holds; tr22's header_done length pe-p-1 cannot underflow because it is only reached with p <= pe-1. The only true out-of-bounds scenario requires an out-of-contract caller to pass off > len into a release build, which the shown code never derives from attacker data, so it is a robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: buffer points to at least len readable bytes (caller-provided buffer contract).
parser and the callback function pointers are non-NULL (caller/library contract, not established in the shown code).
MARK/PTR_TO/LEN implement the offset/pointer/length semantics implied by the callback call sites, so all lengths passed to callbacks are p - (buffer + start) and in [0, len].
limitations: In a release build (asserts compiled out), a caller passing off > len would produce an out-of-bounds read of (*p) at the case 1 switch (and in later states) because the line-16 equality check admits p != pe; this is only reachable via an out-of-scope caller violating the API contract, so it is not reported as a finding (CWE-125 unconfirmed).

snake_upcase_char((char *)p) casts away const and writes into the caller-provided buffer; the write is in-bounds within the len-byte region but mutates caller-visible input and would fault on read-only memory — a design/robustness concern, not a memory-safety flaw under the buffer contract.

header_done is called with p+1 == pe (one-past-end) and length 0 when the terminating LF is the final byte; any failure would depend on callee behavior beyond standard pointer+length semantics and is not confirmable.

The parser tolerates bare LF inside header values (st19 loop) and separates '#' fragments, which could combine with a differently-behaving downstream HTTP layer into request-smuggling/desync behaviors; no such downstream conflict is visible in the shown code.

The final asserts (p <= pe, nread <= len, body_start/mark/field_len/field_start bounds) are debug-only and not relied on as enforcement; nread accumulation across multiple calls can in principle exceed the current len in debug builds, with no memory-safety consequence in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow in find_pattern_in_path: the pattern length parameter `len` is used both to size the heap buffer `pat = alloc(len + 5)` (line 60) and as the `%.*s` precision in `sprintf` (line 63), with no non-negative check. For `len` in [-4,-1] the allocation shrinks to 1-4 bytes while a negative precision is treated as omitted (C99/POSIX), so sprintf writes the whole pattern (plus the \< \> wrappers when `whole` is set) past the end of the heap object, e.g. len=-1 with a 10-char `ptr` overflows a 4-byte buffer by 7 bytes.

evidence.reason: `len` is an internal-helper parameter whose residual range is all of `int`: the shown code imposes no constraint on it before line 60 (`pat = alloc(len + 5)`) or line 63. The guard at lines 55-58 tests only `type`/`compl_status_sol()` and admits every `len`, and the guard at lines 61-62 (`pat == NULL`) passes for the witness `len = -1` because `alloc(4)` succeeds. Sink: for `len = -1`, `whole = 0`, and `ptr` of 10 characters, line 63 passes precision -1, which `%.*s` treats as omitted, so `sprintf` writes 11 bytes (10 chars + NUL) into the 4-byte heap object sized at line 60 — a 7-byte heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-122, unbounded copy over a visible size derived as `len + 5`); with `whole` non-zero the `\<`/`\>` wrappers make the excess 11 bytes.

assumptions: C99 7.19.6.1 / POSIX semantics: a negative precision argument to `%.*s` is treated as if the precision were omitted, so the copy runs to the source NUL.

`alloc(len + 5)` returns a usable object of the requested size (or NULL); `alloc`/`lalloc_clear` fail for huge sizes converted from negative `int` values, which is why `len <= -5` takes the safe NULL path.
limitations: The witness requires a caller to pass a negative `len`; no caller is shown, so attacker-reachability of `len < 0` is established only by the parameter's nominal residual range, not by a visible calling path.

If `ALLOC_MULT` at line 250 fails, `files[depth + 1]` at line 270 indexes `files` at index `old_files == max_path_depth` (out of bounds) and line 281 dereferences `files[old_files].name`; this is excluded by the rules because it requires an unchecked allocation failure with no attacker-controlled allocation-size volume.

At lines 409-410 (`p += ins_compl_len(); vim_iswordp(p);`) a completion prefix longer than the LSIZE `line` could read past `alloc(LSIZE)`; `ins_compl_len()` is bound-unconstrained in the shown code and no concrete in-shown-code value can be derived, so no CWE is attached.
`len + 5` signed overflow for very large positive `len` converts to a huge `size_t`, making `alloc` fail cleanly (NULL → `goto fpip_end`); it does not reach the sprintf sink.

Lines 228-231 (`p[i] = NUL` / restore) and lines 420/443-462 (IObuff completion logic) were walked and are in-bounds; the `IObuff[i-2]` negative-index read cannot fire because `i == 1` forces the increment at line 446 before any `i-2` access.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The only dangerous operation is the derived-pointer call (*mb_ptr2len)(*pp + (*lenp - 1)) at line 35, and it is protected by two shown checks: line 31-32 forces *lenp = 0 when **pp == NUL, and line 33 (has_mbyte && *lenp > 0) admits only *lenp >= 1 into the sink, excluding the offset -1 underflow and any wrapped-negative length from the column arithmetic. limitations: The historical OOB read *pp + (*lenp - 1) with *lenp == 0 (read one byte before the line) is not reachable because line 33 requires *lenp > 0 and lines 24/29 always yield >= 1; the guard at line 31-32 sets *lenp = 0 only for an empty/at-end start, which line 33 then excludes.

When the selection end is exactly the NUL position (lenp == STRLEN+1), mb_ptr2len returns 1 and the returned length includes the trailing NUL; this is a behavior quirk with no memory-safety impact visible in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The interpreter decodes instruction operands with no validation against the current frame's register extent (irep->nregs). A crafted OP_APOST (regs[a]=nil, pre=0, post=255, nregs=8) reaches SET_NIL_VALUE(regs[a+idx]) and writes regs[3..256], 249 mrb_values past the 8-slot frame (CWE-787, stack memory corruption, RCE-capable when untrusted bytecode is executed). Independently, the OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH env-length guards omit the kd flag, so a kd=1 access at e->stack[m1+r+m2+kd+1] is admitted with index == MRB_ENV_LEN(e) and reads one value past the env buffer (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: OOB write (CWE-787): 'a' (1) and 'post' (255) are bytecode operands from the entry-point instruction stream (Phase 1, residual 0..255 each) and are never compared with irep->nregs. With regs[a]=nil the L1499/L1504 guards admit the else branch (len=1 <= pre+post=255); after L1513 'a' becomes 2 and the while loop admits idx=1..254, so the sink writes regs[3..256] against a frame extent of nregs=8 (capacity shown by mrb_stack_extend at L483/L1706 and stack_clear(regs+1, irep->nregs-1) at L1707), an excess of 249 mrb_values.

OOB read (CWE-125): the guard at L1175 (MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1) admits len == m1+r+m2+2 while with kd=1 this sink indexes e->stack[m1+r+m2+kd+1] == MRB_ENV_LEN(e) (stack = e->stack+1, L1179), one mrb_value past the env buffer. Witness: m1=r=m2=0, kd=1, len=2; the admitted set (len >= m1+r+m2+2) intersects the unsafe index set.

OOB read (CWE-125): same guard defect at L648 — admitted set len >= m1+r+m2+2; with kd=1 this sink reads stack[m1+r+m2+1] = e->stack[m1+r+m2+2] == MRB_ENV_LEN(e) when the admitted equality holds (len = m1+r+m2+2, e.g. m1=r=m2=0, kd=1, len=2), reading one mrb_value past the env buffer.

assumptions: Bytecode executed via mrb_vm_exec is treated as attacker-controlled entry-point input (classification rule (a)): the shown code decodes the instruction stream into a/b/c and imposes no constraint on operand values, so residual ranges are the full declared/encodable ranges.
The current frame's register stack has extent irep->nregs, as established in the shown code itself at L483, L524, L622, L942, L1706 (mrb_stack_extend) and L1707 (stack_clear).

Env length MRB_ENV_LEN(e) is the buffer capacity used by the guards at L648/L1175; the actual env length is fixed by bytecode irep metadata (nlocals) when the closure environment is created outside the shown code.
Only base (non-EXT) 8-bit operand encodings are needed for the confirmed witnesses (a=1, pre=0, post=255; b=0x1x for ARGARY/BLKPUSH), so the FETCH macro widths (not shown) do not affect them.
limitations: pool/syms/reps index ranges (OP_LOADL L53, OP_LOADSYM L128, OP_STRING/OP_SYMBOL L1537-1558, OP_ERR L1770, OP_LAMBDA/OP_EXEC L1610/L1691) cannot be confirmed as OOB because the table capacities (plen/slen/rlen) are not identifiable from the shown code.

OP_JMP/OP_JMPIF/OP_JMPUW pc arithmetic (L284, L289, L296, L303, L310, L330) is never runtime-checked against irep->ilen (ilen appears only in an mrb_assert at L316); classified as hardening/robustness under the same missing-validation theme.

The branch-A write sink of OP_APOST at L1508 (regs[a++] = ARY_PTR(ary)[len-post-1]) is an equivalent unvalidated register write with the same root cause as the primary finding; not counted as an additional CWE.
OP_HASH (L1576) and OP_ARYPUSH (L1451) register OOB reads share the missing operand-vs-nregs check; they are the same root-cause family, not additional independent CWEs.
OP_ENTER's m1+len+m2 capacity arithmetic (L666 path) could wrap only on 32-bit with an impractical ~2^31-element array; not confirmed.
Unchecked results of prepare_missing (L430/L578 -> L479/L618) and mrb_proc_ptr(recv) in OP_CALL (L492) rely on valid-bytecode invariants; not confirmed findings.
mruby aborts on allocation failure, so no unchecked-allocation NULL-deref or attacker-volumetric OOM claim is made.

Same wrapped-offset path as line 195: with offsets[y_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 the guard at line 184 admits the value, data_ptr points at head-8, and data_ptr + 4 = head-4; this memcpy reads 4 more bytes before the buffer, another CWE-125 OOB read caused by the CWE-190 wrap in the bounds comparison.

Unconditional on the admitted path (runs before the data_len validation at line 125). CWE-125 OOB read, root cause CWE-190 wrap in the line 94 guard.
Same wrapped offset 2^64-20 admitted by the line 94 guard: data_ptr + 16 = head-4, so this 4-byte memcpy reads before the buffer as well — a second distinct CWE-125 read on the same tiled path.

assumptions: tinyexr::tinyexr_uint64 is an unsigned 64-bit type (uint64_t), so offsets[k] + sizeof(int)*N wraps modulo 2^64 in lines 94, 101, 184, 190.
head points to a readable buffer of exactly size bytes; memcpy/pointer operations are expected to stay within [head, head+size).
sizeof(int) == 4, so sizeof(int)*2 == 8 and sizeof(int)*5 == 20.
limitations: Unbounded chunk count: scanline loop y (line 181) is capped only by offsets.size() and forwarded to DecodePixelData (line 239); whether the callee consumes y as a write row index is not visible in the shown code, and the shown line_no/num_lines guards already confine decoded rows to [0, data_height), so an OOB-write claim via y is unconfirmable from this snippet.

Discarded DecodeTiledPixelData return (line 135) followed by TINYEXR_SUCCESS (line 276) is a real but low-impact error-handling flaw; kept out of the verdict CWE list per single-primary-finding assembly rules.
Unchecked calloc (82-83) / AllocateImage (87-89, 174-176) results: NULL deref on allocation failure is allocation-failure class, treated as a limitation.

Signed-overflow UB at lines 16-17 (data_window subtraction), 209-210 (line_no + num_scanline_blocks; data_window[3] + 1) has no demonstrated security effect inside the shown code beyond the independent OOB-read finding; the line_no adjustment guard (223-232) makes later rows in-bounds.

The line-25 guard's admitted set includes this failing length; CWE-125 OOB read.

Direct read at offset sizeof(*hdr)+1 = 17. For the same witness (length=16, L=3, padlen=0) that passes guards at lines 15, 18, 25, 31, 37, offset 17 is 2 bytes past the buffer end; attacker-controlled bytes are echoed into rpsi->pt. CWE-125 OOB read.

Length argument (rpsi->rpsi_bit_len + 7)/8 is derived entirely from attacker data: rpsi_bit_len = rpsi_len*8 - 16 - padlen (line 44) with rpsi_len = (L-2)*4 (line 24) and padlen in [0,31] (line 31, 37). Maximum string length is rpsi_len - 2, so the last covered offset is sizeof(*hdr) + 2 + strlen - 1 = rpsi_len + 15, while the line-25 guard admits buffers only down to rpsi_len + 12 bytes: the length given to pj_strset exceeds the remaining buffer by up to 4 bytes, and the caller-consuming rpsi->rpsi dereferences the overrun region. CWE-125 OOB read.

assumptions: sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_fb_common) == 16 (PJSIP's RTCP-FB common structure: 8-byte pjmedia_rtcp_common including sender SSRC, plus 32-bit ssrc and ssrc_src fields); with that size the parse cursor at line 28 sits 4 bytes after the 12-byte fixed part implied by the line-25 constant.

The string overread at line 45 materializes when the caller dereferences the returned rpsi->rpsi (the in-function dereferences at lines 29/43 already exceed the buffer for minimal packets).
The overread is bounded to 4 bytes; no write primitive or larger corruption is present, and no integer overflow, NULL-deref, injection, or error-handling flaw was confirmed.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in njs_array_prototype_splice(): converting the deleteCount argument (line 37) invokes attacker valueOf()/toString(), which can shrink the receiver array (a.length = 0) after the length was cached (line 16). The stale start/items/delete are then used to memcpy items into array->start at indices up to start+items-1 (lines 121-122) while njs_array_expand (line 103) only grows the buffer relative to the current (shrunk) length, so start+items exceeds the array capacity and the write runs past the end of the heap buffer.
