sp->buflines entries are non-NULL, NUL-terminated strings; sp->fp is a valid open stream (not verifiable from the shown code).
The USE_CRNL block (lines 42-52, 63-92) only compiles on platforms defining USE_CRNL; the analysis of len guards applies regardless.
limitations: Buffer-source path (line 58): a buffer line whose content plus the appended NUL leaves exactly one free slot (e.g., 248 chars at initial 250-byte capacity) makes ga.ga_maxlen - ga.ga_len == 1, so the next line is concatenated past the first NUL and effectively skipped (data-loss/merge correctness bug, line 58 + line 27). No capacity violation and no security-boundary crossing because :source of attacker content already executes arbitrary code; reported without CWE.
Lines containing embedded NUL bytes (file path line 40, buffer path line 26) are truncated at the first NUL; remaining bytes are re-read (file) or merged/skipped (buffer). Correctness only.

ga_concat (line 26) exposes no return status; internal allocation failure advances sp->buf_lnum (line 27) and can silently skip a line. Allocation-failure-only, no attacker-controlled amplification beyond file size.

Unvalidated internal-helper fields: a NULL sp->fp or NULL/unterminated buflines entry would fault at fgets (line 37) or STRLEN/ga_concat (lines 26/40), but such states are not producible within the shown code.
Multi-gigabyte single lines near INT_MAX terminate via ga_grow FAIL -> break (lines 20-21, 28-29), returning a truncated partial line; no wrap reaches any sink.
sp->sourcing_lnum int overflow requires more than 2^31 sourced lines/continuations (lines 16, 100); not realistic.

verdict.summary: In dostor(), the FTPWHO branch computes a source index with size_t arithmetic that underflows when strlen(name) equals sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename); memcpy then reads out of bounds, producing an OOB read (CWE-125) that crashes the daemon session.

evidence.reason: name is entry-point input (FTP STOR/APPE/STOU argument) with no length cap imposed in the shown code; sl = strlen(name) at L142 is size_t. The guard at L150 admits sl >= sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename); at the boundary sl == N the size_t expression sl - sizeof(...) - 1U (L155) underflows to SIZE_MAX, so &name[SIZE_MAX] is used as the memcpy source and N bytes are read out of bounds (CWE-125, OOB read), reliably faulting the process. A concrete witness is an N-character name (e.g., N copies of 'a') passing checknamesanity at L33.

assumptions: The FTPWHO code path (lines 140-160) is compiled in and shm_data_cur != NULL at runtime.
The FTP command parser accepts an argument of at least sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename) bytes; the shown code itself imposes no length cap on name.

The numeric value of sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename) is fixed at compile time; the boundary failure is proven relative to that named size: the else branch at L153 admits sl == sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename).
limitations: Quota enforcement at L115-123 skips the limit check when quota_update returns nonzero (fail-open), but the shown code gives no attacker-controlled way to make the quota backend fail.

After a failed finalize (get_file_size/tryautorename/rename at L205, L208, L218, L225), control reaches afterquota with ret/overflow still reflecting a successful transfer, so L246-247 can reply 226; triggering requires filesystem/concurrency conditions not derivable from attacker input in the shown code.

If the initial restartat is negative with st.st_size > 0 and append == 0, ftruncate(f, restartat) at L101 is called with a negative length (EINVAL only; no memory impact); the REST parser's accepted range is outside this snippet.
FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) at L180 runs on fd f after close(f) at L174; it fails with EBADF and is checked, but is a closed-fd use with a theoretical fd-reuse race.
The else-branch filename copy at L154-156 writes no terminating NUL, so shm_data_cur->filename may be unterminated; consumers of that field are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: In the ACTION_EXPAND completion path, find_pattern_in_path copies the matched completion word into the fixed-size IObuff with an unguarded STRNCPY (line 420). The length i = p - aux (line 415) equals ins_compl_len() (guard line 417), and neither i nor the helper return is bounded by IOSIZE anywhere in the shown code; the only asserted protection is the comment 'IOSIZE > compl_length' (line 419). A completion leader longer than IOSIZE (e.g., completing a word > IOSIZE bytes in a buffer line, which ml_get supplies without a visible length cap) overflows IObuff, and the later IObuff[i] = NUL (line 462) and IObuff[i++] writes (lines 446, 453) overflow even when i == IOSIZE. CWE-787 out-of-bounds write into a fixed-size buffer.

evidence.reason: Sink for CWE-787: i = (int)(p - aux) (line 415), with aux = p = startp and p = find_word_end(p) (lines 406, 414), is the matched completion word length, unbounded by any shown-code check. The guard at line 417 (i == ins_compl_len()) admits any value of the unconstrained helper return, including values > IOSIZE; the commented invariant at line 419 is not enforced. STRNCPY (strncpy semantics) writes exactly i bytes into IObuff whose capacity is the named constant IOSIZE used by the shown code itself at lines 290, 456 and 462, so a word of length IOSIZE+10 overflows by 10 bytes; even i == IOSIZE overflows at the follow-on IObuff[i] = NUL (line 462). The truncation guard protecting the second copy (lines 456-457) is absent here.

Second out-of-bounds write statement of the same CWE-787 mechanism: i still holds the completion length passed through the unguarded STRNCPY at line 420 (i is not truncated on the first-copy path). When i == IOSIZE the NUL lands at index IOSIZE (one past the last valid byte), and when i > IOSIZE it writes i - IOSIZE + 1 bytes beyond IObuff, after STRNCPY has already overrun the buffer. The in-block writes IObuff[i++] at lines 446 and 453 overflow in the same way.

assumptions: IOSIZE is a named constant equal to the capacity of IObuff; the shown code itself treats it as such at lines 290, 456 and 462.
buffer lines returned by ml_get() (lines 100, 429, 641) are NUL-terminated and not limited to IOSIZE by anything in the shown code.
STRNCPY follows standard strncpy semantics and writes n bytes when the source has no NUL within the first n bytes; aux points at a word token without an embedded NUL.
callers pass a non-negative len, positive start_lnum/end_lnum, and valid curbuf/curwin; these invariants come from outside the shown code.
limitations: The exact witness size for the line-420 overflow depends on ins_compl_len()/compl_length semantics outside the shown code: if some external invariant caps the completion leader strictly below IOSIZE, the overflow would be unreachable; the shown code itself imposes no such cap, which is why the finding is reported at 0.6 rather than higher.

The reads IObuff[i-1] and IObuff[i-2] (lines 443, 445, 449, 451-452) are out-of-bounds only for i == 1 (with p_js true for i-2); this requires an exact small external compl_length and is not an independently demonstrated class, so it is recorded here without its own CWE.

If ALLOC_MULT at line 250 fails while the file stack is full (depth+1 == old_files == max_path_depth), files[depth+1] at line 270 and files[old_files].name at line 281 index one past the allocation; the allocation size is fixed small (2*max_path_depth) and not attacker-controlled, so per the analysis rules this is excluded as an unchecked fixed-size allocation-failure issue.

p += ins_compl_len() at line 409 followed by vim_iswordp(p) at line 410 could read past the end of file_line (LSIZE) if the helper length exceeded the remaining line, but a full-prefix match precondition in the other search branch makes the conflicting conditions inconsistent; not confirmed.
A negative len parameter would defeat the %.*s precision at line 63 and overflow pat (allocated len+5 at line 60); reachability depends on an out-of-scope caller and is not confirmed.
Inverted \zs/\ze matches (endp < startp) used at lines 197-198 and 112-113 would make the derived i negative; whether the regex engine can produce such matches is not visible in the shown code.
curwin->w_cursor.col = (colnr_T)(startp - line) at line 569 could truncate for >2 GB lines; out of practical reach and not claimed as a finding.

mch_fopen at line 270 and getfile at lines 545/558 open files named by include-pattern matches in source text; this is by-design behavior of the include-search feature (:isearch/:psearch) and is not reported as path traversal.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies the unbounded, unvalidated pipe path into the fixed-capacity sun_path stack array with strcpy (line 15), causing a stack buffer overflow for any endpoint name longer than the platform sun_path size (104-108 bytes).

evidence.reason: pipePath is entry-point input from endpoint.name() (line 4) with residual range of any std::string of arbitrary length; the only guard (line 5 map find) constrains set membership, not length or content, and line 15 executes for every admitted path. strcpy writes pipePath.length()+1 bytes into local.sun_path, whose capacity is the fixed standard array size 104 (macOS/BSD) or 108 (Linux/Windows) members of struct sockaddr_un; a 200-byte name admitted by the line 5 guard overflows the stack buffer by 93-97 bytes (CWE-121, unbounded copy over a visible fixed buffer size).

assumptions: FATAL_FAIL(fd) (lines 12, 18, 21) terminates execution on failure of socket/bind/chmod; this only affects Candidates B-D, not the line 15 overflow, which executes before any later FATAL_FAIL.
sockaddr_un.sun_path is a fixed-size array of 104 or 108 bytes per the platform's standard definition; the overflow claim holds on both.
limitations: The discarded return of ::listen (line 19) followed by success-path registration (lines 24-25) is an unchecked-return/robustness concern; no value within the shown code can produce a listen failure once bind at line 18 succeeded, so attacker-triggerability is not demonstrated (error-handling flaw not confirmed).

chmod(local.sun_path, ...) after bind (lines 18-21) is a potential symlink-race/TOCTOU, but requires attacker rename privileges in the parent directory (e.g., world-writable non-sticky dir), which the shown code neither guarantees nor constrains.
The return status of initServerSocket(fd) (line 13) is discarded, but its callee body and error semantics are not shown, so no failure path inside the shown code is demonstrated.
A pipePath containing embedded NUL bytes would be truncated at the syscall layer (bind/chmod/unlink), but this produces no confirmed privilege-boundary crossing beyond the confirmed overflow.

verdict.summary: Use-after-free in eval7(): get_name_len() (line 197) expands a curly-braces name into a heap alias, name_start aliases that buffer (line 245), vim_free(alias) frees it (line 257) while name_start is still live, and the dangling pointer is immediately forwarded to handle_subscript() (line 263) when ret == OK, so a following '->' (e.g., expression {x}->foo()) reads freed heap memory.

evidence.snippet: ret = handle_subscript(arg, name_start, rettv, evalarg, TRUE);
evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled expression text enters get_name_len() at line 197, which (per the guard at line 198 and the vim_free at line 257) returns an owned heap alias for a curly-braces name; line 245 stores that buffer in name_start; after eval_variable() returns OK (line 246, admitted by the guard at line 262), line 257 frees the alias while name_start still points into it, and line 263 passes the dangling pointer to handle_subscript(), which consumes name_start for 'expr->name()' method resolution. This is a confirmed free-then-use: CWE-416 use-after-free read of freed heap memory.

assumptions: The expression string *arg is NUL-terminated (no length is passed; all reads rely on the terminator).
get_name_len() allocates 'alias' with a heap buffer when evaluating a curly-braces name ({expr}) — implied by the shown code's own 'alias != NULL' branch and vim_free(alias).
handle_subscript() consumes name_start as the base-name buffer for the 'expr->name()'/'->method()' subscript handling (name-implied semantics of its parameter).
limitations: The actual dereference of the freed name_start occurs inside the unshown handle_subscript()/eval_method(); the confirmable free-then-use is anchored at the shown call site (lines 257 and 263).
The capacity of the expression buffer is not identifiable from the shown code, so no OOB-read boundary claim beyond the NUL terminator is asserted.
get_reg_contents() (lines 136-137) and the semsg() call (line 36) show no confirmable vulnerability in the shown code.
Termination of the recursive expression parsing (line 172) depends on unshown callees and is not analyzed as a hang finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The only index sink is dp_packet_batch_refill(pb, pkt, pb_idx) at lines 18 and 22, and pb_idx is the loop variable bounded by pb_cnt (= dp_packet_batch_size(pb), line 5) via the loop guard at line 9, so it is always in [0, pb_cnt-1], strictly inside the batch's valid entry range. There are no injection, crypto, auth, or path sinks; the ipf_handle_frag return is consumed consistently (false -> refill/keep, true -> consumed). Residual int-vs-size_t mixing and all behavior of the unshown macro/helpers (batch count finalization, callee-side parsing/freeing) cannot be confirmed from the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The macro DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH (line 9) iterates pb_idx from 0 while pb_idx < pb_cnt and assigns pkt from pb->packets[pb_idx], i.e., it enforces the loop bound visible in the call-site arguments.
dp_packet_batch_size(pb) (line 5) returns the batch's count of valid packet slots, and a batch with count N has valid entries at indices 0..N-1 (name-implied container semantics).
dp_packet_batch_refill(pb, pkt, idx) stores pkt into pb->packets[idx] and is assumed to keep the batch count consistent with the packet-keeping convention of the shown code.
Entries of the caller-constructed batch are valid, non-NULL dp_packet pointers; the shown code derives pkt only from the batch array.
limitations: The batch capacity constant (DP_PACKET_BATCH_SIZE) is not present in the shown code, so the absolute upper bound of pb->packets[] is not identifiable; an OOB claim for dp_packet_batch_refill at lines 18/22 is therefore unconfirmable per the capacity rule, even though pb_idx stays below pb_cnt.

The bodies of DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH, dp_packet_batch_refill, ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, and ipf_handle_frag are not shown; whether the batch count is finalized after drops, whether handle_frag frees pkt, and whether the unlocked validity checks at lines 11/14 race with the locked handle at line 17 (TOCTOU) cannot be established from the shown code.

The int pb_idx vs size_t pb_cnt pairing could only become dangerous for pb_cnt > INT_MAX, which no visible value or constant admits; the mixed-sign comparison itself is inside the unshown macro, so no CWE-195/681 finding can be confirmed.
NULL dereference of pkt is not producible on any path in the shown code, and no allocation failure or failed lookup can supply NULL here.

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The tailroom path is protected by the line 19 tailen<=tailroom check, the page-frag path by the line 25 nr_frags<MAX_SKB_FRAGS guard with refill-failure recovery at lines 37-39, and the cow path by the line 74-76 error check. The suspicious ALIGN(tailen,...) wrap and negative/large tailen cases either fail closed (refill failure falls through to the checked cow path) or require page-frag capacities and caller invariants not identifiable in the shown code, so they are recorded as limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: Callers of esp_output_head pass valid, non-NULL x, skb, and esp, and maintain esp->tailen >= 0 (a non-negative trailer length); the shown code imposes no such bound itself.
skb_cow_data(skb, tailen, &trailer) guarantees that the returned trailer has capacity for tailen bytes and returns < 0 on failure; the shown code checks the failure case (lines 74-76).
skb_page_frag_refill returns false when the requested size cannot be satisfied from the page-frag; the shown code treats that as a recoverable failure via goto cow (lines 37-39).

skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags is maintained by the networking stack within [0, MAX_SKB_FRAGS-1] before this function runs; the shown code additionally re-checks nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS at line 25 before using it as an index.
limitations: ALIGN(tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES) at line 33 can wrap for tailen >= INT_MAX-62 (e.g., tailen=2147483637 gives allocsize=INT_MIN, passed as ~2^31 to skb_page_frag_refill at line 37), but with standard page-frag semantics the refill fails and the code recovers via the checked cow path (lines 38-39, 74-76), so no memory corruption is provable inside the shown code; any downstream overflow would require refill to succeed with the huge size and a tailen-byte copy into a page in caller code, where the page capacity (PAGE_SIZE) is not identifiable from the shown code. This is a defensive-hardening concern, not a confirmed CWE-190 finding.

A negative tailen would underflow unsigned length/accounting sinks (pskb_put at 82, skb_cow_data at 74, refcount_add at 65): branch A (line 19) admits negatives only when tailroom >= 0x80000000, which is not provable from the shown code, and branch B small negatives (-63..-1) make ALIGN=0 so refill succeeds, but the page-frag capacity and esp->tfclen/plen magnitudes are not identifiable in the shown code; non-negative tailen is a caller invariant, so this is unconfirmable.

The capacity of the page-frag object backing `page`/`tail` (lines 42-45) is not identifiable from the shown code, so any boundary claim about esp_output_fill_trailer at line 47 or the frag length at line 52 cannot be confirmed.

A huge positive tailen could drive skb_cow_data at line 74 toward large allocations (potential resource-exhaustion), but attacker control of esp->tailen is outside the shown code and no volume-scaling loop is present, so this is out of scope.

The safe conclusion for the tailroom path relies on the line 19 check tailen<=skb_tailroom(skb) (with int-to-unsigned promotion) plus the skb_cow_data capacity contract on the cow path; the latter is an API contract rather than a check visible in the shown code.

verdict.summary: parse_die computes the loop bound as `abbrev->count - 1` without any lower-bound check. When `abbrev->count == 0` (a zero-attribute abbreviation, reachable from an attacker-controlled DWARF .debug_abbrev section), the unsigned subtraction underflows to SIZE_MAX, so the loop indexes `die->attr_values[i]` (memset write at line 7) and `abbrev->defs[i]`/`die->attr_values[i]` (parse_attr_value arguments at lines 9-10) with effectively unbounded i, causing out-of-bounds reads/writes and memory corruption/crash.

evidence.reason: The CWE-190 root cause: `abbrev->count` is an internal-helper parameter with residual range [0, SIZE_MAX] since the shown code imposes no constraint on it. For the admitted witness `abbrev->count == 0`, the unsigned expression `abbrev->count - 1` wraps to SIZE_MAX (or 0xFFFFFFFF for 32-bit counts), making the loop run nearly unbounded. The wrapped bound is directly consumed by the array-subscript/address-arithmetic sinks at lines 7 and 9-10.

Write sink driven by the underflowed loop bound: with `abbrev->count == 0`, `i` starts at 0 and the guard `i < SIZE_MAX` admits every index up to SIZE_MAX-1, so `&die->attr_values[i]` walks far past the end of the zero-entry `attr_values` array, producing an out-of-bounds write (all-zeros) and memory corruption on the first iteration.

evidence.snippet:
buf = parse_attr_value(buf, buf_end - buf, &abbrev->defs[i],
			&die->attr_values[i], hdr, debug_str, debug_str_len, big_endian);
evidence.reason: Read/write sinks under the same unbounded index: for `abbrev->count == 0`, `&abbrev->defs[i]` (read of a zero-entry array) and `&die->attr_values[i]` (write) at `i = 0` are both out of bounds, and `buf_end - buf` is recomputed from the previous call's unchecked return value, so the failure reaches parse_attr_value as an out-of-domain length and pointer.

assumptions: `abbrev->count` is an unsigned counter (size_t/ut32-family), consistent with its comparison against `size_t i`; if it were signed, 0-1 = -1 would still convert to a huge unsigned bound with the same effect.
`abbrev->count == 0` corresponds to an abbreviation declaring zero attributes; nothing in the shown code forbids this value.
limitations: The concrete capacities of `die->attr_values` and `abbrev->defs` are not declared in the shown code, so the exact exceeded element/offset (CWE-787/CWE-125 mechanism) cannot be pinned from this snippet; only the wrap feeding the unbounded index is fully demonstrated.

The return value of `parse_attr_value` (line 9) is never checked; if the callee can return NULL or advance `buf` past `buf_end` on malformed input (callee body not shown), the subsequent `buf_end - buf` at line 9 and `return buf;` at line 38 are undefined behavior. This is an error-handling concern (CWE-390/703-class) whose failure mode depends on callee semantics outside the shown code.
`strdup(comp_dir)` at line 30 relies on `attribute->string.content` being properly NUL-terminated by the attribute parser; no flaw derivable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The loop bound (pb_idx < pb_cnt) restricts all batch-array indexes used at the dp_packet_batch_refill/delete calls to [0, pb_cnt), the int->size_t promotion is value-preserving over that domain, and no injection, crypto, authz, or error-status sink exists. The int pb_idx vs size_t pb_cnt typing, the batch-array capacity, and the contracts of the unshown helpers/macro remain unconfirmable concerns.

assumptions: DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH implements the standard bounded for-loop over indices 0..SIZE-1 with per-iteration increment and pkt = packets[pb_idx].
ipf_handle_frag returns non-zero exactly when it consumed pkt (caller then deletes it) and zero when the packet must be kept.
dp_packet_batch_refill(pb, pkt, idx) performs an in-place write at pb->packets[idx].
ovs_mutex_lock/unlock and dp_packet_delete operate with their standard semantics.
limitations: The capacity of pb->packets (DP_PACKET_BATCH_MAX_SIZE) is not identifiable from the shown code, so any out-of-bounds claim via pb_idx at lines 18/24 is unconfirmable (no witness excess can be computed).

The int pb_idx vs size_t pb_cnt comparison at line 9 can only misbehave for pb_cnt > INT_MAX, an uncapped but physically implausible batch count; the overflow would occur in the macro's unshown update clause and no shown sink consumes a wrapped value - hardening nit, no CWE.

A use-after-free/dangling refill would require ipf_handle_frag (line 17) to return 0 after freeing pkt, or dp_packet_delete (line 20) to free a packet aliased elsewhere in the batch; the callee contract and aliasing invariants are not shown.
ipf_is_valid_v4_frag/ipf_is_valid_v6_frag (lines 11/14) read ipf without ipf->ipf_lock (taken only at line 16); whether they touch shared ipf state is unconfirmable without their bodies.
NULL ipf or pb would fault at lines 5/16, but no shown path produces NULL; this is an assumed framework contract, not a shown-producible finding.
Single-shot leaks or DoS from unchecked allocation failures are absent (no allocation in the shown code).

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder never validates that the entry coordinates (x, y) lie inside [0, im->sx) x [0, im->sy) before painting. With x >= im->sx (or y < 0 or y >= im->sy), the left-seek loop's first iteration reads a pixel at an index equal to the row/image capacity at line 15 and writes it at line 19, producing an out-of-bounds heap read and write (identical root cause: the missing coordinate-range guard).

evidence.reason: Entry-point x/y carry no upper/lower range check in the shown code; the left loop at line 13 admits i = x for any x >= im->sx (bound is i >= 0 only), and the row capacity im->sx is established by the shown code's own bound at line 28 (i < im->sx). For x == im->sx, i equals the capacity, so gdImageSetPixel performs a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); y == im->sy likewise selects a row index equal to the im->sy row capacity. The write fires when the line 15 OOB read returns a value != border, which its equality guard admits.

Same unvalidated entry coordinate: with x == im->sx (or y >= im->sy, or y < 0), the first iteration of the left loop (line 13 admits i = x >= 0) passes an index equal to the identifiable capacity of the pixel row/array, so gdImageGetPixel performs an unconditional out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125 mechanism) whose result feeds the border comparison; it is part of the same missing-bounds-check root cause as the CWE-787 write.

assumptions: im is a valid gdImage whose pixel rows contain im->sx elements and whose pixel row array has im->sy rows; the shown code itself establishes these as the coordinate domain through the bounds at line 28 (i < im->sx) and line 62 (y < ((im->sy) - 1)).

gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel consume their x/y arguments as image pixel coordinates with that domain (standard pixel-accessor semantics implied by the shown code's own use of im->sx/im->sy as bounds).
limitations: The OOB write at line 19 requires the OOB read at line 15 to yield a value different from border; that poisoned heap value is not derivable from the shown code, so the write's triggering is not backed by a single demonstrated value, though the OOB read itself is unconditional on the first iteration.

Recursion at lines 50-51 and 73-74 has no depth cap in the shown code; for very large images this could exhaust the stack (DoS), but depth is bounded by pixel count and no image-size invariant is visible, so it is not a confirmed finding.
x == INT_MAX would make x+1 at line 28 overflow, but the OOB access at line 15 is already triggered before that arithmetic matters, so no separate integer-overflow finding is reported.
The discarded result of gdImageSetPixel is not a confirmed error-handling flaw because the API family exposes no failure status to check.

verdict.summary: The stroking loops in QPaintEngineEx::stroke parse path elements with `while (points < lastPoint)` (lines 111, 167), advancing `points`/`types` only in the MoveTo/LineTo/CurveTo cases. Any other element type admitted by the switch (e.g. CurveToDataElement from an attacker-supplied QVectorPath) hits `default: break;` (lines 131-132, 193-194), which advances neither pointer, so the loop bound never changes and execution never terminates - an unbounded-loop denial of service in the painting thread (CWE-835).

evidence.reason: Entry-point input `path` (line 84) is consumed with no validation of element-type values; the only guard is `while (points < lastPoint)` at line 111, whose bound was fixed at line 88 from `elementCount()`. For a non-empty path whose `elements()` buffer contains CurveToDataElement (admitted by the switch at line 112, which the shown code never restricts), the `default` case breaks only the switch: `points` and `types` are unchanged, so line 111 re-evaluates identically and the loop never terminates (CWE-835, unbounded/infinite loop).

Same unbounded-loop mechanism in the cosmetic-pen branch: the switch at line 168 consumes `*types` from the unvalidated entry-point path, and the `default` case at lines 193-194 advances neither `points` nor `types`, leaving the loop condition `while (points < lastPoint)` at line 167 permanently true for any attacker-supplied element type outside MoveTo/LineTo/CurveTo - a hang of the rendering thread (CWE-835).

assumptions: `path` is treated as entry-point input per Phase 1 classification: its element-type buffer contents are attacker-controlled because the shown code imposes no constraint on them; well-formedness of QVectorPath/QPainterPath is an invariant that lives outside the shown code and is not used to establish safety.
StrokeHandler's internal output arrays (lines 90-91, 153-156) grow dynamically; their capacities are not declared in the shown code.
limitations: Out-of-bounds reads of `points[0..5]` (lines 124-126, 184-186) and of `*types` after `types += 3` (lines 128, 189) require a QVectorPath whose points/types buffers are shorter or inconsistent with `elementCount()`; those buffer capacities are not identifiable from the shown code, so boundary claims are unconfirmable.
Integer overflow of `pointCount<<1` (line 88) and `elementCount+4` (line 13) would require an element count near 2^30, which cannot be materialized through the shown code.
Unchecked `xf.inverted()` at line 28: a singular transform yields an invalid clip rect with no observable security impact inside the shown code.
NULL `points` dereference (lines 139, 203) when `types==nullptr` requires a malformed direct QVectorPath construction not producible from the shown code.
NaN dash values bypass the qMax clamp at line 37 and propagate into the dasher; the consequences occur outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code alone. The three size/space guards (lines 7, 11, 29) bound the record size to the ring capacity (len <= rb->mask + 1) and cap the producer advance (new_prod_pos - cons_pos <= rb->mask), and all spinlock/error paths pair correctly. The candidate issues (u32 truncation of len/hdr->len, the 8-byte header write when prod_pos & mask == mask, the stale-cons_pos TOCTOU, and busy-bit collision) all require invariants or values not present in the shown code (numeric value of RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ, physical extent/layout of rb->data, consumer_pos monotonicity), so they are recorded as limitations without CWE.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is small enough that u64 `size + 8` (line 10) and `size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT` (line 36) do not overflow u32 after the line-7 check; its value is not shown.
rb->mask + 1 is the ring capacity and rb->data is physically backed to absorb records that wrap the logical end (normal ringbuf design); the physical backing is not shown.
consumer_pos advances monotonically and only after the consumer finishes with a record; this invariant is outside the shown code.
BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT is distinct from every possible size's high bit (i.e., size < 2^31 for valid reservations); the bit's value is not shown.
limitations: u32 truncation of `len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8)` (line 10) and of `hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT` (line 36) would desynchronize producer/consumer record walk, but the witness (size >= 2^32, or >= 2^31 for the busy-bit collision) cannot be shown to pass the line-7 guard because RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ's value is not defined in the shown code (potential CWE-190/195 consumer-side desync, unconfirmed).

When prod_pos & rb->mask == rb->mask, the 8-byte header write (lines 36-37) extends past the logical ring end by up to 7 bytes; the physical capacity of the object at rb->data is not identifiable from the shown code, so this is an unconfirmable boundary claim (potential CWE-787, unconfirmed).

cons_pos is sampled at line 14 before the spinlock and used at line 29 under the lock; a demonstrable overwrite requires consumer-side behavior (mid-record reads, consumer_pos advance timing) not shown, and a stale snapshot is conservative for a monotonic consumer (potential CWE-362, unconfirmed).
producer_pos counter wrap at `new_prod_pos = prod_pos + len` (line 24) is only shown to cause conservative failures at line 29; reaching near-ULONG_MAX counters is not established by the shown code.
Record data written by the caller after `smp_store_release` (line 40) is ordered only by the busy/len flag protocol; consumer-side handling of in-flight records is outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: On a failed lookup (id not present in idInfoMap), the failure branch logs STFATAL at line 5 but does not return, throw, or abort in the shown code, so control falls through and line 7 dereferences the past-the-end iterator returned by find() — undefined behavior (invalid pointer dereference) reachable for any id absent from the map, e.g., an attacker-supplied or stale terminal id.

evidence.reason: The lookup key id is unconstrained by the shown code (any std::string), so when id is absent from idInfoMap the guard at line 4 (it == idInfoMap.end()) admits exactly that failing set; the failure branch only executes STFATAL at line 5 and no return/throw/abort appears in the shown code, so line 7 executes it->second on the non-dereferenceable end() sentinel — an invalid-pointer dereference (CWE-476), reachable for any id not currently in the map, causing undefined behavior such as a crash or out-of-bounds read in the router.

assumptions: idInfoMap is a standard-map-like container whose find() returns end() when the key is absent.
STFATAL's macro body is not shown; the analysis treats the failure path as continuing because the shown code contains no visible termination (return/throw/abort).
id is treated at minimum as an internal-helper parameter with unconstrained residual range; if a caller passes network-derived data, it is directly attacker-controlled.
limitations: If the unshown STFATAL definition aborts or throws, the dereference at line 7 becomes unreachable and the issue reduces to an error-handling/robustness concern with no CWE attributable to the shown code.

The exact memory extent read when dereferencing the end() sentinel is implementation-defined and not identifiable from the shown code; the finding rests on the standard-library domain violation (dereferencing the past-the-end iterator), not on a specific capacity boundary.
No concrete literal id can be enumerated as a witness because the key set of idInfoMap is not shown; the witness is the guard's admitted set itself (any string absent from the map).

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. update_topline() derives only line-number and height arguments for its callees; the fold-count loops are bounded by explicit breaks (lnum >= ml_line_count at line 96; lnum <= 0 at line 199) that keep hasFolding() arguments in [1, ml_line_count] under the editor's cursor-lnum invariant. Behaviors that look dangerous (huge-'scrolloff' arithmetic overflow/underflow, int truncation of save_so, unshown cursor-lnum invariant) do not reach any memory, injection, crypto, or file sink within the shown code.

assumptions: Editor invariant not visible in the shown code: 1 <= curwin->w_cursor.lnum <= curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count on the non-early path (check_cursor_lnum() is only called at line 22 on the screen-invalid/zero-height path).
Called helpers (hasFolding, botline_forw, validate_botline, check_top_offset, scroll_cursor_*) honor in-domain line-number arguments; their bodies are not shown.
p_so and w_p_so are validated elsewhere (not shown); the shown code itself places no magnitude cap on them.
limitations: If *so_ptr could be negative or exceed LONG_MAX scale, the comparisons at lines 92/145/173/195/206/208 could overflow/underflow and misroute scroll decisions, and the restore at line 239 could persist a truncated value; no memory, injection, or file sink exists in the shown code to convert this into a security impact.
The long->int truncation of save_so at line 16 and of n at line 103 is silent and does not reach a security-relevant sink in the shown code.

An OOB read inside hasFolding at lines 98/159/201 would require w_cursor.lnum/w_topline/w_botline outside [1, ml_line_count], which the shown code cannot produce and whose helper-side capacity is not visible — unconfirmable from the shown code alone.

botline_forw's forward-progress contract is not shown; if it could fail to advance, the while loop at 166-176 would not terminate, but that depends on unshown callee behavior and is not attacker-data-driven in the shown code.

verdict.summary: nft_verdict_init validates parse status (lines 11-12), requires NFTA_VERDICT_CODE (14-15), whitelists the verdict code to the five verdict constants or a base verdict whose low byte is NF_ACCEPT/NF_DROP/NF_QUEUE (18-31), and for NFT_JUMP/NFT_GOTO requires a resolvable chain with IS_ERR, base-chain, bound-chain, and set-element-binding checks before chain->use++ and the chain store (35-59). No tainted index, size, length, pointer, format, path, or crypto value reaches a sink in the shown code; residual concerns (chain->use wrap, unshown attribute policy/lookup contracts, stale chain field on base-verdict paths) are unconfirmable from the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: nft_verdict_policy (passed at line 10) enforces standard attribute types/lengths (NLA_U32 for NFTA_VERDICT_CODE/CHAIN_ID, bounded NLA_STRING for NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN), as is conventional for this parse helper; enforcement happens inside nla_parse_nested_deprecated, whose result is checked at lines 11-12.
nft_chain_lookup and nft_chain_lookup_byid return either a valid chain pointer or an ERR_PTR, never NULL, consistent with the IS_ERR protocol used at lines 42-43 and 48-49.
nla is non-NULL when this static helper runs; its producer (nft_data_init) is not shown, so a NULL cannot be constructed within the shown code.

data->verdict.code is a 32-bit unsigned field and struct nft_verdict stores code plus a chain pointer; NF_VERDICT_MASK covers the low byte with NF_ACCEPT=1, NF_DROP=0, NF_QUEUE=3 and the NFT_* verdict constants are negative ints (-1..-5) that match as their u32 two's-complement values.
chain->use is a bounded unsigned counter (per the standard struct nft_chain), though the struct definition is not part of the shown code.
limitations: OOB read via nla_get_be32 at line 16 on an under-length NFTA_VERDICT_CODE attribute is unconfirmable: line 14 checks presence only, and the 4-byte length guarantee lives in the unshown nft_verdict_policy, whose capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.

chain->use++ at line 58 has no upper bound in the shown code, but a u32 wrap requires 2^32 cumulative increments (2^32 netlink messages, no reachable loop), the counter's type is not shown, and the consequence of a wrapped counter is outside this function, so this is a robustness/limitation concern, not a confirmed finding.

A NULL-deref of chain at lines 50/55 would require a NULL (not ERR_PTR) return from the unshown lookup helpers; the shown code's IS_ERR contract does not admit a NULL, so no NULL is producible on a shown path.

data->verdict.chain is not rewritten on base-verdict paths (NF_ACCEPT/NF_DROP/NF_QUEUE/NFT_CONTINUE/NFT_BREAK/NFT_RETURN); any stale-pointer impact depends on unshown callers and consumers, which switch on data->verdict.code before using the chain field.
High-bit values with an accepted low byte (e.g., 0xDEADBE01) are accepted as base verdicts, but no sink in the shown code consumes those bits, so any downstream effect is unconfirmable.

verdict.summary: A crafted CIN file controls image->columns and image->rows (file 32-bit fields at lines 340-341) and the only in-function bound (line 347) admits every pair with columns*rows/8 <= blob size, so SetImageExtent (line 359) sizes the pixel cache from an attacker-chosen product up to ~8x the file size (~48x in bytes), enabling memory-exhaustion denial of service on hosts without sufficient resource limits; the clean-failure path (lines 360-364) only mitigates when ImageMagick resource limits are configured.

evidence.reason: image->columns and image->rows are taken directly from file bytes (line 340 = channel[0].pixels_per_line, line 341 = channel[0].lines_per_image, each ReadBlobLong with residual range 0..2^32-1). The only in-function guard, line 347, admits every (columns,rows) with floor(columns*rows/8) <= GetBlobSize(image), i.e., products up to 8x file size; a witness member of that admitted set is columns=32700000, rows=1 with a ~4.1 MB input (product/8 = 4,087,500 <= 4,096,000; also passes the image_offset>=712 guard at line 75 and the magic check at 68-69). SetImageExtent then allocates the pixel cache from this product (~6 bytes/pixel for 16-bit RGB), permitting a single allocation of roughly 48x the input size before the row loop's truncation break (line 393) can stop consumption; under absent or high memory limits this yields attacker-controlled memory exhaustion (primary CWE-770). The failure-handling branch at 360-364 only triggers when external resource limits reject the allocation.

assumptions: MaxTextExtent (ImageMagick constant, 4096) makes all CopyMagickString(property, member, sizeof(member)) copies safe since every source member is <= 200 bytes.

ReadBlobLong returns an unsigned 32-bit value; ReadBlobByte returns 0..255 or EOF; image->columns/image->rows are size_t on LP64; MagickSizeType is 64-bit, so the line-347 product cannot wrap in 64-bit.
CINInfo channel[0].pixels_per_line and lines_per_image are 32-bit fields per the CIN (SMPTE 268M) header layout.

The severity of the confirmed resource-exhaustion finding depends on resource limits configured outside the shown code; with default ImageMagick memory limits the SetImageExtent failure path (lines 360-364) returns cleanly.
limitations: The staging-buffer read at line 392 (ReadBlobStream(image,length,pixels,&count)) and decode at line 395 (ImportQuantumPixels) cannot be proven out-of-bounds: length=GetBytesPerRow(columns,3,depth,MagickTrue) (line 377) is <= 12*columns, but the capacity of GetQuantumPixels(quantum_info) (line 384) is fixed inside AcquireQuantumInfo/SetQuantumPad, which are not shown; no object capacity is identifiable from the shown code, so no CWE-787/125 claim is made.

The discarded return of SetQuantumPad (line 383, status never checked before pixels is used at 392) could leave pixels NULL on allocation failure, causing a NULL write; this depends on an allocation failing (attacker size control is only indirect) and is therefore not confirmed.

Row-loop break paths (lines 391, 393, 397, 404) can return a partial or blank image with no propagated exception unless EOFBlob fires (line 409); this is an error-handling robustness concern (CWE-754-style) with no confirmed attacker-controlled security transition.
user_length allocation (line 331) is bounded 1:1 by the file size by the guard at line 329 and NULL-checked at 332, so no amplification or overflow is confirmed there.
Potential 32-bit size_t overflow inside GetBytesPerRow for columns near 2^32-1 is platform-dependent and the consuming buffer capacity is not shown; not confirmed.
The pixels=data-read misalignment when image_offset <= actual header length (offset can exceed image_offset, line 349 loop skipped) is semantically wrong but not memory-unsafe.
Line 172 stores green_primary_chromaticity[0] into chromaticity.red_primary.x (copy/paste defect); affects color metadata only, no security impact.

Non-termination via rows up to 2^32-1 is bounded in practice for columns >= 1 because each iteration consumes length file bytes or breaks at line 393; the columns==0 case depends on SetImageExtent/QueueAuthenticPixels semantics not shown.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. Verdict codes are validated by switch/mask checks (lines 18-31) plus exact NFT_JUMP/NFT_GOTO handling with required chain lookup guarded by IS_ERR (lines 33-49); base-chain and set-element binding cases are rejected (lines 50-54); tb[] is only indexed by constants within its declared size; desc->len is a constant store. Residual concerns (short-attribute read at nla_get_be32, NULL from chain lookup, uninitialized chain member, refcount overflow) depend on unshown policy, callee, caller, or volume and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: ctx->net and ctx->table are valid non-NULL pointers supplied by an internal caller (provenance of the helper parameters is not attacker-controlled within the shown code).

nft_verdict_policy (referenced at lines 9-10) validates attribute types/lengths, so nla_get_be32 at line 16 reads an attribute of at least 4 bytes; the policy body is not shown, so this is taken as an assumption, not an observed invariant.
nft_chain_lookup / nft_chain_lookup_byid return ERR_PTR rather than NULL on failure, consistent with the IS_ERR handling shown at lines 42-43 and 48-49.

NF_VERDICT_MASK / NF_ACCEPT / NF_DROP / NF_QUEUE and NFT_* constants use the standard kernel netfilter/nftables values; the signed constants compare correctly against the unsigned u32 code via usual arithmetic conversions.
desc->flags and nft_is_base_chain(chain) semantics are as defined by their kernel callers/callees; only their guards in the shown code are analyzed.
limitations: A 4-byte OOB read at nla_get_be32 (line 16) from an undersized NFTA_VERDICT_CODE attribute cannot be confirmed: whether the parse at lines 9-12 rejects short attributes depends on the unshown nft_verdict_policy; the standard policy (NLA_U32) would prevent it.
NULL-pointer dereference at nft_is_base_chain (line 50) would require a chain lookup to return NULL instead of ERR_PTR; no path inside the shown code produces NULL, so this is unconfirmable.

For accepted non-JUMP/NFT_GOTO codes, data->verdict.chain is not initialized and desc->len (line 61) covers the whole struct; any uninitialized-read/leak consequence depends on downstream copies/dumps and on the unshown initial state of the internal-helper parameter 'data'.

The guard at lines 20-26 admits verdict codes with arbitrary bits outside NF_VERDICT_MASK (e.g., high bits with NF_ACCEPT/NF_DROP, or queue-number encodings with NF_QUEUE); downstream behavior of those residual values is outside the shown code, so no vulnerability is confirmed.
chain->use++ (line 56) has no saturation/overflow guard; a wrap would require roughly 2^32 increments driven by repeated external calls, and the incrementing loop is not part of the shown code.
Concurrency/transaction races (e.g., a referenced chain being deleted in the same batch) and any use-after-free consequences involve state and logic not shown here.

verdict.summary: getInfoForId detects a missing key at line 3 but its failure branch only logs via STFATAL (line 4) and does not return or throw; control falls through to line 6, which dereferences the end() iterator returned by find() at line 2. Any id not present in idInfoMap reaches an invalid/past-the-end iterator dereference (undefined behavior, typically a crash), i.e. the detected failure state is not used to stop execution before a sink that requires success.

evidence.reason: The unconstrained input id (residual range: any std::string, no constraint in the shown code) is used as the lookup key at line 2; for any key absent from idInfoMap, find() returns end(), which is exactly the admitted set of the line 3 guard. The branch body (line 4) contains no return or throw visible in the shown code, so execution reaches line 6 with it == end() and dereferences an invalid iterator — undefined behavior, typically a crash. This is the CWE-754 mechanism: the unusual condition is detected but the function proceeds on the failure state to a sink (line 6) that requires the success state.

assumptions: idInfoMap is a std::map-like container for which find() returns end() if and only if the key is absent.
A string key not present in idInfoMap exists (non-empty admitted set for line 3).
STFATAL is treated as an ordinary log statement that may return, because its termination behavior is not defined in the shown code.
limitations: If STFATAL is defined as a [[noreturn]] fatal-error macro, execution never reaches line 6 and the issue is a code-quality/robustness concern rather than a reachable vulnerability; that invariant is outside the shown code and could not be verified.
The precise undefined-behavior class of dereferencing std::map end() (e.g., CWE-125 vs CWE-476) depends on container internals not identifiable from the shown code, so no OOB-capacity claim is made.
No other vulnerability classes are present in the shown code: no injection sinks, crypto, file handling, numeric conversions, or loops.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmed in SQClass::NewSlot. Every array-store site is protected by a check visible in the shown code: _defaultvalues[_member_idx(temp)] at line 9 is gated by _isfield(temp) at line 7; _methods[_member_idx(temp)] at line 40 is only reachable when temp is a non-field, non-NULL member, and all such markers are created in lockstep with the mandatory append at lines 36-37; _metamethods[mmidx] at line 19 excludes mmidx == -1 at line 18; and both growth paths at lines 36-37 and 47-48 sit behind the member-count cap at lines 12-14. The remaining concerns (array capacities, MEMBER_MAX_COUNT value, an unchecked append failure, and the discarded SQVM::IsEqual status) cannot be demonstrated as reachable, attacker-controlled failures within the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: _isfield/_member_idx/_make_field_idx/_make_method_idx implement the standard Squirrel member-marker encoding: values stored into _members at lines 36 and 47 encode the current array size as their index, and _methods/_defaultvalues only grow (push_back at lines 37 and 48) with no removal path in the shown code, so decoded indices always satisfy 0 <= idx < array.size().
ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName returns -1 for unknown names and otherwise an index bounded by the metamethod-name table (0..MT_COUNT-1), and _metamethods is sized in lockstep with that table.
A default-constructed SQObjectPtr temp has type OT_NULL, so a failed _members->Get at line 7 leaves temp OT_NULL and the new-member path at line 28 is taken.

SQObjectPtrMap::CountUsed counts distinct keys and NewSlot on an existing key replaces the value without growing the count, so the cap at lines 12-14 bounds the number of appends on the two growth paths.
limitations: The capacities of _defaultvalues, _methods and _metamethods, and the value of MEMBER_MAX_COUNT, are not declared or sized in the shown code, so no exact out-of-bounds boundary claim (e.g., index == capacity) can be confirmed for lines 9, 19 or 40.

If MEMBER_MAX_COUNT were >= 2^30, the member-index encoding would collide with the type-flag bit and _isfield/_member_idx (lines 7, 9, 40, 47) could misclassify a marker and produce an out-of-range index; the shown code does not define MEMBER_MAX_COUNT, so no witness value can be exhibited and this is unconfirmable.

Lines 36-37 and 47-48 commit the key into _members before push_back; if that append failed (unchecked allocation), a later override at line 40 or 9 would use a stale index. This requires an allocation failure, is DoS-only, and the allocation size is not attacker-controlled in the shown code.

The return value of SQVM::IsEqual at line 30 is discarded; isconstructor only feeds _constructoridx assignment at line 32, and no error path for the integer-vs-string comparison is demonstrated, so no concrete failure is shown.
The _locked gate at lines 5-6 intentionally admits static/metamethod slots for locked classes; treating that as a bypass would be a design interpretation, not a confirmed authorization flaw.

verdict.summary: No reachable vulnerability is confirmed in SQClass::NewSlot. The array-subscript sinks (_defaultvalues line 9, _methods line 37) are protected by a producer-side bound: member indices are created at lines 33/44 from size() before push_back at 34/45, and the backing vectors never shrink, so the parity guard (_isfield, line 7) and the OT_NULL routing (line 25) admit only in-range indices. The metamethod write (line 16) is guarded by the != -1 check at line 15. The only OOB existential scenarios (index-encoding overflow at >= 2^30 members, or tampering by code not shown) are unreachable from values visible in the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: Default-constructed SQObjectPtr temp holds OT_NULL; a Get miss (line 7) leaves it OT_NULL, which the shown code itself relies on at line 25.
_isfield/_member_idx/_make_field_idx/_make_method_idx implement the standard Squirrel tag encoding implied by their names: even = field, odd = method, and member_idx = encoded >> 1.
_defaultvalues and _methods grow monotonically via push_back (lines 34, 45); the shown code never shrinks them.
The only writers of values into _members in the shown code are lines 33 and 44.
GetMetaMethodIdxByName returns -1 or a legitimate metamethod-array index (guard at line 15).
ss is a valid shared-state pointer supplied by the VM; no NULL path is producible inside the shown code.
limitations: Line 9 (_defaultvalues[_member_idx(temp)].val = val) and line 37 (_methods[_member_idx(temp)].val = theval) would be OOB writes (CWE-787) for any out-of-range member index, but no such index has a producer in the shown code: every stored index equals the pre-push .size() (lines 33/44), and the arrays only grow; an out-of-range index would require >= 2^30 members (encoding overflow, infeasible before OOM) or tampering by code not shown. No concrete witness exists, so this is a hardening concern, not a confirmed finding.

Lines 29, 33, 44: size_t-to-SQInteger narrowing and the <<1 index encoding wrap only for member counts >= 2^30-2^31 (~16-34 GiB), which is not attacker-achievable; unconfirmable as an integer-overflow finding.
Lines 33/44: the return value of _members->NewSlot is discarded; only an allocation failure could desynchronize the table from the arrays, and the single insert per call is not attacker-sizeable.

Line 44 over an existing method key replaces the table binding with a field index, orphaning the _methods entry; a class-layout consistency bug with no demonstrated memory/injection impact in the shown code.
Line 4-5: bstatic=true with a non-closure value bypasses the _locked guard for default-value overrides; no memory-safety consequence is demonstrated.
Line 21: _closure(val)->Clone() is dereferenced at line 22 without a NULL check; only an allocation failure could produce NULL, which is not attacker-controlled here.
Line 15/16 boundary claims for _metamethods rely on the name-implied semantics of GetMetaMethodIdxByName, which is not shown.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies endpoint.name() into sockaddr_un.sun_path via strncpy with no length check, so a name of length >= sizeof(sun_path) (108) leaves sun_path without a NUL terminator; the subsequent unlink() (line 16) and chmod() (line 21) treat it as a NUL-terminated C string, performing an out-of-bounds stack read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: pipePath (endpoint.name(), line 4) is an unconstrained entry-point input; the only guard on it is the duplicate-key check at lines 5-7, whose admitted set includes a 108-character non-NUL name. strncpy at line 15 then copies exactly sizeof(local.sun_path)=108 bytes with no terminator, so sun_path (char[108]) is not a valid C string. unlink() at line 16 consumes it as a NUL-terminated path, reading past the 108-byte capacity (excess >= 1 byte, continuing until the next zero byte on the stack) — an out-of-bounds stack read (CWE-125).

Second sink for the same unterminated sun_path: the same unconstrained pipePath reaches chmod() on the non-Windows path (line 20) whenever bind succeeds; chmod() interprets sun_path as a NUL-terminated string, re-triggering the out-of-bounds stack read (CWE-125) beyond the 108-byte buffer written by strncpy at line 15.

assumptions: FATAL_FAIL is a fatal macro that aborts/throws on failure, so checked calls (lines 12, 18, 21) do not continue after failure.
The code targets POSIX-style sockaddr_un where sun_path is char[108]; sizeof(local.sun_path) is therefore 108 bytes.
limitations: The ::listen(fd, 5) return value (line 19) is discarded: a failure would leave a non-listening socket stored and returned at lines 24-25 (CWE-754/390-class), but no failure of listen on a fresh SOCK_STREAM socket is demonstrably reachable in the shown code.

Unconditional unlink of the unconstrained name (line 16) could delete an arbitrary file the process may remove (CWE-73/22-class), but this only matters if the caller is untrusted; not confirmed under the shown threat model.
An empty endpoint name leads to unnamed-socket bind and a FATAL_FAIL abort at chmod("") (line 21); reachability depends on a caller-supplied empty name.
An embedded NUL in pipePath makes the bound/socket path shorter than the map key used at lines 24-25, causing a key/path mismatch with no memory-safety impact.
The exact number of bytes read past sun_path is not determinable from the shown code (depends on adjacent stack contents); the OOB read itself is confirmed by the absence of a terminator.

verdict.summary: A remote BGP peer can trigger an out-of-bounds heap read in bgp_capability_msg_parse: the memcpy of sizeof(struct capability) (at least 5 bytes per the member accesses cap.code, cap.length, cap.mpc.afi via ntohs, cap.mpc.safi) at pnt+1 is guarded only by the 3-byte remaining-length check at line 16. A capability whose remaining bytes are 3..5 (capability length 0..2) reads up to 3 bytes past the received message, leaking adjacent heap bytes into cap.mpc and into debug logs. Separately, when PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is locally configured, a valid MP capability hits continue at line 58 without the pnt advance at line 104, causing an unbounded loop (configuration-dependent DoS, CWE-835).

evidence.reason: Entry-point input pnt/length; the only pre-copy guard (line 16) admits remaining >= 3 (rejects only 0..2), but this memcpy sink copies sizeof(struct capability) bytes — at least 5 bytes given the shown member accesses cap.code (line 51), cap.length (43), cap.mpc.afi consumed by ntohs (53/72), cap.mpc.safi (54) — from pnt+1, requiring pnt+6 <= end while only pnt+3 <= end is guaranteed. A 3-byte capability {action, code, length=0} passes guard 16 (pnt+3 == end) and reads pnt+1..pnt+5, 3 bytes past end; guard 43 runs after the copy and only protects the pointer advance. This is an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125) whose copied bytes flow into cap.mpc and into zlog_debug output (line 72), an information-disclosure/possible-crash vector.

An attacker-chosen MP capability (cap.code == CAPABILITY_CODE_MP after passing guard 16 and the equality-admitted guard 43) reaches this sink when peer->flags has PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY set (operator-configured state, not attacker-controlled). The continue jumps to the loop condition at line 13 without executing the advance pnt += cap.length + 3 at line 104, so pnt and end never change and the loop spins indefinitely — an unbounded CPU-spin DoS (CWE-835) in the BGP packet-processing path, reachable for any peer configured with override-capability.

assumptions: struct capability contains at least code(1 byte) + length(1 byte) + mpc.afi(2 bytes, consumed by ntohs) + mpc.safi(1 byte) = 5 bytes, inferred solely from the field accesses inside the shown code (lines 39-40, 51-54, 72); its exact layout and padding are not declared here.
The capacity bound for all reads is the received region [pnt, end) defined by end = pnt + length at line 11, which every other check in the shown code uses.
PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is local daemon configuration state; a remote peer cannot set peer->flags.
limitations: Exact sizeof(struct capability) is not shown; the OOB read is confirmed because the struct demonstrably spans at least 5 bytes, but whether the excess past end is exactly 3 bytes or 4 (with alignment padding) cannot be resolved from the shown code.

Crash impact of the OOB read is not guaranteed: heap slab slack normally continues past end, so the primary impact is information disclosure into cap.mpc and debug logs; an unmapped-page crossing is required for a crash.
The infinite-loop DoS (CWE-835) is configuration-dependent: without PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY the loop always advances pnt by cap.length+3 >= 3 and terminates by guard 43.

The afi/safi array writes at lines 80-90 are not OOB: only the values pinned by the equality checks at lines 61-65 (AFI_IP/AFI_IP6 and SAFI_UNICAST/SAFI_MULTICAST/BGP_SAFI_VPNV4, remapped to SAFI_MPLS_VPN) reach the indices.
zlog calls use compile-time constant format strings with data arguments only, and peer->host is only ever a %s argument, so no format-string or log-injection sink exists.

verdict.summary: update_topline() performs scroll-position arithmetic on editor-internal window state. No security-relevant sink (memory copy, index, format string, exec, crypto, authz) is present. The only memory writes are to a scrolloff option pointer, guarded by `mouse_dragging > 0` and always restored by the single fall-through exit; the three loops are bounded by identifiable guards (`n >= halfheight`, `lnum <= 0`/`line_count > w_height + 1`, `loff.lnum < w_botline` with an `n >= *so_ptr` break) and show no attacker-reachable out-of-domain index or size. Candidate issues (long-to-int narrowing of scrolloff, signed overflow of topline+bound expressions, int truncation of `n`) lack a reachable witness value inside the shown code and affect no memory or injection sink, so they are recorded as limitations with no CWE.

assumptions: linenr_T is a signed 64-bit long in this build, so `w_topline + *so_ptr` and `w_botline - *so_ptr` are defined signed arithmetic and underflow yields a negative value, not wraparound.
hasFolding() follows Vim's standard contract: it returns FALSE for lnum outside [1, ml_line_count] without accessing invalid storage, and its fold-start/fold-end outputs stay within the buffer.
botline_forw() advances loff.lnum by at least one line per call (callee contract); without that, the line 168 loop would be a hang, but the shown code provides no witness that it fails to advance.
curwin->w_cursor.lnum and curwin->w_topline are maintained in [1, ml_line_count] by editor code outside this function; the only clamp inside the shown code is check_cursor_lnum() at line 22.
limitations: Line 16 (`int save_so = *so_ptr;`) narrows long to int and line 241 restores the truncated value, corrupting the option only if |*so_ptr| > INT_MAX; the shown code's only assignment to *so_ptr (line 36) yields [0, INT_MAX-1] and option values are validated outside the shown code, so no concrete witness value is reachable — unconfirmed, no CWE.

Signed overflow of `curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr` (line 93) or `curwin->w_botline - *so_ptr` (line 197) would require line counts or scrolloff near LONG_MAX, which the shown code cannot produce; even then only approximation-loop iteration counts are affected — unconfirmed, no CWE.
Truncation of `n` (line 104) and sign of `line_count` (line 208) only alter which scroll routine runs (UI behavior), with no memory or injection sink — no security impact.

Non-termination of the line 168 while-loop is not confirmable from the shown code because botline_forw()'s body is not shown; standard semantics guarantee advancement, and the finite w_botline bound plus the line 175 break bound iteration — recorded as an unconfirmed robustness concern, not a finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable security vulnerability in ReadTGAImage. The most dangerous-looking constructs are each guarded within the shown code: offsets stay strictly below image->rows at every row-loop top (lines 268, 392-400, 269), so the unsigned subtraction at line 273 cannot underflow; colormap lookups are clamped by ConstrainColormapIndex against a colormap whose non-empty size is checked at lines 130/188; the comment NUL write (line 153) is inside a buffer of id_length+MagickPathExtent; and all pixel reads into pixels[4] are length-checked. Remaining concerns (huge canvas/colormap allocation, unchecked comment read count, stale status check) are either enforced by framework resource limits or have no memory-safety impact.

assumptions: TGAInfo.width/height are unsigned short (the casts at lines 85-86 bound them to 0..65535 before use at 97-98); colormap_index/colormap_length are 16-bit values 0..65535 from ReadBlobLSBShort.
ConstrainColormapIndex (lines 310, 346) has its standard contract: clamp index to [0, image->colors-1] and/or raise an exception contained via the passed exception pointer.
AcquireImageColormap fails (with ResourceLimitError) for color counts of 0 or beyond configured limits, making the check at 130/188 effective.
SetImageExtent (line 176) enforces ImageMagick resource/area limits and returns MagickFalse on violation, which is handled at line 177.
QueueAuthenticPixels (line 274) validates x/y/columns/rows and returns NULL for out-of-range coordinates.
ReadBlobByte returns a sentinel on EOF that is cast to unsigned char, so EOF during colormap/pixel decode can only produce a garbage 0..255 sample, never an out-of-bounds access.
limitations: The unsigned underflow at line 273 (real=image->rows-real-1) is not a finding: a witness would require offset >= image->rows at the loop top, but offset is initialized to 0 (line 268) and every update (392-395) is followed by the reset (396-400) that restores offset=base with base <= y and y+1 < rows (line 269), so no member of the guard's admitted set triggers the underflow.

Resource-exhaustion concerns (65535x65535 canvas at line 176; colormap of 2^24/2^32 entries at line 129) are not findings because allocation sizes are bounded by the 16-bit header and the checked SetImageExtent/AcquireImageColormap calls enforce limits; they matter only for non-default unlimited limit configurations.
The unchecked return of ReadBlob at line 152 (comment) can yield a short/garbage comment property but cannot overrun the preallocated buffer; it is a decode-fidelity issue only.
Attacker-controlled comment bytes reach SetImageProperty (line 154), but no log/query/header sink where injection would materialize is present in the shown code, so property injection is unconfirmed.
The stale 'status' check at line 376 and the q==NULL break at 275-276 skipping SyncAuthenticPixels are robustness/dead-path concerns with no confirmed failure-state dereference.

bits_per_pixel values 2..7 and 9..14 decode via the default 8-bit branch, which is a format-conformance deviation (file data width mismatch) but remains bounded by the row/column loops and EOF checks.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in input_bmp_reader: attacker-controlled field biSize (line 75, decoded from file bytes) is accepted as 108 or 124 by the branch guard (lines 189-190), and ReadOK(fd, buffer, biSize-4) then writes 104 or 120 bytes into the 64-byte stack buffer, overflowing it by 40 or 56 bytes (sink at line 194), enabling memory corruption from a crafted BMP file.

evidence.reason: biSize is derived from attacker-controlled file bytes via ToL(&buffer[0x00]) at line 75 with residual range 0..0xFFFFFFFF and is never bounded before this sink; the guard at lines 189-190 admits biSize values 108 and 124, for which biSize-4 equals 104 or 120, exceeding the declared capacity of unsigned char buffer[64] (line 4) by 40 or 56 bytes. ReadOK has standard read semantics (writes size bytes into the destination), so this is a confirmed stack buffer overflow (CWE-121); a concrete witness, biSize=108 with a valid magic, satisfies every guard on the path.

assumptions: Line numbers refer to the code as supplied inline (the workspace directory is empty; no source file was present).
ToL/ToS decode little-endian 32-bit/16-bit integers from the file; biSize is treated as a 32-bit unsigned value ranging 0..0xFFFFFFFF.
ReadOK is an fread-family wrapper that writes exactly `size` bytes into the supplied destination on success.
limitations: ColormapSize computed at line 253 can underflow/overflow if bfOffs < biSize + 14; the cap at lines 261-262 only handles values > 256, and a negative value reaching ReadColorMap (line 334) cannot be confirmed because the signedness of bfOffs/biSize (ToL return type) and ReadColorMap's handling of a negative count are not visible in the shown code.
fclose(fd) at line 352 runs when fopen failed (lines 16-19, fd == NULL); fclose(NULL) is UB by the C standard but its practical impact is platform-dependent and was not confirmed as exploitable.
The return value of fseek (line 338) is discarded; read-at-wrong-offset behavior depends on the unshown ReadImage implementation.

image_storage from ReadImage (line 341) is passed to at_bitmap_init (line 350) without a NULL check, and (unsigned short) truncation of biWidth/biHeight at line 350 could mismatch allocation metadata; both effects depend on callee behavior not present in the shown code.
The 56..=64 branch's ReadOK(fd, buffer, biSize-4) at line 163 is safe because its guard (line 159) caps the size at 60 <= 64.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code. The loop at line 7 indexes `die->attr_values[i]` (lines 8, 11, 13) and `abbrev->defs[i]` (line 10) using `i` derived from `abbrev->count`, whose only shown constraint is the nonzero guard at line 6, but the capacities of those arrays are not identifiable from the shown code, so an out-of-bounds write (potential CWE-787) cannot be substantiated. The unchecked reuse of `parse_attr_value`'s return value (line 10) and the NUL-termination of `attribute->string.content` fed to `strdup` (line 32) likewise depend on unshown callee contracts.

assumptions: `abbrev->count`, `die->count`, and the attribute-kind values are treated as unsigned integer types, consistent with DWARF-parsing conventions; the shown code never reinterprets them.

`parse_attr_value` honors the supplied remaining-length argument and returns a pointer at or below `buf_end` (e.g., `buf_end` on truncation), and the strings it exposes via `string.content` are NUL-terminated; none of these contracts is visible in the shown code.
Callers are assumed to have allocated `die->attr_values` and `abbrev->defs` with at least `abbrev->count` elements; no such invariant is established inside the shown function.
limitations: Potential heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787): `abbrev->count` has no upper bound in the shown code — the only guard, `if (abbrev->count)` (line 6), excludes only 0 — and index `i`, reaching up to `abbrev->count - 2`, is used to write `die->attr_values[i]` at lines 8 and 10-11 and to index `abbrev->defs[i]` at line 10. If either array is fixed-size with a capacity below `abbrev->count - 1`, the writes overflow; the capacity is not identifiable from the shown code, so per the confirmation standard this is a limitation, not a finding.

If `abbrev->count` is a signed type, a negative value passes the truthy guard at line 6, and the comparison `i < abbrev->count - 1` (line 7) converts the negative bound to a huge unsigned value, admitting an enormous index range; whether this reaches a sink depends on unshown type definitions and capacities.

The return value of `parse_attr_value` (line 10) is never checked and is reused as the base for `buf_end - buf` in the next iteration; if the callee can return NULL or overshoot `buf_end` on malformed input, the pointer subtraction at line 10 becomes undefined, but the callee's failure contract is not shown.

`comp_dir` is assigned from `attribute->string.content` (line 16) and passed to `strdup` (line 32); if the underlying DW_FORM_strp/DW_FORM_string data is not NUL-terminated, `strdup` reads past the end of its source. The termination guarantee is enforced (or not) inside the unshown `parse_attr_value`, so this cannot be traced through the shown code.

The loop iterates only `abbrev->count - 1` times (line 7), leaving the DIE's last attribute unparsed and incrementing `die->count` (line 25) short by one; this is at most a functional discrepancy with no demonstrable security impact from the shown code.

verdict.summary: singlevar performs variable resolution and code generation using an internalized identifier; no sink in the shown code consumes attacker-derived indices, sizes, lengths, or format strings, no arithmetic or capacity-based access occurs, and no path inside the shown code can produce NULL or a stale pointer. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: ls is a valid LexState with non-NULL ls->fs and ls->envn, per the parser framework contract (not established by the shown code).
str_checkname returns a valid, internalized TString for a syntactically valid identifier; its error/OOM path aborts outside the shown code.
