limitations: If str_checkname could return NULL without aborting, codestring(&key, varname) at line 8 would dereference NULL (CWE-476), but the NULL-producing path is outside the shown code, so this is unconfirmed.
No capacity-based (off-by-one/boundary) claims are made: the shown code contains no buffers and no size-parameterized calls whose capacities are identifiable from the shown code.
Malfunction of the unshown helpers singlevaraux/codestring/luaK_indexed is out of scope; their arguments here are constants or internalized name pointers, not attacker-derived sizes or indices.

verdict.summary: At line 18, the cursor column `col` (residual range [0, INT_MAX] after the line-3 clamp) is added to the line pointer `p` from ml_get_curline() with no bound against the line length. When `col` exceeds the line's byte length, `p + col` points past the NUL-terminated line object and mb_head_off's backward head-byte scan reads out-of-bounds heap bytes (heap OOB read, CWE-125); the same unbounded `w_cursor.col` is also consumed by curs_columns() on line 20.

evidence.reason: Taint: `col_arg` (internal-helper parameter) is constrained only by the negative clamp at line 3, which admits every value in [0, INT_MAX] and excludes only values < 0; it does not bound `col` against the length of the line returned by ml_get_curline() at line 17. The derivation `p + col` reaches the mb_head_off call on this line entirely within the shown code. The failure set {col > line byte length} intersects the guard's admitted set (witness: col = 1000 on a 3-byte line, which passes line 3 and the environment gates at lines 6 and 12), so `p + col` points beyond the line object and mb_head_off's backward scan reads heap bytes outside the buffer — heap out-of-bounds read, CWE-125. Line 21 cannot protect this sink because it is evaluated after, and `redrawing()`/`has_mbyte` are reachability gates, not value constraints.

assumptions: Reaching the sink requires redrawing() to return true (line 6) and has_mbyte to be true (line 12); these are framework/global states that gate reachability, not constraints on the value of `col`.
`colnr_T` is treated as a signed integer type, as implied by the `col_arg < 0` comparison at line 3.
limitations: The exact heap capacity of the buffer returned by ml_get_curline() is not identifiable from the shown code; the OOB excess is established relative to the NUL-terminated line region, so the witness is range-parameterized (any col > line length) rather than a fixed constant, capping confidence at ~0.65.
curs_columns() at line 20 also consumes the unbounded `w_cursor.col` as a line index, but its body is not shown, so no separate OOB read is confirmed at that call site beyond the same root taint.
The return values of curs_columns() (line 20) and edit_putchar() (line 23) are discarded; no security impact of this status handling is confirmable from the shown code.
Real-world callers might bound col_arg before calling display_dollar, but no such invariant appears in the shown code and it is not relied upon.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The only pointer dereference, `prog->type` at line 5, is fully protected by the NULL check `if (prog)` at line 4 (NULL is in the guard's excluded set). The only sink, `putchar('\n')` at line 13, receives a constant literal, so no attacker-derived index, size, or format data reaches it. The discarded return values (`pstmlist`, `pstm`, `nl`, `putchar`) have no dependent operation that could turn a failure into a security impact, and the unshown callee bodies are out of scope for confirmation.

assumptions: The global `minify` is written at line 3 before its only read at line 12, so no stale global state can influence the shown logic.
`pstmlist`, `pstm`, and `nl` are assumed to validate their own arguments; their bodies are outside the shown-code surface.
limitations: Any vulnerability inside the unshown callees `pstmlist`, `pstm`, or `nl` (e.g., stack exhaustion from recursion on a deeply nested AST, or behavior tied to the global `minify`) cannot be confirmed from the shown code, which forwards only constant indices -1 and 0.
The discarded return value of `putchar` at line 13 has no security impact in the shown code because no later operation depends on the write's success.
A `prog` with internally inconsistent pointer fields could only cause damage inside the unshown callees; the shown code's own dereference at line 5 is NULL-guarded by line 4.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder never clamps negative y: y = -1 (admitted by the L16 guard, which bounds only y >= im->sy) flows as a row index into gdImageSetPixel at L24, an out-of-bounds write through a wild row pointer (CWE-787), after an OOB read of row -1 at L21. Independently, the recursion at L47/L63 has no depth limit and, on a tall image (e.g. 2xN, all pixels != border/color), reaches depth N-1 and exhausts the stack (CWE-674).

evidence.reason: y has residual range (-inf, im->sy-1] after the L16-L18 clamp, which admits every negative int (the guard y >= im->sy is false for y = -1). With x = 0 and y = -1 the L20 loop admits i = 0 and this statement passes row index -1 to gdImageSetPixel, outside the [0, im->sy-1] row domain the shown code itself establishes; confimred OOB write (CWE-787). The same unclamped y also drives the OOB read at L21 and repeats at L33/L36.

First sink reached on the admitted path y = -1, x = 0: the seek-left loop body executes and gdImageGetPixel is called with row index -1, unconditionally an OOB read (CWE-125) outside rows [0, im->sy-1]. Same root cause as the L24 write: the only y check, L16-L18, clamps only the upper side and admits all negative values.

Uncontrolled recursion (CWE-674): no depth counter or iterative bound exists in the shown code. Witness: sx=2, sy=N, all pixels 0, border=1, color=2, start (0,0); every seed admits c=0 at L46 (0 != border && 0 != color), and the recursion descends one row per level, reaching depth N-1 and exhausting the stack for large N.

Second recursion sink with the same unbounded-depth mechanism (CWE-674): the L56 guard admits y <= sy-2 so y+1 is in range, but nothing limits how many times the descent (or the L47 ascent) recurses; a 2xN all-non-border image drives depth N-1 through this line, causing stack exhaustion on attacker-controlled large images.

assumptions: gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel consume (x, y) as row/column indices; the in-range domain [0, sx-1] x [0, sy-1] is the one the shown code itself references via im->sx, im->sy, the clamps (L13-L18), and the boundary guards (L41, L56).
The function parameters x, y, border, color and the image contents read via gdImageGetPixel are entry-point inputs for this analysis; no caller-side validation is shown, so none is relied on.
int is the C int type (32-bit typical); negative values such as -1 are representable.
limitations: The write at L24 (and L36) executes provided the out-of-bounds read at L21 (row -1) does not coincidentally equal border; the OOB read itself is deterministic, and the write is the standard case, but the exact memory contents at the OOB location are platform-dependent.
The exact image height needed to crash via recursion depends on the environment's stack limit and frame size; the shown code confirms unbounded depth, not a specific threshold N.
The bodies of gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel are not shown; they are treated as standard index-consuming pixel accessors per their names and the shown code's use of im->sx/im->sy as the bounds.
If actual callers always pass 0 <= y < im->sy, the negative-y OOB is not triggerable by those callers; the shown code itself imposes no such lower bound.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The newstyle option parser bounds every allocation (optlen capped at MAX_REQUEST_SIZE before malloc(optlen+1), line 34/38), every payload-derived index (optlen>=6 and exportnamelen<=optlen-6 before &data[exportnamelen+4], line 200/207; strict length equality before the INFO loop, line 209/263; opt_index+4>optlen guards before each memcpy in the meta-context parser, line 421/451), and all reads stay within the optlen+1-byte buffer. All return statuses are checked and all loops terminate.

assumptions: MAX_REQUEST_SIZE is a sane constant well below UINT32_MAX (typical nbdkit value 64MB), which makes optlen+1 at line 38 wrap-free and (int) querylen at line 464 exactly representable.

check_export_name (lines 72, 223, 400), check_string (line 457), and finish_newstyle_options (lines 78, 239) honor their maxlen/length parameters before reading data, as implied by their names and by the explicit exportnamelen > optlen-6 guard that makes the line 223 call safe regardless.
GET_CONN, conn->send, conn_recv_full, and the reply helpers have their standard checked-return semantics.
limitations: In the NBD_OPT_LIST/SET_META_CONTEXT path, exportnamelen is bounded only by check_export_name(option, &data[4], exportnamelen, optlen-8) (lines 400-402) before strndup(&data[4], exportnamelen) (line 410) and opt_index computation (line 417); the callee body is not shown, so an OOB read there cannot be confirmed or excluded from the shown code.
malloc(optlen+1) at line 38 would wrap only if MAX_REQUEST_SIZE == UINT32_MAX-0; that constant's value is not shown, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable.
The (int) querylen cast at line 464 and the %.*s log write would only be a problem if MAX_REQUEST_SIZE > INT_MAX, which is unconfirmable from the shown code.
debug() at lines 461-464 logs attacker-controlled bytes verbatim (log-injection shape), but the sink is local stderr and is not treated as a confirmed remote vulnerability.

Per-connection allocation up to MAX_REQUEST_SIZE+1 bytes is attacker-influenced but explicitly capped; exhaustion would require many concurrent connections and is not demonstrated as a loop with attacker-scaled volume in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in the buffer-sourcing branch of get_one_sourceline: `buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL` advances `ga.ga_len` past the terminator, then `STRLEN(buf + ga.ga_len)` starts scanning at the first byte never written by the shown code; when the sourced line exactly fills the garray capacity (e.g., a 249-byte line in the 250-byte allocation from `ga_init2(&ga,1,250)` + `ga_grow(&ga,120)`), `ga.ga_len == 250 == ga_maxtlen` and STRLEN reads one byte past the heap allocation, with the scan continuing until a NUL byte.

evidence.reason: In the `source_from_buf` branch (lines 22-32), `buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL` (line 31) writes the terminator at index `unsigned old_ga_len` and then increments `ga.ga_len` to `line_len + 1`. The unconstrained input is the buffer line copied by `ga_concat(&ga, ((char_u **)sp->buflines.ga_data)[sp->buf_lnum])` (line 26), whose length is never checked (Phase 1 residual range: any byte string, no length cap). STRLEN at line 40 therefore starts at `buf[line_len + 1]`, one byte past the NUL the shown code wrote. `ga_grow(&ga, 1)` (line 28) only guarantees capacity >= line_len + 1, so `ga.ga_len` may equal the capacity: with the 250-byte capacity produced by `ga_init2(&ga, 1, 250)` plus the first `ga_grow(&ga, 120)`, a sourced line of exactly 249 non-NUL bytes makes `ga.ga_len == 250`, so `buf + ga.ga_len` points one byte past the 250-byte heap object and STRLEN performs a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) of at least that first byte, scanning until a heap NUL. The path passes every guard: line 24 admits `buf_lnum < buflines.ga_len` (the line exists), line 28 returns OK (250 - 249 >= 1, no growth), so no guard excludes the 249-byte witness. The fgets path (line 36) is not part of this failure; there STRLEN begins at the start of the freshly read chunk.

assumptions: Capacity for the boundary witness is 250 bytes: `ga_init2(&ga, 1, 250)` (line 13) supplies growth unit/initial size 250 and the first `ga_grow(&ga, 120)` (line 20) results in 250 bytes under standard garray semantics; the shown comment (line 19) guarantees only >= 120, but both readings of the shown `250` constant give 250. If the runtime capacity were larger, the triggering line length scales to capacity - 1 with the same mechanism.

`ga_concat` (line 26) copies `STRLEN(line)` content bytes and advances `ga.ga_len` without counting the terminator; the explicit `buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL` at line 31 otherwise would be redundant. In either variant of ga_concat the conclusion is unchanged: STRLEN at line 40 begins at `line_len + 1`, past the NUL.

A sourced buffer line used as the witness contains no interior NUL before position `capacity - 1`; an interior NUL would only make the line shorter (STRLEN/ga_concat stop at NUL) and cannot create the boundary condition.
Line numbers are relative to the start of the provided snippet.
limitations: How far STRLEN (line 40) reads past the allocation, and the downstream OOB `buf[len - 1]` reads at lines 57 and 60 and `buf[len - 1] = NUL` write at line 103, depend on heap bytes beyond the allocation (no fixed NUL position), so those are not separately confirmed; the deterministic confirmed failure is the first out-of-bounds byte read at line 40.

For shorter buffer lines the read at line 40 is deterministically of uninitialized heap memory (the byte at `line_len + 1` is never written by the shown code); its security impact is limited to steering `len` toward the boundary/index checks, so it is subsumed by the CWE-125 finding rather than reported as an independent uninitialized-use issue.
`(int)STRLEN(...)` narrowing and int overflow of `ga.ga_len`/`len` for lines exceeding INT_MAX bytes cannot be confirmed from the shown code (ga_grow's limits are not shown).

Silent truncation when `ga_grow`/`ga_concat` fail (lines 20, 28, 26) or when `fgets` errors are conflated with EOF (line 36, `ferror` unused) requires an allocation failure or I/O error, not attacker-controlled volume, so they are not findings.

Whether an attacker can make `source_from_buf` true is decided by the caller; within the shown code the branch is reachable without any constraint on `buflines`, and the analysis covers that exact residual range. The fgets path is guarded (ga_grow guarantees capacity >= ga_len + 120 before each read, so fgets writes stay in bounds, and `buf[len-1]` is only evaluated when `ga_maxlen - ga_len == 1`, i.e. `ga_len == maxlen - 1 >= 0`, keeping the index in-bounds), so no finding is reported for it.

After pcim_iomap_regions_request_all(pdev, BIT(0), ...) succeeds at line 80, pcim_iomap_table(pdev) is non-NULL with entry [0] populated (kernel devres invariant), making the line-86 read valid before the line-87 value check.

If the kernel devres invariant were violated, line 86 would read pcim_iomap_table(pdev)[0] before the NULL/value check at line 87; the index and capacity are kernel-managed (BIT(0) requested at line 80), not attacker-controlled, so this is unconfirmable as a finding.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() never validates the parameter col: with has_mbyte set, ml_get_curline()'s NUL-terminated line pointer p is offset as p + col and passed to mb_head_off(p, p + col) (line 17). When col exceeds the current line length, mb_head_off reads bytes past the line's NUL terminator, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose extent grows with col.

evidence.reason: Parameter col is unconstrained in the shown code (no length/bounds check anywhere before this line), so its residual range is the full signed integer domain. Line 16 sets p = ml_get_curline(); by standard NUL-terminated-string/API semantics the line's accessible content is indices 0..L-1 with the NUL at index L. Line 17 derives p + col; for witness col = L + 2 the argument lands two bytes past the NUL, and mb_head_off (a backward byte scan for the character head, per its name and the surrounding comment) dereferences at/just below that pointer, i.e., index L + 1 — at least one byte past the string's storage (excess col - 1 - L bytes for larger col). The guards on the path (redrawing() != 0, has_mbyte != 0) both admit this witness, so the OOB read (CWE-125) is reachable entirely within the shown code.

assumptions: colnr_T is a signed integer type and has_mbyte is a boolean flag (Vim conventions, not re-declared in the snippet).
ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated buffer whose guaranteed accessible contents end at its NUL byte (standard C-string semantics of the accessed API).
limitations: The exact allocated capacity/slack of the buffer returned by ml_get_curline() is not declared in the shown code, so while the read past the NUL terminator is confirmed relative to the string boundary, the number of bytes that fall outside the underlying allocation (as opposed to past the string) is not precisely quantifiable; no slack invariant appears in the snippet.
A negative col makes p + col point before the buffer (pointer-arithmetic UB), but mb_head_off's p <= base convention avoids a dereference on that path, so no read OOB is confirmable there.
curs_columns(FALSE) (line 19) consumes the unvalidated cursor column, but its internal bounds handling is not in the shown code and was not analyzed.
Any caller-side constraints on col cannot be used because they are outside the shown code; analysis treats col as unconstrained per its provenance class.

verdict.summary: Use-after-free: for a curly-braces variable name (e.g. `a{1}` expanding to an existing variable) with evaluation enabled, `name_start` is made to point at the heap-allocated `alias` (line 255), `vim_free(alias)` frees that block (line 267), and the dangling `name_start` is then passed to `handle_subscript` (line 273) with no intervening guard or reset. The unshown callee consumes `name_start` as the base name for the documented subscript handling (`expr[expr]`, `expr.name`, `expr(expr)`, `expr->name(expr)`), so any dereference reads freed, attacker-influenced heap memory — CWE-416.

evidence.snippet: ret = handle_subscript(arg, name_start, rettv, evalarg, TRUE);
evidence.reason: The expression text in `*arg` (entry-point input, residual range: arbitrary NUL-terminated bytes) drives a curly-braces name: `get_name_len` (line 207) allocates `alias`, `s = alias` (209), and `name_start = s` (255) when `evaluate` (7-8) is true and the expanded name is a variable. `eval_variable` returning OK admits this path through the guard at 272. `vim_free(alias)` (267) then frees the block while `name_start` still aliases it, and this call site passes the dangling pointer to a helper that, per the comment at 270-271 and the parameter name `name_start`, consumes it as the base name. Any read inside the callee is a use of freed heap memory whose bytes the attacker influenced via the expanding `{expr}`, i.e. CWE-416; no check or reset exists between lines 267 and 273.

assumptions: The expression string at `*arg` is NUL-terminated, so the reads at lines 31 and 100 (`*(*arg + 1)`, `(*arg)[1]`) are in-bounds.

`get_name_len` (line 207) returns a heap-allocated `alias` only for curly-braces names when `evaluate` is true, and leaves `alias == NULL` otherwise; the shown code's own use at lines 208-209 relies on that.
`recurse` (line 15) is incremented at line 49 and decremented at line 281 on every path of the shown code; there is no early return after line 49, so depth is capped at 1000.
`handle_subscript`'s `name_start` parameter is consumed as the base name for subscript handling, as implied by the comment at lines 270-271.
limitations: The actual dereference of the freed `name_start` occurs inside `handle_subscript`, whose body is not shown; if that callee never reads `name_start` for any suffix reachable after a curly-braces name, the UAF is latent rather than manifest — this caps confidence at 0.6.

`get_reg_contents(**arg, GREG_EXPR_SRC)` (lines 146-147) can return NULL (invalid register / allocation failure) and is stored into `rettv->vval.v_string` with no NULL check, and the historical `@=` use-after-free in this call is internal to the callee; the shown code never dereferences the result, so neither is a confirmed finding.

The dereference `rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func` (line 164) would be a NULL dereference only if `get_lambda_tv` returned OK without setting `v_partial`; NULL is not producible by any statement in the shown code, so this is unconfirmed (CWE-476 possible only with an unshown callee invariant).
The recursion guard uses `recurse == 1000` (line 44) rather than `>=`; this is only brittle if the increment/decrement balance is broken, which does not happen in the shown code.
No loops exist in the shown function, so no loop-bound, parser-position, or sentinel overrun analysis applies to the shown statements.

verdict.summary: Integer-wrap heap corruption in the GBR/GBP brush loader. With width=height=32768 and bytes=1, the pattern-conversion path computes g_malloc(4 * bh.width * bh.height) in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (line 164), wrapping 2^32 to 0; the loop at lines 166-177 then writes up to 4*2^30 bytes into the 0-byte allocation via read() and the store at line 176 (CWE-787, root cause CWE-190). The same wrap on the main path (line 121) makes brush_buf a 0-byte block and gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect (line 261) an out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: width and height are attacker-controlled guint32 values admitted by the sanitizer at lines 47-51; the expression 4 * bh.width * bh.height is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and wraps 2^32 to 0, so the allocation's identifiable capacity is 0 bytes and the subsequent loop writes into it.

For i=0 (admitted because the loop runs while i < ph.width*ph.height with ph.width==ph.height==32768, admitted by lines 151-156), read writes 3 bytes at brush_buf+0, i.e., beyond the 0-byte allocation produced by the line-164 wrap, a heap-buffer-overflow write (CWE-787).

The store at index i*4+3, for i in [0, 2^30-1], targets the 0-byte brush_buf allocated at line 164 after the 32-bit unsigned wrap of 4*width*height; overflow begins at i=0, making this a confirmed out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787) from attacker-chosen header and pattern fields.

assumptions: GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is 32768 (the standard GIMP value for the named constant used at lines 47-48), so width=height=32768 is admitted by the sanitizer.
guint32 arithmetic is 32-bit unsigned on the target platform, so bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes (line 121) and 4 * bh.width * bh.height (line 164) wrap modulo 2^32.
glib g_malloc(0) returns a non-NULL pointer for a 0-sized block, so the overflow happens via writes at brush_buf+0; if it returned NULL the failure would be a NULL dereference instead, still a bug.
gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect with arguments (region, buf, 0, 0, w, h) reads w*h*bpp bytes from buf per its documented semantics.
gimp_any_to_utf8 with len=-1 treats the buffer as NUL-terminated per its documented semantics.
limitations: The same 32-bit wrap at line 121 with width=height=32768, bytes=4 yields size=0 and an out-of-bounds read of ~4 GB in gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect at lines 261-262 (CWE-125 instance of the same root cause; not added as a third CWE).
The confirmed 787 witness requires the file to contain about 1 GB of brush data (the main read at line 124 must return width*height = 2^30 bytes for bytes=1); feasible for an attacker but large.

Line 109 gimp_any_to_utf8(temp, -1, ...) may read past temp when the attacker's name bytes contain no NUL byte (CWE-125), and may return NULL on invalid UTF-8 which is later dereferenced by strlen(name) at line 246 (CWE-476); both depend on the helper's contract and are not counted in the verdict.
Attacker-controlled bn_size up to ~2^31-1 at line 95-97 allows a multi-GB g_new, and glib aborts on OOM: single-shot resource-exhaustion/DoS, not memory corruption.

Return values of gimp_image_new, gimp_layer_new, gimp_drawable_get and gimp_image_attach_parasite are unchecked; NULLs there would be dereferenced later, but the shown code cannot itself produce those NULLs on an attacker path.
The lseek status at line 67 is discarded, but subsequent length-checked reads keep this benign.

verdict.summary: do_put() computes the block-paste (and single-line paste) allocation size from count*(yanklen+spaces) after a one-sided overflow guard (lines 363-365, 509) that only rejects large positive counts. A negative count such as -1, which the function itself treats as a valid sentinel at line 59, is admitted, makes totlen negative, and alloc() an undersized buffer (lines 372, 533); the copy loops then skip all repetitions while the trailing mch_memmove/STRMOVE still writes the full line suffix, producing a heap out-of-bounds write (lines 406-407, 543) of K-delcount (block) or yanklen (single-line) bytes.

evidence.reason: count's residual range from the shown code includes -1 (admitted by the guard at 363-365 whose RHS is positive and by 509; the function explicitly special-cases count == -1 at line 59 with no lower-bound guard before this sink). With count = -1 and K = yanklen+spaces >= 1, totlen (line 371) underflows to -(K) + startspaces + endspaces, so this allocation has capacity oldlen + startspaces + endspaces - K + 1 while the subsequent writes total oldlen + startspaces + endspaces - delcount + 1, an undersized heap buffer (CWE-190 arithmetic underflow feeding the CWE-787 write).

evidence.snippet:
mch_memmove(ptr, oldp + bd.textcol + delcount,
			(size_t)(oldlen - bd.textcol - delcount + 1));
evidence.reason: Tail copy sink in the MBLOCK path for the admitted count = -1 witness: the copy loop at 386 never executes (0 < -1), but this statement still writes oldlen - textcol - delcount + 1 bytes, making total written bytes = oldlen + startspaces + endspaces - delcount + 1 versus the capacity oldlen + startspaces + endspaces - (yanklen+spaces) + 1 allocated at line 372. Excess is (yanklen+spaces) - delcount >= 1 bytes past the heap buffer (e.g., a 1-byte block line at column 0 of a 5-byte line yields a 2-byte overrun), a confirmed out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

Same root cause in the MCHAR/y_size==1 path: with count = -1, the guard at 509 (count > INT_MAX/yanklen) does not exclude it, totlen = -yanklen (line 514), so alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1) (line 533) gives a buffer of oldlen + 1 - yanklen bytes, the copy loop at 538-542 never runs, and this STRMOVE writes oldlen - col + 1 bytes at offset col, total oldlen + 1 bytes, overrunning by yanklen bytes (e.g., yanklen = 3, oldlen = 10, col = 5 writes 11 bytes into 8). Heap out-of-bounds write, primary CWE-787 with CWE-190 as the corrupting size arithmetic.

assumptions: count is treated as an internal-helper parameter per the analysis rules; the shown code imposes no lower bound on it and explicitly handles count == -1 at line 59, so -1 is in the residual range analyzed.
Register contents (y_array entries) are consistent with their STRLEN-derived lengths; the failure requires only yanklen >= 1 and does not depend on attacker-controlling the pasted text itself.

Standard C semantics for alloc()/mch_memmove()/STRMOVE() and INT_MAX = 2147483647 are assumed, and integer arithmetic uses the declared types (count long; totlen, oldlen, yanklen, spaces, delcount, startspaces, endspaces int).
limitations: In a complete Vim build, normal-mode p/P callers pass count >= 1, which would make the negative-count witness unreachable via standard commands; that caller-side invariant is outside the shown code and lowers confidence below a fully demonstrated exploit.

The int wrap of totlen + oldlen + 1 when totlen is near INT_MAX always produces a negative int converted to a huge size_t, so alloc() fails and the NULL checks at 373-374 and 534-535 contain it; not reported as a separate finding.

Mark-field arithmetic such as b_op_end.col = bd.textcol + totlen - 1 (line 423) and b_op_start.col -= first_byte_off can underflow into marks/cursor state but no memory-safety impact is identifiable in the shown code.
The '='-register split writes NUL at line 104 into expr_result in place; no concrete corruption beyond the intended split is demonstrable from the shown code.
No off-by-one claims were made for objects whose capacity cannot be identified from the shown code.

verdict.summary: On the fopen() failure path (lines 16-19) the function jumps to cleanup, where fclose(fd) is called with fd == NULL (line 352). fclose(NULL) is undefined behavior and dereferences the NULL stream pointer on glibc, so any unopenable/unreadable input filename turns a routine open error into a NULL-pointer dereference (crash / DoS). All other suspicious constructs in the shown code are protected by concrete guards (biBitCnt switch, width/height and overflow checks, ColormapSize clamp, bounded header reads), and the remaining concerns depend on unshown callees.

evidence.reason: fd has the residual range {NULL, valid FILE*} from fopen at line 14 (no shown constraint on filename). The guard `if (!fd)` at line 16 explicitly admits the NULL case and routes it via `goto cleanup` (line 19) to the unconditional fclose(fd) at line 352, so a filename that fails to open (e.g., any non-existent or unreadable path) delivers fd == NULL to the fclose sink. fclose(NULL) is undefined behavior per the C standard and dereferences the NULL stream pointer on glibc. Primary mechanism: NULL-pointer dereference, CWE-476; impact is process crash/DoS.

assumptions: Line numbers are 1-based relative to the code block as provided.
fopen/ReadOK/fclose follow standard C semantics (fopen failure returns NULL; ReadOK fails on short reads).
at_exception_fatal returns normally so that `goto cleanup` executes; if it were a noreturn function the fclose(NULL) path would be unreachable.
Target libc is glibc-like, where fclose(NULL) dereferences the NULL pointer; per the C standard the call is undefined behavior regardless.
limitations: An overflow of ColorMap[256][3] (768 bytes) from ColormapSize up to 256 with Maps == 4 at the ReadColorMap call (line 334) is not confirmed: the callee body is not shown and its per-entry write size is not implied by the shown code.

Memory-safety impact of ReadImage (lines 341-348), including allocation failure/DoS for large (but guard-bounded, width*height*4 <= 0x7fffffff) images, is not confirmable from the shown code because the callee is not shown.
A NULL image_storage returned by ReadImage is passed unguarded to at_bitmap_init (lines 341-350); the dereference behavior of that unshown callee is not established.

The (unsigned short) narrowing of biWidth/biHeight at line 350 is a real truncation (e.g., width 65536 becomes 0), but no index/allocation sink in the shown code consumes the truncated value, so downstream memory-safety impact is unconfirmed.
The fseek return value is discarded at line 338; a failed seek would only misposition subsequent reads (data-integrity concern), with no memory-safety consequence shown.

ColormapSize arithmetic at line 253 uses unsigned subtraction, but after division by Maps in {3,4} and the clamp at lines 261-262 the count reaching ReadColorMap is always in [0,256]; no negative-count sink is reachable in the shown code.
Log content (filename passed to LOG) could contain newlines, but LOG's macro behavior and filename provenance are outside the shown code, so log-injection impact is unconfirmed.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. All argv reads are bounded by argc equality guards (lines 267, 280) operating on a provably valid optind-adjusted range; the restricted-user option whitelist (lines 90-94) excludes every disallowed option before the switch; the only allocations are auto-sized xasprintf calls with constant format strings; and the remaining suspicious spots (LABEL/UUID quote wrapping, free-after-set_source, usage(stderr) continuations) depend on library or helper behavior not visible in the shown code, so they are recorded as limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: Standard C argv semantics: argv[argc] == NULL and argv[0..argc-1] are valid strings, so the post-optind reads at adjusted indices 0..1 are in bounds.
getopt_long guarantees optind is in [1, argc] when the loop terminates, so `argc -= optind` (line 218) cannot underflow.
xasprintf follows the x* convention of aborting on allocation failure, so srcbuf is non-NULL when passed to mnt_context_set_source.

libmount setter APIs (mnt_context_set_source/set_target) duplicate the provided strings, making the immediate free(srcbuf) safe; this invariant is from the library contract, not visible in the shown code.
limitations: LABEL/UUID quote injection: optarg is embedded into "LABEL=\"%s\""/"UUID=\"%s\"" without escaping quotes or backslashes (lines 148, 154) and handed to libmount's source parser (lines 150, 156); whether embedded quotes are dangerous depends on libmount parse behavior that is not shown, and the caller already has equivalent source control via --source which is permitted even for restricted users (lines 92-93), so no privilege boundary or memory-safety impact is confirmable.

free(srcbuf) immediately after mnt_context_set_source (lines 150-151, 156-157) would be a use-after-free if that API retained the pointer; the shown code demonstrates no copy, so safety relies on the unshown strdup contract.
Continuation after usage(stderr) (lines 213, 236, 242, 291) is an error-handling/robustness concern only if usage returns; its terminating behavior is not visible in the shown code.
mnt_context_get_cache (line 227) is passed to mnt_table_set_cache without a NULL check; NULL is only reachable on memory exhaustion with no attacker-controlled allocation volume in the shown code.

optarg also flows into libmount APIs for options, patterns, targets, sources, and fstab (lines 137, 141, 166, 206, 210, 246, 248); any misparsing there occurs outside the shown code, and no shell, exec, or user-format sink exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The size arithmetic in load_image is done in 32-bit unsigned int: at line 165, 4 * bh.width * bh.height wraps to 0 for an admitted 32768x32768 brush, so the pattern-extension path allocates a 0-byte brush_buf and the loop then performs heap out-of-bounds writes (read of 3 bytes at brush_buf+4i, and brush_buf[4i+3] = plain_brush[i]) with attacker-controlled bytes.

evidence.reason: Allocation-size sink: 4 * bh.width * bh.height is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned int with bh.width and bh.height from the attacker file header (admitted set [1, GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE] by lines 47-48, GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE assumed 32768). For width=height=32768 the product is 2**32 and wraps to 0, so g_malloc(0) yields a 0-capacity buffer; the 64-bit overflow guard at line 51 cannot bound this 32-bit product, and every later store into brush_buf is out of bounds.

OOB write sink (CWE-787): loop guard at line 167 (i < ph.width * ph.height = 2**30) admits i=0; read writes 3 attacker-controlled bytes into brush_buf + 0, where brush_buf was allocated with wrapped size 0 at line 165. The pattern-header guard (152-159) admits the witness (GPATTERN_MAGIC, version 1, header_size 56, bytes 3, width/height == 32768).

OOB write sink (CWE-787): at i=0 (admitted by line 167) this stores attacker-controlled byte plain_brush[0] at offset 3 of a 0-capacity buffer allocated at line 165 after the 32-bit wrap (4 * 32768 * 32768 == 2**32 == 0 in unsigned int). Indices grow to 4i+3 over 2**30 iterations, far beyond capacity for every iteration.

assumptions: GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is 32768 (GIMP's standard value); the witness width=height=32768 is inside the sanitize guard's admitted set. The value is not defined in the shown code, so the finding is conditional on it.
guint32 is a 32-bit unsigned int, so the multiplications at lines 122 and 165 are computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic before widening to gsize.
sizeof(BrushHeader) == sizeof(PatternHeader) == 28 (7 x guint32), matching the 28-byte reads at lines 31 and 142.
The attack file is a regular file of at least 2**30 + 60 bytes, so read() at line 125 returns the full requested count for the main payload.
limitations: The bytes=4 variant (32768 x 32768 x 4 wraps size to 0 at line 122) would cause an OOB read (CWE-125) inside gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect (lines 262-263) from the 0-capacity brush_buf; not listed as a finding because it additionally requires gimp_image_new (line 242) to allocate a ~4 GiB image successfully and the OOB read happens in the callee.

bn_size (line 95) is attacker-controlled up to ~2**31-1 after the version-2/3 magic check (85-86), so line 97 g_new tries to allocate ~2 GiB from a tiny file; that is a single-shot resource-exhaustion DoS (CWE-400) only when the allocation fails, so it is not a listed finding.

Version-1 files keep bytes=18 (only version 3 converts 18->2 at line 74), so line 122 can wrap to ~2**31 (32768 x 32768 x 18) and line 123 attempts a multi-GiB allocation; same root cause, DoS-only variant.

gimp_any_to_utf8 (line 110) may return NULL for invalid UTF-8 content, which would be dereferenced by strlen(name)+1 at line 247 and gimp_layer_new at line 251; the helper's failure semantics are not shown, so unconfirmed.

Unchecked return values of gimp_image_new (242), gimp_layer_new (251), and gimp_drawable_get (257) (e.g., NULL drawable dereferenced at 259) are GIMP-library-internal error handling, out of scope of the shown code.

verdict.summary: esp_output_head trusts the signed field esp->tailen with no sign/range validation. A negative value (e.g., -1) bypasses the ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen) > ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE cow guard because the sum is computed in unsigned arithmetic, is excluded from the in-place path only by the unsigned tailroom comparison, and then reaches __skb_fill_page_desc and pskb_put, where the int-to-unsigned conversion turns -1 into 0xFFFFFFFF. This records a ~4 GiB fragment size against a page-sized allocation and underflows skb->len/data_len/truesize accounting, enabling downstream out-of-bounds reads and kernel memory corruption (CWE-195).

evidence.reason: The size argument tailen derives from esp->tailen (L8), whose residual range [INT_MIN, INT_MAX] is unconstrained by any shown check. Witness tailen = -1, skb->data_len = 1 passes guard L20 (ALIGN(0) = 0 <= ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE), is steered away from the in-place path by the unsigned comparison at L24 (0xFFFFFFFF <= tailroom is false), and passes the frag-path guards L30-31. At this call site the int is implicitly converted to the unsigned int size parameter, producing 0xFFFFFFFF, which is outside the domain a length may take; the frag descriptor then records a ~4 GiB size for a page of at most one page order, so later frag consumers read or copy far past the page (CWE-195 -> OOB read / kernel corruption).

When the skb is cloned (so the fast paths at L23-74 are skipped), the same negative tailen = -1 reaches pskb_put as its int length; the standard skb_put path converts it to the unsigned 0xFFFFFFFF, wrapping skb->tail and skb->len downward by 1 and corrupting packet accounting on which subsequent crypto/checksum handling depends (CWE-195). No guard in the shown code constrains esp->tailen to a non-negative length before this sink.

assumptions: Standard semantics of the kernel APIs used: ALIGN rounds up via an AND mask; skb_tailroom returns unsigned int; pskb_put/skb_put convert the int length to unsigned int; __skb_fill_page_desc's size parameter is unsigned int; skb_page_frag_refill guarantees sz bytes at pfrag->offset on success; skb_cow_data returns a frag count or negative error.

L1_CACHE_BYTES = 64 and ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE = 32 KiB are not defined in the shown code; the witness only requires ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen) <= ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE, which holds (value 0) regardless of the constants.
skb state (not cloned, nr_frags = 0, no frag list, small tailroom) is chosen as part of the witness; these are struct states, not attacker-supplied values.
limitations: esp->tailen is produced by an unshown caller from packet padding; a negative value cannot arise in the native ESP call chain, so real-world reachability depends on a caller invariant not visible in the shown code. The shown code itself imposes no sign constraint, and this corner is analyzed as the unconstrained residual range per the internal-helper classification.
A fragment-page overflow through esp_output_fill_trailer (L52, L86) is not confirmable: the page_frag capacity and the plen/tailen relationship are not identifiable from the shown code alone.

A 2^32 wraparound of skb->data_len + tailen (L19) would require ~4 GiB magnitudes that no real skb can carry; it is noted only as an additional path to the cow branch and not relied on for the confirmed -1 witness.
Behavior inside skb_cow_data with huge/negative tailbits (L79) is not shown; any failure there is demoted.
The read/write impact of a 0xFFFFFFFF fragment size depends on downstream fragment consumers whose bodies are not in the shown code; the corruption itself is anchored at the shown call sites.

verdict.summary: The shown singlevar snippet performs name resolution and, for globals, builds env[varname] via parser-internal calls. The only attacker-influenced value, varname, is grammar-constrained to an identifier by str_checkname, and the global-name branch is protected by the construction-time _ENV registration (asserted at line 7) which no shown-code input can break. No tainted value reaches a memory, injection, crypto, file, or authorization sink, and no arithmetic/index/size derivation occurs in the shown code, so no three-part-confirmed vulnerability exists in this snippet.

assumptions: ls and var are valid non-NULL pointers per the parser call contract; a NULL ls is only producible by an out-of-scope caller and is therefore not analyzed as an in-path NULL deref.
str_checkname (callee body not shown) enforces the Lua identifier grammar by its standard semantics, so varname reaching lines 3 and 9 is a name token, not arbitrary bytes.

ls->envn is the parser-registered _ENV local of the main chunk, so the second singlevaraux (line 6) always yields a non-VVOID expdesc; the lua_assert at line 7 documents this construction-time invariant.
limitations: If _ENV resolution could fail and lua_assert were compiled out (NDEBUG), lines 8/10 would consume an unresolved expdesc; this is not a finding because no shown-code input can produce var->k == VVOID after line 6 and the ensuing failure would depend on unshown callee internals.

The discarded int return of luaK_exp2anyregup (line 8) is not a status-handling flaw: the call's effect is carried in var, and no prior step has a failure status in the shown code; if this were the only channel of the result, misbehavior would depend on the unshown callee.

Memory-safety or injection claims involving name-length caps inside str_checkname, recursion depth inside singlevaraux, or register/stack handling inside luaK_exp2anyregup/luaK_indexed cannot be anchored: the relevant capacities and callee bodies are not present in the shown code.
Off-by-one or OOB claims for register/stack indices are unconfirmable: no array or object capacity is identifiable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: iwl_trans_pcie_alloc is an initialization routine with fully checked status handling. All allocations (iwl_trans_alloc lines 14/17, alloc_workqueue 32, alloc_percpu 40) are NULL-checked before use; error labels (181-188) preserve the failing errno on every path; the only array subscript is pcim_iomap_table(pdev)[0] (95) with constant index 0 and an immediate element NULL check (96); all format strings are literals and the only string write is snprintf bounded by sizeof(trans->hw_id_str) (146-147). No attacker-controllable value reaches a memory, injection, crypto, or access-control sink. Remaining concerns (unchecked pcim_iomap_table() table pointer, ignored pci_write_config_byte status, signed-overflow wording in the hw_id computation) fail the taint/reachability/impact confirmation and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: pcim_enable_device/pcim_iomap_regions_request_all use standard devres semantics; after the checked success at line 89 the iomap table is expected to exist (if NULL is possible, robust handling is missing — see limitations).

Fields of the freshly allocated trans/trans_pcie are treated per the standard iwlwifi zero-initialization contract; the error-path cleanup is safe even without it because tso_hdr_page receives the NULL result of a failed alloc_percpu at line 40 and alloc_wq is only destroyed on paths where line 32 succeeded.
limitations: pcim_iomap_table(pdev)[0] at line 95 dereferences the framework-returned table without a NULL check; a NULL table would require an unchecked devres allocation failure with no attacker-controlled volume in the shown code, so this is a robustness concern, not a confirmed NULL-deref finding.
The return of pci_write_config_byte (line 104) is discarded; failure only leaves a PCI retry-timeout power/PM register at its default, with no security impact and no dependent operation.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The only memory sink, `&pipe->bufs[i_head & p_mask]` (lines 21 and 30), is bounded to at most `ring_size-1` whenever `ring_size >= 1`, but `ring_size > 0`, its power-of-two property, and the capacity of `pipe->bufs` are not established in the shown code, so an OOB claim is unconfirmable (CWE-125/787 candidates only). Length/offset arithmetic at lines 25, 26, and 42 can in principle truncate or wrap in the declared types, but the required magnitudes and the consuming sinks are outside the shown code, so those are silent/structural concerns, not confirmed findings. The demonstrable failure path is protected in-code: `i->count -= bytes` (line 45) cannot underflow because lines 11-12 cap `bytes` to `i->count`, and the `!bytes`, `sanity`, and `pipe_full` outcomes are all checked before any slot is written.

assumptions: `size_t` is 64-bit and `unsigned int` is 32-bit (standard kernel-header semantics); all wrap/truncation reasoning uses only these standard semantics.
The only in-code relation between `bytes` and `i->count` is the cap at lines 11-12; the safety of `i->count -= bytes` (line 45) rests on that relation alone.
limitations: Index bound unconfirmable: `pipe->bufs[i_head & p_mask]` (lines 21 and 30) cannot be shown out-of-bounds because the capacity of `pipe->bufs` is not identifiable in the shown code, and the only in-code route to an unbounded index is `pipe->ring_size == 0` (line 7, `p_mask = UINT_MAX`), which no shown check either establishes or rules out.

`buf->len += bytes` (line 25) and `buf->len = bytes` (line 39) can truncate to 32 bits once a merged segment reaches 2^32; whether such magnitudes are reachable depends on caller-provided `offset`/`bytes` and merge history, and the corrupted length is consumed only by pipe readers outside the shown code (no in-code index/size/allocation sink), so the security impact is unconfirmed.

`i->iov_offset = offset + bytes` (line 42) and `i->iov_offset += bytes` (line 26) can wrap in `size_t` (e.g., `offset = SIZE_MAX, bytes = 1`), but the wrapped value is read back only at line 20 and used at line 23 in a comparison; it never reaches an index, size, or pointer-arithmetic sink inside the shown code, so part (c) of the confirmation standard fails.

If `ring_size` were not a power of two, the `& p_mask` ring arithmetic (lines 21 and 30) would alias slots and could corrupt live buffers even while staying in-bounds; the power-of-two invariant is not present in the shown code.

A concurrent pipe drain between calls could make `i->iov_offset != 0` while the slot at `i->head & p_mask` is recycled, and the merge check (line 23) does not verify slot ownership or occupancy (`ops`/head-vs-tail); demonstrating this requires an interleaving and page-identity coincidence not derivable from the shown code.
Caller-maintained invariants are not shown: `i->head == pipe->head` when `i->iov_offset == 0`, `max_usage <= ring_size`, and validity of `page`/`offset`/`bytes` (e.g., `offset + bytes <= PAGE_SIZE`).

verdict.summary: No confirmed attack-reachable vulnerability in the shown code. All memory writes (mch_memmove at the visual-range rewrite, STRCPY in the use_plus_cmd branch) stay within the command buffer for every input: the non-plus branch writes at most up to index orig+modlen+4 while the buffer's NUL sits at orig+5+modlen+rest with rest>=1 enforced by the NUL-return/use_plus_cmd paths; the [-1] back-references are bounded by the word-advance guarantees of checkforcmd_noparen; and the modifier loop strictly advances eap->cmd so termination is guaranteed. Candidate NULL-deref and unchecked-pointer issues depend on callee bodies not shown, and the verbose-level branch is a non-security logic flaw.

assumptions: eap->cmd points into a writable, NUL-terminated buffer that contains at least the command string plus its terminating NUL (standard eap->cmd invariant, consistent with the shown rewrite code itself).
checkforcmd_noparen/checkforcmd_opt, on a match, advance the passed pointer only forward by at least the length of the matched word; skipwhite/skip_range/vim_strchr stay at or before the NUL.
mch_memmove/STRCPY operate on the command buffer per their standard semantics; get_address parses only within the NUL-terminated string.
Line numbers in the reasoning are counted from the first line of the provided snippet.
limitations: skip_range's result is dereferenced at the switch without a NULL check, but whether skip_range can return NULL for attacker input is determined by its body, which is not shown; the shown code never produces NULL on that path.
reg_pat is passed to vim_regcomp without a NULL check after skip_vimgrep_pat_ext; reg_pat==NULL reachability depends on the unshown callee.
cmod/errormsg dereferences would crash on caller-supplied NULL, but NULL is not produced anywhere in the shown code.

The verbose modifier has a confirmed logic flaw: for ':verbose N cmd' the digit branch is dead because *eap->cmd still points at the token start ('v') after checkforcmd_noparen(&p, ...) advances only p, so cmod_verbose is always 2; for ':Nverbose cmd' *eap->cmd is the range digit. This only mis-sets a verbosity value and has no confirmed security impact.

The double-memmove rewrite can mangle commands whose modifiers region lacks a trailing space (e.g. "'<,'>silentcmd" becomes "silentcm:'<,'>"), a correctness defect with no memory-safety consequence given the buffer bounds derived above.
Leftover cmod_filter_force state when the filter branch breaks early is a command-semantics concern, not a security mechanism failure visible in the shown code.

verdict.summary: create_cache_bins has a heap out-of-bounds write at deps[dep_index]++ (line 81): dep_index = depArray[k] & 0x7fff is taken from untrusted cache-file bytes and is never checked against the capacity of deps (hdr[0].imagesCount, line 19), allowing an index up to 32767 to write past a small allocation. The same k-loop also reads depArray[k] past its depListCount-element allocation because k is unbounded (CWE-125). Both are reachable with R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER set and a crafted dyld-cache file.

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write (CWE-787): deps is allocated with capacity cache->hdr->imagesCount int elements (line 19), and dep_index = depArray[k] & 0x7fff (line 80) has residual range [0,32767] from attacker-chosen file bytes filled at line 46. The loop guard at line 79 only requires depArray[k] != 0xffff and never compares dep_index to the deps capacity. Witness accepted by every guard: env filter set, N0=1, depListCount=1, depArray[0]=0x0002, extras[0].dependentsStartArrayIndex=0 -> dep_index=2 -> deps[2]++ writes 4 bytes 8 bytes past the 1-int allocation; the write executes before line 83.

Heap OOB read (CWE-125): depArray is allocated with capacity depListCount ut16 elements (line 41), but k is initialized from file-controlled extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex and incremented solely while depArray[k] != 0xffff, with no k < depListCount bound. Witness: depListCount=1 and depArray[0]=0x0002 (no sentinel) -> k reaches 1 and reads depArray[1] (index == capacity); a start index >= depListCount reads OOB on the first iteration. Termination depends entirely on attacker-chosen data.

Heap OOB write (CWE-787): deps capacity is fixed at hdr[0].imagesCount (line 19), while the j-loop at line 58 is bounded by the current header's hdr[i].imagesCount. If a later header reports imagesCount > hdr[0].imagesCount, j passes the allocation size: with hdr[0].imagesCount=1 and hdr[1].imagesCount=2, j=1 writes deps[1] past the 1-int allocation (reads at lines 59/103 are OOB in the same scenario). No guard re-checks the deps capacity inside the loop.

assumptions: cache->hdr, cache->accel, cache->buf, cache->maps_index and the dyld header/accel fields are populated by the caller from the analyzed, attacker-supplied dyld shared-cache file; all values used from them in the shown code are treated as attacker-controlled.
R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER is attacker/user settable; the affected paths require it to be non-empty and to match a library name of an image (line 67 uses substring matching).

R_NEWS0 is calloc-like (returns NULL on failure), R_FREE frees and NULLs, r_buf_fread_at with format "s" reads 2-byte values, and read_cache_images returns an array of at least hdr->imagesCount entries as implied by the shown img[j] pattern with j < hdr->imagesCount.
limitations: img[dep_index] (line 83) is a plausible OOB read when dep_index >= hdr->imagesCount, but read_cache_images' allocation size is not visible in the shown code, so the boundary is unconfirmable.
cache->maps[maps_index] (line 106) and extras[j] (line 79) are indexed with file-derived values, but the capacities of cache->maps and extras are not visible in the shown code; unconfirmable.
Line 111 discards the r_buf_read_at return; a short read leaves magicbytes partially uninitialized before r_read_le32 (line 112) — unchecked-return/uninitialized use, nondeterministic and low impact.
eprintf at lines 72/88 print file-derived lib_name/dep_name with %s and no sanitization (log/terminal injection toward stderr diagnostics); not rated as a security finding.
depListCount * 2 (line 46) could wrap in ut32 only for depListCount > 2^31, which would also require an implausible successful giant allocation; not exploitable.
The unbounded k-loop also implies arbitrarily long execution if the OOB reads keep hitting mapped memory without a 0xffff sentinel; the confirmed finding is the out-of-bounds read itself.

verdict.summary: i2c_ddc_rx reads s->edid_blob[s->reg] with no bounds check, and s->reg is incremented on every call without validation or reset, so once the index reaches the array length the read is out of bounds and the out-of-range byte is returned to the I2C bus master, causing an out-of-bounds read / information disclosure (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: The subscript s->reg is taken directly from device state with no guard in the shown code; its residual range is the full integer domain because no check, cast, or bound is applied, and line 7 (s->reg++) monotonically advances it on every invocation with no reset. Any call with s->reg >= N (N = edid_blob's array length) reads out of bounds, and the byte is returned at line 8, so the OOB value is disclosed to the caller. Primary mechanism: out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Exact excess is uncomputable from the shown code because edid_blob's capacity is not declared there, capping this at range-based confirmation.

assumptions: I2CDDC(i2c) is the standard container_of accessor yielding the device state object that owns edid_blob and reg.
s->edid_blob is a statically sized C array (any subscripted array object has a finite length N), and N is not declared in the shown code.
The I2C bus layer invokes i2c_ddc_rx repeatedly, so s->reg accumulates across calls; within the shown code only the read-then-increment sequence is visible.
limitations: The capacity of s->edid_blob and the integer type/width of s->reg are not declared in the shown code, so the exact N and the precise excess (reg - N) cannot be computed from the shown code alone; the finding is confirmed at the residual-range level (reg >= N) rather than with a numeric witness.
A NULL dereference of s via I2CDDC(i2c) (line 3) is not reportable: NULL cannot be produced by any path inside the shown code.
Overflow/wraparound of s->reg++ (line 7) is not an independent finding; it only feeds the same line-6 subscript already reported as CWE-125.

verdict.summary: The rrlen accumulator is declared uint16_t while the guard at its length check uses a 32-bit threshold (0xffff0000), so a provider name of length >= 65536 (well inside the guard's admitted set) wraps the computed record size; the wrapped size is then passed to malloc and to every snprintf size argument, silently truncating the generated DNSCrypt TXT record and defeating the overflow guard, which breaks the published certificate advertisement (integrity/availability). Writes remain snprintf-bounded, so there is no memory corruption.

evidence.snippet:
rrlen = strlen(dnscenv->provider_name) +
                         strlen(ttl_class_type) +
                         4 * sizeof(struct SignedCert) + // worst case scenario
                         1 + // trailing double quote
                         1;
evidence.reason: rrlen is declared uint16_t (line 19), so this size_t sum is truncated modulo 65536. The guard at line 40 admits every provider_name length < 0xffff0000, so a length of 65536 passes it and yields a sum of at least 65557 (for any sizeof(struct SignedCert) >= 1), which truncates to <= 65535 (e.g., 21). This is the CWE-190 wrap whose corrupted value is consumed by malloc at line 50 and by the snprintf size arguments at lines 55/59/61/70.

Allocation-size sink: for a provider_name of length 65536 (admitted by the line 40 guard), the computed sum >= 65557 is stored in uint16_t rrlen as a wrapped value (e.g., 21), so malloc allocates far fewer bytes than the 65553+ bytes the summing logic reserved, and every bounded snprintf write at lines 55-70 then silently truncates the record, dropping certificate bytes and the closing quote and producing a malformed DNSCrypt TXT local-data entry (impact: broken certificate advertisement / availability).

assumptions: Line 43 is treated as 'continue;' (as written, 'continue' without a semicolon is a syntax error, so the code as shown would not compile; the analysis assumes the author's intent).
On LP64, size_t/int promotions are assumed; the truncation analyzed occurs strictly at the uint16_t assignment.
signed_certs and rotated_certs arrays are assumed to have at least signed_certs_count / rotated_certs_count elements; the shown code does not establish this invariant.
limitations: The unchecked strdup results at lines 6 and 71 and the unchecked malloc inside unshown helpers (cfg_str2list_insert/cfg_strlist_insert) could pass NULL to caller bodies not shown; allocation failure is not attacker-volumed here (record <= 64 KiB), so this is not confirmed (CWE-252/476 not reported).

provider_name is an internal-helper parameter whose ultimate provenance is not attacker-controlled within this function's role; the CWE-190 finding analyzes the admitted residual range per the role classification, but real-world exploitability is limited (DNS provider names are normally far shorter).

The off-by-one 'rrlen - 1' snprintf sizes (lines 55/59/61/70) mean the worst-case record can also lose its closing quote even without wraparound; this is the same undersizing defect as the confirmed CWE-190 and produces no out-of-bounds access, so it is not a separate finding.

No memory corruption occurs despite the undersized allocation because every write is snprintf-bounded; the confirmed impact is silent truncation/integrity and availability of the DNSCrypt certificate advertisement, hence no CWE-787/CWE-122 secondary.
Log injection via provider_name newlines (lines 8-9) depends on operator-controlled configuration and is not a confirmed attacker-triggered flaw.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. Every attacker-derived index/length is bounded by a visible guard before it reaches a memory sink: optlen <= MAX_REQUEST_SIZE (L34) bounds malloc(optlen+1) and all conn_recv_full lengths; INFO/GO bounds exportnamelen <= optlen-6 (L203) and require the exact layout optlen == 4+exportnamelen+2+2*nrinfos (L212), which caps the info loop (L266-267) at byte optlen-1; the meta-context path gates every 4-byte read on opt_index+4 <= optlen (L425, L455) and bounds querylen via check_string's maxlen (L461-462), keeping the loop within optlen bytes and guaranteeing termination. All allocations, receives, replies, plugin lookups, and finalize calls are NULL/-1 checked. The remaining OOB hypotheses depend on the unshown bodies of check_export_name/check_string honoring their maxlen parameters and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: MAX_REQUEST_SIZE (referenced L34) is a small compile-time constant well below UINT32_MAX, so optlen <= MAX_REQUEST_SIZE makes malloc(optlen+1) at L38 overflow-free for every input admitted by the shown guard.

check_export_name (L72, L226, L404) and check_string (L461) honor their final maxlen argument per their names and parameter usage: they reject len > maxlen (and embedded NUL), so exportnamelen <= optlen-8 and querylen <= optlen-opt_index hold on the admitted paths.
finish_newstyle_options, strndup, send_newstyle_option_reply_info_str, and conn_recv_full consume their length/size arguments as bounds (standard or name-implied semantics).
namelen = -1 at L283 and desc length -1 at L305 are deliberately paired sentinels meaning 'NUL-terminated string' (SIZE_MAX), consistent with both call sites, not real lengths.
send_newstyle_option_reply_exportnames at L123 either leaves nr_options unchanged or decreases it (budget accounting); the outer loop (L15) is thus bounded by MAX_NR_OPTIONS.
The line numbers cited are counted from the function body as presented in the task (line 1 = 'negotiate_handshake_newstyle_options (void)').
limitations: An out-of-bounds read in the SET/LIST_META_CONTEXT path (strndup at L414, data[opt_index] reads at L427/L457, debug %.*s at L465, strncmp at L475/L483) would require check_export_name / check_string to fail to enforce their maxlen parameters; their bodies are not shown, so no witness can be constructed as a member of the admitted sets of the shown guards, and the claim cannot be confirmed (no CWE).

If check_export_name admitted exportnamelen near UINT32_MAX, opt_index = 4 + exportnamelen at L421 would wrap to a small value; the shown guards L425/L455 would still only admit in-bounds 4-byte reads, so the shown code's own subscript operations remain in-bounds; only the unshown helper/strndup could fail, which is out of scope.

L434 passes uint32_t nr_queries to a %d specifier (varargs type mismatch, technically UB); the format string is constant and the practical effect is a sign-rendering artifact in a log line, with no confirmed memory-safety or control-flow impact.

Export names and meta query strings are logged without escaping (e.g. L465), but the log sink (nbdkit_debug) and its record separation are outside the shown code, so log injection (CWE-117) is not confirmable.

The trailing byte data[optlen] from malloc at L38 is uninitialized; the shown code never consumes it as a C string (all uses provide explicit lengths: check_export_name, finish_newstyle_options, strndup, %.*s), so it is not a demonstrated flaw here.

The numeric value of MAX_REQUEST_SIZE is not visible in the snippet; a value of >= UINT32_MAX would make the L34 guard ineffective for the L38 allocation, but that contradicts the standard NBD protocol cap and is not confirmable from the shown code.

Resource exhaustion is bounded: at most MAX_NR_OPTIONS options, each with at most MAX_REQUEST_SIZE bytes allocated and read, so attacker-controlled volume per connection is capped by the shown guards.

verdict.summary: thread_call passes sq_gettop(v) (nparams), the source stack-top count that includes the thread slot, as sq_call's parameter count after pushing only nparams-1 argument slots above the child thread's root table. sq_call then consumes nparams argument slots and reads one slot past the region the shown code populated (the child's logical stack top): an out-of-bounds/uninitialized stack read (CWE-125) that can crash the host or feed stale data into the called closure.

evidence.reason: nparams (line 5) is the total number of source stack slots = 1 thread slot + K script-supplied arguments (entry-point input, unconstrained K >= 0), and lines 6-8 push only the roottable plus K = nparams-1 argument slots, leaving the child's logical top at relative index nparams with written slots 0..nparams-1. sq_call consumes params argument slots above the callable; with params=nparams it reads relative index nparams, exactly one slot past the written region (witness: t.call(1) -> nparams=2, child=[roottable,1], callee consumes relative slots 1..2 where relative 2 is unwritten). Guard B1 (line 4, OT_THREAD) admits the witness and guard B2 (SQ_SUCCEEDED) runs after the call, so no shown check constrains the count. Mechanism: out-of-bounds/uninitialized stack read on the child VM (CWE-125).

assumptions: sq_call's params argument counts argument slots above the callable, per standard Squirrel API semantics (documented usage pushes a closure then values and calls sq_call(v, k, ...) for k values).
stack_get(v,1) returns the first script-supplied argument (the thread) and sq_gettop(v) returns the count of slots 1..top, matching the loop's own use of slots 2..nparams as the call arguments.
limitations: Whether the over-read lands past the child thread's stack allocation (heap OOB) or inside spare capacity depends on the child stack size/growth policy, which is not visible in the shown code; only the read past the supplied argument region is confirmed.

The content of the stale slot at the child's logical top is not shown; if the engine clears popped slots the impact reduces to passing one extra value, whereas a dangling reference would make it a use-after-free (CWE-416 unconfirmed).
Pushing a very large attacker-chosen argument count (lines 6 and 8) can overflow the child thread's stack; whether Push grows the stack or raises an error is engine-dependent and not shown.

Under an alternative sq_gettop convention that counts the callee slot, the off-by-one would instead appear as an over-read in the line 7-8 loop bound; either way a mismatch exists, but the anchored mechanism here is the line 9 count.

verdict.summary: create_cache_bins performs heap out-of-bounds writes and reads on attacker-controlled dyld-cache data when R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER is set: (1) the unbounded sentinel loop `for (k = extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex; depArray[k] != 0xffff; k++)` (line 79) reads `depArray` past its `depListCount`-element allocation, and its mask value `depArray[k] & 0x7fff` is used unrestrained as `deps[dep_index]++` (line 81); (2) `deps` is allocated from `cache->hdr->imagesCount` (header 0, line 19) but indexed up to `hdr->imagesCount` of each later header (lines 59/65/75/103), with no equality guard, yielding heap OOB write/read when header counts differ.

evidence.reason: heap OOB read (CWE-125): `depArray` is allocated with `cache->accel->depListCount` elements (line 41, capacity identifiable in the shown code), but `k` starts at the file-derived `extras[j].dependentsStartArrayIndex` and advances until a 0xffff sentinel that the attacker can omit; witness: depListCount=1, depArray={0x0000}, start=0 -> k=1 reads depArray[1] beyond the 2-byte allocation. No guard bounds k against depListCount.

heap OOB write (CWE-787): `dep_index = depArray[k] & 0x7fff` (line 80) ranges over [0,32767] from file bytes, while `deps` was allocated with `cache->hdr->imagesCount` elements (line 19); witness: imagesCount=8, depArray[0]=0x0009 -> deps[9]++ writes past the 8-int allocation. The write occurs before the get_lib_name NULL checks and no guard relates dep_index to the deps capacity.

heap OOB read (CWE-125): the loop admits j in [0, hdr->imagesCount) for every header i (line 58), but `deps` has only `cache->hdr->imagesCount` (header 0) elements (line 19); witness: hdr[0].imagesCount=1, hdr[1].imagesCount=2 -> i=1, j=1 reads deps[1] out of bounds. No check in the shown code equalizes per-header imagesCount.

heap OOB write (CWE-787): same root cause and witness as the line 59 read — j admitted by `j < hdr->imagesCount` (line 58) can exceed the `cache->hdr->imagesCount` capacity of the `deps` allocation (line 19) when later headers declare more images; the identical write also occurs at line 65. No guard admits only j < capacity.

assumptions: `cache` fields (hdr, hdr_offset, maps_index, maps, accel, buf) are caller-populated from the untrusted cache file; the shown code itself imposes no bounds on imagesCount, depListCount, or dependentsStartArrayIndex.
R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER must be non-NULL for the deps/depArray paths to be reachable; it is a user/environment-controlled entry-point input (line 12).
R_NEWS0 is calloc-with-NULL-on-failure and R_FREE frees and NULLs the pointer.
limitations: `&img[dep_index]` (line 83) and `&cache->maps[maps_index]` (line 107) may be OOB, but the capacities of `img` (read_cache_images) and `cache->maps` are not identifiable from the shown code.
`magicbytes` (lines 111-113): the r_buf_read_at return is discarded, so a short read leaves uninitialized stack bytes in the switch value; low impact, no memory-safety failure confirmed.

`file[256]` (lines 126-128): a short read (return < sizeof(file)) is admitted and only the full-read path forces file[255]=0, so strrchr/strdup consume uninitialized stack; whether a NUL is absent within the whole object depends on non-attacker-controlled tail bytes, so an OOB-beyond-object read is not fully demonstrated.
`depListCount * 2` (line 46) wraps in ut32 for depListCount >= 2^31, which could let a short read pass the check; this is not an independent root cause of the confirmed OOB sinks.
eprintf of file-derived lib_name (lines 72, 88) uses a literal format string; only low-impact log-content injection possible, not a confirmed finding.
If n_hdr==0 with R_DYLDCACHE_FILTER set, `cache->hdr->imagesCount` (line 19) could dereference NULL, but header/cache presence invariants are not established in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The security-relevant mechanism historically associated with this function (CVE-2022-0847 'Dirty Pipe' stale PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE in splice-to-pipe insertion) is explicitly neutralized: every new page-cache-backed pipe_buffer is inserted with `buf->flags = 0;` (line 36) before `pipe->head` is advanced (line 42), and the merge path (lines 25-27) requires `buf->page == page` (line 23), so it cannot turn an anonymous buffer into a mergeable page-cache descriptor. Remaining concerns (len narrowing, ring-size invariants, unbounded offset arithmetic) depend on invariants or callers outside the shown code.

assumptions: The caller holds the pipe lock and passes a page slice (page, offset, bytes) fully inside one page; this page-slice contract is not enforced inside the shown code.
pipe->bufs is an array of pipe->ring_size elements with ring_size a power of two >= 1; the allocation invariant lives outside the shown code (pipe allocator).
sanity(i) (line 17) enforces iterator/pipe consistency; its body is not shown, so its exact bound cannot be verified here.
limitations: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) stale-flag mechanism is neutralized by `buf->flags = 0;` (line 36) executed before publication (line 42); the merge path (lines 25-27) cannot create such a descriptor because it requires `buf->page == page` (line 23). A vulnerable verdict would require the flags assignment to be absent, contradicting the shown code. The companion push_pipe() fix in fs/splice.c is outside the shown code.

`buf->len += bytes` (line 25) and `buf->len = bytes` (line 40) narrow size_t to unsigned int; a wrap needs bytes > UINT_MAX - buf->len, i.e. a caller violating the page-slice contract, and no copy sink in the shown code consumes the truncated length.

OOB access to pipe->bufs would require ring_size == 0 or an allocation smaller than ring_size; the allocation is not in the shown code, and the mask confines every index to [0, ring_size-1] (lines 21, 30).

`i->iov_offset = offset + bytes` (line 43) and `i->iov_offset += bytes` (line 26) overflow only for near-SIZE_MAX operands, contradicting the page-slice contract; any resulting over-read would occur in unshown consumer code.
`pipe->head = i_head + 1` (line 42) unsigned wrap would require 2^32 slot advances; `i->count -= bytes` (line 46) cannot underflow because bytes <= i->count is enforced at line 12.

verdict.summary: Every successful `search` result-write block stores the `post` ref into `op[-3]`, two slots below the first operand `op1` that the function establishes (lines 3-4). The type guards and `size <= len` check (lines 12-14) admit calls at operand depth 2-3, where `op[-3]` lies outside the operand-stack region, so line 41 is an out-of-bounds write of the attacker-influenced pointer `ptr + size` (CWE-787); with deeper stacks it instead overwrites the oldest operand while leaving its stale `rsize` intact. Independently, the backward branch at line 47 decrements `op[-3].tas.rsize` before the found path ever initializes it, so the returned `post` ref receives a stale/attacker-influenced length whose uint underflow can reach ~4GB, which later string operators use to read far beyond the text buffer (CWE-457).

evidence.reason: The result store writes into `op[-3]`, i.e. two ref slots below the first operand `op1 = op - 1` (line 4). The only slots the shown code establishes as valid are `op` (line 3) and `op1`; the checks at lines 12-14 admit any two `t_string` operands with `size <= r_size(op1)` and impose no constraint on stack depth or on the result index -3. At depths >= 4 the same statement overwrites the oldest attacker operand, redirecting its bytes pointer into the searched text while its large stale `rsize` survives, enabling later OOB reads.

PostScript string operators then consume that rsize as the buffer length and read out of bounds. Confirmed mechanism: use of an uninitialized/stale value as a length (CWE-457); the OOB read at the consumer is the consequence, not a separate root cause.

For a provider-name length P_r = (65536 - ((16 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert)) mod 65536)) mod 65536 (a value in [0,65535], admitted by every guard in the shown code), rrlen wraps to 0, malloc(0) returns a non-NULL pointer on typical libc, and the snprintf at line 50 receives size arg rrlen-1 == -1 converted to SIZE_MAX, writing P_r+15 bytes into a 0-byte heap allocation (CWE-787; the wrapping size computation is the root cause, CWE-190).

malloc(0) may return a non-NULL unique pointer (glibc behavior), which the NULL check at line 46 admits; the overflow requires this outcome.

limitations: The exact numeric witness depends on sizeof(struct SignedCert), which is not defined in the shown code; the needed length is the symbolic residue (65536 - ((16 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert)) mod 65536)) mod 65536, which exists in [0,65535] for every possible struct size.
On platforms where malloc(0) returns NULL, the path exits at line 48 with return -2 and no overflow occurs.

Unchecked strdup results at lines 6, 7, and 66 could pass NULL into cfg_str2list_insert/cfg_strlist_insert/log_err on allocation failure (potential NULL dereference, CWE-476); this depends on allocation failure and has no attacker-controlled victim-size shown, so it is not confirmed.

verdict.summary: The only security-relevant sink is the array read at line 6. Its index is `s->reg % sizeof(s->edid_blob)`, where the modulus is exactly the byte capacity N of the accessed object and is a size_t operand. Under standard C usual-arithmetic-conversion rules, any integer value of `s->reg` (including negative bit patterns) is converted to an unsigned type before the division on the host LP64 ABI, so the residue — and thus the subscript — lies in [0, N-1]. The maximum admitted index N-1 is strictly below the capacity N, so no out-of-bounds read, off-by-one, injection, crypto, file, authz, or error/status flaw is derivable from the shown code. The unshown declared type and initial value of `s->reg` are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: `I2CDDC(i2c)` is a container_of-style downcast that yields a valid `I2CDDCState *` for the `I2CSlave *` the I2C framework passes to this handler; the shown code contains no check, but nothing in the shown code can produce a NULL or mis-typed pointer.
`sizeof(s->edid_blob)` (size_t) equals the byte capacity N of the array that is subscripted at line 6, per the standard semantics of sizeof applied to that field expression.

On the target ABI, rank(size_t) >= rank(type of `s->reg`), so the usual arithmetic conversions in `s->reg % sizeof(...)` convert the register operand to an unsigned type before the modulo; the residue therefore lies in [0, N-1] for every integer value of `s->reg`.
limitations: The declared type and initial value of `s->reg` are not shown. A negative-index out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) would require `s->reg` to be a signed type with rank greater than size_t's on the host (e.g., a 64-bit signed register on a 32-bit size_t ABI) and to hold a negative value produced outside the shown code; that combination cannot be established from the shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding.

A NULL or invalid `i2c` pointer would be dereferenced at lines 3/6, but NULL cannot be produced by any path in the shown code and the trust invariant for the callback argument is not visible in the shown code.

If `s->reg` is a 32-bit signed int, unbounded sequential reads could eventually overflow the counter (UB) after roughly 2^31 calls; the index remains modulo-bounded and the shown code exposes no attacker-controlled read-count path, so this is a robustness note only.

assumptions: TabPageIdxs is allocated with Columns entries (one per screen column); the shown code's own sibling guard (line 277: mouse_col < Columns) before the same subscript at line 280 establishes the intended valid index domain 0..Columns-1.
mouse_col and mouse_row are OS/terminal-supplied globals (mouse-protocol coordinates); the shown code contains no clamp or trust check for mouse_col on the drag paths.

Preconditions for the sinks are satisfied by normal use: a prior tab-line click sets got_click (line 121) and in_tab_line (line 279), followed by a left-button drag with mod_mask == 0 in the tab-line row.
limitations: The declaration/allocation of TabPageIdxs is outside the shown code; the exact capacity (Columns) is inferred from the sibling guard at line 277 rather than directly observed.

The double-click whitespace-skip loop (while (gc = gchar_pos(&end_visual), VIM_ISWHITE(gc)) inc(&end_visual);) and the cursor-column arithmetic (++VIsual.col; col += (*mb_ptr2len)(ml_get_cursor());) could not be confirmed as out-of-bounds because buffer-line capacities and helper semantics (gchar_pos/inc/find_end_of_word) are not visible in the shown code.
