Operator precedence in 'f != NULL && f->flag & how' (line 12) evaluates as (f != NULL) && (f->flag & how), which is the intended filtering logic.
limitations: Unvalidated index u (residual range [0, UINT_MAX]) is used at fm->hdf[u] (line 6), strchr(fm->hd[u].b, ':') (line 8), and http_hdr_flags(fm->hd[u].b, e) (line 11). If any caller passes u >= the header-array length (e.g., fm->nhd), this is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), but the array capacity is not identifiable from the shown code, so it cannot be confirmed per the boundary-claim standard.
A NULL fm would be dereferenced at lines 6/8/11, but NULL cannot be produced by any path inside the shown code, so it is not a confirmed NULL-dereference finding.

Whether fm->hd[u].b is always NUL-terminated within its storage is not established by the shown code; an unterminated buffer could make the strchr scan at line 8 overrun, but the buffer capacity is not identifiable here.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in reserve_sfa_size(): the fast-path guard (line 11) measures free space against ksize(), the rounded-up slab size, so repeated action reservations can drive next_offset above MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE (e.g., 65536 > 32768). In the growth path, the inner check (MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE - next_offset) < req_size then subtracts two ints into a negative value that is converted to an enormous size_t before comparison with req_size, so the -EMSGSIZE guard is bypassed, a MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE buffer is allocated, and memcpy() copies the full actions_len (up to ~65512) into it, overflowing the heap; the returned pointer at next_offset is likewise past the end of the allocation and is used for a further out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: CWE-787 heap OOB write: the copy length (*sfa)->actions_len can reach ksize(*sfa) - offsetof (e.g., 65512 with a 64 KiB slab), a state admitted by the line 11 guard because it bounds against ksize() rather than MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE, while the destination acts was allocated with new_acts_size = MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE (lines 22-25) and holds only 32 KiB of actions. The -EMSGSIZE guard at line 17 is bypassed for next_offset > MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE because (MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE - next_offset) is a negative int that is converted to a huge size_t before the comparison with req_size (size_t), so the allocation proceeds and memcpy writes up to ~32744 bytes past the requested allocation.

CWE-787 OOB write via returned pointer: next_offset is accumulated by the line 11/line 36 accounting up to ksize(*sfa) (e.g., 65536), exceeding MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE (32768). Because the line 17 guard is defeated for that state (signed subtraction underflow promoted to huge size_t), the new allocation at line 25 is only MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE, so this pointer is ~32768 bytes past the end of the buffer and the caller's write of req_size bytes at it overflows the heap.

assumptions: ksize(*sfa) is the usable slab size and can exceed MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE (a 32 KiB + struct request rounds up to a 64 KiB kmalloc slab), which the shown code itself relies on in lines 11 and 14; workers and callers in the real kernel use nla_alloc_flow_actions() to establish this state.
( *sfa)->actions_len is a u32 accumulator updated only at line 36, and offsetof(struct sw_flow_actions, actions) is small, so next_offset tracks the filled length of the actions area.
MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE is the named 32 KiB kernel constant used at lines 16, 17, and 22; NLA_ALIGN rounds to a 4-byte boundary.
limitations: Extreme attr_len values (near INT_MAX or negative) cause signed overflow UB inside NLA_ALIGN (line 7) and implementation-defined int narrowing of new_acts_size (lines 6/14); those paths would feed a huge size into nla_alloc_flow_actions and fail via IS_ERR, so they were not needed for the confirmed finding and their exact behavior is not further characterized.

The size of the initial *sfa allocation is not shown; the confirmed witness relies on the standard kmalloc/ksize invariant that ksize >= requested size (framework-provided data), which is also the invariant the vulnerable comparison fails to honor.
The discard of memcpy's return value (line 29) and the correct IS_ERR handling (lines 26-27) are not vulnerabilities.
No loops or sentinel-based parsing exist in the shown function, so loop-termination analysis is vacuous here.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML writes one NUL byte one past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-element stack array `line` at line 98 whenever a complete gopher line reaches length TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (guard at 77-79 both admits the boundary and clamps into it), a remotely triggerable CWE-787 OOB write from gopher-server data; additionally, attacker-controlled host/port fields are spliced unescaped into HTML attributes (CWE-79 XSS), and a telnet entry without a port field dereferences NULL at line 225 (CWE-476 DoS).

evidence.reason: inbuf/len are helper parameters with no shown-code cap on len; left = len - (pos - inbuf) (line 69) forwards the full chunk length. For a chunk of TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2 data bytes plus '\n' (gopherState->len = 0), memchr (70) yields llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, which the guard at line 77 admits unchanged (TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE is false); memcpy (96) fills line[0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2], then this subscript writes index TEMP_BUF_SIZE of the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-element stack array declared at line 6 — exactly one byte past capacity (CWE-787 out-of-bounds write). The clamped path (line 79 result TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1) reaches the identical index.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(tmpbuf, TEMP_BUF_SIZE, " %s\n", icon_url, host, gtype, escaped_selector, html_quote(name));
evidence.reason: host is derived from network bytes via line/strchr splitting (lines 115-128) and no shown transformation escapes it; guards at 121 and 126 only test for TAB presence and admit any content. A host value of `x" onmouseover="alert(1)` breaks out of the HREF attribute, and the resulting raw HTML is appended to the StoreEntry at line 331 — CWE-79 attribute-injection/XSS delivered to browsers.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(tmpbuf, TEMP_BUF_SIZE, " %s\n", icon_url, host, rfc1738_escape_unescaped(selector + 5), html_quote(name));
evidence.reason: In the WWW-link branch, host is inserted raw and selector+5 is passed through rfc1738_escape_unescaped (a de-escape, not an HTML filter); both take attacker-controlled bytes from the line buffer, so `"` reaches the HREF attribute unchanged (CWE-79), with no guard on either argument's content.

port = strchr(host, TAB) (line 129) returns NULL when the attacker's gopher line has no TAB after host (e.g. `T\tName\tsel\thost\n`); the if (port) block at 131-153 is skipped, but the GOPHER_TELNET snprintf (223-225) dereferences port here unconditionally — NULL produced inside the shown chain and dereferenced (CWE-476), crashing the proxy.

assumptions: TEMP_BUF_SIZE is a named compile-time constant and LOCAL_ARRAY declares a stack array of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE elements (valid indices 0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1), as evidenced by memset/memcpy at lines 17-18, 96.
inbuf provides `len` readable bytes, the contract the shown code itself enforces via memchr(pos,'\n',left) and memcpy(...,llen) with left,llen <= len.
gopherState->len is initialized to 0 and is maintained in [0, TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1] by the shown code (clamp at 79, increments at 86, resets at 94), so the clamp never produces a negative llen.
The HTML accumulated in outbuf is appended raw to the StoreEntry (line 331) and rendered by client browsers, making injected markup executable.
limitations: The capacity of gopherState->buf is not shown, so whether memcpy at line 85 could overflow it cannot be confirmed from this code (it would be safe if buf has at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE elements).
The OOB write at line 98 is exactly one NUL byte; beyond a guaranteed remote crash, exploitability (targeted corruption of adjacent stack locals) is not demonstrated.
If the unshown caller caps len below TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, the OOB-write witness would be unreachable; no such cap exists in the shown code.
atoi(NULL) is not reachable: the checks at lines 268-269 and 294-295 guarantee that when `result` is non-NULL, strtok produced the earlier tokens too.
xstrdup (156) returning NULL on allocation failure is not attacker-controlled and is treated as out of scope.
The stale byte at line[llen] (NUL placed at llen+1) is a correctness quirk, not a memory-safety issue.

verdict.summary: e1000_send_packet reaches inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count(s, buf) unconditionally (line 12) with no size>=1 or NULL check on buf: size is an unvalidated int parameter (residual [-2^31, 2^31-1]) and the helper reads the frame's first byte (buf[0]) by its name/use. For the admitted value size==0 (line 7's loopback guard constrains only phy_reg), the shown code's own length accounting says the packet is empty, so the 1-byte read is out of bounds relative to that length and can dereference a NULL/too-short buf, letting a guest with control of tx descriptor lengths crash QEMU (host DoS).

evidence.reason: buf (internal-helper parameter, unconstrained residual: any pointer, valid length unknown) and size (int, residual [-2^31, 2^31-1], unchecked) reach this unconditional call on every path; the only guard, line 7, tests s->phy_reg[PHY_CTRL] & MII_CR_LOOPBACK and admits size==0. The callee consumes buf as the transmitted frame's destination-address byte (buf[0]) per its name/use, so the shown code passes a frame it accounts as zero-length to a 1-byte read: 1 byte beyond the frame length the shown code carries, or a NULL/too-short buf dereference. Primary mechanism: CWE-125 out-of-bounds read at line 12.

assumptions: inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count inspects the frame's first byte (buf[0]) to classify broadcast/multicast, as its name/use implies.
buf and size form the packet pointer/length pair supplied by the caller; the shown code performs no validation of either.
limitations: The exact capacity of *buf is not identifiable from the shown code (no allocation or declaration); the fault materializes when the caller supplies buf with fewer than one readable byte (e.g., NULL for an empty frame), which the canonical e1000 transmit path can do.

A negative size forwarded to nc->info->receive / qemu_send_packet (lines 8/10) would be an out-of-domain length, but it is a pure pass-through with no derivation in the shown code and the int-to-size_t conversion occurs only inside unshown callees; not confirmed.
qemu_get_queue(s->nic) (line 6) is dereferenced without a NULL check, but a NULL result is not producible from any shown input/state, so not confirmed.
Return values of receive/qemu_send_packet (lines 8/10) are discarded; no failure state is subsequently used in the shown code, so no error-handling flaw is demonstrable there.

verdict.summary: SProcXkbSelectEvents is the guarded XKB event-swap path: every variable-section read-modify-write (lines 56-57, 60-61) is preceded by a dataLeft capacity check (line 53), out-of-range event bits are rejected with BadValue (lines 49-51), leftover bytes are rejected (line 69), and dataLeft, being req_len*4 - 16 (line 23), is always a multiple of 4, so the size==1 branch's 2-byte guard vs 4-byte consumption can never underflow the unsigned counter or reach an out-of-bounds swap. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: client->req_len is an integer request length in 4-byte words; the shown code multiplies by 4 at line 23, so dataLeft = req_len*4 - SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) is always a multiple of 4 by pure arithmetic.
SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) is 16 bytes (CARD8+CARD8+CARD16*7), a multiple of 4, and REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE (line 6) guarantees req_len*4 >= 16 so dataLeft >= 0.
XkbMapNotifyMask is bit 1; the remaining CARD16 affectWhich bits cover ndx 0..15, so the loop sweeps all possible bits of maskLeft and terminates within 16 iterations.
REQUEST/REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE/swaps/swapl behave per their standard X server definitions: swaps/swapl are in-place read-modify-write on the request buffer.
limitations: In the size==1 branches (XkbBellNotify/XkbActionMessage/XkbCompatMapNotify, lines 44-47, 63-65), the guard at line 53 checks dataLeft >= 2 but the code then consumes 4 bytes (line 66), which would underflow the unsigned dataLeft and allow a later swaps/swapl (lines 56-57, 60-61) to write past the request buffer (CWE-787) if dataLeft could be 2 or 3; that value set is unreachable given the word-aligned arithmetic at line 23, so this is latent robustness debt, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Bits set in affectWhich where selectAll or clear are also set are skipped (lines 29-30), so their arrays are not byte-swapped; whether the not-shown ProcXkbSelectEvents consumes the same layout and whether any unswapped data is interpreted as host-order values cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
ErrorF at lines 70-71 passes an unsigned dataLeft to a %d format specifier; this is cosmetic/type-mismatch only and has no security impact.

verdict.summary: In get_recurse_data_length, the switch arms read bytecode fields at offsets 1 or more past the dispatched opcode (cc[1] at lines 164/176, GET(cc,1) and *alternative at lines 88-89, GET2 at line 73) without any check against ccend; the only guard, 'while (cc < ccend)' (line 20), bounds solely the first byte of each instruction. For admitted internal-helper inputs whose contents are unconstrained by the shown code (e.g. a one-unit region containing OP_MARK/OP_COND), element index of cc[1] reaches the region capacity and the OP_COND link-derived pointer exits the region, causing confirmed out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125) during JIT compilation.

evidence.reason: cc/ccend are internal-helper parameters; the only guard in the shown code is 'while (cc < ccend)' (line 20), which admits any region of length >= 1 and does not bound reads after the dispatch byte. Witness: region [start, start+1) containing OP_MARK is admitted (start < start+1), the switch at line 23 selects the OP_MARK arm (lines 152-164), and line 164 reads cc[1] at element index 1, which equals the region capacity (ccend - cc = 1) — an out-of-bounds read by 1 unit (CWE-125). The identical sink form exists at line 176 for OP_SKIP_ARG.

Same unguarded read as line 164: an admitted one-unit region containing OP_SKIP_ARG reaches line 176 via the switch dispatch (line 23) with no length check on cc[1], reading element index 1 of a 1-unit region (index == capacity), an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) for input in the residual range left by the line 20 guard.

GET(cc,1) reads LINK_SIZE bytes at offsets 1..LINK_SIZE from the dispatched opcode; the line 20 guard bounds only unit 0, so an admitted region of length 1 whose byte is OP_COND makes this read access indexes 1..LINK_SIZE, all >= the region capacity — an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The 16-bit/32-bit code-unit variants only widen the read; the claim holds in units for any width.

alternative is derived as cc + GET(cc,1) at line 88 from stream data that the shown code leaves fully unconstrained; no check confines alternative to [cc, ccend). A link value larger than the remaining region length (a member of the residual range admitted by line 20) makes *alternative dereference memory outside the walked region — an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) at the JIT-compile stage.

assumptions: cc/ccend delimit the instruction stream walked by this function; the shown code's own enforceable bound is the line 20 loop condition and the (debug-only) line 199 assertion, so the region capacity used for boundary claims is ccend - cc.

The bytecode content fields (opcodes, link values, name-length bytes, IMM2 values) read via *cc, cc[1], GET, and GET2 are treated as internal-helper input with the residual range left unconstrained by the shown code.
LINK_SIZE and IMM2_SIZE are positive constants; OOB claims are stated in code units so they hold for 8/16/32-bit PCRE2_UCHAR builds.
No well-formedness invariant of the stream is assumed, because none appears in the shown code.
limitations: The OP_KET arm (lines 41-49) reading PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1) and jumping via cc += PRIVATE_DATA(cc + 1) is in the same OOB family, but PRIVATE_DATA's implementation and the capacity of its backing table are not in the shown code, and the path requires the opaque guard PRIVATE_DATA(cc) != 0 (line 42); a concrete witness cannot be expressed from the shown code alone.
get_class_iterator_size(cc + size) (line 148) is gated only by PRIVATE_DATA(cc) != 0 (line 147), so its reachability/OOB is unconfirmed.

common->optimized_cbracket[GET2(cc, 1 + LINK_SIZE)] (line 73) — the GET2 stream read itself is the confirmed OOB-class sink; whether a 16-bit group number can also index outside optimized_cbracket[] cannot be checked because the array's capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.
next_opcode returning NULL (lines 194-195) would reach *cc at line 23 in release builds only if the stream contains an opcode outside next_opcode's domain; that production path is not shown.

Non-termination candidates — OP_XCLASS with GET(cc,1) == 0 making cc += size (line 149) stationary, or a negative PRIVATE_DATA jump (line 46) — require compiler-internal table/stream values the shown code does not establish.

Practical triggering through a real regex pattern (pattern -> bytecode generator is outside the shown code) is not demonstrated here; this is the historical PCRE2 JIT walker OOB-read class, and the shown code contains no check that would stop the reads.
Integer overflow of the int length counter (lines 4, 44, 63, 70, 80, 96, 105, 114, 123, 129, 135, 202-210) needs a stream size not bounded by the shown code and is not claimed.
SLJIT_ASSERT failures (lines 26, 64, 156, 180, 195, 199) are debug-only aborts and are not treated as exploitable.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in apprentice_load: the filearr capacity growth maxfiles = (maxfiles + 1) * 2 wraps a 32-bit size_t after 2^31-1 regular directory entries, so mlen wraps to 0 and the subsequent filearr[files++] store writes far past a 0-byte allocation (CWE-787, with CWE-190 as the corrupting integer overflow).

evidence.reason: With a 32-bit size_t and files == maxfiles == 2147483646 (admitted by the equality guard files >= maxfiles at line 52), (2147483646 + 1) * 2 = 2^32 wraps to 0, so mlen = 0; the CWE-190 wrap corrupts the allocation size consumed by erealloc at line 56-57, producing the undersized capacity that line 64 then indexes out of bounds (CWE-787).

Sink store at index files: after the line 54-55 size_t wrap, the erealloc'ed buffer has 0-byte capacity while files == 2147483646, so this char* write exceeds capacity by 2147483646 elements — a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The index is the unbounded, attacker-reachable regular-file count from the readdir loop (lines 41, 49), which the shown code never caps.

assumptions: size_t is 32-bit (ILP32/LP32) for the wrap at maxfiles = 2^31 - 2; on LP64 the same wrap would require ~2^63 entries.
PHP allocators (erealloc/emalloc family) return a non-NULL minimal block for size 0 and abort on genuine OOM, so the NULL check at line 56-57 does not fire for mlen == 0.
php_stream_readdir returns each entry once, yields a NUL-terminated d_name without '/', and returns NULL at end-of-directory.
limitations: Exploitation requires ~2^31 regular files in one directory; OS/filesystem limits make this practically unreachable, which is why severity is medium despite the confirmed arithmetic.
On LP64 builds the maxfiles growth cannot wrap at any feasible entry count, so the finding is platform-dependent.

The line 68 processing loop uses uint32_t i: if files exceeded 2^32 on LP64, i would wrap to 0, causing repeated load_1/efree on filearr[0] (infinite loop/double free); needs >4e9 entries, not confirmed reachable.
filearr is leaked if snprintf fails at line 42 after entries were collected (lines 42-48); a single-shot leak without attacker-controlled volume, no CWE.

Defects inside unshown helpers (load_1, set_text_binary, set_last_default, coalesce_entries, magic_entry_free), including a possible NULL mset[j].me[i].mp at line 81, cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
stat (line 49) followed by load_1 (line 69) is a TOCTOU window on directory entries, but no security impact is demonstrable within the shown code.

verdict.summary: unsquashfs_opendir reads the directory table at an attacker-controlled offset `bytes` with no bounds check against the table's actual size: `bytes` is derived from `lookup_entry` (only `-1` excluded, line 44) plus `(*i)->offset` (line 48), and the only loop bound `size` (line 49) is itself computed from attacker-controlled inode data, so a crafted filesystem drives `directory_table + bytes` far past the end of the allocated table at lines 52, 66, and 76-77, yielding an unbounded heap out-of-bounds read (crash / heap contents disclosure).

evidence.reason: `bytes` carries the residual range 'any long long except -1' from `lookup_entry` (line 42, guard at 44 excludes only -1) plus the unconstrained `(*i)->offset` (line 48). The only guard on the path, `while(bytes < size)` (line 51), admits every value below `size`, and `size` (line 49) is itself attacker-derived from `(*i)->data`. No check bounds `bytes` against the directory table's allocation, so for e.g. `(*i)->data = 0x40000000` with `bytes` inside the table at loop start, `directory_table + bytes` walks past the table end and this read becomes an out-of-bounds read of the heap buffer (CWE-125).

Same attacker-derived `bytes` (lines 42, 48; only guard on the path is the attacker-computed `bytes < size` from lines 49 and 51) is used to read `sizeof(*dire)` bytes from `directory_table`. Once `bytes` exceeds the table allocation — reachable by choosing a large `(*i)->data` so `size` is huge — this performs an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125).

The source address `directory_table + bytes` uses the same unconstrained `bytes` as above; the guard at line 71 only constrains the copy length (`dire->size + 1` in 1..SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN), not the source offset. With `size` (line 49) driven arbitrarily large via `(*i)->data`, `bytes` passes `while(bytes < size)` far past the table end, so the memcpy reads out of bounds from the heap buffer (CWE-125).

assumptions: `directory_table` is the in-memory copy of the on-disk directory table backed by an allocation of finite size established outside the shown code; that exact capacity is not visible in the snippet, so the precise excess cannot be stated, only that reads continue unbounded past it.
`SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_HEADER`/`SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_ENTRY` read `sizeof(dirh)`/`sizeof(*dire)` bytes from the pointer argument, as implied by their destination-object sizes.
limitations: The exact OOB excess (index minus directory-table capacity) is not quantifiable because the table's allocation size is not declared in the shown code.
NULL dereference of `*i` after `read_inode` (lines 17, 25-29) is not confirmed: no NULL-producing path for `read_inode` is visible in the shown code.

`strcpy` into `dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name` (line 90) cannot be confirmed as a buffer overflow because the capacity of `dir_ent.name` is not shown; the copied string is at most `SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN` bytes due to the line 71 guard.

`lookup_entry` returning negative values other than `-1` (lines 42, 48-49) could feed odd `bytes`/`size` values, but the callee's return-value contract is not visible, so no separate finding is claimed.

`realloc` size arithmetic `(dir->dir_count + DIR_ENT_SIZE) * sizeof(struct dir_ent)` (lines 83-84) and the 32-bit wrap of `start` (line 41) are only DoS-scale/unquantifiable given attacker-controlled volumes and are not independently confirmed memory-corruption root causes.

The unbounded iteration count of `while(bytes < size)` (line 51) terminates (bytes strictly increases) and is therefore not a hang finding; its security impact is the out-of-bounds read reported above.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir copies a directory entry name with an untrusted length: the only guard (line 81) rejects dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN but enforces no lower bound, so an image-supplied negative size (e.g., 0xFFFE = -2 as signed short) is admitted; dire->size + 1 = -1 is widened to a ~2^64-byte size_t at the memcpy on lines 86-87, overflowing the fixed stack buffer declared on line 5 (attacker-controlled bytes written onto the stack, source over-read) — stack buffer overflow (CWE-121) driven by the signed-to-unsigned length conversion (CWE-195), resulting in memory corruption and crash/DoS.

evidence.reason: dire->size originates from image bytes copied at lines 72-77 (swap path preserves the 16-bit value). The guard at line 81 (dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) admits every value below 256 including negatives, i.e., it leaves the lower bound completely unconstrained; with the on-disk field's signed 16-bit semantics, size = 0xFFFE (-2) passes (admitted by 64 since dir_count=1 <= SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, and by 50 with data >= 1). dire->size + 1 = -1 is then converted to size_t at the memcpy length parameter (2^64-1/2^32-1), so the copy writes attacker-controlled bytes far past dire->name inside the fixed stack buffer of capacity sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_2)+SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1 (line 5) and over-reads directory_table — fixed-stack buffer overflow (CWE-121) caused by the negative-to-size_t length conversion (CWE-195). The finding stands only under the signed-type assumption; if the member is unsigned the copy is bounded to 1..256 and fits the buffer.

assumptions: squashfs_dir_entry_2.size is a signed 16-bit integer (short int), matching the SquashFS v2.0 legacy on-disk entry layout implied by the _2 structs and SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_ENTRY_2; the type is not declared in the shown snippet.
SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN = 256, so guard 81 admits exactly 0..255 for a non-negative field, bounding a benign copy to 1..256 bytes.
SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT = 256 bounds dir_count per header after guard 64; DIR_ENT_SIZE >= 1.
limitations: The negative-size finding collapses if dire->size is unsigned in the actual build, because the guard then restricts the memcpy length to 1..256 which fits the stack buffer on line 5; the signedness is not declared in the shown code (confidence 0.6).

Out-of-bounds reads of directory_table (lines 53, 56, 72-77, 86) driven by attacker-inflated (*i)->data / (*i)->offset (lines 47-48) are unquantifiable because directory_table's capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.
NULL dereference of *i is unconfirmed: read_inode (line 17) is not shown, so NULL producibility cannot be established.

Integer overflow of the realloc size (lines 93-94) requires ~millions of directory entries and a 32-bit build; otherwise directory growth is attacker-volume-scaled DoS only (allocation failure exits).
TRACE() at lines 89-91 passes image-controlled dire->name containing embedded control characters to a %s format (log injection), but TRACE is a debug macro without an established security-log sink.
Integer wrap in bytes/size (lines 47-48) can only skip or extend the directory parse; extension beyond directory_table is covered by the capacity limitation above.

verdict.summary: inflate() dereferences state->head unconditionally at line 142 in the gzip EXTRA case before the NULL checks at lines 143-144, so decompressing a crafted gzip stream that sets the FEXTRA flag with a nonzero extra length causes a NULL pointer dereference (crash/DoS, CWE-476) whenever the caller has not installed a header struct (state->head == Z_NULL, the default).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled gzip header bytes set state->flags (line 85, FLG=0x04 -> flags & 0x0400 admitted by the FLAGS guards at lines 86/91) and state->length (line 126, EXLEN >= 1), and EXTRA executes the statement when copy != 0 (lines 139-141), i.e. length >= 1 and have >= 1. state->head has residual range {Z_NULL, non-NULL} in the shown code (guarded as possibly NULL at lines 52, 96, 105, 114, 127, 133, 143); the NULL check at line 143 runs only after this dereference, so head == Z_NULL (the default when inflateGetHeader was not called) is dereferenced at line 142: NULL pointer dereference, CWE-476, leading to a crash on attacker-supplied input.

assumptions: GUNZIP is compiled in and the caller configured gzip decoding (state->wrap & 2), which reaches the FLAGS/EXTRA path via the magic check at line 43.
LOAD()/RESTORE() and the NEEDBITS/BITS/DROPBITS/PULLBYTE macros behave as standard zlib bit-buffer helpers; inflateStateCheck passes for a valid stream.
state->head is Z_NULL by default when the application does not call inflateGetHeader, a value the shown code explicitly accommodates at every other use.
limitations: No heap overflow via the gzip extra field is confirmed: the len < state->head->extra_max check (line 145) and the min-length selection (lines 146-148) keep the zmemcpy within the caller-declared buffer when head is non-NULL.
Match/window copy bounds (MATCH case) rely on default state->sane == 1 and on updatewindow maintaining whave <= wsize; neither is established in the shown code, so no window OOB claim is made.
Correctness of the decode tables (LENLENS/CODELENS/LEN/DIST) depends on the not-shown inflate_table/fixedtables semantics; no shown-code boundary violation was found in the table-building loops.
Decompression-bomb resource exhaustion is inherent to the inflate API contract and not bounded by the shown code.

verdict.summary: In squashfs_opendir, dire->size is a signed short parsed from the filesystem image. The guard if(dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) (line 71) admits all negative values, so a crafted image with dire->size == -2 makes dire->size + 1 == -1, which memcpy converts to SIZE_MAX (2^64-1). The memcpy at lines 76-77 then overruns the stack buffer 'buffer' (declared at lines 5-6) and reads out of bounds from directory_table: a signed-to-unsigned length conversion (CWE-195) causing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), reachable with dir_count=1 and (*i)->data=4.

evidence.reason: dire->size is a signed short loaded from the image at line 66; the only guard (line 71) has admitted set [-32768, 255] because it rejects only values >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, so negative sizes pass. Witness dire->size = -2 (image bytes 0xFFFE): dire->size + 1 = -1 (int) converts to size_t 2^64-1 as the memcpy length, which is out of domain for the destination 'buffer' declared at lines 5-6 (capacity sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1, with at most SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1 bytes remaining at dire->name), producing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and out-of-bounds read from directory_table. The path is admitted by every prior guard: (*i)->data = 4 passes line 32 and makes size = bytes + 1 so line 51 holds; dirh.count = 0 gives dir_count = 1 which passes line 60. Root cause is the signed-to-unsigned conversion of the negative length (CWE-195).

assumptions: struct squashfs_dir_entry::size is a signed short (per squashfs_fs.h used by this build); SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN = 256; SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT = 256; memcpy's third argument is size_t.

The parser consumes a fully attacker-crafted squashfs image, so lookup_entry can be made to return a non-(-1) block offset and the directory block bytes (including the entry size field) are attacker-chosen.
Line numbers count the shown snippet from line 1 (the function signature).
limitations: Out-of-bounds read of directory_table at lines 52, 66, 76 for large bytes is not reported as a standalone finding because the directory_table capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.

Potential integer overflow of (dir->dir_count + DIR_ENT_SIZE) * sizeof(struct dir_ent) at lines 90-91 requires roughly 2^31 directory entries (multi-GB image) and is pre-empted by the line 76 overflow; not a demonstrated reachable witness.
Dereference of *i after read_inode at lines 25-30 without a NULL check cannot be confirmed because read_inode's failure behavior is outside the shown code.
Narrowing long long to int for size at line 49 can truncate, but only shortens the loop (early exit); no corrupted value reaches a sink.

Negative bytes advance at line 103 can make the outer loop non-terminating for admitted negative sizes, but the memcpy at line 76 faults first for size <= -2, so this is dominated and not independently demonstrated.
The null-terminator write at line 78 with a negative index corrupts only bytes inside 'buffer' (within the struct's storage); not an out-of-bounds write of the buffer object.
Inode allocated by read_inode is not freed on the corrupted path (lines 109-112); single-shot leak with no attacker-controlled volume inside the shown code.

verdict.summary: reserve_sfa_size never constrains the signed int attr_len; NLA_ALIGN of a negative value at line 7 converts it to size_t 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC, and line 36 wraps the u32 actions_len to 0xFFFFFFFC (4294967292). A subsequent growth-triggering reserve (e.g. attr_len=244 after attr_len=-4) reaches line 29 memcpy(acts->actions, (*sfa)->actions, (*sfa)->actions_len) with a ~4 GiB length, causing a heap out-of-bounds read and write (CWE-787), rooted in the signed-to-unsigned conversion (CWE-195).

evidence.reason: Primary sink. The memcpy length is the u32 (*sfa)->actions_len, which the shown code corrupts to 0xFFFFFFFC via line 36 (attrs_seq: attr_len=-4 → req_size=0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC at line 7 → +0 mod 2^32). On the next call with attr_len=244 the guard at line 11 admits the growth path (244 <= ksize(256)-20 = 236 fails), the cap check at line 16 is skipped (new_acts_size=512 <= MAX), and memcpy copies 4,294,967,292 bytes out of a ~256-byte source object into a ~536-byte destination object: heap OOB read and OOB write (CWE-787).

Corruption step: req_size holds size_t 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC (derived from the unconstrained negative attr_len at line 7), and adding it into the u32 actions_len wraps it to 4294967292. This corrupted counter is later consumed as the memcpy length at line 29. The increment has no upper-bound check and the parameter's residual range (full int per Phase 1) admits the triggering value.

Root conversion: attr_len is int; NLA_ALIGN(-4) = -4 as int, and the implicit conversion to size_t yields 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC. The shown code imposes no constraint on attr_len before this conversion, making this a signed-to-unsigned conversion of a negative value into a huge size (CWE-195) that is the independent root cause of the later u32 wraparound and the oversized memcpy at line 29.

assumptions: attr_len is classified per Phase 1 as an internal-helper parameter; the shown code imposes no constraint, so the analyzed residual range is the full int range.

Fresh flow-actions state before the two calls: (*sfa)->actions_len = 0 and a modest initial object (example ksize=96), matching standard creation; the witness holds for any initial ksize whose doubled allocation is below the MAX cap.
offsetof(struct sw_flow_actions, actions) is a small constant (e.g., 24 for a 16-byte rcu_head plus two u32); the failure does not depend on its exact value.
MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE is the module constant (32*1024); the witness values (192, 512, 244) are far below it, so the result holds for any cap >= 512.
limitations: In the real OVS kernel, callers pass nla_len() >= 0 after netlink attribute validation, which would make the negative attr_len input unreachable; that caller-side invariant is not present in the shown code, so attacker reachability of the negative value is not established here.

The MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE cap can be exceeded by roughly 2x through the ksize() fast path when the allocator rounds the object up past the requested size, letting actions_len approach 64 KiB; this is not confirmable as memory-unsafe from the shown code because the allocator's rounded ksize is not observable in the shown code and any effect would be in unshown consumers.

Truncation of the size_t expressions (next_offset + req_size, ksize(*sfa)*2) into the int new_acts_size at line 14 cannot be triggered with in-range nonnegative attr_len since all values stay far below INT_MAX.
A NULL dereference of *sfa could not be produced by any path inside the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmed within the shown code. The only dangerous-looking mechanism, unbounded case-fold alternative expansion, is capped by the visible guard at lines 94-95: alt_num *= (n + 1); if (alt_num > THRESHOLD_CASE_FOLD_ALT_FOR_EXPANSION) break;. Since the else path guarantees n >= 1 via the guards at lines 27 and 34, alt_num grows by a factor >= 2 and breaks at the first product > 8, bounding consecutive expansion steps to at most 3 (alt_num 2, 4, 8) and steering the remaining input into the bounded remainder block at lines 135-159. All allocation results are NULL-checked before use, and the local index/size arithmetic (p += len at line 132, byte-range copies at lines 79 and 87) cannot be shown to go out of domain; the remaining stack-exhaustion, non-termination, and size-contract concerns depend on callee bodies and encoder contracts not present in the shown code and are recorded as limitations with no CWE attached.

assumptions: onig_node_list_add returns NULL without linking its argument on allocation failure, and onig_node_new_str / onig_node_str_cat / swap_node / onig_node_free have their standard library semantics (copy bytes, append bytes, swap node content, recursively free a tree).
The encoders reached at lines 25-26 and 62-63 honor their API contracts: n does not exceed the items array size (line 10) and fold_len does not exceed sizeof(buf) (line 11).
enclen (line 32) returns a positive byte length for every position the regex parser admitted, so p += len (line 132) strictly advances towards end.
The string node content [sn->s, sn->end) consists of complete encoded characters, as it was produced by the regex parser.
limitations: Potential stack-exhaustion DoS: the remainder at line 138 (expand_case_fold_make_rem_string, body not shown) could recurse back into this function on the remaining input after the line 95 break; with an input of threshold-triggering characters this would create recursion depth scaling with input length. The recursion is not visible in the shown code and the callee is not a standard operation, so this is unconfirmed and carries no CWE.

Non-termination claim: if an encoder's enclen returned 0, line 132 would not advance p and the while loop (line 24) would not terminate. No witness is derivable from the shown code because the encoder bodies are not shown.
OOB-read claim: the copies at lines 79 and 87 trust fold_len <= MAXLEN / len <= end - p from unshown encoder and parser invariants; a concrete overshoot cannot be demonstrated from the shown code.

Stack-array overflow of items (line 10) or buf (line 11) would require an encoder to exceed its API bounds; that contract is not stated in the shown code and is not attacker-selectable independently of the encoder.

Minor error-handling note: line 139 forwards any failure of expand_case_fold_make_rem_string to mem_err (line 168), masking the specific error code with ONIGERR_MEMORY; the function still returns failure, so this has no security impact.

verdict.summary: add_mtab writes devname, mountpoint, fstype, and the user-name-derived options string verbatim into the mount-table file via addmntent (line 86) with no content validation or escaping; a value containing a newline or field separators injects forged mount records into a root-owned control file consumed by privileged mount/umount tooling (CWE-74).

evidence.reason: devname (line 58), mountpoint (59), fstype (60), and mount_user (via strlcat at 79-81) are internal-helper parameters with residual range 'arbitrary C string' — the shown code imposes no length or content constraint on any of them. They are assigned unconditionally into the mntent struct and passed to the addmntent sink, which emits the fields as whitespace-separated text. The only guards on the path (pmntfile non-NULL at 51, mnt_opts non-NULL at 62) do not constrain string content, and line 86 executes for every admitted value. A witness such as devname="/dev/sda1\nJUNK /junk ext4 0 0\n" passes every guard and terminates the current mtab record early, injecting a forged mount record into the root-owned file opened at line 50 (MOUNTED) — improper neutralization of special elements in output used by a downstream component (CWE-74).

assumptions: MOUNTED names a root-owned mount-table file (e.g., /etc/mtab) opened for append at line 50; addmntent formats mnt_fsname/mnt_dir/mnt_type/mnt_opts as text fields per its standard contract.
getusername(uid) returns either NULL or a NUL-terminated string (only the NULL case is guarded at line 78).
SAFE_FREE is a NULL-safe free macro; EX_FILEIO is a nonzero error code.
The process is privileged (setreuid to effective uid and toggle_dac_capability imply a setuid-root mount helper context).
limitations: End-to-end attacker reachability of devname/mountpoint/fstype is not provable from this snippet alone: they are internal-helper parameters and the shown code never parses argv/env; no protective check exists in the shown code either, so the residual range remains fully unconstrained.
mount_user (lines 10-12, 79-81) is derived from the password/NSS database for the real uid, not directly chosen by the caller; newline-bearing usernames would require exotic NSS/LDAP configurations.

calloc failure at line 61 passes a NULL mnt_opts to addmntent at line 86; allocation size is a compile-time constant (no attacker control), and NULL handling depends on unshown callee internals — not a confirmed NULL deref.

Lock lifecycle: atexit(unlock_mtab) at line 42 is registered before lock acquisition (43); the lock-failure path (47) exits with an unlock-in-atexit of a lock never held, and the success path unlocks twice (line 92 plus atexit). Whether this can break another process's lock depends on unshown lock_mtab/unlock_mtab internals.

Discarded return values (endmntent at 91, toggle_dac_capability(1,0) at 95, restore sigprocmask at 96) are robustness concerns whose impact would land in the unshown caller; e.g., failure of line 95 would leave DAC override raised at return.

verdict.summary: In win_redr_status(), when get_trans_bufname() fills NameBuff to capacity (STRLEN == MAXPATHL-1), the status-marker code overwrites the trailing NUL at line 54 and sets len == MAXPATHL; the following vim_snprintf calls get size 0 and write nothing, and lines 58/64/74/79 then call STRLEN(p + len) on the one-past-the-end pointer, causing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) during statusline redraw that can crash or leak memory.

Line 73's vim_snprintf then has size MAXPATHL-len == 0 and writes nothing under standard snprintf size-0 semantics, so line 74 reads at index MAXPATHL, exactly one past the MAXPATHL-capacity object identified by the MAXPATHL-len size arguments at lines 57/63/73/78 — an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

vim_snprintf follows standard snprintf size-0 behavior (writes nothing when size is 0).

limitations: The witness L == MAXPATHL-1 is a member of the residual range but depends on get_trans_bufname() (not shown) producing a name that fills NameBuff; no single concrete filename can be demonstrated inside the shown code, so confidence is range-based (0.5-0.7).

A potential out-of-bounds write via MAXPATHL - len underflowing to a huge size_t (CWE-681/787) depends on STRLEN(p+len) returning at least one garbage byte, which is not derivable within the shown code.

If vim_snprintf with size 0 wrote a terminating NUL at p+MAXPATHL (non-standard behavior), that would be a one-byte OOB write, but the callee body is not shown; the OOB-read mechanism is the confirmed one.
The same buffer-full trigger also makes mb_string2cells/loop reads (lines 95, 99) and screen_puts (line 118) read past the unterminated string, but these are not reported as separate findings.
The '*'='<' truncation branches (lines 103-108 and 111-116) are guarded and keep their writes in-bounds; no finding.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code. The suspicious derivations — the pointer-difference casts at lines 53 and 68, the MAXCOL+1 arithmetic at line 55, the end-1 arithmetic at line 69, and the line-number addition at line 47 — either require invariants about rex.input/rex.line that are established only outside the shown code (so no in-code witness exists), or, where a witness shape exists (bot.col == MAXCOL with exclusive selection), the overflow result feeds only a comparison whose failure mode is over-rejection with no memory-safety, injection, or authorization impact. All are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: linenr_T is a signed long (64-bit on LP64) and colnr_T is a signed 32-bit int with MAXCOL == 0x7fffffff, per Vim's standard typedefs; these widths are not defined in the shown code.
getvvcol() computes virtual columns from a position and win_linetabsize() scans line[0..len) stopping at NUL; their bodies are not shown, but their name-implied semantics are standard.

The regex engine that calls reg_match_visual is assumed to keep rex.line pointing at the start of the current matched line and rex.input within that line's storage (or one past its NUL); this invariant is not restated in the shown code.
limitations: Potential OOB read at line 68: win_linetabsize(wp, rex.line, (colnr_T)(rex.input - rex.line)) receives a length the shown code never bounds. A negative length makes the callee loop not execute; a length exceeding the NUL-terminated storage reachable from rex.line would read past it. No witness for rex.input/rex.line violating the engine invariant is derivable from the shown code, so this is unconfirmed.

Negative column at line 53: (colnr_T)(rex.input - rex.line) with rex.input < rex.line yields a negative col; both guards at lines 54-55 then reject the match, so no unsafe operation follows, and the precondition cannot be produced from the shown code.

Signed overflow at line 55: bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e') with bot.col == MAXCOL and exclusive selection overflows colnr_T (UB; wraps to INT_MIN in practice), causing every match to be rejected. This is a correctness concern only — the result feeds a comparison, not a memory sink — and whether bot.col can actually equal MAXCOL in characterwise exclusive selection is not established by the shown code.
Underflow at line 69: end - (*p_sel == 'e') with end == 0 and exclusive selection yields -1, causing only rejection of all matches; no security impact.
Line-number addition at line 47 (rex.lnum + rex.reg_firstlnum) could overflow linenr_T only with both operands near the type maximum, which the shown code cannot produce.

Window/buffer consistency: wp is taken from rex.reg_win without an in-code check that it displays curbuf, so getvvcol() at lines 60-61 could index a different buffer's line table by lnum if the engine violated its invariant that rex.reg_win->w_buffer == rex.reg_buf == curbuf; that invariant is outside the shown code, so this is unconfirmed.
The dangerous-looking length/pointer paths are not asserted safe by an identified in-code guard; they are simply not confirmable as vulnerabilities from the shown code alone.

verdict.summary: add_mtab writes the caller-supplied mount fields (devname, mountpoint, fstype) and the non-escaped user name (mount_user) into the system mount table via addmntent at line 104 with no character filtering or escaping: embedded spaces, tabs, newlines, or commas survive verbatim (strlcat only bounds length) and can forge extra mtab entries or inject options into the entry that privileged mount/umount-style consumers parse (mtab injection).

evidence.reason: Sink statement: addmntent writes the already-populated struct mntent to MOUNTED. devname (L76), mountpoint (L77), and fstype (L78) are internal-helper parameters that the shown code leaves fully unconstrained (no length cap, no character filter, no escaping of space/tab/newline/comma), and mount_user is copied verbatim into mnt_opts at L98-99. There is no transformation between these assignments and line 104 that removes or quotes separator characters, so a value such as mountpoint="/mnt/x\nFORGED /dev/sda1 ext4 rw 0 0" (a member of every guard's admitted path set on this flow) causes addmntent, which separates fields by spaces and terminates the entry with a newline, to write a forged line/fields into /etc/mtab. Confirmed mechanism: CWE-74 improper neutralization of special elements in output fed to the mtab format consumed by downstream privileged tools.

Distinct option-embedding sink: mount_user is the unvalidated result of getusername(uid) (L13) with a residual range of arbitrary strings; strlcat performs no escaping, so a comma or newline in the user name survives into the mnt_opts field after the literal ",user=" (L97) and reaches addmntent at L104, injecting an option or terminating/breaking the mtab entry line. Same confirmed CWE-74 mechanism (failure to neutralize special elements before the mtab output is written).

assumptions: Constants (EX_FILEIO, MOUNTED, MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN, MS_*) and helpers (getusername, lock_mtab/unlock_mtab, my_endmntent, toggle_dac_capability, SAFE_FREE) are defined outside the shown code.
addmntent follows its standard semantics: fields written space-separated, entry terminated by a newline, with no escaping.
The shown snippet ends at the sigprocmask restore without a visible final return; a trailing 'return rc;' is assumed as a truncation artifact.
MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN is a positive constant, so all strlcat calls are bound-safe regardless of its exact value.
limitations: NULL deref candidate: if calloc at L79 returns NULL, addmntent at L104 is still called with mountent.mnt_opts == NULL; excluded from findings because the allocation size is a fixed constant (MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN), not attacker-controlled, so the failure is an unchecked fixed-size OOM case.

Actual attacker control over devname/mountpoint/fstype depends on callers not shown; they are classified as internal-helper parameters whose residual range the shown code leaves fully unconstrained, per the input-classification rules.

Ignored strlcat return values can only cause silent truncation of option text (no security impact), and the discarded returns on ftruncate (L107), toggle_dac_capability (L118), and the restore sigprocmask (L119) have no demonstrated exploitable consequence inside the shown code.
Whether a forged mtab entry escalates further depends on downstream mount/umount parsing behavior, which is not part of the shown code; the confirmed mechanism is the injection itself.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds heap read in mobi_parse_index_entry: control_bytes is set to buf->data + buf->offset (L41) and advanced by control_bytes++ (L62) for every tag with control_byte == 1, with no check against buf->maxlen — the buffer bound the code itself enforces at L16. tagx->tags_count is unconstrained by the shown code, so a crafted file can set tags_count = M with the first M-1 tags control_byte == 1 and the last non-control; the loop then executes L66 with control_bytes[0] reading buf->data[M], one byte past the end (index == capacity), a CWE-125 heap OOB read causing a crash (DoS) or disclosure of adjacent heap bytes.

evidence.reason: control_bytes = buf->data + buf->offset (L41) is advanced by control_bytes++ (L62) per tag with control_byte == 1, with no bound relative to buf->maxlen, the capacity the shown code itself uses as the valid-content bound (L15/L16/L145). tagx->tags_count is left unconstrained by the shown code, so a file-derived witness sets tags_count = M, tags[0..M-2].control_byte = 1, tags[M-1].control_byte != 1, entry_length = 1 and label_length = 0 (all guards at L10, L16, L22 admit this path; ptagx allocation of M*12 bytes at L52 succeeds). After M-1 advances, the L60 loop reaches the non-control tag and line 66 dereferences control_bytes[0] at buf->data + M, i.e., index == capacity — a one-byte OOB heap read (CWE-125), yielding crash/DoS or heap information disclosure.

mobi_buffer_setpos (L8) assigns buf->offset = idxt.offsets[curr_number] (standard set-position semantics), which makes the L16 sum equal offsets[curr_number+1] exactly.

INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX >= 256 would make the label path safe only if the label helpers also honor it; neither is shown.

OOB reads of idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] (L7) and tagx->tags[i] (L61/L66/L89/L90) cannot be confirmed because those arrays' capacities are not identifiable in the shown code.
Discarded return values of mobi_buffer_setpos (L8) and mobi_buffer_seek (L42) are noted; no error-handling flaw is confirmed without the helpers' failure semantics.

All value/decoding loops (L83-L86, L111, L120) are bounded and terminate; no hang or sentinel-overrun is confirmed.

Use-after-free of nfc_dev/ndev would depend on unshown callee behavior of nci_unregister_device freeing those objects before line 6; the shown code's own deferred-free ordering (line 14) contradicts that, so the claim is unconfirmed.

No attacker-controlled input, loop, index, size, or arithmetic exists in the shown code, so no memory-safety, injection, or resource-exhaustion vulnerability can be demonstrated from the shown code alone.

verdict.summary: The shown code is the hardened Expat addBinding: every input-derived size is bounded by explicit guards (len <= INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE before len+EXPAND_SPARE arithmetic at lines 69/97; a 32-bit size_t guard at 78/105; copy length len into capacity len+EXPAND_SPARE at 119; guarded constant-array reads at 46/50 with short-circuit len > xmlLen/xmlnsLen; allocation NULL checks at 85/93/112). No reachable out-of-bounds, integer-overflow, injection, or error-handling flaw is demonstrable from the shown code.

assumptions: uri is a NUL-terminated XML_Char string; the loop at 45-52 and memcpy at 119 consume it under standard C string semantics.
prefix->name is NUL-terminated, which is required for the short-circuit reads at lines 33-41.
EXPAND_SPARE is the small positive Expat constant (4); the observed bound INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE then admits len <= INT_MAX-4.
