evidence.reason: arg.length and arg.chars originate from table-file argument tokens read at lines 130-131 (entry-point input; residual range unconstrained by the shown code, up to the MAXSTRING capacity named at line 157). The sibling definition-copy branch is guarded by line 157, which admits only writes with linelen <= MAXSTRING-1 and thus fixes tmpFile.line's capacity at MAXSTRING; the substitution branch (166-174) applies no equivalent check. Witness accepted by every guard: macro name matches (111), exactly one argument (129/135), prefix of L=2 chars written at indices 0-1 (admitted by 157), substitution taken (166); with arg.length=439 the write at line 170 reaches index 440 == MAXSTRING, i.e. one element past the stack buffer (two elements with arg.length=MAXSTRING). Confirmed mechanism: unbounded element-wise copy into a fixed stack buffer — CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow.

assumptions: CharsString carries at most MAXSTRING widechars and getToken returns whitespace-delimited tokens up to that size, so an argument token of length 439 is producible; MAXSTRING is the named capacity used by the shown code's own guard at line 157.
tmpFile.line has MAXSTRING elements, which is why the guarded sibling branch at lines 157-164 refuses writes at linelen >= MAXSTRING.

The macro metadata (definition, substitutions, counts) is produced by compileMacro (line 37) with at least one substitution whose argument index is in range, so the substitution branch at 166 is reachable for expansion.
_lou_showString is assumed to neutralize control characters when used in _lou_logMessage/compileError format arguments; log/format string injection was not treated as a finding.
limitations: Heap OOB read at line 168 via an out-of-range substitution index would depend on compileMacro emitting invalid substitution entries; that validator is not shown, so the residual range of m->substitutions is not confirmable as containing an OOB value.
NULL dereference at lines 131/168 requires the unchecked malloc at lines 127-128 to fail; the allocation size is not attacker-scaled within the shown code.

Discarded return values of getCharacters/getRuleCharsText/getRuleDotsPattern in the CTO_Match/CTO_BackMatch cases can leave ptn_before empty so the ptn_before.chars[0] test reads an uninitialized slot; no memory-safety or injection sink follows, so it is a robustness concern only.

Appends into seqAfterExpression, ruleDots, and the multind ruleChars array lack bounds checks, but the capacities of those objects are not identifiable from the shown code, so OOB claims there are unconfirmable.
CTO_Match/CTO_BackMatch pattern-buffer sizing (27720 = 2*13841 + slack) is safe only if _lou_pattern_compile honors its maxlen argument; its contract is not present in the shown code.
The widechar-to-char cast when building emphasis-class name strings truncates wide characters; this is a data-integrity issue, not a security finding.
Line 16 reads token.chars[0] assuming getToken guarantees a non-empty token; getToken's contract is not shown.

verdict.summary: The LZW decoder's own guards neutralize the dangerous-looking memory operations. code_new is bounded to [0, current_entry] by the check at line 28, and in the 'code not in table' case (code_new == current_entry) the entry at index current_entry is always initialized first by the add at lines 44-50 before it is read at line 62: the code-size cap at lines 54-55 forces current_code_size <= LZW_CODE_MAX, hence code_new <= (1<<LZW_CODE_MAX)-1, so code_new == current_entry implies current_entry < 1<<LZW_CODE_MAX and the add guard at line 44 always admits that path. Dictionary chains strictly decrease (line 71's previous_entry is always < its entry index as provable from lines 39, 48, 49), so the walk at lines 68-72 terminates and never reads an unadded index. The only truly unguarded quantity is the number of *stack_pos++ writes (lines 38, 70, 73), but the stack buffer capacity is not declared in the shown code, so no out-of-bounds write can be confirmed.

assumptions: ctx->table has at least (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) entries, matching the add guard at line 44 (indices 0..(1<<LZW_CODE_MAX)-1 are the only ones ever written or read by the shown code).
ctx->stack_base points to a buffer large enough for the longest decodable string (bounded by (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) bytes per call, i.e. ~4096 for the standard 12-bit GIF case).

lzw__clear_codes (called at line 22) initializes literal entries 0..clear_code-1 and the previous-code state; this invariant is required by the reads at lines 35, 62, 70, 73 but its body is not shown.
LZW_CODE_MAX is a small standard constant (e.g. 12), so the signed shifts at lines 44 and 57 are well-defined.
limitations: Per-call output-stack writes (*stack_pos++ at lines 38, 70, 73) are bounded only by the decoded string length (<= (1<<LZW_CODE_MAX)), and no stack buffer capacity is identifiable from the shown code; a single-call stack overflow would be CWE-121/122 only if that external capacity were smaller, which cannot be confirmed here.

Reading table[code_new] at line 62 with code_new == current_entry is safe only because the add at lines 45-48 always executes before the read on that path (code_new == current_entry forces current_entry < 1 << LZW_CODE_MAX given the code-size cap), and because the table holds at least (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) entries; if the table were smaller, the add at line 45 would be the first overflow.
A 'code not in table' code as the first code after a Clear (lines 36-40) decodes from previous context; this is a correctness/robustness concern with no demonstrated memory impact in the shown code.

Signed 32-bit shifts (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) at line 44 and (1 << ctx->current_code_size) at line 57 would be UB for LZW_CODE_MAX >= 31, but the constant is not defined in the shown code; no exploitable wrap is demonstrated.

verdict.summary: The viewlog handler streams log-file contents into the HTML response body (inside a <textarea>) with no HTML escaping, allowing a stored XSS via textarea-breakout when attacker-influenced data is present in the monitored log file.

evidence.reason: Log-file bytes are entry-point input (file contents, unconstrained by any shown-code filter): fread (line 13) accepts up to 511 bytes per chunk into buf[512], adds a NUL at buf[n] (line 14), and appends the chunk verbatim with "%s" (line 15) into the HTML page body established by do_head (line 6) and the literal <textarea> markup (line 12). No transformation removes or escapes '<', '>', '/' or quotes; only NUL truncation applies. A log line containing </textarea><script>alert(document.cookie)</script> passes every guard on the path (line 2 is_readonly admits non-readonly users; line 7 selects file logging; line 9 fopen success; none inspect content) and reaches the sink unchanged, terminating the textarea and executing script in the monit web session. Primary CWE-79: improper output encoding of untrusted content during web page generation.

assumptions: StringBuffer_append into res->outputbuffer writes the HTTP response body of an HTML page rendered in a browser (supported by do_head's 'View log' page and the literal <textarea> markup in the shown code).
A non-readonly (write-capable) authenticated user is required to reach this page; that is the only access-control gate present in the shown code.

The log file consumed by fopen (line 8) may contain attacker-influenced content; the shown code imposes no content constraint, so per entry-point classification it is attacker-controlled unless constrained, which it is not.
limitations: Whether a remote attacker can actually place the payload into the monitored log depends on the log-writing path, which is outside the shown code; a deployment whose log contains only trusted daemon-generated messages would not be remotely triggerable.

Resource exhaustion: the loop (lines 13-16) streams an unbounded log into res->outputbuffer and all StringBuffer_append/fclose return values are discarded; exploitation requires attacker-controlled log growth and allocation failure behavior not establishable from the shown code.
fread error vs EOF is not distinguished (ferror never checked), so an I/O error silently truncates the page output; robustness concern only.

Rejected candidates: no off-by-one (fread limited to sizeof(buf)-1=511, max index 511 < capacity 512), no format-string bug (literal "%s" format at line 15), no path traversal (Run.files.log is a global value).

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in the window-wrap match path of qtm_decompress: the unsigned difference match_offset - window_posn (line 102) is narrowed into signed int j, so a difference >= 2^31 becomes negative and passes the signed bound check `j > (int) qtm->window_size` at line 103. A negative j then inflates the copy count at line 110 (`i -= j`, e.g. i = 1048579 from j = -1048576 and match_length = 3), and the loop at line 113 writes i bytes from &window[window_posn], overflowing the window_size-byte window buffer by an attacker-controlled amount (CWE-787, secondary CWE-681 for the conversion that both bypasses the guard and corrupts the length).

evidence.reason: Sink: the post-increment copy writes i bytes from rundest = &window[window_posn]. With window_posn = 0 and match_offset = 0xFFFFF000 (residual range [0, 2^32-1] left unconstrained by the shown code for the helper-supplied position_base/extra values), line 102 computes j = (int)(0xFFFFF000 - 0) = -1048576; the signed guard at line 103 admits every j <= window_size including all negative j, so it does not reject this value; line 108 admits -1048576 < 3 and line 110 sets i = 3 - (-1048576) = 1048579 without overflow. The loop then writes 1048579 bytes while the window has only qtm->window_size = 524288 bytes (the capacity the shown code uses at lines 92/103/107/140), an out-of-bounds heap write of 525291 bytes (CWE-787), rooted in the unsigned-to-signed narrowing of the difference (CWE-681).

assumptions: The window buffer is exactly qtm->window_size bytes: the shown code uses window_size as the window length in the wrap test (line 140 window_posn == qtm->window_size), the bounds guards (lines 92, 103), and window indexing (line 107 &window[qtm->window_size - j]).
qtm->window_size < 2^31 so (int) qtm->window_size preserves its value; int is 32-bit two's complement for the implementation-defined unsigned-to-signed narrowing (line 102).
QTM_GET_SYMBOL/QTM_READ_BITS consume the attacker-supplied compressed stream, and values sym/extra are input-derived with no bound imposed by the shown code.
Initial state has window_posn = 0 and o_end == o_ptr at stream start so the outer loop (line 37) is enterable with out_bytes > 0.
limitations: Literal writes (line 59 window[window_posn++] = sym) can pass the end of the window when frame_end (lines 46-49) exceeds window_size; reaching that state requires window_size not to be a multiple of QTM_FRAME_SIZE, a relation not visible in the shown code, so it is unconfirmable here.

out_bytes > INT_MAX would make (int) out_bytes negative at lines 17/158, but the final flush at line 158 is unreachable for such values because the line-37 loop would only exit via an error return while remaining < out_bytes; no confirmed path.

frame_end is computed in wider arithmetic and truncated to unsigned int at line 46; a wrap below window_posn would stall progress (infinite decode loop) but only for out_bytes >= 2^32 and it is bounded by input exhaustion (DoS only); the read-position invariant depends on unseen macro error semantics.

The sentinel align loop at line 136 (do { QTM_READ_BITS(i, 8); } while (i != 0xFF)) terminates only if QTM_READ_BITS errors on input exhaustion; the macro body is not shown, so a hang claim is unconfirmable.

In the real host program the position_base/extra_bits tables (not shown) may bound match_offset below 2^31 and make the demonstrated witness unreachable in deployment; the shown code itself imposes no such bound, and the finding is confirmed within the shown code's residual ranges.

If |j| exceeds INT_MAX - match_length, the i -= j at line 110 overflows signed int (UB, practically wraps negative and the line-113 loop is skipped), producing no memory write; this variant was not reported.
The unsigned sum at line 92 (window_posn + match_length) could wrap in a 32-bit type only for window_posn near 2^32, excluded by sane window sizes not shown in this code.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in the size_t expression `dl->length + so_ext_len + 1` (line 8): for `dl->length` near SIZE_MAX the unsigned addition wraps, so `alloc_root` returns a 1-byte block while `memcpy(s, dl->str, dl->length)` (line 9) and `strcpy(s + dl->length, SO_EXT)` (line 10) write `dl->length` bytes into it, causing a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) whose root cause is the wrap (CWE-190). No upper-bound guard on `dl->length` exists in the shown code.

evidence.reason: Allocation-size sink: `dl->length` (size_t, residual range [0, SIZE_MAX]; the only guard on it is the lower bound at line 4) is added unchecked to `so_ext_len + 1`. With the admitted witness `dl->length = SIZE_MAX - 2` and `so_ext_len = 3`, `SIZE_MAX - 2 + 3 + 1` wraps mod 2^64 to 1, so the allocation is 1 byte — the corrupted capacity is consumed directly as alloc_root's size (CWE-190 corrupting the size, feeding the CWE-787 write at lines 9-10).

Out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787): `dl->length` (residual [0, SIZE_MAX] after the guard at line 4, which admits the value SIZE_MAX - 2 since SIZE_MAX - 2 >= so_ext_len and suffix "aaa" != ".so") is used as the copy count into the 1-byte block produced by the wrapped allocation at line 8; the write exceeds the destination capacity by roughly SIZE_MAX bytes.

Second out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787): the destination pointer is `s + dl->length` with `dl->length = SIZE_MAX - 2` from the same admitted residual range, and `strcpy` writes `so_ext_len + 1` bytes past the wrapped 1-byte allocation from line 8, compounding the same integer-wrap root cause (CWE-190).

assumptions: SO_EXT is a non-empty NUL-terminated string literal (e.g., ".so"), so `so_ext_len = sizeof(SO_EXT) - 1 >= 1` and equals 3 in the witness.
size_t is 64-bit unsigned on the target, so the arithmetic wraps modulo 2^64; on a 32-bit size_t the same overflow class applies with the modulus 2^32.
alloc_root returns a contiguous block of the requested (wrapped) size.
limitations: `dl` is an internal-helper parameter; the shown code does not demonstrate a caller that supplies attacker-controlled length, so the finding rests on the unconstrained residual range [0, SIZE_MAX] rather than a demonstrated external origin.
A length near SIZE_MAX presumes `dl->str` references a region of that size; real callers typically derive length from actual string buffers, making the near-SIZE_MAX witness practically unreachable.
Before the write completes, memcpy's source read of ~SIZE_MAX bytes would fault on real hardware, so the realistic impact is a crash/DoS rather than a clean controlled overflow.
Unchecked alloc_root result (line 8) dereferenced at line 9: single-shot OOM, not attacker-scaled and not attacker-controlled in the shown code; demoted, no CWE.
No explicit loops exist in the shown code; the internal my_strcasecmp loop is bounded by SO_EXT's NUL terminator and is not attacker-elongatable.
The read `dl->str + dl->length - so_ext_len` (line 5) is guarded by the `length < so_ext_len` check; no out-of-bounds read is confirmed there.

verdict.summary: An attacker-controlled FLX frame chunk with flxfh.size in [0, FlxFrameChunkSize] (e.g., 0) passes the upper-bound-only guard at line 105; the unsigned expression flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize at line 112 underflows (or is 0 for size == FlxFrameChunkSize), gst_adapter_take returns NULL, and the unguarded dereference ((FlxFrameType *) chunk)->chunks at line 114 NULL-pointer-crashes the decoder (CWE-476, enabled by CWE-191 unsigned underflow), a remotely triggerable denial of service via a crafted media stream.

evidence.reason: flxfh.size is attacker-controlled (guint32 copied from adapter bytes at line 98) and its only shown constraint is the upper bound `avail < flxfh.size` at line 105, admitting [0, avail]. For flxfh.size = 0 the unsigned subtraction wraps to 0xFFFFFFFA, an out-of-domain length for gst_adapter_take (documented precondition 0 < nbytes <= available bytes, here at most the small buffered amount), so the call returns NULL and the shown code dereferences that NULL at line 114, crashing the pipeline. Primary mechanism CWE-476 (NULL deref); CWE-191 (unsigned underflow) is the independent root cause corrupting the size argument.

chunk is NULL on the fully shown path: guard line 105 admits flxfh.size = 0 (avail >= 6 > 0), line 112 derives the wrapped size, gst_adapter_take (line 111) returns NULL, and no NULL check exists between assignment and this dereference at line 114 (also the macro at line 113). Dereferencing NULL reads/writes nothing valid and crashes the process (CWE-476), a confirmed denial of service from an 6-byte attacker chunk header.

assumptions: FlxFrameChunk has a 32-bit unsigned size field followed by id, FlxFrameChunkSize == 6 per the FLIC format/GStreamer headers, so `flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize` uses unsigned arithmetic and wraps for flxfh.size < 6.
width/height are 16-bit unsigned (implied by the explicit `(guint)` casts at line 78 and FLIC format), giving flxdec->size range [0, 4294836225].
gst_adapter_take(nbytes) returns NULL unless 0 < nbytes <= bytes available in the adapter (documented GStreamer precondition); standard build with GLib checks enabled.
flxdec->size is 32-bit `guint` in the real struct; the shown code does not declare it, so the `flxdec->size * 4` wrap is handled as an assumption-dependent limitation.
limitations: Heap overflow via flx_dec->size * 4 wrapping to a tiny/zero allocation (line 124) and flx_colorspace_convert (lines 140-141) writing past `map.data` is not confirmed: the width of `flxdec->size` is not declared in the shown code and the write extent is inside the unshown callee (would be CWE-190/CWE-787).

flx_decode_chunks (lines 127-129) receives an attacker count (`((FlxFrameType *) chunk)->chunks`) and pointer `chunk + FlxFrameTypeSize`; overflow of `flxdec->frame_data` or reads past the chunk buffer depend on the unshown callee, so not confirmed (FlxFrameTypeSize is also not shown).

For depth > 8 the converter is never created (lines 67-69) but is still passed to flx_colorspace_convert at line 140; a NULL-converter dereference would occur inside the unshown callee and is not confirmable from the shown code.
Attacker-controlled allocation sizes (lines 81-82 and 124, up to ~4.29 GB each) can cause memory-exhaustion DoS, but this is secondary to the confirmed NULL deref.

With flxfh.id not equal to FLX_FRAME_TYPE and flxfh.size = 0, the default branch (lines 151-154) flushes zero bytes, so the loop at line 90 makes no progress and spins forever on that input (hang DoS, CWE-835) — noted, not part of the primary finding.
The discarded return of gst_buffer_map (line 138) is not attacker-triggerable on a freshly allocated writable buffer and was not reported.

verdict.summary: In the buf != NULL branch, check_termcode() writes a NUL terminator at tp[len] == buf[*buflen] without ever relating *buflen to the buffer capacity bufsize. When *buflen == bufsize (a value inside the admitted set of the line-51 guard), the write lands exactly one byte past the end of buf, a one-byte out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) that can corrupt adjacent heap/stack memory for attacker-supplied terminal data of the exact input length.

evidence.reason: len is derived from *buflen at line 54 (len = *buflen - offset); the only guard on the path, line 51 (offset >= *buflen -> break), admits offset=0 with *buflen == bufsize, so tp[len] indexes buf[*buflen] == buf[bufsize] — index equals the capacity bufsize, i.e. one byte out of bounds. The write is a 1-byte NUL overflow of buf (CWE-787 primary); the shown code imposes no constraint *buflen <= bufsize-1 before the write, and termleader-membership of buf[0] (e.g. ESC) plus default p_ek/State let the witness reach line 85.

assumptions: buf[0] is chosen as ESC and ESC is present in the global termleader[] (standard Vim termcap configuration with ESC-starting termcodes); termleader content is not shown.
p_ek (esckeys) is set and/or State is not MODE_INSERT so the line-82 skip does not fire for the witness.
termcodes[]/tc_len and the inner modifier/keypad matching code are the normal internal state; none of the inner loops produced an independent finding.
limitations: The equivalent typebuf-branch write typebuf.tb_buf[tb_off + tb_len] = NUL cannot be confirmed: the capacity of typebuf.tb_buf is not identifiable from the shown code.

GUI scrollbar loops (lines 479-480, 508-509) read tp[j], tp[j+1], tp[j+2] with j advanced past len without a len-based bound; reachable only in GUI builds from GUI-generated event data (framework provenance), and the byte/long reader helpers have bounds logic not shown.

atoi() at line 251 has undefined behavior on very long digit strings, but reads are NUL-bounded at tp[len] and the result only ORs decode_modifiers() bit constants; no memory-safety impact is confirmable.

Writes into string[] via modifiers2keycode()/mb_char2bytes() (lines 567-591) cannot be confirmed: callee bounds are not shown and modifiers is a bounded bit-OR of decode_modifiers() constants, so an input-scalable size reaching MAX_KEY_CODE_LEN is not derivable in the shown code.

get_bytes_from_buf/get_long_from_buf/handle_csi/put_string_in_typebuf bodies are not shown; no out-of-domain index or size argument is derivable from the shown code at those call sites (slen <= len holds on every match path before line 593).

verdict.summary: On the non-cancelled connect-failure path (lines 28-34), connection_attempt_remove (attempt) unlinks the attempt from data->connection_attempts and drops the list-held reference, but the callback-owned reference that every other exit releases via connection_attempt_unref (attempt) (lines 15, 39, 56) is never dropped. Each failed connection attempt therefore leaks a ConnectionAttempt along with its GSocket, GIOStream, GCancellable, GSocketAddress and attached timeout GSource, enabling memory/resource-exhaustion DoS whose volume scales with attacker-influenceable address enumeration and repeated failed connects (CWE-401).

evidence.reason: The guard at line 28 admits every connect_finish failure whose attempt->cancellable is not cancelled (e.g., peer ECONNREFUSED or ETIMEDOUT), with the early guard at line 12 also FALSE. On that path, connection_attempt_remove (attempt) unlinks the attempt from data->connection_attempts and consumes the list-held reference, after which enumerator_next_async and the implicit return at line 42 release nothing further; the separate callback-owned reference that the other three exits release with connection_attempt_unref (attempt) (lines 15, 39, 56) is stranded, and the unlink at line 32 prevents the data-free g_slist_free_full cleanup from reaching it. Result: every such failed attempt leaks the ConnectionAttempt and its GSocket/GIOStream/GCancellable/GSocketAddress/timeout GSource, compounding with the address count from the enumerator (CWE-401, improper cleanup / missing release of memory).

assumptions: In-flight attempts are registered in data->connection_attempts and the list membership holds a distinct reference from the callback user_data reference; this is the only model consistent with the shown code's four exit paths (lines 15/39 unref without unlinking; lines 52+56 unlink then unref).
g_socket_connection_connect_finish returning TRUE implies attempt->socket and attempt->connection are non-NULL (standard API contract; used at lines 45-46, 58, 62).
g_proxy_address_get_protocol (line 70) returns a non-NULL scheme string for a valid GProxyAddress.
Standard GLib semantics for g_slist_*, g_steal_pointer, g_clear_pointer, g_cancellable_*.
limitations: Success-path double-unref of the current attempt (loop at lines 48-53 then line 56) would be a CWE-416/415 only under single-owner reference accounting; that model is contradicted by the shown code's own branches (lines 15 and 39 unref without unlinking), and the two-owner invariant needed to confirm is not declared in the snippet, so this is not reported as a finding.

NULL protocol from g_proxy_address_get_protocol reaching g_hash_table_contains (line 86) or g_set_error with %s (line 107) is not producible on any path inside the shown code (provenance of data->proxy_addr not visible); unconfirmed.

Double/non-balanced g_object_unref (data->task) across multiple concurrent attempts (lines 14, 38, and inside g_socket_client_async_connect_complete) depends on per-enumeration task ref accounting outside the shown code; unconfirmed.
g_set_error at lines 107-109 uses a fixed format literal with protocol passed as an argument; no format-string injection is possible, so CWE-134 is excluded.
Leak severity is bounded by the number of failed attempts an attacker can drive (address-enumeration/DNS volume and repeated connects); assessed as low rather than medium/high.

verdict.summary: S3 GET response construction echoes stored object metadata into HTTP response headers without control-character filtering: user metadata is dumped as a header name+value at line 165 and mapped attributes are copied into response_attrs (only trailing NULs stripped, lines 144-150) and dumped at line 199. The function's only CRLF guard, str_has_cntrl at line 122, is scoped to response-content-* query parameters and never constrains attr names/values, so CR/LF bytes in stored metadata survive to the header sinks and enable HTTP response splitting (CWE-113).

evidence.reason: Taint: attrs keys/values have no shown-code constraint (residual range includes CR/LF; the str_has_cntrl guard at line 122 applies only to the query-arg value val in the response-param loop). Reachability: with op_ret==0 (line 92) and an attr key whose first bytes match RGW_ATTR_META_PREFIX (lines 161-162 admit "user_meta" + any tail), line 164 advances name past the prefix and this sink emits the remaining key bytes as the header name and iter->second as the header value with no filtering. Concrete witness: key "user_meta\r\nX-Injected: 1" or value containing "\r\n". Impact: CRLF reaches HTTP header serialization -> header injection/response splitting; primary CWE-113.

Taint: attr values copied verbatim at lines 144-145 and shrunk only by removing trailing NUL bytes at lines 146-149; CR (0x0D) and LF (0x0A) survive into response_attrs at line 150. Reachability: op_ret==0 (line 92) and the attr key present in rgw_to_http_attrs (lines 140-141) admit any value bytes; the str_has_cntrl check at line 122 is not on this path. Concrete witness: attr value "public\r\nX-Injected: 1" -> this sink writes it as a response header value at line 199. Impact: stored-object-metadata CRLF reaches HTTP header serialization -> header injection/response splitting; primary CWE-113.

assumptions: attrs is the object's stored metadata; the shown code imposes no character constraint on attr names/values and no trust invariant for attrs is visible in the shown code, so their residual range is treated as arbitrary bytes including CR/LF.
dump_header/end_header serialize header lines as 'name: value\r\n' per standard RFC7230 semantics, so a value or name containing CRLF terminates the header line.
limitations: Line 218 dump_body(s, bl.c_str() + bl_ofs, bl_len): OOB read if bl_ofs < 0 or bl_ofs + bl_len exceeds the bufferlist's data; bl_ofs/bl_len are internal-helper parameters with no visible bounds and bl's capacity is not identifiable from the shown code, so the excess cannot be quantified - unconfirmed, no CWE.

Whether CRLF can actually be stored into object metadata depends on upload-path and HTTP-frontend sanitization that is not present in the shown code; the shown code itself leaves attribute bytes unconstrained.

The Content-Type attr path (lines 155-156 -> end_header at line 208) is the same injection class but requires RGW_ATTR_CONTENT_TYPE to contain CRLF, which HTTP frontends typically preclude by splitting header lines on CRLF at upload.
Integer overflow of total_len at line 54 needs metadata_bl.length() near 2^63 (unreachable magnitudes); not a finding.
Potential NULL dereference of s->auth.identity at line 112 has no NULL-producing path inside the shown code.
crypt_http_responses and object-lock attr values are populated by server-side code not shown; no attacker path to controlling them is demonstrable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in compileRule's macro expansion: macro argument characters are appended to the fixed MAXSTRING-widechar tmpFile.line (line 170) without the linelen >= MAXSTRING guard that protects the definition-character path (line 157), so a macro whose definition fills the line and whose argument token is long enough writes at index == MAXSTRING, overflowing the stack buffer with attacker-controlled widechars.

evidence.snippet:
for (int j = 0; j < arg.length; j++)
								tmpFile.line[tmpFile.linelen++] = arg.chars[j];
evidence.reason: arg.length and arg.chars are macro-argument token data read from the attacker-controlled table file at line 130, with no length cap imposed by any shown check. linelen is admitted up to MAXSTRING-1 by the sibling guard at line 157 (which rejects linelen >= MAXSTRING only on the definition-copy path, line 164) but is not checked on this path; with a macro definition prefix of MAXSTRING-1 non-newline chars (all prefix writes admitted by 157) and an argument token of length >= 2, the loop writes tmpFile.line[linelen++] at index == MAXSTRING, one past the MAXSTRING-capacity buffer identified by the named constant and error message at 157-161. This is a confirmed stack-buffer overflow (CWE-121) via an unbounded copy in the macro expansion substitution loop.

assumptions: MAXSTRING is the capacity in widechars of tmpFile.line, as implied by the guard at line 157 and the error message at lines 158-161.
CharsString.length fields are non-negative integers and CharsString.chars arrays have at least MAXSTRING elements.
Embedded helpers (getToken, compileMacro, _lou_pattern_compile) honor their documented caps; _lou_pattern_compile caps its output at its maxsize argument (13841).
Macro metadata (definition[], substitutions[], argument_count, substitution_count, definition_length) is generated from the same attacker-controlled table file by the unseen compileMacro.
limitations: OOB read of arguments[] via m->substitutions[2*subst+1]-1 at line 168 when a substitution argument index falls outside [1, m->argument_count]: no range check in the shown code, but the values are built by the unseen compileMacro, so no witness value is derivable from the shown code alone.

NULL dereference at line 131 if the unchecked malloc at lines 127-128 fails: allocation size is small (m->argument_count * sizeof(CharsString)) and not attacker-scaled, so failure is not attacker-controlled.

CTO_MultInd ruleChars.chars[ruleChars.length++] and CTO_RepEndWord x.chars[x.length++] and ruleDots.chars[ruleDots.length++] have no identifiable capacity in the shown code; boundary claims are unconfirmable (CTO_MultInd is additionally bounded by tokens per line).

Discarded return statuses of getCharacters/getRuleCharsText/getRuleDotsPattern in CTO_Match/CTO_BackMatch/CTO_Replace may propagate stale or empty lengths; impact within the shown code is limited to incorrect parsing, not confirmed memory unsafety.

If macro metadata is internally inconsistent (e.g., a substitution position beyond definition_length), the while loop at line 144 could read past m->definition; consistency depends on the unseen compileMacro.
_lou_showString-based log output is passed as a %s argument with fixed format strings, so format-string injection is not present; log-injection behavior depends on unseen escaping in _lou_showString.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read of cp950_pua_tbl in mbfl_filt_conv_big5_wchar: the row-search loop (L47-L51) can exit with k == N when no row contains the attacker-controlled byte pair c2 = c1<<8|c; the code then indexes cp950_pua_tbl[k] unconditionally at L53/L54-L55/L57, reading one row (4 unsigned shorts) past the array. The only gate, is_in_cp950_pua(c1,c) at L45, is a call to an unshown helper; the shown code contains no visible bound that a true return forces a matching row, so the k == N path stays inside the guard's residual range.

evidence.reason: First post-loop OOB read: k is derived entirely from attacker-controlled c2 (L46: c2 = c1 << 8 | c, with c1 from filter->cache set at L20 and c the case-1 input byte), and the loop at L47-L51 leaves k == N (the row count from sizeof(cp950_pua_tbl)/(sizeof(unsigned short)*4)) whenever no row covers c2. The gate at L45 (w <= 0 && is_in_cp950_pua(c1, c)) does not bound k or demonstrate, in the shown code, that a true helper result implies a row match; no k < N check exists after L51. Index k == capacity N reads one row (8 bytes) past cp950_pua_tbl => CWE-125.

Second post-loop OOB read on the k == N path from the exhausted L47-L51 loop: cp950_pua_tbl[N][2] and cp950_pua_tbl[N][0] are read (8 bytes past the array's last row) when the OOB bytes on the L53 condition evaluate to the 0x40 low byte; attacker-controlled c1 and c (residual ranges [0x81,0xfe] and [0x3a,0x7e]∪[0xa1,0xfe] under L31) select this path via c2 and the unconstrained helper gate at L45 => CWE-125.

Third post-loop OOB read on the k == N path: executes whenever the L53 OOB condition evaluates non-0x40; cp950_pua_tbl[N][2] and cp950_pua_tbl[N][0] are read one row past the array for any attacker pair (c1, c) admitted by L45 whose c2 matches no row => CWE-125.

assumptions: int is 32-bit and sizeof(unsigned short) == 2, so one cp950_pua_tbl row is 8 bytes (4 unsigned shorts).
The encoding framework passes input bytes as int values; the shown code itself never caps c to 0..255, but no confirmed sink depends on that cap.
cp950_pua_tbl has at least one row (N >= 1), matching the explicit row-width sizeof expression at L47.
limitations: The bodies of is_in_cp950_pua and the contents of cp950_pua_tbl are not shown; if the helper's true-return exactly mirrors the row coverage of the table, the loop always breaks and the post-loop reads stay in bounds. That invariant is not visible in the shown code, so it cannot support a safe verdict.
No single numeric trigger pair can be enumerated from the shown code because the table rows are not shown; the confirmation is residual-range based, hence confidence 0.65 rather than >= 0.7.
The CK macro (return-error handling of (*filter->output_function)) is not defined in the shown code, so output-callback error/status handling cannot be classified.
The final `return c;` (L83) returns the consumed byte rather than a status; callers are outside the shown code, so misuse cannot be confirmed here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability within the shown code. Every length reaching a memcpy/read/write sink is guard-bounded to {1..16}, {12}, or {13} (lines 39, 45, 56, 65, 71), the TLS1_AAD length discount is protected against underflow (lines 82-84), and allocation results are checked (lines 11, 31). The remaining candidates (actx/dst NULL dereference, EVP_CTRL_COPY and SET_TAG success-without-effect, OOB bounds on tag/tls_aad, short nonce) depend on caller-supplied NULL pointers, external call ordering, allocation failure, or capacities not identifiable from the shown code, so they are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE == 16, CHACHA_CTR_SIZE == 16, and EVP_AEAD_TLS1_AAD_LEN == 13 (standard OpenSSL constants used by the shown guards; their numeric values are not defined in the shown code).
aead_data(ctx) returns ctx->cipher_data, so actx can be NULL before EVP_CTRL_INIT completes successfully (INIT itself checks and sets it).
actx->tag and actx->tls_aad are assumed wide enough for the guarded copy lengths (16 and 13); their capacities are not declared in the shown code.
limitations: NULL dereference of actx (lines 41, 47-52, 59, 67, 77-96) or of dst derived from ptr (lines 27-30) requires a caller to invoke a ctrl case before successful EVP_CTRL_INIT or to pass ptr == NULL; the shown code never constructs NULL on any path, so this is a limitation rather than a confirmed CWE-476.

EVP_CTRL_COPY returns 1 even when actx == NULL after skipping the copy (lines 26-36), and EVP_CTRL_AEAD_SET_TAG returns 1 without setting tag_len when ptr == NULL (lines 58-62); these are status-handling concerns of the CWE-703/754 shape, but the operation that runs on the failure state is in the unshown caller, so no confirmed impact can be established from the shown code.

Boundary/OOB claims for memset(actx->tls_aad, 0, 16) (line 22), memcpy(actx->tag, ptr, arg) (line 59), memcpy(ptr, actx->tag, arg) (line 67), and memcpy(actx->tls_aad, ptr, 13) (line 77) cannot be confirmed because the capacities of actx->tag, actx->tls_aad, and the caller's ptr buffers are not identifiable from the shown code; the guards admit at most 16/13 bytes.

EVP_CTRL_AEAD_SET_IVLEN admits nonce lengths as low as 1 (line 39), but nonce_len has no consumer in the shown code and the function does not choose a weak algorithm, PRNG, or seed, so weak-entropy claims are unconfirmable here.
There are no loops in the shown code, so no loop-bound or sentinel-termination analysis applies.

A path where OPENSSL_zalloc fails (lines 9-10) and subsequent ctrl cases dereference the still-NULL actx depends on an uncontrolled allocation failure and is not a confirmed attacker-triggerable path.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only security-relevant sink is ctx->set_output(output_port, shape) at line 8; output_port is an int parameter forwarded unchanged with no range check, but the valid output-index range and the capacity of InferenceContext's output storage are not identifiable from the shown code, so the out-of-bounds hypothesis is unconfirmable and recorded as a limitation.

assumptions: int is the platform 32-bit signed type with full range INT_MIN..INT_MAX.
GetContext returning nullptr is the only failure signal the shown code needs to handle, and it is handled at lines 5-7.
limitations: output_port (line 1) reaches the index argument of ctx->set_output (line 8) unvalidated; if it left the valid output range, set_output could perform an out-of-bounds access (CWE-787/CWE-125), but the capacity/bounds of the callee's output storage and the parameter domain are not identifiable from the shown code, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable.

The ShapeHandle returned by GetUnknownOutputShape (lines 2-3) is never validated before being passed to set_output (line 8), and the function returns Status::OK() (line 9); if the helper returned an invalid handle on failure, this would be an error-status handling concern, but the helper's failure semantics are not visible in the shown code.
node is not null-checked in the shown code, but no dereference of node occurs in the shown code and no NULL-producing path exists inside it; any NULL dereference would happen in unshown helpers.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability in the shown code. The only index-bearing sink, node.input(0) (lines 19 and 21), is protected by the input_size() < 1 guard at line 14, whose excluded set {0} exactly covers the only unsafe value; the GetNode result is null-checked at line 20 before any dereference (lines 26, 33); and the consumer loop (lines 29-40) performs only string equality and pointer dereferences with no index/size derivation. The historical zero-input crash pattern for this function is patched. Remaining concerns (log injection via VLOG, unguarded consumer pointers, returning true for non-identity nodes) are provenance- or caller-contract-dependent and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: node_map_ refers to a consistent NodeMap whose GetOutputs returns only live, valid consumer NodeDef pointers for the given node name.
callers of SafeToRemoveIdentity invoke it only for nodes they intend to remove based on this function's decision (the non-identity early return at line 3 relies on that contract).
node.name() is used strictly as a key/comparison/log operand; no downstream operation in the shown code interprets it as a path, format, command, or index.
limitations: CWE-117 log-injection candidate at the VLOG(1) sink on line 21: node.name() and node.input(0) are internal-helper parameters with unconstrained string range in the shown code, but attacker provenance cannot be established from the shown code alone, and no log-consumer sink is shown; therefore not confirmed.

Potential null/invalid consumer pointers from node_map_->GetOutputs (dereferenced at lines 30 and 34): the invariant that the returned collection contains only valid non-null NodeDef pointers is not visible in the shown code, so a NULL-dereference claim cannot be produced inside the shown code.

Early return true for non-identity nodes (lines 2-4) is only a flaw if a caller uses this function to bless removal of arbitrary nodes; the caller contract is not shown, and no failure mechanism is demonstrable within the shown code.
No explicit cap on node input count or string lengths exists; this has no security impact in the shown code because no index/size/length is derived from those values.

verdict.summary: In qtm_decompress, the window-wrap match path (match_offset > window_posn) copies match_length bytes to window[window_posn] with no clamp to window_size — unlike the else branch which clamps i at lines 112-113. Decoding a match with window_posn near the window end (e.g., window_size-2 with selector 5, match_length fixed at 4) writes past the end of the heap window buffer (indices window_size and window_size+1), a heap out-of-bounds write driven by attacker-controlled compressed input.

evidence.reason: Sink of the confirmed heap OOB write. i = match_length (line 93) is attacker-derived (selector 5 gives fixed match_length 4 at line 74; selector 6 gives length_base[sym]+extra+5 at line 80) and is never clamped to window_size - window_posn in this wrap branch (contrast lines 112-113 in the else branch). With window_posn = window_size - 2 admitted by the inner-loop guard (line 51, window_posn < frame_end = window_size), this loop writes indices window_size and window_size+1, exceeding the window_size-byte capacity the shown code itself enforces at lines 102, 112 and 135. Guard at line 98 admits j = match_offset - window_posn up to window_size and bounds only the source index at line 102, not the destination extent. Line 123-127 checks run after the write and cannot prevent it. Primary mechanism: CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write; excess = window_posn + match_length - window_size = 2 for the demonstrated witness.

Second distinct sink of the same finding: the first copy run in the wrap branch writes j bytes to window[window_posn .. window_posn+j-1] with no clamp to window_size - window_posn. j is admitted up to window_size by the line 98 guard (j > window_size errors); combined with the unclamped remainder copied at line 108, a match decoded at window_posn = window_size - 2 with match_length 4 (selector 5, line 74) and j = 1 (match_offset = window_posn + 1 admitted by lines 95 and 98) produces writes at indices window_size and window_size+1, past the window buffer's window_size-byte capacity. Same missing destination bound as the line 108 sink; CWE-787.

assumptions: window is a heap buffer of exactly qtm->window_size bytes; the shown code treats it as such (source index at line 102 uses window_size - j, clamp at lines 112-113 uses window_size - window_posn, flush condition at line 135 tests window_posn == window_size).

window_size is a multiple of QTM_FRAME_SIZE (or frame evolution otherwise permits a frame to reach the window end), so a frame can bring window_posn to window_size - 2 while frame_end = window_size, per normal frame boundaries at line 147 and the flush-at-capacity check at line 135.

QTM_GET_SYMBOL and QTM_READ_BITS succeed for attacker-crafted input (they do not set qtm->error) and the position/length model tables defined outside this function cover the offset/length intervals the guards admit.
out_bytes is non-negative per the line 12 guard and can be large enough to demand a full frame's worth of output.
limitations: The concrete sym/extra pair producing match_offset = window_posn + 1 (and any numeric window_size / QTM_FRAME_SIZE values, and position_base/length_base/extra_bits contents) is defined outside the shown code; the witness is therefore confirmed over the guards' admitted residual range rather than a fully enumerated symbol value (supports confidence 0.5-0.7).
do { QTM_READ_BITS(i,8); } while (i != 0xFF) at line 131 may overrun or hang on a stream lacking the 0xFF sync byte; behavior depends on the unshown QTM_READ_BITS macro's end-of-input handling.

Unsigned wrap of frame_end at line 46 (potentially a non-advancing infinite loop) requires out_bytes near 2^32, i.e., a ~4 GiB output request from the caller; not confirmable as a reachable DoS from the shown code.

Signedness/truncation at line 97 (j into int), line 98/112 ((int) casts of window_size), and line 153 ((int) out_bytes) would only matter for values > INT_MAX / > 2 GiB, which cannot be established from the shown code.
A downstream OOB at line 59 via exact-aligned window_posn overshoot past window_size depends on window_size not being a multiple of QTM_FRAME_SIZE, which is not identifiable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code. Every attacker-derived size and index is either bounded by checks present in the shown code (m and basis exponents capped by OPENSSL_ECC_MAX_FIELD_BITS at lines 56/151 together with the trinomial/pentanomial ordering guards at lines 79 and 101-103; order bit-length bounded by the Hasse check at line 209) or used with a matching same-size allocation (seed allocation at line 172 and memcpy at lines 176-177). Plausible issues such as the non-prime-p/compressed-point infinite-loop class (CVE-2022-0778) reachable through EC_POINT_oct2point at lines 194-195 and a length-0 read of params->base->data[0] at lines 190-191 depend on callee behavior or buffer capacities not present in the shown code, and are recorded as limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: OPENSSL_ECC_MAX_FIELD_BITS is a small fixed constant (661 in OpenSSL), so every m/k value surviving the line 56/152 checks is within safe BIGNUM and int range.

ASN1_STRING length fields (curve->a->length, curve->b->length, seed->length, base->length) are non-negative per the ASN.1 decoder invariant; their data/length are consistent within the parsed structure.
BN_set_bit with a negative index returns failure (library semantics), and EC_GROUP_new_curve_GFp/GF2m initialize ret->seed before it is freed at line 171.

EC_POINT_oct2point, EC_GROUP_new_curve_GFp/GF2m, EC_GROUP_set_generator, and ec_curve_nid_from_params are treated as opaque with their documented contracts; any vulnerability inside them is not visible in the shown code.
limitations: Non-prime field modulus p (only checked for negativity/zero at line 146) combined with a compressed base encoding at lines 190-195 can drive EC_POINT_oct2point into an unbounded BN_mod_sqrt loop (CVE-2022-0778 class); the infinite loop is inside the callee and is not anchorable in the shown code.

The read of params->base->data[0] at line 191 lacks a length>0 check (only data!=NULL is enforced at line 181); whether this is a 1-byte OOB depends on the ASN1_STRING zero-length buffer capacity, which is not identifiable from the shown code.

ASN1_INTEGER_to_BN failures at lines 201 and 218 leave the reused BIGNUMs a/b in callee-defined state; a double free at lines 309-310 is unconfirmed (callee semantics not shown) and would require an allocation failure.

EC_GROUP_set_generator receives an unvalidated cofactor (lines 215-221); negative or zero cofactors are accepted, but no security-relevant consumer exists in the shown code, so this is a robustness concern.
Potential free/realloc of an uninitialized ret->seed at line 171 relies on an initialization invariant inside EC_GROUP_new_curve_GFp/GF2m that is not present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: SetUnknownShape uses output_port as an output-index argument to GetUnknownOutputShape (line 3) before validating it; the bounds check at lines 8-12 runs only afterward, so any int value (e.g., -1 or >= ctx->num_outputs()) is forwarded to a name-implied shape-array lookup, producing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The check fully protects the later set_output call but not the earlier call; it must be hoisted above line 3.

evidence.reason: output_port (int, internal-helper parameter) has no constraint applied anywhere before this call: its residual range here is the full int domain, including -1 and values >= ctx->num_outputs(). It is forwarded unchanged as an output-port index to GetUnknownOutputShape, whose parameter is consumed as an index by name and use; the only bounds guard (lines 8-12, admitting [0, ctx->num_outputs()) and excluding negative/too-large ports) executes after this call and therefore cannot protect it. Witness output_port = -1 reaches line 3 unconditionally and triggers the out-of-range shape lookup, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) that can crash the process or disclose adjacent memory.

assumptions: GetUnknownOutputShape consumes output_port as an index into per-output shape storage whose valid domain is [0, ctx->num_outputs()), as asserted by the shown code's own guard and error message at lines 8-11.
ctx->set_output's storage has capacity num_outputs(), making the guarded write at line 13 in-bounds for the admitted range.
limitations: The exact capacity of the object indexed inside GetUnknownOutputShape is not declared in the shown code; the OOB claim rests on the name/use-implied index semantics permitted for call-site anchoring.

If GetUnknownOutputShape ignores output_port or uses only bounded lookups internally, the impact would be limited to returning a shape for an invalid port; that behavior is not visible in the shown code.
No other security-relevant sinks (injection, crypto, file, auth) exist in the shown code; the line-13 set_output call is fully guarded by lines 8-12.

verdict.summary: In the else branch of the shape-dtype dispatch, ConstantFolding::IsSimplifiableReshape reads every element of the attacker-supplied constant shape tensor as int64 (line 62) after only checking that the dtype is not DT_INT32 (line 52). For any non-INT32/INT64 dtype (e.g., a DT_FLOAT constant with 4 elements, 16 bytes), NumElements() counts elements by the tensor's actual element size while flat<int64_t>() indexes 8-byte slots, so index i=2 reads bytes [16,24) past the 16-byte heap buffer. This is a confirmed heap out-of-bounds read (type confusion as root cause) reachable from a crafted model with no protective dtype check in the shown code.

evidence.reason: Sink for the heap OOB read: outputs[0] holds the evaluated constant shape tensor whose dtype is attacker-controlled with residual range 'any DataType except DT_INT32' (the only discriminator is the dispatch at line 52). The loop bound at line 61 is NumElements() in units of the tensor's actual element size, while flat<int64_t>()(i) reads byte offset 8*i..8*i+7. Witness: DT_FLOAT constant with 4 elements (16-byte buffer) is admitted by all guards (IsReshape line 3, input_size>=2 line 6, constant line 12, EvaluateNode OK line 25, outputs.size()==1 line 28, props/shape checks lines 36-49); the else branch at line 59 admits it; with N=4, i=2 reads bytes [16,24), 8 bytes past the 16-byte capacity, and i=3 reads 16 bytes past. Primary CWE-125 OOB read caused by type-confused access (CWE-843): the tensor is bit-reinterpreted as int64 without an int64 dtype check.

assumptions: Tensor::flat<T>() is a raw, unchecked bit-reinterpretation in release builds: index i addresses byte offset i*sizeof(T) with no dtype or bounds check (standard Tensor semantics).
TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape / TensorShape::AddDim treat negative dims as invalid, and TF_CHECK_OK aborts the process on a non-OK status.
NodeMap::GetNode returns nullptr for a name absent from the node map.
The serialized graph/model, including the constant shape node's dtype and values, is attacker-controlled entry data; the shown code imposes no constraint on it beyond the checks named above.
limitations: Potential null-pointer dereference at line 12: GetNode's return is never null-checked, but confirming a dangling node.input(1) reference reaches this function requires graph-validation behavior outside the shown code; not counted as a verdict finding.

Potential reachable-assertion DoS via TF_CHECK_OK on lines 58/65: an unchecked negative dim (e.g., -1 from the constant, or garbage dims from the type confusion) can make MakeShape fail and TF_CHECK_OK abort the process (CWE-617); real but secondary and not added to the cwe list.
Line 8's diagnostic says 'must have at most 2 inputs' although the guard at line 6 enforces at least 2 inputs; cosmetic message bug, no security impact.
If an external, unshown pass guarantees the shape input dtype is DT_INT32 or DT_INT64, the OOB read would be unreachable; such an invariant is not present in the shown code and cannot be used.

verdict.summary: The bool function optimize_unflattened_subqueries has no return statement on the success path: normal list exhaustion (line 5) or the break after un->exclude_level() (lines 19-23) flows off the end of the function (line 128), which is undefined behavior in C++ (CWE-758) and returns an indeterminate status to the subquery-optimization caller, potentially spuriously aborting otherwise successful statements. No memory-safety, injection, crypto, or file-handling defect exists in the shown code.

evidence.reason: The function is declared bool (line 1) but its only returns are the error returns at lines 57, 77 and the dead check at 104-105; on every successful pass (outer loop exhausted at line 5, or break at line 23 after exclude_level() at line 20), control reaches the closing brace at line 128 without returning a value. Flowing off the end of a non-void C++ function is undefined behavior, so the returned bool is indeterminate (primary mechanism CWE-758). Concrete witness admitted by every guard: const_only=false with any fixed inner unit whose sl->join is non-NULL and inner_join->optimize() returns 0 (guards at lines 11, 13, 25-29, 32, 60, 76, 86, 89 all admit this state); the residual ranges of these inputs are unconstrained by the shown code, and the missing return makes the mainline path UB.

assumptions: The supplied snippet is treated as complete: there is no return false at the end of the function body.
Framework invariants relied on: un->thd and inner_join->thd point to a valid THD with a non-NULL lex; first_inner_unit()/next_unit()/next_select() return valid nodes or NULL.
sl->join may be NULL and is handled by the continue at line 60.
limitations: if (res) return TRUE; at lines 104-105 is dead code (res is always 0 there because a non-zero optimize() result returns at line 77); it has no security impact.

If every union member has NULL sl->join, empty_union_result stays true and no_rows_in_result() fires (lines 60-61, 107-108); whether that produces a wrong query result is unconfirmable from the shown code.

On the early failure returns (lines 57, 77), THD state (current_select, inner_join->select_options, sl->options) is left modified; any downstream unsafe consumption occurs outside the shown code, so no impact is confirmed.
The impact of the confirmed missing return (indeterminate bool) is consumed by a caller outside the shown code, which caps confidence at 0.6; no memory corruption is demonstrated, hence severity low.
No memory-safety, injection, crypto/entropy, or file/access-control sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: SafeToRemoveIdentity aborts the process when an Identity/IdentityN node's input edge names a node absent from the node map: node_map_->GetNode returns nullptr and the CHECK at lines 20-21 terminates the program instead of returning false. A malformed graph (e.g., an Identity node with input "ghost:0" or "^ghost") reaches this point because the only prior guard, node.input_size() >= 1 (line 14), validates the edge index but not that the referenced node exists. This is an attacker-triggerable denial of service (CWE-617) in any pipeline that runs the grappler optimizer on externally supplied graphs.

evidence.reason: node.input(0) has residual range "any edge string" because the only prior constraint (input_size() >= 1, line 14) bounds the edge index, not the referenced name. NodeName(node.input(0)) at line 19 is passed to node_map_->GetNode, which returns nullptr for names absent from the map (a possibility the CHECK itself acknowledges). Many earlier guards each admit this case: identity-family (line 2), node not preserved (line 6), fetch_nodes_known_==true (line 9), input_size==1 (line 14). Witness: Identity node "id" with input(0)="ghost:0" (or "^ghost") where node_map_ contains no "ghost"; every guard admits the witness and the CHECK then aborts the process (SIGABRT) instead of returning false. This is a reachable assertion on attacker-influenced graph data: primary mechanism CWE-617, denial of service; the affirmatively-checked-but-fatal handling of the GetNode status is the error/status-handling root cause.

assumptions: node_map_->GetNode returns nullptr for names not present in the map; the CHECK at line 20 confirms the shown code treats nullptr as a possible outcome.
AsControlDependency(node.name()) follows standard TensorFlow semantics (prepend '^' unless the name already starts with '^'); it is used only in a string equality comparison.
limitations: Whether an out-of-scope caller always pre-validates graphs so every input edge resolves is not shown; if such validation existed elsewhere it would reduce real-world reachability, but no such check is visible in the shown code.

For IdentityN nodes with multiple inputs, the checks at lines 28-33 do not protect consumers that read output slots > 0 via regular edges such as "id:1" (such edges pass the input_size>1 Retval/Merge guard and are never equal to the control-dep form "^id"); the resulting unsafe return true at line 39 is only harmful if the caller's rewrite logic mishandles multi-output nodes, which is outside the shown code.
Consumers returned by node_map_->GetOutputs are dereferenced at lines 28 and 32 without null checks; the non-null invariant of that collection is not established by the shown code.

Node names that are empty or begin with '^' interacting with AsControlDependency at line 33 depend on name-validation invariants not present in the shown code; no concrete failure is derivable in-scope.

verdict.summary: Unauthenticated remote DoS via NULL pointer dereference: an attacker-supplied JSON body with a non-string "scheme_type" passes the existence-only guard on line 16, makes json_string_value() return NULL, and crashes the strcmp-family call o_strcmp(NULL, "password"). A secondary log-injection issue lets attacker-controlled username/scheme strings inject newlines into y_log_message audit output.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled "scheme_type" from the parsed JSON body (line 3) reaches the o_strcmp sink at line 16. The guard only tests json_object_get(...) == NULL, whose admitted set includes every present JSON value; for any non-string value (e.g., the number 1 in {"username":"u","password":"p","scheme_type":1}, which also passes the line 15 non-empty-string check) json_string_value() returns NULL and o_strcmp(NULL, "password") dereferences NULL, crashing the process (CWE-476).

The attacker-controlled "username" JSON string is passed verbatim as the %s argument with no escaping, filtering, or length/character constraint anywhere between the body parse (line 3) and this log sink, so embedded newline and control characters survive and forge log entries (CWE-117); identical behavior exists at the audit-log sinks on lines 35, 70, 85, 105, 118.

assumptions: Jansson semantics: json_string_value() returns NULL and json_string_length() returns 0 for non-string JSON values; json_decref(NULL) is safe.
o_strcmp is the orcania strcmp wrapper (name-implied standard semantics); strcmp on a NULL pointer is undefined behavior and faults on standard libcs.
ulfius_get_json_body_request returns either NULL or a JSON object whose fields the attacker selects.
limitations: NULL-capable session_uid from get_session_id is passed unguarded to get_users_for_session (line 46) and its value is used for the refresh cookie (line 53); whether the callee accepts NULL is not shown, so no NULL-deref finding is confirmed there.
u_map_get(request->map_cookie, config->session_key) may return NULL at line 49; user_session_update's tolerance of NULL is not shown.

json_string_value(json_object_get(j_result, "username")) at lines 113/118 is not type-guarded; whether auth_check_identify_scheme returns G_OK without a string "username" is not visible in the shown code, so NULL flow there is unconfirmed.
ip_source (lines 35/70/105) and issued_for (lines 23/49/80/113) may be NULL from unshown producers; %s with NULL is UB but not a confirmed crash.
Session cookie is set with HttpOnly flag 0 (lines 27/53/84/117); this only matters given an out-of-scope XSS, so it is recorded as hardening, not a confirmed finding.
strftime(expires, 128, ...) against expires[129] is bounded and safe; the remaining y_log_message calls with attacker data share the reported log-injection mechanism but are not separate root causes.
No loops exist in the shown code, so loop-bound and parser-invariant analysis is vacuous.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code alone. The pps_id subscript (&avc->pps[pps_id], line 13) is guarded to the admitted set 0..255 (lines 11-12), and the sps subscript (&avc->sps[sps_id + GF_SVC_SSPS_ID_SHIFT], line 17) has no shown bound on sps_id, but in both cases the array capacities, the field types/ranges, and the constant value are not identifiable from the shown code, so no concrete witness index or exact excess can be derived. All other reads (bit counts, slice_type wrap) reduce to hardening concerns with no consuming security-relevant sink in the shown code.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_ue_log / gf_bs_read_int_log / gf_bs_read_se_log are GPAC bitstream-layer calls whose bodies are not shown; their results are treated as unsigned and attacker-influenced values within the residual ranges fixed by the shown guards.

The declarations of AVCState (capacities of pps and sps arrays) and the field types of AVC_PPS, AVC_SPS, and AVCSliceInfo are outside the shown snippet, so capacities, types, and value ranges are treated as unidentifiable.
limitations: CWE-125 candidate at line 17 (&avc->sps[si->pps->sps_id + GF_SVC_SSPS_ID_SHIFT]): the shown code imposes no constraint on pps->sps_id, but the field's type/range, the value of GF_SVC_SSPS_ID_SHIFT, and the capacity of avc->sps are not shown, so no admissible witness index or exact excess can be derived; demoted per the capacity rule.

CWE-125 candidate at line 13 (&avc->pps[pps_id]): the guard at lines 11-12 admits exactly 0..255, but the capacity of avc->pps is not identifiable from the shown code, so a boundary violation can be neither confirmed nor excluded.

If a PPS slot admitted by the pps_id guard was never populated by parser code outside the snippet, fields such as sps_id are uninitialized; the line 15 check tests only slice_group_count, so a stale nonzero value could steer the line 17 index, but the provenance is not attacker-controlled within the shown code and the index is not quantifiable.

Bit counts passed at lines 21 and 35 (log2_max_frame_num, log2_max_poc_lsb) are only constrained by the nonzero check on log2_max_frame_num at line 18; spec-invalid values could be passed to gf_bs_read_int_log, but no OOB is derivable in the shown code and the callee semantics are not shown.

slice_type, stored from an unsigned read into an s32 field (line 7), can wrap negative for values >= 2^31 and pass the >9 filter at line 8, but no security-relevant sink consumes slice_type in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmed in the shown code. evalUnaryOperator only dispatches on kind, negates a floating-point literal (a total IEEE-754 operation with no wrap), returns hard-coded strings, and fully consumes the results of its guard predicates; no attacker-influenced value is used as an index, size, length, pointer, format string, path, or any other security-relevant sink. The only dangerous-looking construct, the unguarded dereference of the `operand` parameter, is not a finding because no statement in the shown code can produce a null operand.

assumptions: `operand` is a valid non-null `Literal*` by caller contract; the shown code dereferences it at lines 8 and 30 without a check.

`LiteralNumber::getValue()` returns a double (Hermes API), so the negation at line 11 is total floating-point negation, not an integer negation subject to wrap; this return type is not redeclared in the snippet.
`evalIsTrue`/`evalIsFalse` are trusted predicates whose bodies are outside the shown code; their boolean results are fully consumed as branch guards, and the false/false case safely yields nullptr.
`builder` is a valid `IRBuilder&` reference (guaranteed by C++ reference semantics for a well-formed caller).
limitations: A null `operand` would be dereferenced at lines 8 and 30, but null is not producible by any path inside the shown code; only an out-of-scope caller could supply it, so it is not a confirmed finding.

If `LiteralNumber::getValue()` returned a narrow signed integer type (contrary to the Hermes API), negating the minimum value could wrap; the return type is not declared in the snippet, so this is unconfirmable and no CWE is attached.
Behavior of callers of `evalUnaryOperator` when it returns nullptr (line 63) is not shown; the null return is a conservative constant-folding bail-out, not a success-after-failure path.
A kind/type inconsistency where `getKind()` reports a kind but `dyn_cast` fails is not reachable through values the shown code can produce.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The stack name buffer is exactly protected: the guard at line 81 admits dire->size 0..SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1, and the copy plus NUL (memcpy lines 86-87, NUL line 88) touch at most index SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, the last valid index of the SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1-byte name region in the line 5-6 buffer. The dir_count guard (line 64) caps the inner loop, and the realloc scheme (lines 99-106) keeps dir->dirs[dir->dir_count] in range. Remaining concerns (reads past 'size' from the global directory_table, strcpy target capacity, NULL from read_inode, integer wrap in lines 47-48, negative dire->size if signed) all depend on types or capacities not present in the shown code, so they are unconfirmed limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: lookup_entry returns a valid non-negative position or -1 per its name/use; only -1 is treated as failure in the shown code.
read_inode returns a valid struct inode pointer on success; its NULL behavior is not shown.
dire->name is a trailing (zero-length/flexible) member of squashfs_dir_entry_2, so its region in the line 5-6 buffer is SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1 bytes; the struct definition is not shown.
SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, DIR_ENT_SIZE are positive constants as implied by the comments and guard usage.
directory_table points to a readable mapping whose capacity is not determinable from the shown code.
limitations: OOB read from directory_table (sinks at lines 53/56, 72/76, 86-87): the inner loop advances 'bytes' past 'size' without a per-entry re-check (bytes += sizeof(*dire) line 78, bytes += dire->size + 1 line 113), but the buffer capacity of directory_table is not identifiable from the shown code, so no exact excess can be demonstrated (CWE-125 unconfirmed).

If squashfs_dir_entry_2.size were a signed type, a negative value would pass line 81, underflow the memcpy length at lines 86-87, and overflow the stack buffer; the field's signedness is not shown, so this is unconfirmable.
strcpy at line 107 into dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name could overflow if struct dir_ent.name is smaller than the (bounded) source length; struct dir_ent is not shown.
NULL dereference of *i at lines 25-48 if read_inode returns NULL; the callee body is not shown.
Integer wrap in 'bytes += (*i)->offset' (line 47) and 'size = (*i)->data + bytes' (line 48) could yield negative indices or a corrupted loop bound, but the inode field types and ranges are not shown.

'(dir->dir_count + DIR_ENT_SIZE) * sizeof(struct dir_ent)' (lines 100-101) could wrap only for unrealistically large counts unreachable through the int 'size' loop bound; not demonstrated with shown types.
Log injection / content injection through dire->name at TRACE (lines 96-98) cannot be confirmed because check_name's rejected-character set (line 91) is not shown.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in the FEAT_GUI scrollbar-event loops of check_termcode: the loop conditions at lines 479-480 and 508-509 probe tp[j], tp[j+1], tp[j+2] with no bound against len (= *buflen - offset or typebuf.tb_len - offset). A crafted terminal stream beginning with CSI, KS_VER_SCROLLBAR (or KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR) and continuing the pattern advances j to 8+ per event, so index j+2 reaches and then exceeds len, reading past the input's codified extent. The only terminator is a data-dependent NUL byte that the shown code never guarantees for the buf path (and never proves for typebuf).

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; tp[j] == CSI && tp[j + 1] == KS_VER_SCROLLBAR
						     && tp[j + 2] != NUL; ++i)
evidence.reason: Sink: the loop condition dereferences tp[j+2] (and tp[j], tp[j+1]) with index j+2 unconstrained by len, the shown-code capacity (len = *buflen - offset at line 54, or typebuf.tb_len - offset at line 47). Taint: externally supplied bytes at tp, admitting any content; the GUI branch (lines 97-101) admits len >= 3 with key_name[0] = tp[1] = KS_VER_SCROLLBAR (line 100), and the else-if at line 471 is admitted. After one body pass j = 3 + 1 + sizeof(long_u) = 8 (lines 482-495); with *buflen = 10 the next condition read is tp[10], index == capacity, i.e. one element past the valid range, and nonzero trailing memory lets the loop continue further. No guard in the shown code bounds this loop; the sole terminator tp[j+2] != NUL depends on a NUL byte the shown code never establishes for buf. Confirmed OOB read (CWE-125), heap read beyond the input extent in GUI builds.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; tp[j] == CSI && tp[j + 1] == KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR
						     && tp[j + 2] != NUL; ++i)
evidence.reason: Sink: identical unbounded probe reads tp[j], tp[j+1], tp[j+2] for the horizontal-scrollbar code, with the same derivation as the KS_VER_SCROLLBAR case: j advances via j += 3 and j += num_bytes (lines 511-516) without re-checking len. Attacker terminal bytes make key_name[0] == KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR via line 100, the else-if at line 501 is admitted, and on the second iteration j = 8 reads tp[10] at or beyond the shown-code extent len (index == capacity with *buflen = 10), with continuation gated only by a data-dependent NUL not guaranteed in the shown code. Confirmed OOB read (CWE-125).

assumptions: Build flags FEAT_GUI enabled and USE_ON_FLY_SCROLL not defined, and gui.in_use is TRUE so the GUI special-key branch (lines 90-102) is taken.
The byte CSI is present in termleader so the early-out at lines 72-76 does not skip the position.

get_bytes_from_buf and get_long_from_buf have their name-implied semantics: they read the requested 1 / sizeof(long_u) bytes and return the byte count (or -1), so j advances to 8 after one full event on the crafted input.
Input bytes at tp (typebuf/tb_buf or buf) are treated as externally supplied terminal data.
limitations: For the typebuf path, whether the reads past tb_len stay inside the allocation depends on a NUL byte at tp + len that the shown code never establishes; the excess is confirmed only against the shown-code extent len, not against the allocation size.
Allocation sizes of typebuf.tb_buf and of caller-supplied buf are not visible in the shown code.
Bounds of the helper calls get_bytes_from_buf / get_long_from_buf at lines 361, 427, 448, 461, 483, 491, 512 cannot be confirmed because their bodies are not shown.
A possible overflow of string[MAX_KEY_CODE_LEN + 1] at lines 576, 578, 589-591 cannot be confirmed because modifiers2keycode / mb_char2bytes output bounds are not shown.
KS_MENU pointer fabrication from input bytes at line 431 (current_menu = (vimmenu_T *)val) is only mitigated by check_menu_pointer, whose body is not shown, so arbitrary-pointer use is unconfirmed.
handle_csi, handle_osc, handle_dcs and put_string_in_typebuf are called with buffer/length arguments but their bodies are not shown; any flaws inside them are out of scope for this analysis.
The always-compiled parser paths were checked and are protected by explicit len guards (lines 126-127, 148/155, 175/180, 239-244); no other confirmed finding was identified in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in evalUnaryOperator: the shown code contains no loops, no memory operations, and no attacker-derived index, size, length, format string, path, or query reaching a security-relevant sink. All handled literal cases fold to JS-correct values, and every path either returns a builder-created literal or the normal nullptr fallback. The dangerous-looking constructs (unguarded dereference of the internal-helper 'operand' parameter at lines 8 and 30, unary negation whose operand type is hidden by 'auto' at line 11, and the llvm_unreachable default at line 43) cannot be confirmed as reachable with an attacker-controlled value from the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: LiteralNumber::getValue() returns a double (Hermes convention), in which case the negation at line 11 is total IEEE negation; this type is not visible in the shown code.
evalIsTrue/evalIsFalse (used at lines 18, 47, 50) are helpers whose bodies are not shown; their truthiness results are only used as branch conditions returning defined literals.
The caller of evalUnaryOperator is expected to supply non-NULL, appropriately filtered Literal operands; no such invariant is established inside the shown code.
limitations: NULL operand dereference at 'switch (operand->getKind())' (lines 8 and 30) is not confirmable: the shown code never produces a NULL operand, and a NULL supplied only by an out-of-scope caller is excluded by the CWE-476 confirmation standard.

Integer overflow or signed-negation UB at 'auto V = -literalNum->getValue();' (line 11) is unconfirmable: the return type of getValue() is hidden by 'auto', no wrap can be shown in the shown types, and the result is consumed by a literal factory, not by a size/index/length/pointer-arithmetic sink.

llvm_unreachable('Invalid literal kind.') at line 43 is reachable in principle for any ValueKind not listed in the TypeofKind switch (e.g., a BigInt literal), but reachability depends on a caller that constant-folds typeof over such a literal; no such caller or guard appears in the shown code, so no attacker-controlled path is demonstrated.

Unchecked builder.getLiteral* allocations (lines 12, 16, 19, 21, 24, 33, 35, 37, 39, 41, 48, 51, 55) would only manifest as NULL literals returned to the caller or out-of-scope OOM; the shown code contains no loop over attacker-controlled volume and never dereferences these results.

verdict.summary: Null pointer dereference in ConstantFolding::EvaluateOneFoldable: the result of node_map_->GetNode(input) at line 24 is not checked for nullptr, and is dereferenced at line 25 through '*input_node'. An attacker-controlled graph whose node.input() references a name absent from the node map (e.g., "absent_node:0", admitted by the index() >= 0 guard at line 20) triggers a crash (DoS).

evidence.reason: The input name from node.input() (Phase 1 residual range: any parse with index() >= 0 after the line 20 guard) is passed to node_map_->GetNode at line 24; GetNode returns nullptr for a name absent from the map (standard lookup semantics, and the shown code neither guarantees presence nor checks the result). The only guard on this path, line 20's `index() < 0` break, admits all indices >= 0, including witness "absent_node:0" (index 0), so the dereference at line 25 runs on a null pointer, causing CWE-476 (NULL pointer dereference, process crash / DoS).

assumptions: node_map_ and the CheckAttrExists helper behave per their names: GetNode returns nullptr on lookup miss, CheckAttrExists returns non-OK when the 'value' attribute is absent.
outputs and result_too_large are non-null caller-provided pointers.
Tensor::TotalBytes() reflects bytes actually allocated after a successful FromProto (line 45).
limitations: Integer overflow of total_inputs_size (line 52) fed to CreateNodeDef (lines 67-68): each TotalBytes() term belongs to a materialized tensor, so the sum is bounded by real memory and a mod-2^64 wraparound is not demonstrable with values the shown code can produce; the callee's use of the 4th argument is also not visible, so no confirmed sink.

Denial of service via attacker-crafted tensor_shape (line 44) or a large output_tensors.size() (line 60) is resource exhaustion inherent to processing an attacker-chosen graph; allocation-failure behavior of the callees is not observable in the shown code.

An upstream graph validator outside the shown code could reject dangling input references before this function runs; per the shown-code-only rule this is not used to dismiss the finding, only to bound confidence.
Unchecked .at("value") at line 31 is presumed covered by CheckAttrExists at line 30; a defect inside CheckAttrExists would be outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: NULL-pointer dereference in ConstantFolding::IsSimplifiableReshape: the result of node_map_->GetNode(node.input(1)) is dereferenced at line 12 (*new_shape) with no null check. For a crafted graph whose reshape shape-input names a node absent from the node map, GetNode returns nullptr and IsReallyConstant dereferences it, crashing the optimizer (denial of service).

evidence.reason: node.input(1) is an entry-point input whose residual range is any node-name string; the only admission constraint is input_size() >= 2 (line 6), which the witness input_size() == 2 satisfies. GetNode is a name lookup returning a raw pointer, and the shown code imposes no check on it, so on a map miss the pointer is nullptr. Line 12 dereferences *new_shape with no intervening guard, yielding a NULL-pointer read/crash (primary CWE-476, DoS).

assumptions: NodeMap::GetNode returns nullptr when the requested node name is absent (standard raw-pointer lookup semantics; its body is not shown).
The GraphDef/node being optimized is attacker-controlled input, so node.input(1) is an externally influenceable entry-point input.
limitations: The element loops (lines 54-55 and 62-63) use int i against int64 NumElements(); an overflow/OOB read would require NumElements() > INT_MAX (a >2^31-element shape constant, about 8-16 GiB), and the vector push_back would exhaust memory first — not a demonstrated attacker value.

The inverted input-count guard at line 6 admits more than 2 inputs despite the message saying 'at most 2', but the shown code only ever indexes input(1), so no security impact is confirmable from the shown code.
