No runtime check on the path bounds the write; the only guards are assert() at lines 90/94/etc., which are not runtime bounds. Primary mechanism: heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) caused by u32 wraparound (CWE-190).

In the GF_EOS accumulation path, the allocation size is computed as ctx->hdr_store_size + pck_size - vosh_start and stored through an explicit (u32) truncation at line 299. When the accumulated header data plus the current packet reaches >= 2^32 (e.g., hdr_store_size=0xFFFFFFF0, pck_size=0x100, vosh_start=0), the stored hdr_store_alloc becomes 240 while the guard at line 298 compares against the wrapped value, so no realloc is performed and this memcpy writes pck_size-vosh_start (0x100) bytes at offset 0xFFFFFFF0 of a ~0xFFFFFFF0-byte buffer — an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-controlled size. Primary CWE-787; explicit u32 truncation/wraparound is CWE-190.

Identical sink statement to line 302 for the MPEG-4 (M4V_VOL_START_CODE) branch: hdr_store_alloc is truncated to u32 at line 343 after the wrapped sum at line 342, and this memcpy then copies an attacker-controlled pck_size-vosh_start bytes at offset hdr_store_size, past the end of the under-sized/realloc-skipped heap buffer once the accumulated header size crosses 2^32. Primary CWE-787, secondary CWE-190.

assumptions: Packet payloads and pck_size returned by gf_filter_pck_get_data (line 31) are derived from the media input and are attacker-controllable.

ctx->hdr_store_size and ctx->hdr_store_alloc are 32-bit unsigned fields: all shown aggregates are u32-width (pck_size u32, assignments at lines 69/79/299/303/343/347) and the EOS paths explicitly truncate with (u32).

The accumulation of hdr_store_size across packets is reachable while gf_m4v_parse_config keeps returning GF_EOS for an attacker-crafted, structurally incomplete VOL/config header (lines 292-306, 336-350), and hdr_store_size is reset only at line 398 on the successful-parse path.
limitations: The initial/allocation capacity of ctx->hdr_store is not identifiable from the shown code, so the fixed-size window writes/reads (lines 129, 139, 151, 172, 217, 256, 486, 524) cannot be assessed for OOB independent of the wrap finding.

The resume_from resume path (lines 89-99) is guarded only by assert() (90/94); an OOB there would require the filter framework to deliver a different or smaller buffer than the one in which resume_from was recorded without the packet having been dropped (lines 393-395) — the same-buffer invariants are framework contracts not established inside the shown code.

Post-parse consumption (lines 444-456, 528-530) and vosh obj_size consumption (lines 360-362) rely on gf_m4v_parse_frame / gf_m4v_get_object_start returning sizes no larger than the remaining buffer; a violation (negative remain reaching memcpy at line 129) would depend on callee behavior beyond its name-implied contract.
gf_realloc return values (lines 70, 300, 344) are unchecked; NULL dereference would additionally require allocator failure, whose behavior is outside the shown code.
The u64 DTS subtraction (lines 51-52) can underflow, but the result only affects FPS/timing fields, not a security-relevant sink.
The confirmed wrap requires roughly 4 GiB of adversarial input in the accumulate state; this is the practical (resource) gate on the finding, not a denial of its reachability.

verdict.summary: The non-scalar scatter path validates only the RANK of updates (line 10-11) and that indices.shape is a prefix of updates.shape (line 58), but never compares updates.shape[indices.dims():] against params.shape[1:]. With params [5,3], indices shape [8], and updates [8,7], line 63 derives updates_flat of width 7 while params_flat rows (line 43) have width 3; ScatterFunctor (line 66-67) then writes out of bounds on the heap for in-range indices, and since all indices are valid it returns bad_i=-1 so the op completes 'successfully'.

evidence.snippet:
const Index bad_i = functor(c, c->template eigen_device<Device>(),
                                    params_flat, updates_flat, indices_flat);
evidence.reason: ScatterFunctor sink: params_flat is a {5,3} view (line 43) over a 15-element buffer, while updates_flat is derived at line 63 as {N, num_updates/N} = {8,7} from entry-point indices shape [8] and updates shape [8,7] (Phase 1 residual ranges: rank check line 10-11 admits 2 == 1+2-1; prefix check line 58 admits [8,7] with prefix [8]; no inner-dim check exists anywhere in the shown code). For in-range index values in [0,5), the functor writes 7 columns per params row of width 3: index 4 writes physical offsets 12..18, exceeding the 15-element capacity by 3 elements - a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Because all indices are in range, bad_i == -1 and OP_REQUIRES(bad_i < 0) at line 68 passes, so the corruption occurs on the success path.

assumptions: ScatterFunctor follows its name-implied standard semantics: for each position i it writes updates_flat(i, 0..num_updates/N-1) into params_flat(indices_flat(i), ...) and returns -1 when every index lies in [0, params->dim_size(0)).
flat_outer_dims<T>() and shaped<T,2>() create non-padded reshaped views over the existing buffers.
Index is a signed integer type (int32/int64) as implied by the kIndex/newer two's-complement usage (numeric_limits<Index>::max()).
limitations: The functor bodies are not shown; the confirmed derivation is the out-of-domain width created at line 63 (num_updates/N = 7) relative to the params row width (3), and the finding relies on the standard scatter semantics implied by the call site rather than the callee source.

The DIV zero-validation at lines 36-39 runs only for CPU devices; on GPU, zero updates with op==DIV could trigger division-by-zero behavior (e.g., UB for integer T) - not a memory-safety issue and not confirmed as a vulnerability from the shown code.

The error-path read indices_flat(bad_i) (lines 53, 71) is in-bounds under the assumed functor contract bad_i in [-1, N-1]; if a functor variant returned bad_i outside that range it would warrant a separate review, but that behavior is not established by the shown code.
Truncation of N_big to Index (line 27) is guarded by the max() comparison at line 22 and is not independently exploitable.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. All array processing is delegated to unshown kernel bodies, and the only local arithmetic (negation of params.zero_point at lines 4-5) can overflow for INT32_MIN but the corrupted value reaches only arithmetic fixed-point offsets in op_params, never an allocation-size, index, length, or pointer-arithmetic sink in the shown code.

assumptions: TfLiteTensor.params.scale and params.zero_point are populated by the interpreter before this kernel executes for quantized tensors; this invariant is not enforced by the shown code and is not relied on for any safety conclusion.
Every field of ComparisonParams is assigned in the shown code (lines 18-24), so no default/zeroed struct state is relied upon.
QuantizeMultiplierSmallerThanOneExp is the TFLite reference helper that writes both output parameters via pointers; its body is not shown.
limitations: NULL tensor pointers (input1/input2/output) are never checked in the shown code, but NULL cannot be produced on any path inside the shown code, so a NULL dereference is only reachable from an out-of-scope caller.

Negating params.zero_point when it equals INT32_MIN (lines 4-5) is signed overflow (UB, wraps to INT32_MIN); the value flows only into arithmetic op_params fields consumed by the kernels, with no memory-index/size/pointer sink in the shown code, so CWE-190 cannot be confirmed here.

params.scale is passed to QuantizeMultiplierSmallerThanOneExp (lines 10, 14) without validation (e.g., 0, negative, or NaN); the helper body is not shown and its outputs reach no memory sink in the shown code.

The branch at line 3 validates input1->type only; input2->type and output->type are never checked in the shown code, but any impact (e.g., reading params of a non-quantized input2) depends on unshown callee arithmetic.

All actual bounds/indexing occur inside reference_ops::BroadcastComparison4DSlowWithScaling and ComparisonWithScaling (lines 26-34), whose bodies are not shown; any OOB or status-handling flaw there is unconfirmable from this snippet.
input1_shift/input2_shift are uninitialized until the helper writes them (lines 9, 13, 10-11, 14-15); uninitialized use would require helper misbehavior that is not shown.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad kernel performs an out-of-bounds heap write into in_backprop_tensor_temp: row/col pooling-sequence values (context inputs 2/3) are used as in_row_start/in_col_start with no lower-bound check. A negative sequence value yields a negative in_index (line 103) that is passed to Eigen coeffRef (line 109) and written through the returned reference (lines 110-111), corrupting memory before the buffer. The guards at lines 38/44 only bound the seq-array indices and the std::min caps at lines 89/94 only bound the upper end.

evidence.reason: in_index (line 103) is derived from in_row_start = row_seq_tensor_flat(r) (line 86) and in_col_start = col_seq_tensor_flat(c) (line 91), whose values are attacker-controlled int64 with residual range [-2^63, 2^63-1] (only the element count of the seq tensors is checked, lines 38/44). The guard at line 89 (std::min(in_row_end, in_max_row_index)) caps only the upper end; in_row_start is unconstrained, so the loop at line 101 admits negative in_r. Witness: orig shape [1,4,4,1], out_backprop [1,1,1,1], row_seq=[-1,0], col_seq=[0,1], overlapping=false => in_row_start=-1, in_row_end=-1, in_col_start=0, in_col_end=0, in_index=(0*4+(-1))*4+0=-4; coeffRef(0,-4) with column-major storage yields storage offset 0+(-4)*1=-4, i.e. a reference 32 bytes before the in_backprop_tensor_temp buffer, written by in_backprop_ref += (lines 110-111): out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787).

assumptions: overlapping_ is the op attribute exposed as a bool member used at lines 87/92.
Eigen::Map<Eigen::Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic>> is column-major by default, so coeffRef(row, col) accesses data()[row + col*rows].
out_backprop.dim_size(i) is non-negative for an allocated tensor.
limitations: Same sink is also reachable with valid sequences when out_depth (line 36) exceeds in_depth (line 58/75): the d-loop at line 105 indexes in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat (rows = in_depth) with d < out_depth, so storage offset d + in_index*in_depth can equal the buffer length; e.g. in_shape [1,2,2,1], out_depth 2, row_seq=[0,2], col_seq=[0,2] yields a one-past-the-end write at d=1, in_index=3. Not reported as a separate CWE since it is the same sink statement.

A negative value in orig_input_tensor_shape (lines 55-58) reaches in_shape.AddDim (line 64) unconstrained and would trigger the framework's hard CHECK_GE abort (availability/DoS only; not counted in the verdict CWE).

int64 overflow of in_cols*in_rows*in_batch (line 76) and of num_elements_in_pooling_cell (lines 96-97) is conceivable only with implausibly large positive dims that would fail allocation first; a negative divisor yields only IEEE double Inf/NaN, not memory corruption.
No analysis performed on callee internals beyond standard Eigen coeffRef index semantics and TensorShape::AddDim's documented dimension check.

verdict.summary: FractionalAvgPoolGrad::Compute indexes the heap temporary buffer with unvalidated pooling-sequence values. row_seq_tensor/col_seq_tensor values have no value-range guard (only element counts are checked, lines 38-49), so a negative in_row_start/in_col_start (line 98/103) makes the inner loops (lines 113-114) run with negative in_r/in_c, and line 115 derives in_index = -2, which line 121 passes to Eigen coeffRef -> out-of-bounds heap read-modify-write before in_backprop_tensor_temp (CWE-787). The same sink is also reachable past the end when out_depth > in_depth (line 117 vs. the in_depth rows of the map at lines 86-88).

evidence.reason: row_seq_tensor values are entry-point data whose only shown guard (lines 38-43) limits element count (NumElements > out_rows), leaving each flat<int64> value unconstrained in [INT64_MIN, INT64_MAX]. Line 98 assigns in_row_start = row_seq_tensor_flat(r) with no lower clamp (line 101 caps only in_row_end), so -1 is in the admitted set. With overlapping_=false, out_backprop shape (1,1,1,1), orig shape [1,2,2,1], row_seq=[-1,0], col_seq=[0,1], all guards (38/44/59-70) admit these values; the loop at line 113 runs in_r=-1 and line 115 derives in_index=(0*2-1)*2+0=-2 against a 4-double temp buffer allocated from in_shape at lines 74-83 and mapped at lines 86-88. coeffRef(0,-2) at line 121 dereferences 16 bytes before the heap buffer: confirmed out-of-bounds read-modify-write (CWE-787).

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK abort Compute on failed conditions (standard TF macros), so failed allocations and the sequence-length guards are effective at blocking those specific failures.
Op inputs (orig_input_tensor_shape, out_backprop, row/col sequence tensors) are attacker-controllable per the TF op/kernel threat model (malicious graph/model).
out_backprop dims are non-negative per the framework Tensor invariant; the attacker controls their values within that invariant.
The Eigen matrix-map OOB claim holds for either storage ordering: an index of -2 maps below the buffer start in column-major (offset -2*in_depth) and row-major (offset -2) alike.
limitations: out_depth > in_depth reaches the same coeffRef sink at line 121 one element past the end for the outermost valid in_index column; it is a second manifestation of the same missing-value-validation root cause and is not reported as a separate CWE.

Negative dims in orig_input_tensor_shape (covered only by the != 0 guards) would likely fail at the temp allocation (lines 81-83) and abort via OP_REQUIRES_OK before use, so no separate memory-safety vector is claimed for them.
Division by zero at line 123 is not reachable: a zero denominator implies start == end+1 for a dimension, which empties the corresponding inner loop so the division statement never executes.

Int64 overflow of in_index/num_elements_in_pooling_cell with extreme dimension values was not separately confirmed; such dimensions generally fail allocation first, and any such path is dominated by the confirmed OOB.
No hang finding: each inner loop is bounded once start/end are fixed; adversarial values yield immediate OOB rather than unbounded execution.

verdict.summary: In VNC_MSG_CLIENT_SET_ENCODINGS, the attacker-controlled uint16_t encoding count 'limit' (read from data[2..3]) drives a loop that reads (read_s32) and writes (memcpy, 4 bytes) at data+4+i*4 without any check that len >= 4 + 4*limit. A crafted message with a large limit but a small received length causes a remote heap out-of-bounds write/read on the VNC server, enabling memory corruption or crash. The shown code never validates len against the dereferenced offsets.

evidence.reason: Primary CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write. The destination pointer data+4+i*4 and i are derived from the attacker-controlled uint16_t 'limit' (0..65535, from read_u16(data,2) at line 27/31) with no len>=4+4*limit check. For i=limit-1 the 4-byte memcpy ends at data+4+4*limit, which exceeds the len-byte buffer whenever len<4+4*limit; every shown guard (len!=1, and len!=4 or limit==0) admits such input.

OOB read of the same root cause: index 4+i*4 up to 4+(limit-1)*4 reads beyond the len-sized data buffer when len<4+4*limit, with limit attacker-controlled and unvalidated. Same primary CWE-787 root; noted to reinforce the confirmed mechanism.

set_encodings is handed attacker-controlled count 'limit' over data+4 without a len>=4+4*limit check; its standard semantics consume limit*4 bytes, producing the same OOB read when len is insufficient. Same root cause as the primary CWE-787 finding.

assumptions: data is a buffer of len bytes allocated by the VNC read path (len is the actual received length passed to this handler).
limit is fully attacker-controlled with residual range 0..65535 (uint16_t).
limitations: Reachability of len<4+4*limit at loop entry depends on the unseen vnc_read_when/caller sizing behavior; the nominal return-4+limit*4 handshake may size the buffer to match, which is why confidence is ~0.6 rather than higher. The shown code itself provides no in-function length validation, so the missing check is genuine.

The other message cases (e.g., pixel-format reads at offsets 4..16 with 2<=len<=16, and the else-branch read_u16(data,2) when len<4) exhibit the same missing-len-validation root cause as OOB reads (CWE-125) but are not added as independent CWEs since they share the same root and are less severe than the encoding write.

CUT_TEXT's return 8+dlen uses uint32_t arithmetic; a dlen near 0xFFFFFFFF would wrap 8+dlen, but the resulting behavior depends on unseen read-layer handling and is not a confirmed independent finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown PQconnectPoll. Each dangerous sink is protected by an in-code guard with a stated admitted set: server-supplied msgLength is range-validated to [8,2000] for 'R' (line 1056) and [8,30000] for 'E' (line 1064) before any use, the message body is only processed after avail >= msgLength-4 with bounded buffer growth (1095, 1102), and the length passed to pg_fe_sendauth exactly matches the remaining buffered bytes. SSL/GSS negotiation rejects non-'S'/'N'/'E' (resp. non-'E'/'N'/'G') replies, fails closed on require/verify downgrades (810-818), and aborts on any unencrypted data left after the handshake (860-865, 972-977). Port input is clamped to [1,65535] (132) before use and requirepeer peer-credential checks fail closed (567-623). All return statuses in the function are consumed; format strings are literal with matched arguments. Residual concerns are DoS-only or rely on OS invariants not restated in the shown code and are listed in notes.limitations.

assumptions: conn is a fully initialized PGconn whose connhost[] array is populated by the caller; the shown code bounds every access to it via nconnhost (lines 86-106, 100).
pqGetc/pqGetInt/pqGets_append/pqCheckInBufferSpace and the PQExpBuffer helpers enforce inBuffer/PQExpBuffer bounds and return failure without advancing the cursor when data is short.
getaddrinfo (via pg_getaddrinfo_all) returns sockaddr records that fit in struct sockaddr_storage, so memcpy at 281-283 stays in bounds (POSIX-level invariant; see limitations).
conn->sslmode/gssencmode were validated to known values before this function runs; only their first character is consumed here.
PQgetvalue returns a NUL-terminated string, so strncmp(val, "on", 2) / strncmp(val, "t", 1) are bounded regardless of row content.
conn->inCursor and conn->inEnd are non-negative and satisfy inStart <= inCursor <= inEnd, making avail = inEnd - inCursor non-negative.
limitations: The Unix-socket path check at line 174 (strlen(portstr) >= UNIXSOCK_PATH_BUFLEN) can never fire: the standard UNIXSOCK_PATH macro writes at most UNIXSOCK_PATH_BUFLEN-1 chars plus NUL into portstr. The failure mode is silent truncation of a path the client itself supplied (connect would fail or target a path the client chose), with no memory-safety effect. UNIXSOCK_PATH_BUFLEN is not defined in the shown snippet, so any explicit boundary claim is unconfirmable.

The pre-3.0 error fallback (lines 1064-1087) rewinds inCursor to inStart+1 and re-appends buffered bytes to conn->errorMessage on each poll when the peer never sends a newline (pqGets_append returns EOF without advancing inStart). A malicious pre-3.0-protocol peer can make errorMessage grow without bound across repeated polls. This is a resource-exhaustion-only concern whose volume scales with attacker input in a reachable loop, so it is not reported as a finding.

The memcpy at 281-283 forwards getaddrinfo's ai_addrlen into a sockaddr_storage-sized destination. The shown code does not restate the OS invariant ai_addrlen <= sizeof(sockaddr_storage), and no attacker-controlled value derives the length in the shown code, so no OOB write is confirmable.
The ignored strdup return at line 296 leaves conn->connip NULL on failure; conn->connip is not dereferenced anywhere in the shown code.

Error-message formatting of client-supplied connection parameters (ch->host, ch->port, requirepeer) into conn->errorMessage is same-principal data with no distinct trust boundary and no non-literalf format string; no injection finding.
strcmp(conn->last_sqlstate, ...) at line 1127 relies on pqGetErrorNotice3 (callee not shown) having set last_sqlstate after a successful parse; a NULL there is unconfirmable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code alone. All memory-touching behavior is inside the unshown reference_ops comparison helpers, and the shown code forwards only params, shape objects, and data pointers — it derives no index, size, or length from input at any call site. Candidates (missing input2/output type validation, INT32_MIN zero_point negation overflow, discarded QuantizeMultiplier status, trusted requires_broadcast flag) fail the impact/reachability confirmation standards and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: Template parameters input_dtype/opname are instantiated consistently with input1->type by an unshown dispatch.
QuantizeMultiplier and GetTensorShape/GetTensorData behave per their standard TFLite semantics; QuantizeMultiplier's own body is unshown and is assumed to initialize its out-parameters.
Tensor data buffers are allocated with capacity matching each tensor's own shape and element size (standard TFLite invariant, not visible in the shown code).
limitations: The only tensor type guard is on input1->type (line 3); input2->type (and output->type) are unconstrained in the shown code, so GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2) (lines 26, 31) can reinterpret mismatched-type storage (e.g., uint8 vs float). Element-wise reads over each tensor's own shape keep reads inside each buffer, so no OOB or memory-corruption impact is derivable; the observable effect is incorrect results — a robustness/type-confusion concern, not a confirmed CWE.

Negating zero_point at lines 4-5 overflows for zero_point == INT32_MIN, but the wrapped value only reaches op_params.input*_offset (lines 17, 20) as numeric data and is not consumed by an allocation-size, index, length, or pointer-arithmetic sink in the shown code, so no CWE-190/CWE-195 finding is confirmable.

QuantizeMultiplier return values (lines 12-13) are discarded; the callee declaration is unshown (standard signature returns void) and no failure-state-dependent operation follows, so no error/status-handling flaw is confirmable.

requires_broadcast (line 23) is trusted without shape-equality validation; if false while shapes differ, the non-broadcast helper could index the smaller tensor, but the flag's correctness is a caller-established invariant outside the shown code and the failure would occur inside the unshown callee.

All actual memory operations (comparison loops, broadcast indexing, quantized arithmetic) reside in the unshown reference_ops helpers, so buffer capacities and boundary behavior there are unconfirmable from the shown code.
Pathological scale values (0, NaN, negative, >1) are passed to QuantizeMultiplier (lines 12-13) without checks in the shown code; resulting behavior is callee-internal and unconfirmed.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown fragment. Every flat-tensor index derives at least partly from out-of-scope helper results: output_flat capacity from GetOutputShape (line 31), big_stride/small_stride from GetStrides (line 52), and relative_offset_set contents/size from GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets (line 54). The present segment-id guard (line 43) admits exactly [0, num_segments) for each element and runs before the work loop, and all OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK failures abort Compute; the remaining OOB/overflow candidates lack a witness traceable entirely within the shown code and are recorded as limitations without CWEs.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES and OP_REQUIRES_OK abort Compute and return the error status on failure (standard TensorFlow macro semantics).
flat<T>() views (lines 36-38) have element counts equal to the tensors' element counts, and operator()(i) reads element i for i in [0, size).
TensorShape::dims()/dim_size() return the tensor's rank/dimensions (non-negative for a live tensor).
INDICES_TYPE and NUM_SEGMENTS_TYPE are the intended signed integer instantiations for the guard analysis; unsigned or mixed-signedness behavior is not fixed in the shown code.
separator_ is a valid std::string member; append/c_str() on tstring follows standard sized, checked semantics with no OS/command/shell interpretation.
limitations: OOB write to output_flat (CWE-787): output_index (line 57) used at lines 59-61; output_flat capacity is set by GetOutputShape (line 31), whose body is not shown, so no boundary witness (index >= capacity) can be derived from the shown code.

OOB read of flat_input (CWE-125): offset (line 58) = start_offset + relative_offset_set[i]; the range of relative_offset_set elements and its size come from GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets (line 54), not shown, so the derivation cannot be traced entirely within the shown code.

OOB read / unvalidated flat_segment_id(i) in the work loop (line 57): the guard loop (line 40) bounds i by flat_segment_id.size(), but the work loop (line 56) bounds i by relative_offset_set.size(); a size mismatch is only possible if the unshown helper returns more elements than the segment_id tensor, which cannot be established here.

Integer overflow of flat_segment_id(i) * big_stride (line 57, CWE-190): operand magnitudes (num_segments, big_stride from GetStrides at line 52) are unconstrained by the shown code, and the allocation at line 31-32 must first have succeeded with sizes derived from the same values, making the overflow path unconfirmable.

int loop counters at lines 40, 55, 56 (int vs int64/size_t bounds): non-termination or signed-overflow UB would require an element count or stride above INT_MAX, which needs tensors beyond limits not stated in the shown code.

num_segments < 0 with an empty segment_id skips the validation loop (line 40); rejection then depends on GetOutputShape/allocate_output, which are not shown. Signedness issues from template types INDICES_TYPE/NUM_SEGMENTS_TYPE are also not fixed in the shown code.

Large num_segments leads to a proportional output allocation (lines 31-32): resource exhaustion is intrinsic to the op's documented output size; allocation failure is handled by OP_REQUIRES_OK, and no attacker-controlled amplification beyond output sizing is shown.

verdict.summary: TransposeShapeFn's reshape loops (lines 49, 58) compare a 32-bit counter (int32_t/int) against attacker-influenced int64 'rank' with no upper bound in the shown code. When rank >= 2^31 (reachable via a perm_shape whose declared dims make NumElements(perm_shape) = 2^31, e.g. perm_shape = [2^31], perm == nullptr), ++i at the loop increment wraps to -2^31 and the body still executes because i < rank promotes true, indexing data[i] (line 50) and dims[i] (lines 55, 59) far out of bounds — an attacker-controlled heap OOB write (CWE-787) caused by the counter overflow (CWE-190), with a corresponding OOB read at line 50.

evidence.reason: Rank (residual range [2, INT64_MAX], uncapped by the shown code) is entry-point derived from NumElements(perm_shape)/perm->NumElements()/c->Rank and is the loop bound at line 49. The int32_t counter wraps to -2^31 at rank = 2^31 (line 49 condition i < rank stays true after promotion), so data[-2^31] reads 2^31 elements before the start of the rank-element vector data — confirmed OOB read (CWE-125 within the same CWE-787/CWE-190 root cause).

The in_idx guard at lines 51-54 admits in_idx in [-(rank-1), rank-1], but it protects only the c->Dim argument, not the vector index i. For rank = 2^31 (perm != nullptr variant with a 2^31-element constant, or input-rank variant), int32_t i wraps negative after 2^31-1 and the shown code writes dims[-2^31], 2^31 elements before the 2^31-capacity dims vector — confirmed heap OOB write (CWE-787), root cause integer overflow of the counter (CWE-190).

Cleanest witness path: perm == nullptr, input rank unknown, perm_shape = [2^31] makes perm_elems value-known, so line 9 is skipped, line 18 gives rank = 2^31, lines 23/33/35/36 all admit it, and this else-branch loop uses int i; after i = 2^31-1, ++i wraps to -2^31 and this statement writes dims[-2^31], an index 2^31 elements before the 2^31-capacity vector — confirmed heap OOB write (CWE-787) caused by the 32-bit counter overflow (CWE-190); no guard in the shown code bounds rank above 2^31-1.

assumptions: Framework invariants in the shown code's environment: RankKnown(input) implies rank >= 0, known dimension values are non-negative, and input(1)/input_tensor(1) describe the same tensor so perm->NumElements() equals NumElements(perm_shape); AsInt64<T>(perm, rank) reads exactly the rank elements its num_elems argument specifies.

The witness path assumes the dims.resize(rank) allocation at line 32 succeeds for rank = 2^31 (16 GiB for 8-byte handles); the attacker controls rank directly, but the OOB write manifests only if that allocation does not throw.
Signed overflow of ++i (lines 49/58) is formally undefined behavior in C++; the analysis assumes the standard two's-complement wrap in effect.
limitations: Negative in_idx values admitted by the guard at lines 51-54 reach c->Dim(input, in_idx) at line 55; whether this is a memory-safety failure depends on callee behavior not shown here (standard TensorFlow Dim semantics range-check and return UnknownDim), so it is not reported as a finding.

dims.resize(rank) at line 32 with a huge attacker-controlled rank can abort via bad_alloc/length_error before the OOB loop path executes, which is a DoS/resource-exhaustion concern (CWE-770) rather than the confirmed memory-corruption mechanism.

Practical TensorFlow constraints outside the shown code (graph serialization/tensor-size limits) may cap achievable rank below 2^31 in deployment, which narrows reachability of the confirmed overflow but does not remove the shown code's own absence of an upper-bound check.
The OOB read at line 50 requires the perm-branch variant (a constant perm of 2^31 elements), which is heavier to instantiate than the else-branch write path at line 59.

verdict.summary: The shown code is a standard device release callback: it recovers the containing rtrs_clt_sess via container_of with a compile-time constant offset and frees it exactly once. No input is parsed or attacker-controlled within the shown code, no branch or loop exists, and every potential failure (invalid pointer, NULL dev, double free) requires caller/device-core state that is not producible inside the shown code. verdict.summary: Run-mode decoding uses the attacker-controlled run length returned by DecodeRun as an unvalidated write count: when run exceeds the remaining line pixels (m_ulWidth[0]), the stores at *lp[cx]++ advance past the end of the per-component line sample buffer (heap OOB write), and run--,length-- underflows length below zero so the while(--length) pixel loop never terminates, continuing unbounded stores.

evidence.reason: run, returned by DecodeRun at line 66 from the attacker-controlled bitstream, is used as the write count of while(run) (line 69) with no clamp to the remaining line samples (length initialized from m_ulWidth[0] at line 36); the guard at line 61 only tests gradient run-conditions and does not bound run. For run = W+1 where W = m_ulWidth[0], the loop performs W+1 stores per component via lp[cx] (set to line[cx]->m_pData at line 41), 1 element past the W-sample per-component line buffer (CWE-787); run--,length-- at line 77 underflows length to -1, making the truthy if(length) at line 83 and while(--length) at line 155 keep firing further stores.

After run = W+1, length has been underflowed to -1 by run--,length-- (line 77); the guard if(length) at line 83 is truthy for the admitted negative value (it excludes only 0), so this run-interruption store executes as an additional out-of-bounds write past the same W-sample per-component buffer, compounding the CWE-787 heap overflow.

assumptions: Each Line's m_pData holds exactly m_ulWidth[0] samples per component; the only capacity evidence in the shown code is its own accounting (LONG length = m_ulWidth[0] at line 36 and exactly W stores per component on the well-formed path), since the buffer allocation is not shown.
m_ulRemaining, m_ulWidth, m_ucCount, and m_lRunIndex are decoder state derived from the JPEG-LS header/scan; only the residual ranges left by guards visible inside this function are analyzed.
limitations: The concrete value run > length cannot be traced through the shown code because DecodeRun's body is not shown; whether a crafted bitstream can make it return a run exceeding its length argument (versus capping internally) is not demonstrated here, so the finding is range-confirmed rather than single-value-confirmed.

If DecodeRun internally caps run at the passed length, the overflow is not reachable for non-negative lengths; the shown code still does not enforce the invariant itself, so safety cannot be concluded from that unshown callee behavior.

A negative m_ulRemaining[0] would make while(--lines) (line 164) non-terminating, but the shown state machine cannot drive remaining negative from a valid non-negative start (it subtracts at most the remaining value and returns false at lines == 0), so the negative value requires external corrupt state.

CurrentLine(cx) results are dereferenced (lines 41/161) with no NULL check; NULL is not producible by the shown code.

The falsy result of BeginReadMCU (line 45) only skips decoding, and ParseMCU unconditionally returns false (line 172) after success; these are error-status/decode-correctness concerns (CWE-703/754 candidates) with no demonstrated memory-safety consequence.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled length (argv[3], e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF) is held in an unsigned int and assigned to a signed int nbytes at line 65, becoming negative on two's-complement targets. The ternary at line 70 admits the false branch for every nbytes <= DISP_LINE_LEN, including all negatives, so linebytes = -1. Passing -1 as the read length for the DISP_LINE_LEN-byte linebuf is a negative signed size that the callee consumes as a huge unsigned length (CWE-195), overrunning the stack buffer linebuf; the ret check at line 77 executes only after the overflow.

evidence.snippet: ret = i2c_read(chip, addr, alen, linebuf, linebytes);
evidence.reason: Same taint and derivation as the DM path: length >= 0x80000000 from argv[3] yields negative nbytes at line 65, the line 70 guard admits it (false branch, nbytes <= DISP_LINE_LEN), and linebytes = -1 is forwarded as the buffer length for linebuf (capacity DISP_LINE_LEN). The negative signed size is converted to a huge unsigned size by the callee (CWE-195), writing far beyond the 16-byte stack buffer linebuf (CWE-787 impact); the post-call ret check at line 77 cannot prevent it.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled delay_den from an APNG fcTL chunk (line 147, residual range [0,65535]) reaches the integer division at line 78 (bundle.duration = delay_num * 1000 / delay_den) with no zero check anywhere in the shown code; a crafted APNG with delay_den=0 and a valid 1x1 IDAT triggers division by zero (SIGFPE/abort), a remotely triggerable denial of service in decoders processing untrusted images.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in xfrm_migrate(): the Stage-2 loop (lines 23-35) stores migration states into the fixed-capacity arrays x_cur and x_new (declared with XFRM_MAX_DEPTH entries at lines 9-10) at indices nx_cur/nx_new, which are incremented once per successful state find/migrate and never bounded against XFRM_MAX_DEPTH. With num_migrate = XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 and every state lookup/migration succeeding, the (XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1)-th iteration writes x_cur[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] at line 25 (and x_new[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH] at line 29), corrupting the kernel stack (CWE-787).

For num_migrate = XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 with xfrm_migrate_state_find returning non-NULL each iteration (admitted by the guard at line 24), the write at line 25 executes with index nx_cur == XFRM_MAX_DEPTH, exactly one past the maximum valid index — an out-of-bounds stack write of a pointer-sized value (CWE-787).

With num_migrate = XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 and all migrations succeeding, the write at line 29 uses index nx_new == XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (index equals capacity), an out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787).

assumptions: XFRM_MAX_DEPTH as used in the declarations at lines 9-10 is the capacity of both arrays, giving valid indices 0..XFRM_MAX_DEPTH-1.
xfrm_migrate_state_find (line 24) and xfrm_state_migrate (line 27) can return non-NULL for consecutive migration entries so the loop body admits non-NULL values on every iteration.

limitations: The body of xfrm_migrate_check (line 13) is not shown; if that helper enforced num_migrate <= XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (as later upstream fixes do), the overflow would be unreachable. The post-corruption OOB reads implied at lines 44-45, 61, and 63 use the same unbounded nx_cur/nx_new counts and are the same root cause, not an independent CWE.

Bodies of xfrm_migrate_policy_find, xfrm_state_migrate, xfrm_policy_migrate, km_migrate, xfrm_states_put, and xfrm_states_delete are not shown; their semantics are assumed only as implied by name and usage in the shown code.

verdict.summary: In ljpeg_start, the JPEG segment length is converted to int `len` at line 14 with no range check; a length word of 0x0000 yields len=-2, which is passed as a huge size_t element count to fread at line 16, making fread copy the entire remaining file into the 65536-byte stack buffer `data` (declared line 4) and overflow it with attacker-controlled bytes (CWE-787 stack out-of-bounds write, root-caused by CWE-195 signed-to-unsigned conversion of the negative length). A crafted file starting with FF D8, then marker FF 01 and length 00 00, followed by at least 65537 bytes, triggers the overflow.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled file bytes data[2..3] (read at line 12 with return discarded) are reduced by 2 into int `len` at line 14 with residual range -2..65533 and no validity check; the only prior guard, line 15, constrains tag (admits 0xff01..0xffff) but is independent of the length field, so tag=0xff01 with length word 0x0000 (len=-2) passes. At this fread sink the negative int is converted to a huge size_t nmemb ((size_t)-2 = SIZE_MAX-1), so fread reads to EOF and writes the remaining file contents into the 65536-byte stack buffer declared at line 4, writing at least one byte past data[65535] for a file with >=65537 trailing bytes — a stack out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) enabled by the signed-to-unsigned conversion of the negative length (CWE-195).

assumptions: `ifp` is the input stream whose bytes are attacker-controlled file content consumed by fread/getc; no further constraint on those bytes appears in the shown code.
`data` is a stack buffer of exactly 0x10000 = 65536 bytes (declared at line 4).
Standard `fread` semantics: it reads up to nmemb one-byte items or until EOF/error, and a negative int passed as nmemb is converted to a huge size_t before the call.

`dng_version`, `zero_after_ff`, `merror`, `FORC`, `make_decoder_ref`, and the `jhead` struct fields are defined outside the shown code; merror is treated as abort-on-failure, so no NULL-deref is derivable from the shown code.

`make_decoder_ref` body is not shown; any over-read past the Huffman table segment performed inside it cannot be confirmed from the shown code.

Unchecked `fread` returns at lines 9/12/16 mean truncated files cause stale/uninitialized stack bytes to be parsed; this has no attacker-controlled OOB beyond the confirmed negative-length case and is treated as stale-data processing only.

After the negative-length fread consumes the stream to EOF (lines 16/39 path), the main loop can spin forever when the stale tag never equals 0xffda; this attacker-triggerable hang shares the same missing-length-check root cause and is noted as a secondary DoS consequence, not a separate CWE.
The `calloc` at line 47 is bounded by the shown guards (wide <= 65535, clrs <= 6 via line 41) and the int product cannot wrap; no finding there.

verdict.summary: The release callback performs container_of-derived pointer arithmetic, two mutex_destroy calls, and a single kfree. Every dangerous operation is safe only under invariants established outside the shown code (that the device model passes the embedded &clt->dev, that release runs exactly once, and that the mutexes are initialized and quiescent). No failure witness is derivable from values visible in the shown code, so no vulnerability is confirmable.

assumptions: The device model passes a struct device * that is the dev member embedded in a struct rtrs_clt_sess, because a caller registered &clt->dev; this invariant is established outside the shown code.
The release callback is invoked exactly once per registered device by the kernel's kobject/device reference-counting.
paths_ev_mutex and paths_mutex were initialized before the session could reach release, and are not held at release time.
limitations: If dev were not the embedded dev member of a struct rtrs_clt_sess, the container_of at line 3 would compute an invalid clt, making the mutex_destroy calls at lines 5-6 and kfree at line 7 operate on a bogus pointer (OOB/invalid free). This is not confirmable because the shown code establishes no constraint on dev and relies entirely on the caller-side registration invariant.
A double-free or use-after-free of clt at line 7 would require the release callback to fire more than once or clt to be referenced after release; no such path exists within the shown code.
mutex_destroy at lines 5-6 would be unsafe if the mutexes were never initialized or were destroyed while in use; initialization and quiescence are established outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: Compute derives the per-channel output-scale vector `scales` from min/max-vector length (`depth`, lines 18, 42) but never checks that the input's channel count equals `depth` (only rank-4 at line 20 and vector self-consistency at lines 23-30 are checked). An attacker-supplied input with more channels than `depth` (e.g., shape [1,1,1,8] with 2-element min/max vectors) makes MKL-DNN's per-channel reorder (mask 2, lines 51 and 91) index `scales` past its capacity, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: `scales` was allocated with exactly `depth` entries (line 42), where `depth = input_min_vec.NumElements()` (line 18) and the only guards on the path (lines 20-30) enforce rank 4 and `dim_size(0) == NumElements` — none relate `depth` to the input's channel count `C = input.dim_size(3)` used at lines 53-62. Mask `2` requests one scale per channel; with a concrete admitted witness (input [1,1,1,8], min/max vectors of 2 elements), the callee indexes `scales[channel]` for channel 0..7, reading 4-byte floats at indices 2..6 beyond the vector's capacity — heap OOB read (CWE-125).

The reorder primitive built from `dims_mkl_order` (channel count `C`, NHWC->NCHW at line 53) executes with the undersized per-channel `scales` vector bound at line 51, so the channel-indexed scale lookups occur here; for `C > depth` the reads exceed the capacity of `scales`, confirming the heap OOB read (CWE-125) at the consuming sink.

assumptions: The tensor element types match the `flat<float>()` / `flat<qint32>()` casts (framework kernel-registration invariant).
`input_requested_min`/`input_requested_max` are scalars with exactly one element, enforced by op shape registration outside the shown code.
`TFShapeToMklDnnDimsInNCHW` converts an NHWC [N,H,W,C] shape to [N,C,H,W], so mask bit 1 selects the channel dimension.

MKL-DNN per-channel output scales are consumed by indexing with the channel index (the standard, name-implied semantics of `set_output_scales` with mask `2`), and the scales count must equal the masked dimension.
limitations: Division by zero when both requested min and max are 0.0f (lines 35-37, 46-47) yields IEEE ±inf/NaN `scales` without any fault in the shown code; the resulting crash/corruption would occur only inside the unshown oneDNN body, so no CWE is attributed.

Signed/unsigned loop mismatch (`int i` vs `size_t depth`, lines 43-48) becomes signed-overflow UB only for `depth > INT_MAX`; the array reads remain in-bounds for all shown indices, and triggering it needs a >2^31-element tensor, so no memory-safety witness is confirmable.
The `DCHECK(input_requested_min_float < 0.0f)` at line 32 is compiled out in release builds (NDEBUG) and has no production impact.
`input_requested_min/max.flat<float>()(0)` (lines 13, 16) lacks an element-count check in the shown code; safety relies on the scalar shape enforced by op registration outside the shown code.
`reorder_stream` is dereferenced at line 91 with no null check on `CreateStream` (line 85); a null can only arise from an unshown framework helper.
`static_cast<float>(1L << 31)` (line 47) relies on `long` being at least 64-bit; on ILP32 platforms the shift is signed-overflow UB, out of scope for this target.

verdict.summary: SWTPM_NVRAM_CheckHeader verifies the input length against sizeof(bh) (the size of a pointer, 8 bytes) instead of sizeof(blobheader). This admits buffers of only 8 bytes, yet the function subsequently reads the blobheader tail fields (min_version, flags), causing an out-of-bounds read that can leak adjacent memory and fault.

evidence.reason: Entry-point input length is only constrained by line 8's guard `length < sizeof(bh)`, which compares against the pointer size (8) rather than sizeof(blobheader) (>= 11 bytes of fields visible in the shown code). A blob of exactly length=8 with totlen=htonl(8) passes lines 8 and 15, then this statement reads bh->min_version at an offset >= 8 inside an 8-byte buffer — an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) by at least 1 byte, exposing adjacent memory in the comparison and the %d logprintf at line 27.

For a short header of length=8 (admitted by the line 8 guard `length < sizeof(bh)` = 8, and passing the line 15 totlen==length check), this statement reads bh->flags at offset >= 8 beyond the 8-byte buffer, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) caused by the pointer-size length check instead of the full blobheader size.

assumptions: 64-bit build so sizeof(bh) for a blobheader* equals 8 bytes.
The blobheader structure contains at least the fields accessed here (totlen, hdrsize, version, flags, min_version), summing to at least 11 field bytes, so sizeof(blobheader) > sizeof(bh).
data points to a buffer of exactly `length` bytes (the contract implied by line 8's own 'not enough bytes' check).
limitations: The exact struct layout/field offsets are not shown, so the precise number of bytes read past the buffer depends on the standard swtpm blobheader layout.
The read of bh->version at line 40 may or may not be out of bounds depending on layout; not reported as a separate finding.
A NULL `data` pointer is not checked; that NULL is not produced by the shown code and is attributed to the caller.
Minor printf-family format-type mismatches (e.g., %u with a uint16_t promoted to int at lines 36) are technically undefined but not attacker-exploitable here.
The function can return TPM_SUCCESS for a short buffer while setting *dataoffset=16; the resulting downstream read is outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: inbound_cap_ls assembles a CAP REQ buffer from server-supplied capability tokens, but every buffer append uses g_strlcat bounded by sizeof(buffer)=256 (lines 31, 42, 43), so no buffer overflow is possible. Additionally, non-literal content reaching the tcp_sendf sink is restricted to byte-exact members of the supported_caps whitelist by the g_strcmp0 guards (lines 26, 41), which excludes arbitrary attacker bytes such as CR/LF, preventing command/CRLF injection. assumptions: supported_caps entries are fixed, non-hostile constant strings (their contents are not shown in the provided code).
extensions_str is a NUL-terminated non-NULL C string supplied by the caller/server.
limitations: If a supported_caps whitelist entry itself contained a CR/LF, it could reach the tcp_sendf sink; not verifiable from the shown code.
A NULL extensions_str (g_strsplit returning NULL followed by extensions[i] deref) is not producible by any shown code path and depends on the caller; out of scope.
Return values of g_strsplit/g_strlcat are discarded, but their failure modes do not lead to a dangerous operation in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The error paths in load_buffer jump to the 'beach' cleanup label while 'obj' is still NULL (line 11, before the R_NEW0 at line 18) or after R_FREE has nulled it, and the cleanup unconditionally executes 'obj->cache_buf = NULL;' (line 67), writing through a NULL pointer. An attacker-supplied Mach-O whose prelink-info extraction returns NULL (guard at line 14 admits exactly NULL) triggers a NULL-pointer write and crashes the loader (DoS).

R_FREE nulls its argument after freeing (standard macro semantics, relied on to classify the line-67 failure as NULL deref rather than use-after-free).
get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 can return NULL for malformed or unsupported Mach-O input, since the shown code explicitly handles a NULL outcome as an error path.
limitations: A refcount leak of fbuf occurs at line 7 when MACH0_(new_buf) fails before r_buf_free(fbuf); single-shot leak with no attacker-controlled volume, so no CWE.
rebase_info is not freed on the error paths; leak only, no security impact.

prelink_range->range.offset/size flow into r_cf_value_dict_parse at lines 26-27; whether those bounds are internally validated is not visible in the shown code, so an out-of-bounds claim is unconfirmable here.
io = bf->rbin->iob.io at line 59 is dereferenced without a NULL check, but a non-NULL io is a framework invariant not established in the shown code.
The R_NEW0-failure path (line 19) reaches the same NULL write but depends on allocation failure, which is less attacker-controllable than the prelink_range-NULL path.

verdict.summary: SWTPM_NVRAM_CheckHeader validates the header length against sizeof(bh) — the size of a blobheader pointer (8 bytes on LP64) — instead of sizeof(blobheader). The header fields span at least 10 bytes given the member types read here, so a length of 8 passes every guard and the member reads, e.g. ntohs(bh->hdrsize) at line 32, dereference offsets 8-9 past the end of the attacker-supplied data buffer (CWE-125).

The blobheader read set spans at least 10 bytes (4-byte totlen + 1-byte version + 1-byte min_version + 2-byte flags + 2-byte hdrsize), so the admitted value length=8 with data={0,0,0,8,0,0,0,0} passes line 7 (8 < 8 false), line 14 (ntohl(totlen)==8), and line 22 (min_version=0), and reaches this sink where ntohs(bh->hdrsize) reads offsets 8-9 beyond the 8-byte buffer: out-of-bounds read, primary CWE-125.

assumptions: length is the byte capacity of the buffer pointed to by data, as implied by the guard's own semantics at lines 7-10 ('not enough bytes for header').
BLOB_HEADER_VERSION is non-negative, so min_version=0 always passes the line 22 guard.
sizeof(blobheader) >= 10 is derived from the member types accessed in the shown code; any extra padding only increases it.
limitations: The exact blobheader declaration is not shown, so which specific member read lands past the buffer depends on layout; however the >=10-byte extent guarantees at least one member read is out of bounds for length in [8, sizeof(blobheader)-1] on LP64.
dataoffset (line 32) is not checked against length here; any downstream use of dataoffset as an index into data is outside the shown code and unconfirmable.
If a caller passes a data pointer to a physically larger allocation while declaring the smaller length, the read stays within the real allocation — a defensive concern, not this finding.

verdict.summary: The kernel validates tensor shapes before use: input_min has exactly depth elements (lines 8, 16), input_max has at least depth elements (line 12), and input is a non-empty 4-D NHWC tensor whose channel dim equals depth (lines 20-25). The loop at line 53 iterates i in [0, depth) against objects whose capacities are all >= depth (ranges, input_min_data, transposed_input), so no index can exceed any buffer capacity and no out-of-bounds access is reachable. Allocation failures are handled by OP_REQUIRES_OK before the output writes. Remaining concerns (abs of INT32_MIN, MSVC-only OpenMP data race on out_min_max, NaN/Inf propagation) affect only numerical output values, not memory safety, and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The kernel is registered such that input is of dtype qint32 and input_min/input_max are of dtype float; dtype conversion invariants are established outside the shown code.
input_max.NumElements() is non-negative (TensorShape semantics), so the cast to size_t depth cannot underflow.
flat_inner_dims<qint32>() on a validated 4-D tensor yields [N*H*W, C], so transposed_input.chip<0>(i) indexes C = depth rows.
limitations: std::abs(min_per_channel) at line 61 is undefined behavior when a qint32 element equals INT32_MIN (-2147483648), which is admitted by all guards; the corrupted abs_max only flows into float scale math (lines 64-65) and output scalars, never into an index/size/allocation sink, so no memory-safety CWE is confirmable.

Under ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPENMP with _MSC_VER (line 47), the reduction(max: out_min_max) clause is omitted, creating a data race on out_min_max at line 69; impact is nondeterministic calibration output rather than memory corruption or an access-control failure.

NaN/Inf values in input_min/input_max are unconstrained by the shown code and propagate through scale (lines 62-65) into output_min/output_max; this can corrupt downstream quantization results but reaches no security sink.

ranges(depth) at line 32 allocates from the input-derived depth; a denial-of-service via a huge but framework-bounded tensor is not demonstrably attacker-controlled within the shown code, and failure would be an unchecked-allocation throw, not an out-of-bounds use.

TensorShape::dim_size(0) on a 0-d (scalar) input_min/input_max is not confirmable from the shown code and would anyway be precluded for input_min by the NumElements == depth guard on the executed path.
1L << 31 at line 65 is a signed left-shift UB on platforms where long is 32-bit (e.g., MSVC); this affects only the float divisor/correctness, not memory safety.

verdict.summary: r_bin_ne_get_entrypoints reads file-controlled NE entry-table data with inconsistent bounds. The movable-entry branch allows segnum in 1..255 to index bin->segment_entries[segnum-1] with no upper-bound check against SegCount (unlike the fixed branch), producing an out-of-bounds heap read (line 61, CWE-125). Two further 1-byte OOB reads occur: bundle_type is read after off++ without a bounds check (line 38), and the movable ut16 segoff read extends one byte past the +4 guard margin (line 59). Impact is OOB heap read leading to crash/DoS and OOB data exposure.

evidence.reason: segnum is a ut8 read from the attacker-controlled entry table (line 57); the only guard, line 60 (`segnum > 0`), admits 1..255 and never bounds segnum against bin->ne_header->SegCount, unlike the fixed branch guard at line 64 (`bundle_type < SegCount`). With the array's shown-code capacity SegCount (e.g., SegCount = 2), a movable bundle (bundle_type == 0xff) with segnum = 100 yields index 99, an out-of-bounds heap read of segment_entries[segnum-1].offset — CWE-125 OOB read.

The line-30 guard (tableat + off >= r_buf_size -> break) protects only the bundle_length read at line 33; off is incremented at line 37 and this read executes with no bounds check for the new position. When tableat + off == r_buf_size - 1 and the last file byte is nonzero (bundle_length != 0 passes line 34), the read at line 38 accesses buffer position r_buf_size — one byte past the buffer of size r_buf_size(bin->buf) — CWE-125 1-byte OOB read.

For a movable bundle the line-42 guard (tableat + off + 4 >= r_buf_size -> break, evaluated with off = bundle_start + 2) admits bytes through buffer position tableat + bundle_start + 6. The ut16 read here consumes positions tableat + bundle_start + 6 and +7, so when the file ends exactly at tableat + bundle_start + 6 the second byte is at buffer position r_buf_size — one byte past the buffer — CWE-125 1-byte OOB read.

assumptions: bin->entry_table points into bin->buf at buffer position tableat = header_offset + EntryTableOffset, consistent with the code's own bounds-check arithmetic (lines 28, 30, 42) and reads (lines 33, 38, 57, 59, 66).

capacity of bin->segment_entries is SegCount, inferred from the shown code's own safety guard on the same array at line 64 (bundle_type < bin->ne_header->SegCount); the allocation itself is not visible.
bin->ne_header is non-NULL on entry (no NULL-producing path exists inside the shown code).
NE header fields and entry-table bytes are attacker-controlled file contents, as the function is the parser's consumer of them.
limitations: A NULL dereference of bin->ne_header would require a caller-supplied partially initialized object; no path inside the shown code produces NULL, so it is not reported.
size_t addition in tableat = header_offset + EntryTableOffset could wrap on 32-bit builds, but the wrapped value only feeds bounds comparisons and no independently confirmed sink is shown.
Unaligned ut16 reads through *(ut16*)(bin->entry_table + off) are undefined behavior on some targets, but no attacker-controlled impact is demonstrable from the shown code alone.
Discarded r_list_append return values could leak a single RBinAddr on failure; single-shot leak with no attacker-controlled volume compounding, so not a finding.

Candidate A's exact over-read magnitude (index up to 254 vs SegCount) depends on the allocation of segment_entries outside the shown code; the shown-code bound (SegCount via line 64) is the basis for the boundary claim.

verdict.summary: Stack out-of-bounds write in xfrm_migrate(): the entry-point int num_migrate bounds the loop at line 29 and, via nx_cur/nx_new, indexes the fixed-size arrays x_cur/x_new (capacity XFRM_MAX_DEPTH, lines 9-10). The shown code imposes no visible cap on num_migrate (line 14's xfrm_migrate_check body is not shown), so for num_migrate = XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 with all m entries matching existing states that migrate successfully, the writes at lines 31 and 35 store one pointer past the arrays (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: The index nx_cur is incremented once per loop iteration in which xfrm_migrate_state_find returns non-NULL (lines 30-32), so with attacker-supplied num_migrate = XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 (admitted by line 14's gate since the shown code never bounds num_migrate) and all N+1 iterations taking the non-NULL branch, the iteration i = XFRM_MAX_DEPTH writes x_cur[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH], one element past the declared capacity at line 9 (valid indices 0..XFRM_MAX_DEPTH-1). Primary mechanism: CWE-787 out-of-bounds write via array index derived from unvalidated input.

The same num_migrate-derived count drives nx_new (line 36) whenever xfrm_state_migrate returns non-NULL (line 34). With num_migrate = XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 and all migration calls succeeding, nx_new reaches XFRM_MAX_DEPTH and this store writes x_new[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH], one element past the declared capacity at line 10. Confirmed secondary sink of the same CWE-787 stack out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: XFRM_MAX_DEPTH is the compile-time capacity N >= 1 of both arrays declared at lines 9-10, making the object capacities identifiable from the shown code.
dir and type are u8, so the XFRM_POLICY_MAX comparison at line 17 is well-defined within 0..255.
num_migrate, i, nx_cur, nx_new are all int; no cast, truncation, or signedness change occurs between the count and the array subscripts.
limitations: Reachability of num_migrate values above XFRM_MAX_DEPTH depends on the unshown body of xfrm_migrate_check() at line 14; the shown code contains no numeric cap on num_migrate, and no outside invariant may be imported, so the confirmation is a residual-range analysis (hence confidence 0.7).
Out-of-bounds reads of m[] and a NULL m are not confirmable because the allocation/contract for the caller-supplied m buffer is outside the shown code.
Duplicate m entries resolving to the same state (potential double-put/use-after-free) cannot be confirmed because deduplication, if any, is performed only by the unshown xfrm_migrate_check().
Severity assumes a caller (e.g., the XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE netlink handler) can supply an arbitrarily large num_migrate; that entry path is outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow in fiber_switch: in the MRB_FIBER_CREATED path, the unconstrained parameter len (no guard in the shown code) sizes the stack extension as len+2 (line 35) and then bounds the argument-copy loop e = b + len (line 37) which writes indices 1..len of c->stbase (lines 38-39). When len is at the top of the mrb_int range, len+2 wraps negative, no stack growth occurs, and the loop performs an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787) caused by the integer overflow in the extension size (CWE-190 secondary).

evidence.reason: Confirmed OOB heap write sink (CWE-787). len is an internal-helper parameter whose residual range the shown code leaves as the full signed mrb_int domain (no length guard anywhere before this point). The loop bound e = b + len makes the loop run len times, writing c->stbase indices 1..len. The only capacity-establishing step, mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2) at line 35, yields a non-positive extension for len = MRB_INT_MAX (e.g., 0x7fffffff + 2 wraps to -0x7fffffff), so the writes exceed the fiber stack allocation; the witness len = 0x7fffffff with status == MRB_FIBER_CREATED and a valid proc passes every guard (switch default at lines 23-24, !c->ci->proc check at line 32), since none constrain len.

evidence.snippet: mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2); /* for receiver and (optional) block */
evidence.reason: Confirmed integer-overflow size derivation (CWE-190, secondary root cause of the CWE-787 write). len is unconstrained in the shown code (residual range = full mrb_int); the addition len+2 in the signed mrb_int type wraps to a non-positive value at len = MRB_INT_MAX, corrupting the number of guaranteeable stack slots so the subsequent loop at lines 37-39 writes len values without a corresponding extension.

assumptions: fiber_check, fiber_check_cfunc, fiber_switch_context, and mrb_raise are raise-style (longjmp) and never return on failure, so no shown path 'continues after a failed step'.
mrb_stack_extend's parameter is consumed, by its name and the line-35 comment, as the number of mrb_value slots to guarantee on the current (post-switch) context stack.
MRB_FIBER_CREATED is admitted by the switch default branch (lines 23-24).
limitations: The mrb_int width (32- vs 64-bit) is not shown; the len+2 overflow occurs at either width's top of range, but the exact wrap magnitude depends on the build configuration.

If mrb_stack_extend internally promotes the wrapped len+2 to a huge unsigned size, its allocation would likely fail with a raise instead of reaching the write loop; its body is not shown, so the observable outcome (raise vs OOB write) is not fully pinned down.

Practical callers (mrb_fiber_resume-style argument unpacking) derive len from a bounded argument count, so len = MRB_INT_MAX may not be attainable in real builds; the shown code itself imposes no bound on len.
Lines 42 and 50 (c->ci-- and c->ci[1].stack[0] = value) are unconfirmed: the callinfo array's capacity and occupancy are not identifiable from the shown code, so no boundary claim can be made.
A negative len stores a negative arity in c->cibase->n at line 44; the consuming sink is outside the shown code, so no confirmed finding is derivable from the shown code alone.

Allocation-failure behavior inside mrb_stack_extend and fiber_result is not visible; unchecked-allocation-failure claims are out of scope unless the size is attacker-controlled in a shown reachable loop.

verdict.summary: gf_hinter_finalize dereferences the return value of gf_isom_get_esd() without a NULL check: assignments at lines 66 and 105 feed unconditional writes `esd->OCRESID = 0` at lines 98-99 and 134-135 (and derefs at 84/121/126-127 on the embeddable path). A crafted MP4 whose in-root-OD OD/SCENE track cannot be materialized into an ESD makes the lookup return NULL, and the subsequent field write crashes the process (NULL-pointer dereference, CWE-476, DoS). The same API call is explicitly null-checked later at line 144, showing the guard is required and missing here.

evidence.snippet:
if (remove_ocr) esd->OCRESID = 0;
		else if (esd->OCRESID == esd->ESID) esd->OCRESID = 0;
evidence.reason: esd is assigned from the unchecked lookup `esd = gf_isom_get_esd(file, sceneT, 1)` at line 105. The guards along the path—line 47 (sceneT != 0) and lines 106/108 (sample count and samp/embeddability)—constrain only sceneT and samp, leaving esd's residual range {NULL, non-NULL} unconstrained. A crafted SCENE track whose ESD fails to materialize yields esd == NULL, which reaches this unconditional write; line 144 shows the same API call being null-checked elsewhere, confirming the missing guard. Primary mechanism: NULL-pointer write (CWE-476).

evidence.snippet:
if (remove_ocr) esd->OCRESID = 0;
			else if (esd->OCRESID == esd->ESID) esd->OCRESID = 0;
evidence.reason: esd comes from the unchecked `gf_isom_get_esd(file, odT, 1)` at line 66 and is dereferenced unconditionally whenever odT is nonzero; the guard at line 65 admits every in-root-OD OD track index and says nothing about esd's nullness. NULL from a failed ESD materialization on a crafted OD track reaches this sink (and the same NULL is then added to the IOD via gf_list_add at line 102). Primary mechanism: NULL-pointer write (CWE-476).

assumptions: gf_base64_encode honors its outSize argument as a hard cap (name-implied standard semantics), so size64 <= 2000, buf64[size64] stays within the 5000-byte declaration, and every sprintf into sdpLine[5100] stays below 5100.
gf_isom_get_esd returns NULL on failure per its lookup contract; that NULL is the un-guarded value reaching the deref.

limitations: Stack overflow via `gf_base64_encode`/`buf64[size64] = 0` (lines 81/118/172) and the `sprintf(sdpLine, ..., buf64)` `%s` expansions (82/119/175) is NOT confirmed: with the explicit outSize=2000 cap, writes are bounded to ~2050 bytes and never exceed sdpLine[5100] or buf64[5000]. An overflow would require the callee to ignore outSize, i.e., behavior beyond name-implied semantics that is not evidenced in the shown code.

The NULL trigger for gf_isom_get_esd lies inside the callee (crafted sample-description state); a concrete file-bytes witness cannot be derived from values visible only in the shown code, capping confidence at 0.6.

The return value of gf_odf_desc_write (line 167) is discarded; on failure the buffer/size state is unspecified and a base64 read of size bytes plus a malformed IOD SDP line could result. No confirmed failure path.
gf_malloc at lines 90/126 is unchecked; an OOM would feed NULL into strcpy (NULL deref), but sizes are small (<= ~5.1 KB) and not attacker-controlled in volume, so it is not a confirmed finding.
Line 15 passes u32 bandwidth to `%d`, which is a format/type mismatch for values > INT_MAX; it has no buffer consequence in the shown code.
