verdict.summary: The only check on the first splits tensor is a rank check (dims() > 0, line 16), which admits a 1-D tensor with zero elements. Line 18 then computes num_params = dim_size(0) - 1, underflowing to -1, and line 19 forwards that negative count to ValidateIndices(indices_in, num_params) as the admissible-index bound. With a negative bound the validation invariant is unsatisfiable: all indices are spuriously rejected, or negative indices escape the guard and are consumed as gather indices/offsets by the downstream MakeSplits/WriteValues calls (lines 30-38), where they can index splits and dense-value buffers out of bounds. The confirmed mechanism is a signed count underflow to -1 (CWE-190) that is consumed as a count/bound at the call site.

evidence.reason: params_nested_splits_in[0] is entry-point input; the only guard (line 16, dims() > 0) admits a rank-1 tensor of shape [0], so dim_size(0) has residual range including 0. The subtraction then produces num_params = -1 in the signed SPLITS_TYPE, a count below its legal minimum of 0 (CWE-190 signed underflow), which is forwarded to the sink at line 19.

ValidateIndices consumes num_params, by name and use, as the exclusive upper bound/count of admissible indices. The shown code derives -1 for this count from a zero-length split tensor (line 18), which is out of the domain the parameter requires; with the standard semantics (0 <= index < num_params) the guard admits no index, and any lower-edge check not enforced in the callee leaves negative indices to flow into MakeSplits (line 30) and WriteValues (line 36), where they index the splits/dense-value buffers.

assumptions: The TF runtime enforces the op's declared input arity, so context->input(params_nested_splits_in.size()) and context->input(params_nested_splits_in.size() + 1) (lines 12-14) reference valid inputs; this framework invariant is not visible in the shown code.
SPLITS_TYPE is a signed integer template parameter (int32 or int64), so 0 - 1 yields exactly -1 without an unsigned wrap.
limitations: The concrete OOB read/write that a negative index could cause inside ValidateIndices, MakeSplits, or WriteValues cannot be anchored to the shown code because those callee bodies are not provided; only the invalid -1 bound at the call site is confirmed.
For SPLITS_TYPE == int32, dim_size(0) values >= 2^31 would also truncate when assigned to SPLITS_TYPE (line 18); this requires a multi-GB input tensor and is not the demonstrated witness.

Consistency between split-derived value counts and params_dense_values_in's dimension is not validated anywhere in the shown code, but any resulting overrun would occur in the unshown helper bodies, so it is not a confirmed finding.

With a correct two-sided index validator, num_params = -1 causes only spurious rejection of all indices (correctness/availability of a single op), and the security impact (negative-index escape) depends on the unshown callee implementation.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in inbound_cap_ls: attacker-controlled CAP LS extension tokens are appended to a fixed 256-byte stack buffer via unbounded strcat calls (e.g., line 25) inside a loop with no capacity check. An input of 20 space-separated 'identify-msg' tokens (or enough copies of any recognized extension) writes past buffer[255], corrupting the stack.

evidence.reason: Entry-point taint: extensions_str (arbitrary length, no constraint in shown code) is split at line 15 into an unbounded token list iterated at line 19. Guard at line 23 (!strcmp(extension,"identify-msg")) admits exactly the token "identify-msg"; there is no count/length guard. Each pass appends the 13-byte constant to buffer[256] (line 4, capacity 0..255): after 19 passes the string is 9+247=256 chars and strcat writes its NUL at index 256 (OOB); with 20 passes 14 bytes are written past the end. Confirmed CWE-121 stack OOB write.

Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached when the loop (line 19) sees repeated "multi-prefix" tokens admitted by guard line 28. Each append adds 13 bytes with no capacity check, so enough copies push strlen(buffer) past 255 and this strcat writes out of bounds (CWE-121).
Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached via repeated "away-notify" tokens admitted by guard line 33; no capacity check precedes it, so enough copies overflow buffer[256] (CWE-121).

Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached via repeated "account-notify" tokens admitted by guard line 38; 15-byte constant appended without a capacity check, so 17+ copies overflow buffer[256] (CWE-121).

Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached via repeated "extended-join" tokens admitted by guard line 43; 14-byte constant appended without a capacity check, so 18+ copies overflow buffer[256] (CWE-121).

Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached via repeated "userhost-in-names" tokens admitted by guard line 48; 19-byte constant appended without a capacity check, so 14+ copies overflow buffer[256] (CWE-121).

Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached via repeated "znc.in/server-time-iso" tokens admitted by guard line 57; 23-byte constant appended without a capacity check, so 11+ copies overflow buffer[256] (CWE-121).

Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached via repeated "znc.in/server-time" tokens admitted by guard line 62; 19-byte constant appended without a capacity check, so 14+ copies overflow buffer[256] (CWE-121).

Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached via repeated "server-time" tokens admitted by guards at lines 67-68 (which also require the framework flag prefs.hex_irc_cap_server_time); 12-byte constant appended without a capacity check, so 21+ copies overflow buffer[256] (CWE-121).

Same unbounded-append sink as line 25, reached via repeated "sasl" tokens admitted by guards at lines 75-77 when loginmethod/password/cert state permits; 5-byte constant appended without a capacity check, so 50+ copies overflow buffer[256] (CWE-121).

assumptions: g_strsplit (line 15) follows GLib semantics: returns a NULL-terminated array of tokens, with max_tokens=0 meaning unbounded splitting.
strcpy/strcat follow standard C semantics (copy/append plus NUL termination); the length arithmetic in Phase 2 relies only on these semantics and the visible constant strings.
extensions_str is a valid (possibly arbitrarily long) C string; a NULL value would additionally crash the loop at line 19 but that path is not confirmable from the shown code.
limitations: NULL extensions_str would make g_strsplit return NULL and the loop condition/deref at line 19/21 dereference NULL; the shown code neither produces nor guards this, so it is unconfirmed (no CWE).

Beyond a guaranteed crash, exploitation depth (precise control of the saved return address) is not confirmed: overflow bytes are fixed ASCII constants plus a single terminating NUL, and code execution depends on the surrounding stack layout.
Any IRC message-length limit imposed outside the shown code is not relied on; the demonstrated ~259-byte witness input fits within typical IRC message limits regardless.
EMIT_SIGNAL_TIMESTAMP is a macro whose body is not in the shown code, so no format-string or injection claim is formed against it.
Unbounded g_strsplit allocation scales with attacker input volume but is only a DoS concern with no additional confirmed mechanism.

verdict.summary: On the decrypt path, `ilen = aes->src_len - authsize;` (line 61) computes an unsigned subtraction with no `src_len >= authsize` guard. For attacker-supplied `src_len < authsize` (e.g., 0 with authsize 16) `ilen` wraps to 0xFFFFFFF0 and is consumed as an SG-forward offset in `scatterwalk_ffwd` (line 62), as the DMA length in `ccp_init_data` (lines 148-151, 158-159), as the tag source in `ccp_set_dm_area` (line 249), and as the GHASH length word (line 217), driving an out-of-bounds DMA/SG walk and memory corruption (CWE-125/CWE-787 impact root-caused by the CWE-191 wrap).

evidence.reason: CWE-191: `aes->src_len` has residual range [0, 2^32-1] (no constraint in the shown code) and `authsize` is confined by the switch at lines 34-45 to {4,8,12,13,14,15,16}. On the decrypt branch (admitted set: action != CCP_AES_ACTION_ENCRYPT), the guard at the action branch admits src_len=0, so 0 - 16 wraps in `unsigned int` to 0xFFFFFFF0; this wrapped length is then consumed as an offset/length by the sinks at lines 62, 148-151, 158-159, and 249.

The wrapped 0xFFFFFFF0 from line 61 is used as a forward offset over the residual source SG mapping `p_inp` (built at line 54 from the two-entry `sg_inp`). The offset exceeds the SG-backed data extent, so the standard scatterwalk forward walks past the available chain and reads out of bounds before any data can satisfy 4 GB, an out-of-domain length argument derived entirely in the shown code.

evidence.snippet:
ret = ccp_init_data(&src, cmd_q, p_inp, ilen,
				    AES_BLOCK_SIZE,
				    in_place ? DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL
					     : DMA_TO_DEVICE);
evidence.reason: The guard `ilen > 0` (line 144) admits the wrapped value 0xFFFFFFF0, so `ccp_init_data` is called with a DMA length of ~4 GB against an SG mapping that covers only the actual input data; the GCTR loop (lines 167-186) then reads out of bounds from `src` and writes the decrypted output out of bounds to `dst` (same wrapped length at lines 158-159).

On the decrypt path this reads `authsize` bytes from `p_tag`, whose position was derived at line 62 from the wrapped `ilen` (0xFFFFFFF0). The tag source is outside the valid source-data mapping, so the DMA copy of the tag reads out of bounds; the tag mismatch check then compares garbage, additionally corrupting the authentication result (line 255).

assumptions: AES_BLOCK_SIZE is 16 and CCP_SB_BYTES/CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT are small positive constants, so the workarea sizes at lines 77, 98 are fixed small buffers and the key placement at lines 82-83 stays in bounds for key_len in {16,24,32}.
cmd_q is an initialized engine queue whose sb_key/sb_ctx are pre-allocated and whose perform->aes method is valid (shown only by unconditional dereference at lines 130, 178, 236).
The `aes->src`/`aes->dst` scatterlists are expected by the driver contract to cover aad_len + src_len (+ authsize); their actual capacity is not visible in the shown code.
limitations: The exact excess of the out-of-bounds access caused by the wrapped `ilen` cannot be quantified because the SG chain length is not identifiable from the shown code; the wrap itself (CWE-191) and its consumption at the length/offset sinks are fully traceable, which is the reported root cause.

Separate confirmed concern, not added to the verdict CWE array per single-finding discipline: `aes->iv_len` is unvalidated, and `dm_offset = CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->iv_len` (line 103) wraps for iv_len larger than the workarea sized at line 98, so `ccp_set_dm_area(&ctx, dm_offset, aes->iv, 0, aes->iv_len)` (line 104, reused at 197) performs an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); attacker-reachability of an oversized iv_len via upstream callers is outside the shown code.

The encrypt path uses `src_len` without validating it against the actual destination SG capacity (lines 57-58, 242); the destination SG size is not identifiable from the shown code, so any boundary claim there is unconfirmable.
The wrapped `ilen * 8` at line 217 corrupts the GHASH length word (mod 2^32 arithmetic) but only affects the tag computation, not memory safety; treated as part of the same root cause.
aad_len * 8 at line 216 could wrap only for aad_len >= 2^29, which is far beyond realistic aead constraints and is not reported.

verdict.summary: A crafted DimFlag=16 MAT file with Frames=0 (read unvalidated at line 133) makes the pre-decrement at line 417 underflow to UINT_MAX, so the inner frame loop never exits at EOF; every iteration allocates a new Image via AcquireNextImage (line 407), growing the image list without bound and causing memory/CPU exhaustion (DoS).

evidence.reason: Frames is declared unsigned (line 18) and read from the file with no validation (line 133, residual range [0, 2^32-1]). When Frames==0 the pre-decrement at line 417 evaluates to UINT_MAX, which is a member of the admitted set of the guard, so the loop re-enters NEXT_FRAME (line 180); EOF does not terminate it because the short-read path at line 299 only jumps to ExitLoop and the check at line 417 is reached again. Primary mechanism is unbounded resource allocation (CWE-770), with one new Image allocated per iteration at line 407.

Executed once per frame iteration for attacker-controlled Frames (line 133); each call grows the image list by one Image with no bound tied to file data or any shown resource cap, compounding with the un-terminated frame loop into memory/CPU exhaustion (CWE-770).

assumptions: 64-bit build (size_t/ssize_t 64-bit), matching the MagickOffsetType/filepos arithmetic that is overflow-free in the shown code.
Framework calls (SetImageExtent, AcquireNextImage, RotateImage, ReadBlob) behave per standard ImageMagick semantics; the shown code only exploits the standard failure/short-read behavior of ReadBlob.
z2qtype is indexed only with z values in {0,1,2,3} produced by the shown code.
limitations: 32-bit wrap in ldblk computations (lines 196/202/208/217/230) yielding an undersized BImgBuff (line 270) and a potential heap over-read at ImportQuantumPixels (lines 304/314) is not a confirmed finding: the width of MATHeader.SizeX is not declared in the shown code, and the witness column count (~2^30..2^31) must be admitted by SetImageExtent (lines 265-267) whose limit is not visible here.

image->colors = one << image->depth (line 242) with depth==64 (lines 207/221) is a shift-by-width undefined behavior, but no allocation/index/length sink in the shown code consumes image->colors, so no memory-safety impact is confirmed.
goto ExitLoop (line 332) skips DestroyQuantumInfo (line 331), leaking one QuantumInfo per object; treated as a low-impact DoS/resource-leak concern rather than a confirmed vulnerability.

The unbounded frame loop is capped in principle at 2^32 iterations of unsigned arithmetic, but memory exhaustion (one Image+QuantumInfo per iteration) occurs long before that, so it is practically unbounded on attacker input.

verdict.summary: In njs_await_fulfilled, the non-terminal interpreter status NJS_AGAIN (line 39) is flattened to NJS_OK at line 55 and returned at line 67, so a continuation that suspends again (e.g., a nested await in attacker-supplied async/await code) is reported to the enclosing promise/event machinery as fully completed while its async context stays live and unsettled; the reject dispatch status at line 71 is likewise discarded with (void) before the context is freed at line 74. This is an improper-check/unusual-condition status-handling flaw (CWE-754) that can desynchronize the async event loop and leave suspended coroutines to resume against advanced VM state.

evidence.reason: ret is the status returned by njs_vmcode_interpreter at line 39. Its value NJS_AGAIN (a suspended, not completed, continuation that occurs when the resumed async function awaits again on attacker-controlled JS) is admitted by the equality test at line 54 and then rewritten to NJS_OK at line 55 and returned at line 67. The enclosing machinery therefore learns that the fulfillment event succeeded while the coroutine is still suspended and ctx is neither settled nor freed, an improper check of an unusual condition (CWE-754).

The return status of the reject dispatch is discarded with (void). If the dispatch itself suspends (returns NJS_AGAIN, e.g. an async rejection handler) or fails (NJS_ERROR), no action is taken on that status and njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx) at line 74 frees the async context unconditionally, compounding the CWE-754 status-handling flaw at a second sink: a suspension/failure is swallowed and the context is torn down underneath the in-flight dispatch.

assumptions: njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) bounds the argument read to args[1] when nargs > 1 and yields a shared default value otherwise (standard njs_arg guard semantics).

The VM status contract is: NJS_AGAIN means the native call chain suspended and the enclosing event machinery normally relies on that status to keep the VM/pending work alive; NJS_OK means the event completed. If, in this specific build, flattening NJS_AGAIN to NJS_OK is the intended hand-off (because the nested suspension registers its own follow-up event), the finding degrades to a robustness limitation; the shown code contains no guard or comment establishing that intent.

vm->levels[], vm->top_frame, vm->active_frame, and ctx->await/index/pc/capability are managed by the unshown promise/async machinery; their invariants are not independently verifiable from the shown code.
limitations: Line 34 (*njs_scope_value(vm, ctx->index) = *value) is an unchecked write, but the capacity of the target scope and the admissible range of ctx->index are not identifiable from the shown code, so no OOB write (CWE-787) can be confirmed.

Lines 58-60 return NJS_ERROR on a memory error without njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx); this leaks the async context, but it is a one-shot leak on an OOM path with no attacker-controlled volume scaling in the shown code, so it is recorded here rather than as a finding.

All freeing paths (lines 52 and 74) run while vm->top_frame is still the promise-callback frame whose function->context equals ctx; any use-after-free of that dangling pointer would occur in unshown caller code and cannot be confirmed from the shown code alone.
The two njs_async_context_free sites (lines 52, 74) do not constitute a double free in the shown code: the paths are mutually exclusive and each returns immediately after its single free.

A promise fulfillment that carries an Error value is diverted to the failed: path (lines 13-15) without resuming the continuation; this is a semantic/logic quirk whose security impact cannot be confirmed from the shown code.

The resolve dispatch at lines 49-50 stores its status into ret and returns it, but njs_async_context_free at line 52 runs regardless of that status; whether incorrect handling of an NJS_AGAIN/NJS_ERROR from resolve has security impact depends on unshown caller behavior.

verdict.summary: pjstun_parse_msg performs out-of-bounds reads of the STUN message header (lines 10 and 25) before any check that buf_len >= sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr), and reads the attribute header's length field (line 41) when only 1-3 bytes remain, because the guard at line 44 runs after the read. Truncated attacker packets with buf_len < 4 or msg_len in {1,2,3} trigger CWE-125 OOB reads whose values are then logged, enabling information disclosure and potential faults.

evidence.reason: buf_len is entry-point input with residual range [0, SIZE_MAX] (no shown constraint precedes this statement); msg->hdr->type is a 16-bit read at buf[0..1] requiring capacity >= 2. For buf_len in {0,1} (a truncated packet) the read exceeds the buffer. No guard exists before the sink; the switch at line 12 only filters msg_type and runs after the read. Primary CWE-125 OOB read.

Still unconstrained buf_len: this 16-bit read at buf[2..3] requires capacity >= 4. Witness: buf_len = 2 with wire type 0x0001 (BINDING_REQUEST) passes the switch (admitted set of lines 12-23), then this line reads buf[2..3] out of bounds by 2 bytes. The length check at line 26 runs afterward, underflows for buf_len < 4, and logs the OOB-derived value via 'invalid msg_len %d' (lines 27-28), disclosing adjacent memory. Primary CWE-125 OOB read.

After the line-26 check, remaining in-bounds bytes from p_attr equal msg_len with buf_len = msg_len + 4. The loop condition 'while (msg_len > 0)' (line 35) admits msg_len in {1,2,3}; this line reads the 16-bit length field at p_attr+2, requiring 4 remaining bytes. Witness: msg_len = 1, buf_len = 5 -> read at buf[6..7] exceeds the 5-byte buffer. The guard at line 44 ('if (msg_len < len)', always true because len >= 4) executes after the read, so the guard's admitted-continue set (msg_len >= 4) does not protect this sink. Primary CWE-125 OOB read.

assumptions: sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr) == 4 and sizeof(pjstun_attr_hdr) == 4, matching the standard STUN layout (16-bit type + 16-bit length) that the shown arithmetic (p_attr = buf + sizeof, len = attr_len + sizeof, 4-byte rounding) relies on.
pj_size_t is unsigned, so buf_len - sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr) underflows to a huge value when buf_len < 4; this only forces the error return and is not itself a finding.
PJ_CHECK_STACK() has no security-relevant effect on the shown data flow.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds write via msg->attr[msg->attr_count] (lines 36/40/61): the loop can iterate up to 16383 times with attr_count incremented without any bound check, but the capacity of msg->attr is declared in the pjstun_msg struct, which is not shown, so the overflow is unconfirmable from the shown code; no CWE attached.
NULL dereference of msg (lines 9/32/36/40) is not producible within the shown code - only an out-of-scope caller could supply NULL.
Unaligned/strict-aliasing concerns from casting buf and p_attr to struct pointers (lines 9/40) are ABI-dependent and no attacker-triggerable failure is demonstrated.

The remaining bytes read at lines 10/25 assume buf points to a buf_len-byte object per the function's own contract; if a caller instead guarantees a larger backing buffer, the header reads would be in bounds, but no such invariant appears in the shown code.

verdict.summary: mobi_decode_infl's delete branch decrements pos from 0 to -1 (line 41) when dir=='<' and pos==0, then reads decoded[pos] (line 49) one byte before the buffer on every such parse. With *decoded_size==1 and rule {0x04,0x0B,0x03,0x61}, every guard on the path admits the negative index: line 22 admits pos=0 after the jump, and line 45's boundary check (l>=0 and d+l<=decoded+INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX) passes because d+l=decoded+size. The same negative pos also makes memmove (line 53) write one byte before the buffer when decoded[-1] equals the rule byte, and decrements the used size below zero.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Attacker-controlled rule byte reaches the delete branch with pos==0 and dir=='<': line 41 executes pos--, making pos=-1. The only guard before this access, line 45, admits the path because l = *decoded_size - pos = size+1 >= 0 and d+l = decoded+size <= decoded+INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX; it is a high-end/length check and cannot reject a negative index. Witness: *decoded_size==1, rule={0x04,0x0B,0x03,0x61} — line 22 admits pos=0 (0<=pos<=1) after the jump, line 41 yields pos=-1, and decoded[-1] is read unconditionally.

Same negative-pos root cause escalates to a one-byte out-of-bounds write: with pos=-1, d=decoded-1 and l=size+1, so memmove writes starting one byte before the buffer. It is gated by the line-49 match test (requires decoded[-1]==c, the byte preceding the allocation), so the guaranteed violation is the line-49 read; when the match occurs, memory before the allocation is corrupted and *decoded_size is decremented below zero at line 54. The length cast (size_t) is safe here (l>=0 enforced at line 45); the failure is the out-of-domain destination pointer.

assumptions: Line numbers are 1-based as the code was presented in the prompt.
The buffer capacity equals INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX, as implied by the upper-bound comparisons at lines 32 and 45; the actual allocation is not shown.
rule is a NUL-terminated string (the sentinel loop at line 7 depends on c==0 to terminate).
MOBI_RET, MOBI_DATA_CORRUPT, MOBI_SUCCESS, INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX, and debug_print are library-provided names with their standard libmobi semantics.
Initial *decoded_size is taken at face value (shown code imposes no constraint on it); the confirmed witness only requires the ordinary value 1.
limitations: The OOB write at line 53 requires the byte at decoded[-1] to equal the attacker-chosen rule byte; the byte preceding the allocation is not attacker-visible from the shown code, so a full write witness cannot be demonstrated. The guaranteed, always-triggered violation is the one-byte OOB read at line 49 (CWE-125).
debug_print("%s", decoded) at lines 23/33/46/50 reads decoded as a C string; whether decoded is NUL-terminated (or zero-initialized) is not shown, so a string-read overflow there is unconfirmed.
If the caller ever passed a non-NUL-terminated rule buffer, the line-7 sentinel loop would read past rule; the rule's storage/length is outside the shown code.

A negative initial *decoded_size (e.g., -1) would allow an immediate OOB write at decoded[pos] on line 37 (line 32's l = 0 passes); this is the same underflow family and is listed here because real callers are unlikely to pass negative sizes.
If the real allocation of decoded is smaller than INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX, the insert branch's tail check (line 32) would also be insufficient; capacity is not declared in the shown code.
The second evidence item and the conditional write are not reported as a separate CWE because they share the line-41 negative-pos root cause with the CWE-125 read.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in the NE entry-table parser: the guard at line 30 protects only the bundle_length byte, so the bundle_type read at line 38 can read one byte past r_buf_size when the buffer ends right after bundle_length; the per-iteration guard at line 42 admits tableat+off+4 < r_buf_size while the moveable branch's r_read_le16 at line 62 reads offset +5, so its second byte can read one byte past the buffer end, with the OOB byte flowing into entry->paddr.

evidence.reason: CWE-125: file-controlled bundle_length (1..255 after the line-34 break) is read under the line-30 guard that only admits tableat+off < r_buf_size; after off++ (line 37) this read targets buffer index tableat+off+1. When a truncated/crafted NE file has r_buf_size == tableat+off+1 (bundle_length is the last byte), the read is at index r_buf_size — one byte past the heap buffer. The witness (bundle_length=1, tableat=0, buffer size 1) is a member of every guard's admitted set (lines 29, 30, 34).

CWE-125: the line-42 guard admits tableat+off+4 < r_buf_size, but the moveable branch advances off by 3 (lines 50, 56, 58) so this 2-byte read spans buffer indices tableat+off+4..+5. When r_buf_size == tableat+off+5 (witness: bundle_length=1, bundle_type=0xff, EntryTableLength=255, buffer size 7), the second byte is read at index r_buf_size — one byte past the heap buffer; line 59's EntryTableLength check bounds the header field, not the buffer. The OOB byte is consumed into segoff and stored into entry->paddr at line 64. The witness passes lines 30, 42, and 59.

assumptions: bin->entry_table is a view of bin->buf at offset tableat = header_offset + EntryTableOffset, which the shown guards themselves enact by comparing tableat + off against r_buf_size(bin->buf) before dereferencing entry_table + off. If entry_table pointed elsewhere, the shown guards would not protect any read and the OOB would be even less constrained.
bin->ne_header, SegCount and segment_entries are consistent with a successfully parsed NE object (segments list non-NULL at lines 9–13).
limitations: NULL dereference of bin->ne_header / bin->segment_entries is not confirmable from the shown code: no in-scope path produces NULL for those fields; only caller-supplied invalid state could.
On 32-bit builds, tableat = header_offset + EntryTableOffset could wrap if header_offset is near UINT32_MAX; not demonstrable as a reachable witness from the shown code's constraints.
The discarded return status of r_list_append (lines 25, 77) can silently drop entries on allocation failure but has no memory-safety or attacker-scalable impact.
Both overreads are exactly one byte past the buffer end; practical impact is an ASAN-detectable crash and at most a one-byte heap disclosure into paddr, not a bulk read or write.

verdict.summary: ccp_run_aes_gcm_cmd performs unsigned-subtraction underflows on unvalidated lengths that feed out-of-bounds memory operations in the kernel crypto driver. On the decrypt path, ilen = aes->src_len - authsize (L61) wraps to ~2^32 when src_len < authsize and is passed as the offset to scatterwalk_ffwd (L62), walking past the end of the source scatterlist to an OOB read/NULL dereference. Independently, dm_offset = CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT*CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->iv_len (L103) underflows for iv_len > 32 and is used as a workarea offset in ccp_set_dm_area (L104, echoed at L197), producing an out-of-bounds write beyond the 32-byte ctx area. Both fail because the shown code never bounds src_len against authsize or iv_len against the SB area size.

evidence.snippet:
ilen = aes->src_len - authsize;
		p_tag = scatterwalk_ffwd(sg_tag, p_inp, ilen);
evidence.reason: In the decrypt branch, src_len has residual range [0, 2^32-1] (no guard in the shown code) and authsize is constrained to {4,8,12,13,14,15,16} by the L34 switch. Witness src_len=0, authsize=16: the unsigned subtraction at L61 wraps to ilen=0xFFFFFFF0 (CWE-191). That out-of-domain offset is consumed at the L62 sink: scatterwalk_ffwd subtracts each SG entry's length and calls sg_next(), whose standard end-of-list result is NULL, so a chain shorter than 0xFFFFFFF0 makes the walk dereference NULL/read past the list — an OOB read (CWE-125) in kernel context. The guard set (L21 iv!=NULL, L24-27 key_len=16, L29 key!=NULL, L34 authsize=16, L56 else-branch) all admit the witness.

evidence.snippet:

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-reachable vulnerability. The dma-buf attach callback validates the kzalloc result (line 9) and the dma_get_sgtable status (line 14), returns proper error codes, and serializes the list insertion with the buffer mutex (lines 23-25). dmabuf->priv points to a valid struct fastrpc_buf established at export time outside the shown code; the shown code derives buffer->dev/virt/phys/size/lock/attachments from it without a guard.
dma_get_sgtable returns 0 on success and a negative errno on failure, and on failure owns no success-path resources other than the caller's a->sgt being unusable.
limitations: Missing kfree(a) at the dma_get_sgtable failure branch (lines 14-16) leaks one struct fastrpc_dma_buf_attachment per failed attach (CWE-404/CWE-401-style resource flaw). This is a single-shot leak: the shown code contains no loop or mechanism by which attacker-controlled input forces repeated failures, and the failure itself depends on driver-internal arguments/environment, so attacker-reachability and compounding volume are not established; no CWE is attached.

A NULL dmabuf->priv would dereference NULL at lines 12-13, but NULL is not producible by any path in the shown code (it would require a framework/export-site violation), so it is out of scope per the NULL-dereference standard.

The positive (success) return of dma_get_sgtable is not validated beyond the ret < 0 check; any content or size of a->sgt reported by the API on success is assumed valid per the API contract, and no mis-handling is demonstrable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: In ReadMATImage, the per-scanline byte count ldblk is computed as 4*MATLAB_HDR.SizeX in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic (line 202). With SizeX=0x40000001 the product wraps to 4, so BImgBuff is allocated as only 32 bytes (line 270) while image->columns=0x40000001; ImportQuantumPixels (line 314) then imports 0x40000001 LongQuantum samples (~4.29 GiB) from this 32-byte heap buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) rooted in the integer overflow (CWE-190). A crafted MAT file reaches this path through guards that all admit the witness values (endian, identifier, mix type, mxINT32_CLASS, DimFlag 8, non-zero dims, miINT32).

evidence.reason: MATLAB_HDR.SizeX is attacker-controlled with residual range [1,0xFFFFFFFF] (assigned from unsigned int reader at line 119; only the columns!=0 guard at lines 243-244 constrains it). 4 * SizeX is performed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic for the standard 32-bit MATHeader member; for SizeX=0x40000001 the product 0x100000004 wraps to 4, so ldblk=4 although image->columns is set to 0x40000001 at line 236. This CWE-190 wrap corrupts the size later consumed by the allocation at line 270.

evidence.reason: The buffer is allocated as ldblk elements of sizeof(double): for the wrapped ldblk=4 (SizeX=0x40000001) this is 32 bytes, while the row imported at line 314 is image->columns=0x40000001 samples wide. The allocation size is too small for the data ImportQuantumPixels consumes; the wrap at line 202 flows into this size.

With CellType=miINT32, DimFlag=8, StructureFlag=0, SizeX=0x40000001, SizeY=1 (all members of the admitted sets of guards at lines 60/68, 79, 105, 143-154, 123-135, 156-170, 181-234, 243-244; line 301 is false, so this else branch runs), ImportQuantumPixels reads image->columns=0x40000001 LongQuantum samples (4 bytes each, ~4.29 GiB) from BImgBuff whose capacity is only 8*ldblk=32 bytes after the line 202 wrap; the first read past byte 32 is a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: MATLAB_HDR.SizeX/SizeY are 32-bit unsigned members of MATHeader; their value domain is forced to [0,0xFFFFFFFF] by the unsigned int return of ReadBlobXXXLong assigned at lines 119-120, making 2*/,4*/,8*SizeX 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and the line 202 wrap (and lines 196, 208, 217, 230) effective.

limitations: The declared width of MATLAB_HDR.SizeX is not visible in the shown code (struct definition elsewhere in the file); if it were 64-bit the product would not wrap and AcquireQuantumMemory would fail cleanly instead of returning an undersized buffer.

Reachability of the over-read depends on the huge pixel-cache allocation succeeding; under restrictive memory/map/disk limits (e.g., a 256 MiB policy) SetImageExtent fails and the impact is limited to clean resource rejection.

image->colors = one << image->depth (line 242) is undefined shift behavior for depth==64, but no shown operation uses that value as a size, index, or allocation count, so no memory impact is demonstrated.

On 32-bit size_t targets, size = 4*(ssize_t)((size+3+1)/4) (line 160) can wrap and misalign parsing, but no memory-safety sink is reached by that value.

verdict.summary: ljpeg_start() enters an unbounded do-while loop when the input stream ends before the SOS marker. The fread return values at lines 10/13/17 are discarded, so once EOF is reached data[0..3] (and therefore tag) stay constant; the guard at line 16 keeps admitting the stale marker (e.g. 0xffc0 > 0xff00) and the loop condition at line 40 (tag != 0xffda) is never satisfied. A crafted truncated lossless-JPEG file (FF D8 FF C0 00 0A followed by exactly 8 payload bytes) provably spins forever, causing a CPU-spin denial of service (CWE-835).

evidence.reason: Entry-point file bytes are read into the stack buffer and the return status is discarded. At EOF the call returns 0 without modifying data[0..3], so tag (line 14) is identical on every re-entry, and no later statement in the shown code can change tag or advance the stream, feeding the non-terminating loop.

The segment length len is derived from file bytes at line 15 and the return value is discarded; on EOF 0 bytes are read and the stale segment contents are re-parsed each iteration. Note the ushort underflow at line 15 (length field 0x0000/0x0001 -> len 65534/65535) stays below the 0x10000-byte capacity, so this statement is not an OOB write, only the feed into the hang.

CWE-835 sink: the loop exits only when tag == 0xffda. Witness file FF D8 FF C0 00 0A plus 8 payload bytes leaves the stream at EOF; tag = 0xffc0 passes the line-16 guard, the 0xffc0 switch case contains no return, and with fread returning 0 forever the identical state repeats, so execution is unbounded on attacker-chosen input.

assumptions: ifp is a FILE* positioned at the start of a JPEG stream; FORC and make_decoder_ref follow dcraw/libraw semantics, but their bodies are outside the shown code.
dng_version is a global set by code outside this function; it only gates the optional getc() at line 26.
limitations: The ushort underflow at line 15 (length field 0x0000/0x0001 -> len 65534/65535) is NOT a memory-safety bug in the shown code: the buffer is data[0x10000] (65536 bytes) and fread at line 17 never writes more than 65535 bytes (max index 65534), so the corrupted length is in-domain; only one spare byte remains.

Whether make_decoder_ref (line 31) can advance dp past data+len or read out of bounds cannot be confirmed because its body is not shown; the shown guard dp < data+len bounds the loop's own dereferences within the 65536-byte buffer.

Short reads leave data stale/uninitialized, so reads at lines 11, 14-15, 20, 22-25, 34-35 and 38 can parse garbage, but all indices (max 7 and 511) remain inside the stack buffer, so no OOB read is confirmable from the shown code.
jh->wide <= 65535 and the line-42 guard caps jh->clrs at 6, so calloc at line 48 (wide*clrs <= 393210) cannot overflow; CWE-190 is not confirmed.
The discarded fread/getc statuses (lines 10, 13, 17, 26) are the mechanism of the confirmed hang rather than an independently exploitable second root cause, so no second CWE is reported.

verdict.summary: 32-bit unsigned overflow in APNG frame-buffer sizing (rowbytes = w*4; imagesize = h*rowbytes) lets attacker-chosen IHDR dimensions wrap the computed size, so frameRaw.p is allocated too small (e.g., 0 bytes for w=h=65536) while the PNG decode writes h*rowbytes scanline bytes through it via processing_start, producing a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) rooted in the unchecked wrap (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: w is attacker-controlled (png_get_uint_32 of IHDR bytes, line 40), admitted range [0, cMaxPNGSize] after guard 43-45; the unsigned-int multiply wraps to 0 for w >= 2^30 and drives the size wrap for w >= 2^15 since the required product is 4*w*h. No overflow check follows the dimension guard, so the admitted set contains wrap witnesses (w=h=2^16 -> rowbytes=2^18).

The 32-bit product h*rowbytes wraps: for w=h=65536 (admitted by guard 43-45 whenever cMaxPNGSize >= 2^16), imagesize = 2^34 mod 2^32 = 0 while the true required size is 2^34 bytes. This corrupted value is the allocation size consumed at line 56.

Allocation sized by the wrapped imagesize (e.g., 0 bytes for the w=h=65536 witness) while the decoder later writes h*rowbytes = 2^34 bytes into it; the corrupted allocation size is the direct CWE-190 consumption that turns the decode into a heap OOB write (CWE-787).

Name-implied PNG decode semantics write one scanline of rowbytes=w*4 bytes per row via the rows pointers installed at line 58 (rows[j] = frameRaw.p + j*rowbytes), totaling h*rowbytes bytes into frameRaw.p, whose capacity is the wrapped imagesize (0 for the witness). The decode therefore performs an out-of-bounds heap write of 2^34 bytes from a 0-capacity buffer; chunkIHDR still carries the true w,h, so libpng produces full-size scanlines.

assumptions: cMaxPNGSize is a large constant (at least 2^16, e.g., 2^30) since the shown code uses it to cap PNG dimensions read from 32-bit fields; the wrap witness w=h=65536 belongs to the guard's admitted set only under this assumption. If cMaxPNGSize < 2^15, no 32-bit product wrap is possible.
Standard libpng semantics: png_get_uint_32/16 return unsigned 32/16-bit values, and processing_start/processing_data decode scanlines into the supplied frame buffer (frameRaw.rows into frameRaw.p).
sizeof(png_bytep) == 8, so the rows allocation at line 57 is computed in size_t and does not itself wrap for h <= 2^30.
limitations: The fcTL branch reads chunk.p+12..+33 (lines 142-149) with no shown check that chunk.size >= 34; whether read_chunk guarantees a minimum size is not visible in the shown code, so this potential OOB read is unconfirmed and carries no CWE.
x0+w0 / y0+h0 can overflow only if cMaxPNGSize >= 2^31 (sums >= 2^32); with a 2^30-class constant the check at line 153 is sound. Unconfirmed, no CWE.
fdAT chunk.size-16 and chunk.size-4 (lines 181, 183) can underflow only if read_chunk can return size < 16, which is not observable in the shown code. Unconfirmed, no CWE.
The immediate JXL_FAILURE return at lines 84-86 leaks the current chunk and frame allocations; single-shot, non-compounding leak with no security impact, no finding.
Image3F/ImageF sub_frame allocation of huge w0*h0 (lines 105-106) fails by throwing/aborting; DoS-only via unchecked allocation failure without volume scaling, placed in limitations per standard.
io->dec_pixels += w0*h0 (line 103) can wrap in unsigned arithmetic but feeds no memory-safety sink.
The precise numeric value of cMaxPNGSize is not present in the shown code; all boundary claims about the dimension guard hinge on it.

verdict.summary: pjstun_parse_msg performs unguarded reads before validating lengths: it dereferences the STUN header (msg->hdr->type/->length) without checking buf_len >= 4, and it reads an attribute header (*attr)->length when fewer than 4 bytes remain, because the size check at line 45 runs after the read. Attacker-supplied truncated datagrams (e.g., a 21-byte packet with header length field = 1) cause an out-of-bounds heap read of up to 3 bytes beyond the buffer, which can crash the process or disclose adjacent heap bytes (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: OOB read (CWE-125). The attacker-controlled 16-bit msg_len field retains residual range [1,65535] after the equality check at line 27 (msg_len == buf_len-20) and the loop guard at line 36 (msg_len > 0), which admit msg_len=1. With msg_len=1 (buf_len=21), p_attr = buf+20 and only byte offset 0 of the attribute region is in-buffer, but this 2-byte read of (*attr)->length touches buffer offsets 22-23, i.e., 2 bytes beyond a 21-byte buffer. The only size guard (if (msg_len < len), line 45) executes after the dereference and cannot protect it.

OOB read (CWE-125). buf_len is entry-point input with no size constraint before this dereference. With buf_len=2 and type bytes 0x0001 (admitted by the switch at lines 13-24), this 2-byte read at buffer offsets 2-3 reads entirely past the 2-byte buffer; the length validation at line 27 runs only afterwards (and rejects via unsigned underflow), so it cannot protect the read.

OOB read (CWE-125). buf_len is unconstrained before this dereference; with buf_len=1 the 2-byte read of msg->hdr->type extends 1 byte past the buffer. The read occurs before the switch and before any length check, so the later equality at line 27 cannot protect it.

assumptions: pjstun_msg_hdr is 20 bytes (type, length, magic, transaction id) and pjstun_attr_hdr is 4 bytes (type, length), per the standard STUN layout and consistent use of sizeof in the shown code; PJ_ARRAY_SIZE returns the element count of msg->attr; pj_size_t is unsigned; pj_ntohs returns a 16-bit value; buf/buf_len is the full buffer contract of the parser.
limitations: The bytes read out of bounds are not attacker-controlled; after each OOB read the function returns an error, limiting impact to a crash if the over-read crosses an unmapped page or a minimal leak of adjacent heap bytes.
Real callers may allocate buffers larger than the datagram length, which would reduce the practical crash likelihood while still violating the declared buf_len contract.
PJ_LOG at line 28 passes a size_t expression to %d (varargs width mismatch); noted as a code-quality issue, not a security vulnerability.
The loop is guaranteed to terminate (msg_len strictly decreases by at least 4 per iteration), so no hang or unbounded-iteration finding was made.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. Every access to buffers allocated inside the shown code (orders, insParaPtrs, patParaPtrs, samplePtrs, pattern, packed) stays in bounds: the pattern loop is guarded by the row>=64 break (lines 310-316) and the pi&31 channel mask (line 320) against the identifiable 10240-byte allocation (line 249), and all count-sized allocations match their file-derived sizes (lines 26/75, 90/95, 97/105, 115/123, 285/295-296). The clearly dangerous unbounded writes into module's fixed arrays - header->ord[j++] (line 83), smp[s]/instr[i] (lines 139-203), phead[i] (line 359) - driven by 16-bit counts (lines 24, 30, 31) cannot be confirmed as out-of-bounds because the capacities of TXMHeader::ord, module->smp, module->instr, and module->phead are not identifiable from the shown code; they are recorded in limitations per the boundary/capacity rule.

assumptions: mp_uword is a 16-bit unsigned type and mp_uint32/mp_sint32 are 32-bit, per the codebase naming; f.readWord() therefore yields counts of 0..65535 (used to size arrays at lines 26, 90, 97, 115) and the *16 computations at lines 128/145/271 fit in mp_uint32.

XMFileBase::read(dst,size,count)/readWords(dst,n) copy at most size*count bytes / n 16-bit words and do not write past the supplied destination; the shown code passes sizes matching the allocations it creates (lines 26/75, 90/95, 97/105, 115/123, 285/296).

limitations: header->ord[j++] (line 83) can write indices j up to ordnum-1 <= 65534 (ordnum from line 24, no cap in the shown code), but whether this overflows depends on the capacity of TXMHeader::ord, which is not identifiable from the shown code; per the boundary/capacity rule the OOB claim is unconfirmable and carries no CWE.

smp[s] (lines 139-182), instr[i] (lines 194, 200-202), and phead[i] (line 359) are indexed by file-derived s <= 65535 / i <= 65534 with no in-code cap; the capacities of module->smp/instr/phead are not visible in the shown code, so the OOB write/read claims (potential CWE-787/CWE-125) are unconfirmable.
