All f.read/f.readWords/f.readByte/f.readWord/f.readDword return values are discarded (e.g., lines 15, 75, 95, 105, 296); on a truncated file, uninitialized heap bytes in orders/packed and struct fields can be consumed (lines 80-83, 304-342) and parsed as data, which is a robustness/error-handling concern (CWE-754 candidate) with no security sink in the shown code.

Line 152 casts two uint32 file values to int32 and subtracts; the subtraction can overflow int32 (UB), but the result is clamped to >= 0 (lines 153-154) and is only stored in smp[s].looplen, whose downstream consumption as a length is outside the shown code - no confirmed integer-overflow sink.

The second instrument loop (lines 380-398) skips s++ when smp[s].samplen is 0, while the first loop (lines 198-204) only increments s when both samplePtrs[i] and samplen are non-zero; a zero-length sample can desynchronize s so a later instrument's sample is loaded under a stale smp index - a logic flaw whose security impact cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
strcpy(header->tracker, "Screamtracker 3") (line 408) copies a fixed constant; the capacity of tracker is not shown and the size is not attacker-controlled.

Bodies of safeRead, loadModuleSample, and convertS3MPattern are not shown; internal bounds of packed reads (lines 304-342), sample-data allocation from smp[s].samplen (line 385), and pattern conversion (line 359) are therefore unconfirmable.

verdict.summary: The signed int loop counters (auto start_offset at line 57; int i at lines 42/58) are incremented against int64/ size_t bounds derived from attacker-controlled tensor shapes (GetStrides, line 54). For a shape with big_stride = 2^31 (e.g. input [1, 2^31], segment [1], num_segments = 1, id 0, all guards at lines 15-28 and 42-49 admit the witness), start_offset wraps to INT_MIN after 2^31-1 iterations; the re-admitted iteration then computes output_index = INT_MIN and offset = INT_MIN (lines 59-60), producing out-of-domain accesses into output_flat (lines 61-62) and flat_input (line 63) - a heap OOB write/read (CWE-787) rooted in signed wraparound (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: The counter is a plain int (auto from 0) while big_stride is int64, derived from the attacker-controlled input shape (line 54, GetStrides). big_stride = 2^31 is admitted by every guard (segment_dims=1 <= input_dims=2 at lines 15-21; dim equality at lines 22-28; id 0 in [0,1) at lines 42-49), so the int counter wraps at INT_MAX and the loop re-admits the negative value, whose use at lines 59-63 causes the out-of-domain index (primary CWE-787, root cause CWE-190).

After the line-57 wraparound, start_offset = INT_MIN is fed here; with flat_segment_id(0) = 0 and big_stride = 2^31, output_index = INT_MIN, which is out of domain for output_flat's non-negative index space and is consumed at lines 61-63.

The wrapped start_offset = INT_MIN is added to relative_offset_set[0] = 0, yielding offset = INT_MIN, which is consumed as an index into flat_input at line 63 (OOB read, CWE-125 mechanism subsumed by the confirmed CWE-787/CWE-190 finding).
output_flat(output_index) with output_index = INT_MIN (line 59 after the line-57 wrap) is an out-of-domain read on the output tensor.

Primary sink: an out-of-domain write into output_flat at output_index = INT_MIN (CWE-787). The index is derived entirely in the shown code from the wrapped int counter (line 57) and the admitted witness shape.

Sink: writes output_flat(output_index) and reads flat_input(offset) at the out-of-domain values INT_MIN/INT_MIN produced by the line-57 counter wraparound; both the write (CWE-787 primary) and read (CWE-125 mechanism, secondary to the wrap) are traceable to the same wrapping int counter.

assumptions: Helper semantics follow the standard TensorFlow implementation: GetOutputShape returns [num_segments] + input dims beyond the segment rank; GetStrides returns (big_stride = product of input dims past segment rank, small_stride = product of segment dims); GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets returns {i * big_stride | 0 <= i < small_stride}.

The giant allocations required by the witness (input and output each with 2^31 tstring elements, tens of GiB) succeed; an allocation failure at line 34 would abort cleanly via OP_REQUIRES_OK before the loop is reached.
Two's-complement wraparound is assumed to observe the signed int overflow (UB per the C++ standard) as it manifests on mainstream compilers.
limitations: For every shape where big_stride and small_stride are <= INT_MAX, all derived indices are in-bounds (max output_index = num_segments*big_stride - 1; max offset = input.NumElements() - 1), so no small-input out-of-bounds condition exists.

The output tensor's capacity C_out is not directly identifiable from the shown code because GetOutputShape's body is not shown; the confirmed OOB rests on the negative-index out-of-domain argument, not on a comparison against C_out.
num_segments positivity is never checked (line 13), but values <= 0 are neutralized by the segment-id guard (lines 43-48) for any non-empty segment tensor and by zero iterations for an empty one.

A multi-element num_segments tensor passes the emptiness check at lines 11-12 while scalar<NUM_SEGMENTS_TYPE>() at line 13 relies on a one-element tensor contract enforced outside the shown code (op shape function).
The same int-versus-int64 wrap class also affects the counters at lines 42 and 58 (flat_segment_id.size(), relative_offset_set.size()).
The error message at lines 26-27 prints input_dims (the rank) instead of input_shape.dim_size(i); cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. Every interpreter/function-call return status is tracked and propagated, VM frame state is restored on all paths, and njs_async_context_free is invoked only after ctx's last use on each path (resolve at line 58 before free at line 61; reject at line 80 before free at line 83). The scope-index write (line 37), the ctx/async-frame dereferences, and the nargs==0 edge case depend on invariants established outside the shown code, so they are recorded as limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: vm->top_frame->function->context is a live njs_async_ctx_t, ctx->await is a valid frame, and ctx->index lies within the capacity of the buffer returned by njs_scope_value — none of these invariants is established in the shown code.
njs_vmcode_interpreter returns only NJS_OK, NJS_AGAIN, or NJS_ERROR and sets vm->retval accordingly on non-OK returns.
njs_function_call reads its args before writing the retval slot, making the &vm->retval aliasing at lines 58-59 and 80-81 safe under standard njs semantics.
njs_arg safely handles nargs values below the requested index via its own (unshown) definition.
The awaited continuation was suspended earlier by the njs async machinery, which also guarantees that on NJS_AGAIN the current ctx must remain alive for a later nested resume.
limitations: Line 37 (*njs_scope_value(vm, ctx->index) = *value;): ctx->index is passed through unchanged and the capacity of the indexed scope buffer is not identifiable from the shown code, so no boundary excess and no effective guard can be computed; an OOB write cannot be confirmed.
Lines 11-22: ctx, ctx->await/async_frame, and function could only be NULL if supplied by unshown VM state; no path inside the shown code produces NULL, so NULL-dereference is unconfirmable.
Line 13: nargs is unconstrained in the shown code; whether nargs < 1 is safe depends on njs_arg's unshown definition and the VM call site.

Lines 67-69: on a memory error the function returns NJS_ERROR without rejecting ctx->capability and without calling njs_async_context_free, leaking the context and leaving the promise pending; this is a single-shot leak with no attacker-controlled compounding volume in the shown code while the VM is unwinding on OOM.

The NJS_AGAIN path (lines 63-64) returns success while the continuation remains suspended without freeing ctx; its correctness depends on unshown nested-await resume machinery and cannot be verified from this function alone.
No loops, injection sinks, crypto/entropy operations, file/path handling, or authorization checks exist in the shown code, so those vulnerability classes are not applicable.

verdict.summary: The result of gf_isom_get_esd(file, odT/sceneT, 1) is dereferenced without a NULL check in the IOD-embedding path (esd->OCRESID, esd->decoderConfig, esd->URLString), so an attacker-crafted MP4 whose root-OD OD/SCENE track lacks an ESD drives a NULL-pointer dereference and process crash.

evidence.reason: esd (line 105) comes from the lookup gf_isom_get_esd, which returns NULL for a SCENE track that lacks an ESD; sceneT is admitted non-zero by the line-47 guard, and the NULL guard present for the same call in the loop (line 144: if (!esd) continue;) is absent on this path. esd is then dereferenced unconditionally at lines 134-135 (esd->OCRESID) and at 121/126 (esd->decoderConfig, esd->URLString), yielding a NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476) on attacker-controlled file input.

esd (line 66) is an unchecked lookup result; if an OD track in the root OD has no ESD, gf_isom_get_esd returns NULL and the code dereferences esd->decoderConfig (line 84), esd->URLString (line 90), and esd->OCRESID (lines 98-99) without any NULL check, causing a NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476) on attacker-supplied file input.

assumptions: gf_isom_get_esd is a descriptor lookup that returns NULL when the queried track has no ESD; the code's own NULL check at line 144 (if (!esd) continue;) confirms this return value can be NULL.
gf_base64_encode is treated as a bounded encoder that honors its outSize argument (2000) and returns the number of bytes written.
limitations: A potential stack-buffer overflow of buf64[5000] / sdpLine[5100] via gf_base64_encode of large attacker-controlled sample/IOD data (lines 80-82, 117-119, 171-175) cannot be confirmed from the shown code: the outSize=2000 argument implies bounded output, so any overflow would depend on the unshown callee ignoring outSize, which is beyond the name-implied semantics. The gf_hinter_can_embbed_data guard's exact bound is also not visible in the shown code.
All sprintf calls use constant literal format strings, so there is no format-string injection; the destinations are large enough for the bounded inputs under the assumed base64 semantics.
The OD-branch NULL deref (lines 66-99) is somewhat less certain than the scene-branch one because an OD track normally carries a mandatory ESD, but the shown code imposes no check to guarantee it.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability in the shown code. All fprintf calls use literal format strings with input passed only as %s/%d arguments, all return values are checked (L15, L20, L23, L29, L30), and the STRNEQ at L35 is reachable only with non-NULL xml (L30) and non-NULL data->expect (L23). Remaining concerns are caller-contract NULL handling, unescaped newlines in unit-test stderr output, and strict expected-error-code equality — none have an in-scope security impact.

assumptions: struct testBackingParseData provides rv (int), backing (const char *), expect (const char *) as implied by usage at L8/L12/L15/L23.
STRNEQ follows the libvirt convention of strcmp(a, b) != 0, requiring non-NULL operands; reachability analysis shows both operands are non-NULL at L35.
virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute, virDomainDiskSourceFormat, and virBufferContentAndReset behave per their documented contracts; their bodies are outside the shown code.
limitations: args == NULL would dereference NULL at L8 (data->rv); the shown code has no path producing NULL for args, so this is a caller-contract limitation, not a confirmed finding.
NULL data->backing or data->expect would reach %s (undefined behavior per C11) or callee NULL handling; NULL cannot be produced within the shown code.

Unescaped newlines in data->backing/data->expect reach fprintf at L24-25 and L36-39 (log/console-injection hardening concern); the sink is a unit test's stderr stream with no security-relevant log or authz mechanism demonstrable from the shown code, so no CWE-117 finding is confirmed.
L12-13 forces erc = -1 when data->expect is NULL, so L15 misreports an expected parse failure that returns a code other than -1; this is test-logic robustness, not a security vulnerability.

Memory-safety inside virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute / virDomainDiskSourceFormat cannot be confirmed from the shown code; no index, size, length, or format argument is derived from input at those call sites.

verdict.summary: params_nested_splits_in[0].dim_size(0) is never required to be >= 1; the only structurally near guard (DCHECK_GT, line 11) checks list length and is compiled out in release builds. An attacker-supplied empty first splits tensor makes num_params underflow to -1 (line 12), and this out-of-domain negative bound is passed as the validation/index bound to ValidateIndices (line 13) and drives the row/slice index and count derivations consumed by MakeSplits and WriteValues (lines 24-26, 30-32), enabling out-of-bounds accesses for crafted inputs.

evidence.reason: Entry-point tensor shape dim_size(0) has residual range int64 >= 0 with no in-code lower-bound constraint; the witness 0 is admitted by every shown guard (line 11 checks only list length and is debug-only). 0 - 1 wraps to -1 in signed SPLITS_TYPE, an out-of-domain index/count (CWE-191) consumed as the validation bound at line 13.

Consumes num_params == -1 derived from the zero-sized splits tensor at line 12 as the maximum-index/count parameter, whose domain is non-negative; the corrupted bound then governs which indices/rows reach MakeSplits (lines 24-26) and the slice extents/counts in WriteValues (lines 30-32) that index into the 0-element splits and dense-values tensors, yielding out-of-bounds access based on attacker-controlled input.

assumptions: SPLITS_TYPE is signed (TensorFlow Tsplits, int64 by default); a 1-D tensor with dim_size(0) == 0 is a valid tensor value an attacker can supply as params_nested_splits[0].
OpInputList::operator[] and Tensor::dim_size behave per standard TensorFlow semantics; tensor shapes and values are attacker-controlled in this kernel's trust domain.
limitations: Accessing params_nested_splits_in[0] with a zero-length OpInputList would be an OOB read, but that case is blocked by the REGISTER_OP registration invariant asserted only in a comment, not by shown code — unconfirmed.

The concrete memory-corruption step (row indexing / slice copy in MakeSplits/WriteValues) occurs in unshown callee bodies; the confirmed shown-code mechanism is the -1 bound derivation and its out-of-domain consumption, so OOB details are range-based, not a demonstrated single crashing offset.

If ValidateIndices is fully sound it rejects all indices when num_params == -1; exploitation then depends on indices that survive the corrupted validation or on the empty-indices path combined with inconsistent splits — neither is fully demonstrable from the shown code.
Potential int64-to-int32 narrowing if Tsplits is registered as int32, and DoS via oversized indices_in, are not confirmable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled row_remapping values are not bounded by the shown code (only their count is checked against num_rows_). A value of INT64_MAX makes max_old_row = INT64_MAX, so the slice loop's slice_length computation (max_old_row - row_start + 1) overflows to INT64_MIN. slice_length is then used as a slice length and as the loop increment, driving row_start to INT64_MIN where row_start <= max_old_row always holds, producing an unbounded loop and unbounded growth of tensor_slices (CPU/memory denial of service).

evidence.reason: row_remapping values have residual range any int64 (only the count equals num_rows_, line 9, is enforced). With row_remapping = [0, INT64_MAX], min_old_row=0 and max_old_row=INT64_MAX pass line 106 and the line 110 guard row_start <= max_old_row. In line 114/115, INT64_MAX - 0 + 1 overflows int64 to INT64_MIN (std::min also yields INT64_MIN), so slice_length is negative; line 119 row_start += slice_length gives INT64_MIN, which still satisfies row_start <= max_old_row, so the loop re-enters with slice_length = INT64_MAX - INT64_MIN + 1 = 0 and never advances. This is an unbounded loop pushing unbounded tensor_slices entries (lines 117-118): integer overflow (CWE-190) as the root cause producing a loop with unreachable exit (CWE-835) and CPU/memory exhaustion (DoS).

assumptions: The body of RemapVectorToMap is not shown; if it rejected or bounded old-row-ID values, the slice-loop overflow would be unreachable. Based on the shown code alone, no value bound is imposed on row_remapping entries, so INT64_MAX is admitted.
num_rows_, num_cols_, max_rows_in_memory_ are op attributes (framework constants) not treated as attacker inputs.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK are assumed to abort the op on failure, so out-of-range values reaching guarded sinks are converted to errors rather than memory corruption.
limitations: A potential OOB write at line 192 is NOT a finding: the line 183-191 guard aborts before the write for any new_row/new_col outside [0, num_rows_)/[0, num_cols_), and map values (new_row) are bounded indices.

A possible uninitialized-output / out-of-range-read result when old-row IDs exceed the old tensor's row count, or when a non-wrapping huge slice_length reaches LookupSlice/SliceTensorShape, is unconfirmed because those callee bodies are not shown.
Path/other robustness concerns (e.g., BundleReader on attacker-controlled ckpt_path) are not analyzed further since no flaw is demonstrable within the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability in the shown code. Every memory sink is bounded (snprintf into strport[8] at L22 with a max 6-byte output; getsockname at L73 capped by naddr_len=sizeof(naddr) and post-checked at L79; net_address_get receives sizeof(addr)); every syscall return (getaddrinfo L23, socket L35, setsockopt L40/44/51, bind L56, getsockname L73) is checked before use; the addrinfo walk at L30 terminates and never indexes; fd management (close at L33/L93) neither double-closes nor leaks; DPRINTF calls use only literal format strings. The remaining concerns (log-injection content and getaddrinfo error-sign portability) lack a taint origin or platform witness derivable from the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: A successful getaddrinfo (checked at L24 on glibc, where EAI_* are negative) returns a valid, finite, NULL-terminated addrinfo list whose fields follow standard POSIX semantics.

union net_sockaddr is at least the size of any sockaddr it can receive, or, if not, getsockname's write is still bounded by the initial naddr_len = sizeof(naddr) (L7) and any mismatch is rejected at L79 before use.
net_port_get and net_address_get honor their out-parameter buffer sizes (L85/L86); their bodies are not shown.
DPRINTF is a standard variadic logger whose format argument is the string literal; the strings passed at L26/L67/L76/L81/L88 are format arguments, not formats.
cfg/cfg_getsec/cfg_getstr/cfg_getbool are trusted local-administrator configuration reads (L16/L19).
limitations: Log injection via log_service_name or cfgaddr reaching DPRINTF (L26/L67/L76/L81/L88) is unconfirmed: no sanitization exists, but attacker control of these values is not established anywhere in the shown code.

The getaddrinfo error check 'ret < 0' at L24 would treat a non-negative EAI_* error code (non-glibc platforms) as success and use uninitialized servinfo at L30; the required platform constant behavior is not visible in the shown code.
The reported errno at L67/L76 may reflect a different syscall than the one the message implies; informational only, no security impact.

The exact capacity of union net_sockaddr is not identifiable from the shown code; the post-getsockname length check at L79 is the bound relied upon, so no OOB can be confirmed even if the union were undersized.
SO_KEEPALIVE on SOCK_DGRAM, IPV6_V6ONLY=0 dual-stack behavior, and SOCK_NONBLOCK flowing through 'type' at L35 are functional/portability concerns with no demonstrated security impact.

verdict.summary: The shown decode/clear logic is protected by concrete bounds: the descriptor boundary check (offset_x+width<=gif->width, offset_y+height<=gif->height) keeps every frame_scanline write within the gif->width x gif->height frame buffer, and the gif_bytes guards keep all gif_data reads in range. Remaining suspicious patterns (colour_table[colour] with a table smaller than 256, frames[frame] off-by-one at frame_count_partial, early returns that skip cleanup) cannot be confirmed as vulnerabilities because the relevant buffer capacities and callee invariants are not established by the shown code.

assumptions: frame_data from bitmap_get_buffer is the gif->width x gif->height frame buffer (consistent with the memset sizes at lines 187-189 and 216-218).
gif_interlaced_line(height, y) returns a value in [0, height-1].
lzw_decode maintains the invariant stack_pos >= stack_base after returning LZW_OK.
GIF_COLOUR_TABLE_SIZE_MASK is a 3-bit mask so colour_table_size ranges over {2,...,256}.
gif->width and gif->height are bounded by 16-bit GIF logical screen dimensions, so width*height does not overflow 32-bit.
limitations: colour_table[colour] (line 265) and colour_table[gif->background_index] (line 294) can read past the logical colour-table size when the table is smaller than the decoded colour value, but whether this exceeds the allocation is unconfirmable because the capacity of local_colour_table/global_colour_table is not shown; if they are fixed 256-entry arrays, index 255 stays in bounds (no confirmed CWE).

gif->frames[frame] is read at line 25 before the range check at line 30, and line 30 admits frame == gif->frame_count_partial; a potential off-by-one/OOB depends on the frames-array capacity, which is not identifiable from the shown code (no confirmed CWE).

The early returns at lines 157, 228, and 240 bypass the gif_decode_frame_exit cleanup (buffer_position restore at line 321 and bitmap callbacks), leaving state inconsistent, but no subsequent operation in the shown code operates on that failure state, so this is a robustness concern, not a confirmed error-handling flaw.

burst_bytes = stack_pos - stack_base (line 254) would wrap to a huge unsigned value if stack_pos < stack_base, and the inner loop could then read below stack_base (line 261); this requires the unshown lzw_decode to produce stack_pos < stack_base, so it is unconfirmable from the shown code.
Deep recursion through the CLEAR/RESTORE disposal paths is bounded by the strictly decreasing frame index and frame count, so no unbounded-stack claim is confirmed.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The function only allocates fixed-size objects and stores or walks caller-supplied values (name, src_buf/src_buf_sz, es_pid, head); no sink in the shown code consumes an input-derived index, size, or pointer. The risky consumers (vidtv_s302m_encode, clear, destroy) are outside the shown code, and the remaining candidates (unchecked kstrdup/vzalloc returns, unterminated-name over-read, cyclic-list hang, error-path leak, unvalidated es_pid) fail taint, reachability, or impact requirements and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: Field types of struct vidtv_s302m_encoder_init_args are inferred from use (es_pid is u16 for cpu_to_be16, src_buf_sz is a size-like value); the struct definition is not part of the shown code.
VIDTV_S302M_BUF_SZ and sizeof(struct vidtv_s302m_ctx) are positive compile-time constants, so lines 16 and 28 allocate fixed capacities not derived from input.
The consumers of the stored state (vidtv_s302m_encode at line 37, vidtv_s302m_clear at line 38, vidtv_s302m_encoder_destroy at line 48) are not shown; their invocation is outside the shown code.
Line 1 omits the return type in the snippet, but line 59 (`return e;`) indicates the function returns struct vidtv_encoder *; this is a transcription artifact, not a security issue.
limitations: src_buf/src_buf_sz (lines 22-23) are stored without cross-validation against the actual buffer capacity; an inconsistent pair would only be consumed by vidtv_s302m_encode, which is outside the shown code, so an OOB-read (CWE-125) claim is unconfirmable here.

args.name (line 13-14) is assumed NUL-terminated; an unterminated string would over-read in kstrdup's internal strlen because the shown code imposes no length or termination constraint, but the violating input is a caller-contract value with no attacker path shown.

The kstrdup (line 14) and vzalloc (line 16) results are unchecked; a NULL there would be dereferenced only in unshown functions and requires OOM of fixed-size allocations, which is not attacker-controlled.
The line 29-31 error path frees only e, leaking e->name and e->encoder_buf when their allocations succeeded; this is a single-shot, OOM-gated leak with no attacker-controlled volume.
A cyclic args.head list would make the walk at lines 51-52 non-terminating, but no cycle can be produced from values inside the shown code (e is fresh and e->next is NULL at line 57).
es_pid (line 40) is stored unvalidated (e.g., could be the null PID 0x1FFF), but its only consumers are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: The password check compares binary digests with strncmp, which stops at the first NUL byte in the attacker-derived digest. When the stored digest contains an early 0x00 and the attacker obtains a password whose derived digest matches the prefix ending at that NUL (e.g. 1/256 per trial for a leading-NUL stored digest), strncmp returns 0 on a partial match and check_passwd grants authentication, bypassing the digest-verification mechanism with far less than full preimage effort.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled passwd (line 1, no constraint) is hashed at lines 43-44 into passwd1_sum, which is compared at this sink with NUL-terminated strncmp. The stored bytes in key (written at line 29 with no content constraint) may contain early 0x00; when the derived and stored digests agree through that 0x00, strncmp returns 0 on a partial (j+1)-byte match, causing ret=1 at line 49 and bypassing authentication (CWE-347).

In the non-PBKDF2 path, attacker-derived digest passwd1_sum (line 51) is compared to the unconstrained stored digest passwd2_sum (line 29/31) with NUL-terminated strncmp. Equal bytes through the first 0x00 in both buffers make strncmp return 0 on a partial match, setting ret=1 at line 57 without a full digest match, bypassing the password check (CWE-347).

assumptions: Compile-time constants satisfy 0 < PBKDF2_SALT_LEN < PBKDF2_LENGTH and PBKDF2_LENGTH >= 1, and digest_length(d) >= 1.
read_env_passwd/read_default_passwd write at most hash_len bytes on success; pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1 writes exactly keylen bytes and digest_digest exactly hash_len bytes, all returning 0 on success.
The password being verified is externally supplied at the boot gate, so passwd/length are treated as entry-point input with no pre-check range.
limitations: A fully concrete byte-for-byte witness for the strncmp bypass requires the stored digest contents (produced by unshown callees) and a concrete PBKDF2/SHA-1 preimage, which cannot be derived entirely from the shown code; confirmation rests on the residual-range/probabilistic analysis (stored digest bytes uniform over 0..255, so an early 0x00 occurs with probability ~7.5% within a 20-byte digest, dropping the effective match from the full digest length to the first-NUL position).

If PBKDF2_SALT_LEN >= PBKDF2_LENGTH (build misconfiguration), keylen <= 0 would be converted to a huge size_t length at the pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1 call site; this is not attacker-controlled and unreachable under sane configuration.
Unbounded attacker-controlled length could scale work inside the KDF/digest (resource exhaustion), but no loop over length exists in the shown code and the volume depends on unshown callees.
The early exit also leaks prefix-match information through timing; this is the same root cause as the truncated comparison, not an independent CWE.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in r_bin_java_bootstrap_methods_attr_new: R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) reads the 2-byte num_bootstrap_methods field at offset 6 before any bounds check. With attr non-NULL and sz in {6,7} (witness sz=7, valid indices 0..6), the read touches indices 6-7, reading up to 2 bytes past the end of buffer (CWE-125). The only bounds guard (if (offset >= sz) break, lines 14-16) is inside the loop and executes after this read.

evidence.reason: Entry-point buffer has capacity sz (declared parameter semantics); after offset += 6 (line 6), R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) reads bytes at indices 6 and 7 with no sz check protecting it. The line-7 guard (if (attr)) admits non-NULL, which is the success path for sz >= 6, so witness sz = 7 reaches index 7 == capacity and reads 1 byte out of range (2 bytes for sz = 6). The only bounds check, if (offset >= sz) break (lines 14-16), is inside the loop and covers only the later read at line 17, not line 9. Confirmed CWE-125 out-of-bounds read of up to 2 bytes past the heap buffer.

assumptions: R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT reads exactly 2 bytes big-endian at buffer + offset (standard, name-implied macro semantics).
r_bin_java_default_attr_new can return non-NULL after parsing the in-bounds 6-byte attribute header when sz >= 6, making the line-7 guard's admitted set reachable.
The capacity of buffer is sz bytes, as declared by the parameter shown in the code.
limitations: Line 19 (offset += bsm->size) is not re-validated against sz; it can inflate attr->size, but every subsequent parse at line 17 is re-guarded by line 14, so no memory-safety impact is confirmed from the shown code.
Line 11's unchecked r_list_newf result would make r_list_append at line 20 crash on NULL, but only via a small, non-attacker-controlled allocation failure; not a finding.
Further bounds issues inside r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new are outside the shown code; the call site passes an in-bounds (offset, sz - offset) pair, so they are unconfirmed here.
The loop is bounded by the 16-bit num_bootstrap_methods (max 65535), so non-termination is not a concern.
Severity is low because the confirmed excess is at most 2 bytes read past a heap buffer.

verdict.summary: pgpPrtParams parses attacker-controlled PGP packet data and never validates the decoded body length pkt.blen against the remaining buffer: after decodePkt (L11) fills pkt.body/pkt.blen, the body is consumed by pgpPrtPkt (L22) and the same decoded length is used to advance p (L25) with no check that pkt.body + pkt.blen <= pend (capacity pktlen set at L5). A header encoding blen=16 in an 8-byte buffer (6-byte header, 2 body bytes available) makes pgpPrtPkt read 14 bytes past the end of the buffer, an out-of-bounds read over attacker-chosen data.

evidence.reason: pkt.blen is a length decoded from attacker-supplied header bytes via decodePkt (L11) with a residual range [0, 2^32-1], because no constraint in the shown code bounds it against the remaining buffer. The loop guard (L10, p < pend) bounds only the header position, not the declared body length. Witness: pktlen=8, tag byte + 0xFF + 4-byte length 0x00000010 gives header size 6 and pkt.blen=16 while only 2 body bytes remain; the guard admitted set (valid header, p < pend) contains this value, so pgpPrtPkt's 16-byte body read at this call site exceeds the pktlen-byte capacity (L5) by 14 bytes — heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The p == pend gate at L30 runs only after this read and cannot protect it.

The same unvalidated decoded length pkt.blen (residual range [0, 2^32-1] per Phase 1) is consumed here as a size for pointer advancement; with the witness above, p advances to pkts+22, past one-past-end pend = pkts+8 (UB pointer arithmetic; on 32-bit size_t the sum can also wrap). This is the same missing bound (no check that header+blen <= pend-p) feeding the CWE-125 read at L22; the overshoot itself only causes the loop to exit and rc=-1 (L30) without a dereference in the shown code.

assumptions: pkts points to a readable allocation of pktlen bytes (capacity = pktlen, fixed at L5), and decodePkt/pgpPrtPkt read the bytes passed to them.
pkttype is a caller-chosen tag filter, not attacker-parsed data.
decodePkt parses a PGP header (tag and length encoding) into pkt.head/pkt.body/pkt.blen/pkt.tag; the length argument it is given (pend - p) bounds only its own header reads.
OpenPGP length-encoding semantics (1-, 2-, or 5-octet lengths up to 2^32-1) are used only to establish the residual range of the decoded length field.
limitations: decodePkt's body is not shown; if the real decodePkt validated body-fit against its length argument, the OOB read would be prevented — however, no such protective check exists anywhere in the shown code, and the shown code itself consumes pkt.blen unvalidated at L25, so a not-vulnerable reading cannot name a protecting guard.

The L25 pointer overshoot and the subsequent p == pend comparison are technically undefined behavior, but the shown code performs no dereference after the overshoot; the only security impact confirmed is the out-of-bounds read at L22.

On a 32-bit build, (pkt.body - pkt.head) + pkt.blen can wrap in size_t arithmetic (CWE-190 candidate), but the wrapped value is not independently confirmed to reach a dereferenced address in the shown code, so it is not reported as a CWE.

pgpDigParamsNew (L18) return is not checked; a NULL digp would be forwarded to pgpPrtPkt (L22), but the allocation size is fixed and failure is not attacker-scalable — robustness concern only, no CWE.
The success gate p == pend (L30) makes malformed/truncated inputs fail closed; it is not a bypass vector itself.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. Every gif_data read is preceded by an exact gif_bytes guard (>=12 at lines 43/61 for indices 0..9, >=3*colour_table_size at line 111 for the local palette copy, >=1 at line 144, >=2 at lines 171/179/246), and every frame-pixel write is bounded by the boundary check at lines 92-93 to at most width*height elements. The burst pop count (line 266) exactly equals the stack fill, so *--stack_pos cannot underflow. Remaining concerns (colour-table/frames/bitmap capacities, gif_skip_frame_extensions and gif_interlaced_line invariants, buffer_position not restored on the direct insuff-memory returns) depend on capacities or callee behavior not identifiable from the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: gif->gif_data/gif->buffer_size delimit one contiguous decoded buffer, and offsets frame_pointer/buffer_position are populated by other stages of the shown file's decode pipeline.
The LZW stack semantics of lzw_decode/lzw_decode_init keep stack_pos within [stack_base, stack_base + fill] after a successful call, so burst_bytes at line 266 is an exact pop count.
gif_interlaced_line(height, y) returns a value in [0, height) for y in [0, height), matching GIF interlacing semantics.
bitmap_get_buffer returns a buffer of at least width*height unsigned ints for gif->frame_image, and the local/global colour tables hold at least 256 entries.
The frames array has at least frame_count_partial+1 valid entries.
limitations: Line 19 reads gif->frames[frame].display before the line 24 range check, so an out-of-range frame (internal-helper parameter, unconstrained at that point) would be an out-of-bounds read only if the frames array capacity is smaller than any admitted-frame value; capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.

colour_table[colour] (line 277, colour in 0..255 from the LZW stack) and colour_table[gif->background_index] (line 306) would be OOB only if a colour table has fewer than 256 entries; capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.

memset sizes (gif->width * gif->height * sizeof(int), width * 4) and scanline writes are in-bounds relative to width*height but assume the bitmap buffer allocated by the callback matches those dimensions.

The direct returns at lines 159 and 236 skip restoring gif->buffer_position to save_buffer_position (line 333); the misbehavior of downstream stages on that stale state occurs outside the shown code, so this error/status-handling concern cannot be fully confirmed here.

Bounds of gif->buffer_position after gif_skip_frame_extensions (line 52) and of gif->frames[frame].frame_pointer (line 35) are not established in the shown code; a negative gif_bytes is caught by the line 43/61 guards before any dereference.
No format-string, command, SQL, or crypto sinks exist in the shown code; no such vulnerabilities are present.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write past big_buffer in readconf_main: when CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE/EUID is defined, a filename item of length near big_buffer_size (copied at line 10) leaves fewer bytes at suffix (line 16) than the constant-format sprintf appended text, producing a heap/global OOB write at lines 25, 30, and 41 with no runtime length guard.

evidence.reason: filename (residual range 0..big_buffer_size-1 chars from the string_nextinlist copy at line 10) sets suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename) at line 16, leaving big_buffer_size-len(filename) bytes of capacity. This sprintf writes up to ~277 bytes (euid digits + '.' + 256-char nodename + NUL); with len(filename) = big_buffer_size-10 (a member of the admitted set, no runtime length guard exists) the write extends up to ~267 bytes past the end of big_buffer, an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) into the global buffer in a root-privileged startup path.

Same mechanism as line 25: append of up to 258 bytes at suffix; overflow past big_buffer occurs when len(filename) > big_buffer_size-258, which the admitted item-length range (0..big_buffer_size-1) permits (e.g., big_buffer_size-10 with a 258-byte nodename). Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), sink reached when the EUID variant fopen fails (config_file == NULL at line 27) and this branch executes.

Same mechanism: append of up to ~21 bytes at suffix; overflows big_buffer when len(filename) > big_buffer_size-21, which the unconstrained filename-length range from line 10 admits (e.g., big_buffer_size-10). Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) on the EUID-only suffix path, reachable when config_file is still NULL after the node-specific attempts.

assumptions: Line numbers are counted from the first line of the provided fragment (line 1 = readconf_main(void)).
big_buffer is a global buffer whose capacity the shown code itself treats as big_buffer_size bytes, as used in the string_nextinlist call at line 10.
string_nextinlist copies each list item into big_buffer and returns a NUL-terminated string of length at most big_buffer_size-1.
The analyzed suffix-append path is compiled only when CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE and/or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID is defined at build time; the #else branch at line 57 is the default Exim configuration.
limitations: The confirmed OOB write requires a build that defines CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE and/or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID, plus uname() success (line 22); the default build taking the #else path (line 57) is not affected by this sink.

Triggering the overflow requires a config_main_filelist item of length > big_buffer_size-278 (admin/command-line controlled, i.e., trusted input); there is no way for a remote unauthenticated party to reach it through the shown code.

Line 390-391: the expand_string(host_number_string) return is not NULL-checked before Ustrtol(s, &end, 0), so an expansion failure (e.g., host_number_string = "${") dereferences NULL; a separate, config-controlled CWE-754/CWE-476 flaw of low severity, not added to the verdict CWEs.

Line 396-400: only n > LOCALHOST_MAX is rejected, so a negative value (e.g., "-1") passes and is stored into host_number; the downstream use of host_number is not shown, so the impact is unconfirmable.
Ustrtol overflow (LONG_MAX + errno) is not checked, but line 396 rejects LONG_MAX as exceeding LOCALHOST_MAX.
log_write calls use constant format strings and trusted config values, so log/format-string injection is not confirmed.

verdict.summary: print_media_desc's only length guard (line 9) sizes the buffer for the m= line only (media.slen + transport.slen + 36) and never accounts for the per-format writes in the loop at lines 27-31. m->desc.fmt_count and m->desc.fmt[i].slen reach pj_memcpy at line 29 (and the trailing '\r\n' at lines 32-33) with no capacity check, so with a single format of slen >= 31 and len at the admitted minimum, the copy writes past end = buf+len — an out-of-bounds write of input-controlled SDP format data (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: the memcpy size m->desc.fmt[i].slen is input-derived with a residual range left fully unconstrained by the shown code, and the loop at line 27 never checks it against end-p. The line-9 guard admits len >= media.slen+transport.slen+36 only; for media.slen=transport.slen=0, port=0, port_count=1, fmt_count=1, fmt[0].slen=31, len=36 (a member of that guard's admitted set), the pre-loop writes leave p=buf+6 and line 29 copies 31 bytes over the 30 bytes remaining before end=buf+36, writing index 36 past capacity. Confirmed CWE-787 heap/stack buffer overflow.

Consequent OOB write of the same finding: after the unchecked format loop has advanced p past end, the '\r\n' terminator writes beyond buf+len (e.g., with fmt[0].slen=30 the loop fills indexes 6..35 exactly and these two writes hit indexes 36-37 while capacity is 36). Same root cause and guard admission as the line-29 memcpy sink; CWE-787.

assumptions: buf has usable capacity of exactly len bytes, as made explicit by end = buf+len at line 4.
pj_memcpy behaves like memcpy and consumes its third argument as the exact number of bytes copied.
m->desc.port/port_count are at most 32-bit unsigned, so pj_utoa emits at most 10 digits; even that worst case stays within the +36 slack of the line-9 check, so port-digit writes are safe.

In the real callers (PJSIP SDP serialization) m is built from network-supplied SDP, making fmt_count/fmt[i].slen attacker-influenced; the verdict itself relies only on residual ranges left unconstrained by the shown code.
print_connection_info/print_bandw/print_attr honor their length argument and return a negative value on shortfall, as the shown code's own checks assume.
limitations: Integer overflow of the unsigned sum at line 9 (CWE-190) requires media.slen and transport.slen individually near 2^63-1 (pj_ssize_t max), magnitudes that cannot be produced by any real SDP token or string storage visible to the shown code; not confirmed.

The casts (int)(end-p) at line 37, (int)print_bandw/print_attr at lines 46/55, and (int)(p-buf) at line 62 only corrupt values when capacities exceed INT_MAX (>= 2 GiB), which no identifiable capacity in the shown code supports.
An OOB read would occur if fmt[i].slen exceeded the real storage behind fmt[i].ptr, but that pointed-to capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.
The helper calls at lines 37, 46 and 55 receiving negative or huge lengths after the format loop overruns are consequences of the confirmed overflow, not independent findings.

verdict.summary: One-byte out-of-bounds read of the attacker-controlled cipher-suite buffer in the first scan loop (lines 13-39): for odd datalen the final iteration i = datalen-1 evaluates data[i+1] = data[datalen] at line 30 (and line 17), because the datalen % 2 guard only executes at line 78, after the read. The index equals the buffer capacity (datalen), an excess of exactly one byte; the read value is used in equality comparisons (SCSV/fallback detection).

evidence.reason: datalen is an attacker-controlled entry-point input with no parity constraint before loop 1 (the datalen % 2 check at line 78 runs after the loop). For datalen = 3, i = 2 is admitted by 'i < datalen' with i += 2, and data[2] = GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR is admitted by the equality at line 29 (attacker sets the byte). Line 30 then reads data[3], i.e. index == datalen on a datalen-byte buffer, a confirmed 1-byte OOB read (CWE-125); the guard at line 78 is too late to protect this access.

Same mechanism on the safe-renegotiation branch: for odd datalen (witness datalen = 3) the last iteration has i = 2; with data[2] = 0x00 (GNUTLS_RENEGO_PROTECTION_REQUEST_MAJOR per the comment at line 14, admitted by line 16) and sr != SR_DISABLED (line 15), line 17 reads data[3], one byte past the datalen-byte buffer (index == datalen). CWE-125 OOB read; the line-78 parity guard executes only after this loop.

assumptions: data points to a buffer of exactly datalen bytes; datalen is the only capacity indicator for data in the shown code.

GNUTLS_RENEGO_PROTECTION_REQUEST_MAJOR == 0x00 and GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR correspond to the standard SCSV first bytes {0x00, 0xff} and {0x56, 0x00}; the witness only requires the attacker to match the named constant, which data bytes fully control.
For the line-17 witness, session->internals.priorities.sr != SR_DISABLED is assumed (the line-30 witness needs no session state).
limitations: A potential OOB read on cipher_suites[i + 1] at lines 98/108/124/134 when cipher_suites_size is odd is unconfirmable: the evenness and the value of MAX_CIPHERSUITE_SIZE are callee/constant invariants not visible in the shown code.
datalen == UINT_MAX would make 'i += 2' wrap and loop 1 non-terminating, but requires a ~4 GiB attacker buffer, unreachable under upstream handshake size limits not shown here.
session == NULL would crash at first dereference, but NULL can only originate from the caller (out of scope).
Impact assessed as low: the leaked byte is used only in equality comparisons (equality oracle / possible page-boundary crash), with no attacker-controlled write.

verdict.summary: The shown function applies complete guards to every security-relevant sink: kzalloc failure returns -ENOMEM (lines 9-10), the full failure set of dma_get_sgtable (negative errno, per its standard contract) is excluded by `ret < 0` (line 14), the dev_err is a constant format string (line 15), and list registration is serialized under buffer->lock (lines 24-26). No attacker-controlled value is derived, transformed, or consumed within the shown code, so no confirmed vulnerability exists; residual concerns (unvalidated dmabuf->priv, buffer->size source-region bounds, error-path sgt cleanup) depend on out-of-scope caller state or callee internals and are recorded in limitations.

assumptions: dma_get_sgtable returns 0 on success and negative errno on failure (standard API contract), so `ret < 0` at line 14 covers its complete failure set and admits only success into the continuation.

The dma-buf framework invokes this attach op only for a dmabuf exported by this driver, whose ->priv is a valid struct fastrpc_buf with initialized fields, and with a valid attachment; that invariant is not visible in the shown code.
buffer->size matches the region described by buffer->virt and buffer->phys, established at allocation time outside the shown code.
limitations: A NULL dereference of buffer (dmabuf->priv) at lines 12-13 is unconfirmed: line 5 performs no operation that can yield NULL inside the shown code, so the NULL would have to come from an out-of-scope caller/framework contract violation.

The capacity of the memory region described by buffer->virt / FASTRPC_PHYS(buffer->phys) / buffer->size is not identifiable from the shown code, so any sgtable size-mismatch or out-of-bounds claim is unconfirmable here.
FASTRPC_PHYS is not defined in the shown code, so any masking/truncation it applies to buffer->phys cannot be evaluated.

If a platform's dma_get_sgtable allocated sg resources before returning an error, `kfree(a)` at line 16 would leak them; this contradicts the standard contract and generic implementation (internal cleanup on failure), cannot be confirmed from the shown code, and is a single-shot leak without attacker-controlled volume.
Racing invalidation of buffer via concurrent detach/release cannot be assessed because those callbacks are not shown; the shown registration path itself holds buffer->lock (lines 24-26).
Returning -EINVAL at line 17 discards the specific error code from `ret`; informational only, with no demonstrated security impact.

verdict.summary: One-byte out-of-bounds read of the peer ciphersuite list: the scan loop at lines 13-39 evaluates data[i+1] on its last iteration (i = datalen-1) whenever datalen is odd, and the only parity guard (lines 78-81) executes after this loop, so it does not protect it. A concrete trigger is datalen = 1 with data[0] = GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR, which forces the OOB load data[1] at line 30 (CWE-125, one-byte read past the data buffer identified by the (data, datalen) contract).

evidence.reason: datalen (unsigned int) has no constraint before loop line 13; the parity guard at lines 78-81 runs only after this loop, so odd values are admitted here. For odd datalen the last iteration has i = datalen-1, and this expression loads data[i+1] = data[datalen], one byte past the datalen-byte buffer identified by the (data, datalen) contract. With datalen = 1 and data[0] = GNUTLS_RENEGO_PROTECTION_REQUEST_MAJOR (and sr != SR_DISABLED), the load occurs — a confirmed one-byte out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Same loop (line 13) and same unguarded odd-datalen path, reachable without the sr precondition: with datalen = 1 (odd, admitted — the parity check at line 78 is after this loop) and data[0] = GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MAJOR, line 29's first operand is true so this expression loads data[1], i.e., index == capacity (1) of the datalen-byte buffer — one-byte out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: data points to a buffer of exactly datalen bytes — the extent the shown code uses as the bound for every access (lines 13, 43, 92, 123) and that the parity comment at lines 74-77 relies on.

server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites and _gnutls_supported_ciphersuites honor the capacities passed to them (pk_algos_size = MAX_ALGOS; sizeof(cipher_suites)), so cipher_suites_size <= MAX_CIPHERSUITE_SIZE.
session is non-NULL; a NULL session could only be supplied by an out-of-scope caller.
limitations: The parity check at lines 78-81 does effectively protect the later data[j]/data[j+1] loops at lines 92-145; those accesses are safe for the residual range of datalen.
Whether the callees _gnutls_ext_sr_recv_cs or server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites perform their own OOB reads for odd datalen cannot be confirmed from the shown code (bodies not shown).
Unsigned wrap of i += 2 (line 13) could make Loop 1 non-terminating, but only for datalen near UINT_MAX, requiring a buffer size not identifiable in the shown code.
The (int) datalen cast at line 89 is implementation-defined only when datalen > INT_MAX and is used solely in a log statement — no security impact.

An odd return value from _gnutls_remove_unwanted_ciphersuites would make cipher_suites[i+1] touch within-capacity uninitialized bytes; the callee contract is not shown and no OOB of the cipher_suites allocation is derivable.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The function only performs a plain struct write, two guarded regex evaluations, and a guarded home-replacement path; every callee return status is checked, and no index/size/injection/crypto sink exists in the shown code.

assumptions: name is a NUL-terminated Vim string as required by vim_regexec and home_replace_save (a Vim invariant not restated in the shown code).
vim_free(NULL) is safe (free(NULL) semantics); this matters only for the allocation-failure path at line 21.
regmatch_T is an opaque struct whose only touched field is rm_ic; the shown code performs no arithmetic on regex match offsets.
limitations: NULL dereference of rmp at line 12 is not confirmable: the shown code never produces a NULL rmp, so a triggering call (rmp == NULL with name != NULL) would have to originate from an out-of-scope caller; no CWE attached.

On the match-success path at lines 19-20, match is set to name while the regex matched the home-replaced copy p and rmp's match offsets refer to p, which is freed at line 21; any consumer of rmp's offsets after this call could observe stale data, but that consumption is outside the shown code and no memory operation on freed p occurs here; no CWE attached.
ReDoS or other regex-engine behavior inside vim_regexec cannot be assessed because its body is not shown and the shown code performs no filtering or escaping of the matched string.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Every input-derived size is clamped before use: linebytes = min(nbytes, DISP_LINE_LEN) bounds the linebuf reads/writes by the buffer's own declared capacity, alen is restricted to {0,1,2,3} by the guard before either I2C sink, argc guards protect argv dereferences, and nbytes decreases monotonically without unsigned underflow, so the read loop provably terminates. The only security-relevant gap is the absence of any cap on the display length (up to 2^32-1 bytes, ~2.68e8 loop iterations), which is a finite, console-privileged resource-exhaustion/robustness concern, not an exploitable memory-safety, injection, or logic flaw in the shown code.

assumptions: linebuf's capacity is DISP_LINE_LEN (line 67) and the clamp at line 70 uses the same named constant, so the bound is identifiable from the shown code alone; upstream defines DISP_LINE_LEN 16, which only confirms, not required for, the safety argument.
hextoul/simple_strtoul cannot signal parse failure and wraps modulo 2^64 on 64-bit builds; this is why remaining range is [0, 2^32-1] after uint assignment.
argv strings are NULL-terminated and argv[0..argc-1] valid per the console-command parser contract; guards at lines 21 and 47 keep argv[1..3] in range.
In the DM path, i2c_get_cur_bus_chip writes *dev exactly when ret == 0 (line 52), so dev is initialized on the only path where it is used (lines 54, 73).
get_alen (body not shown) returns the ".N" modifier digit or the default; the shown guard at line 40 leaves only {0,1,2,3} admitted.
limitations: Resource exhaustion: argv[3] of "0xffffffff" yields up to 268,435,456 iterations (line 66-98) of I2C reads and console output; the loop is provably finite (nbytes strictly decreases by >=1 per iteration and cannot underflow), so this is a hardening/DoS robustness gap (no length cap), not a confirmed vulnerability; requires console or boot-script access and a responding I2C device.

uint alen (vs upstream int alen): in DM builds DEFAULT_ADDR_LEN=-1 makes get_alen return UINT_MAX, which the guard at line 40 now rejects, so 'i2c md <chip> <addr>' without a ".N" modifier fails with CMD_RET_USAGE; the alen != -1 check at line 53 is dead for admitted values. Functional regression only, no unsafe value is admitted.
Silent ulong->uint truncation of chip/addr/length on 64-bit builds (lines 32, 38, 48) has no security impact because the only size consumed (linebytes) is clamped by min() at line 70.
addr wraps only after 2^32 increments (unreachable with max length 2^32-1) and is a bus-offset value, not a host index; no host memory impact.
No CWE is attached to any of the above per the stated standards because none satisfies all three parts of confirmation with a concrete witness.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability. Every security-relevant operation is protected by an identifiable guard in the shown code: the fd passed to ioctl is guaranteed >= 0 by the checks at lines 37 and 42-43 (exactly excluding -1); oldflags is used only after the GETFLAGS ioctl succeeds (line 58); errno is read only immediately after a failing syscall (lines 71, 89); open() uses O_NOFOLLOW|O_RDONLY (lines 38-39); close() at line 93-94 only closes the self-opened descriptor exactly once. The unsigned-long-to-int narrowing of set/clear at line 62 is silent truncation feeding a fixed-width int ioctl argument, with no memory-safety, injection, or privilege impact.

assumptions: __archive_ensure_cloexec_flag is the standard fcntl-based libarchive helper whose contract is to tolerate invalid descriptors (it performs no dereference on -1); the call at line 40 with myfd == -1 after a failed open is benign, and even without that assumption the guard at lines 42-43 prevents any later use of the invalid descriptor.
ioctl(FS_IOC_GETFLAGS, &oldflags) writes all sizeof(int) bytes on success, per the kernel API contract; the shown code checks the return (line 58) before using oldflags.
errno is meaningful immediately after a failed ioctl; all reads of errno (lines 71, 89) immediately follow the failing syscall with no intervening calls.
limitations: set/clear are unsigned long but are narrowed to int newflags at line 62 (e.g., set = 0x100000000UL truncates to 0); this is a CWE-681-style truncation concern, but no security impact is confirmed because the consuming sink (ioctl at lines 63-84) accepts a fixed-width int argument and no size, index, length, or pointer value is derived from the truncated bits.
A NULL a would crash at archive_set_error (line 89), but the shown code never produces NULL and such a value is only reachable from an out-of-scope caller.

Passing myfd == -1 to __archive_ensure_cloexec_flag (line 40) relies on the helper tolerating invalid fds; the constant -1 is not attacker-controllable in magnitude and no dereference is implied by the call site.

External file-replacement races between open (line 38) and the ioctls are outside the shown code's scope; the fd pins the opened inode and O_RDONLY/O_NOFOLLOW prevent symlink following, so no privilege boundary is crossed within this function.
The EPERM subset retry (lines 75-84) may return ARCHIVE_OK while some superuser-only flags were silently dropped; this is a functional semantics nuance, not a security flaw.

verdict.summary: lprn_is_black divides by unconstrained device members: lprn->nBh is used as a divisor at line 9 with no nonzero guard, and the derived maxY is used as the modulus at line 11. A zero denominator (nBh == 0, or BlockLine < nBh making maxY == 0) causes integer division by zero (SIGFPE/UB) on the unconditional entry path, enabling a crash/denial of service (CVE-2017-8291 pattern) from crafted device state.

evidence.reason: lprn->nBh is framework/device state whose residual range in the shown code is all int values — no guard checks nBh != 0 anywhere before this statement, so the admitted set reaching the division is the full int range including 0. With the witness nBh == 0 the denominate of '/' is 0, producing integer division by zero (SIGFPE/UB) on the unconditional entry path; this is the confirmed CWE-369 mechanism (DoS via crash). The only absent link is that nBh's attacker influence originates in device-state flow outside the snippet, hence the range-based 0.7 confidence rather than a fully traced entry-point value.

maxY is computed at line 9 as BlockLine / nBh * nBh; for the unguarded, positive-state witness BlockLine == 1 and nBh == 2 (both within the residual ranges the shown code leaves unconstrained) the quotient is 0 and maxY == 0. Line 11 then evaluates (r + h - bh) % 0, a second zero-divisor sink of the same CWE-369 failure: no guard checks maxY != 0 before the modulo. An attacker-controllable/transitional device state making BlockLine < nBh crashes the interpreter on every call.

assumptions: int is 32-bit two's complement and C99 truncated division applies, so a negative (r + h - bh) yields a negative y0.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The unguarded writes in the "m=" line (lines 12-26) are bounded by the line-9 length check, which admits only len >= media.slen + transport.slen + 36 while the worst-case overhead of those writes is 25 bytes (2 + 1 + 10 digits port + 11 digits port_count + 1), leaving at least 11 bytes of headroom (p <= end - 11) before the independently guarded fmt/CRLF/conn/bandw/attr sections. The fmt guard (end-p > fmt[i].slen) admits exactly slen <= end-p-1 so the 1+slen-byte write cannot pass end, and the CRLF guard (end-p >= 2) writes exactly 2. Claims requiring field widths or callee/parser invariants not visible here are demoted to limitations.

assumptions: pj_utoa writes exactly the decimal digits of the value (no NUL) and returns the digit count; for 32-bit unsigned values that is at most 10 digits.
desc.port is a 16-bit (<=5 digits) and port_count/fmt_count/bandw_count/attr_count are 32-bit unsigned fields of pjmedia_sdp_media_desc (types not declared in the shown code).
pj_memcpy has memcpy semantics; print_connection_info/print_bandw/print_attr honor the passed remaining length and return bytes written or a negative error.
buf/len describe a valid buffer, so end = buf + len is the true capacity.
limitations: If desc.port or desc.port_count were wider than 32 bits (not visible in the shown code), pj_utoa digit counts could exceed the 36-byte reservation (e.g., 20+20 digits -> 45 bytes of overhead) causing an unguarded overflow of the m= line; unconfirmable because the field types are not shown.
OOB reads from media.ptr/transport.ptr/fmt[i].ptr would require the SDP parser to store a .slen larger than the backing allocation; that invariant is outside the shown code.
If print_connection_info/print_bandw/print_attr returned a byte count larger than the remaining buffer, p += printed could advance p past end; their bodies are not shown.
A size_t overflow of media.slen + transport.slen + 36 in the line-9 check would require slen values near SIZE_MAX, which the shown code cannot produce.
(int) casts of (end-p) and (p-buf) only wrap for buffers larger than INT_MAX (2 GB), not attacker-controllable within the shown code.

verdict.summary: In _gdContributionsAlloc, the error-cleanup path decrements unsigned u past zero (lines 29/32) and tests it with 'while (u >= 0)' (line 30), which can never be false for unsigned arithmetic. On the overflow_error/allocation-failure branch (line 28), the loop indexes res->ContribRow at u = UINT_MAX (line 31) — far beyond the line_length-element array — performing an out-of-bounds read and calling gdFree on the resulting invalid pointer, then repeating indefinitely. Reachable with line_length = 1 and windows_size in the overflow-flagged range admitted by line 23 (e.g., UINT_MAX), or on any weights-allocation failure (line 26 -> line 28).

evidence.reason: Sink line 31: u is unsigned int; after the failure branch (line 28) executes u-- (line 29), u wraps from 0 to UINT_MAX (for the witness line_length=1, windows_size=UINT_MAX, where line 23's overflow2 admits the value and sets overflow_error=1). Line 30's 'while (u >= 0)' is always true for unsigned u, so this statement reads res->ContribRow[UINT_MAX], which exceeds the line_length-element capacity established at line 17 (excess UINT_MAX elements), an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), and passes that out-of-bounds pointer to gdFree (invalid free). The same statement is reached for the Weights==NULL arm of line 28 (line-26 allocation failure) for any line_length >= 1, since the cleanup loop cannot terminate.

assumptions: overflow2(a, b) returns nonzero exactly when a*b exceeds the checked representation, its standard meaning; its body is not shown, so the precise threshold is assumed per the name and use.
sizeof(ContributionType) defines the element size of the array allocated at line 17, so the array has exactly line_length elements.
gdMalloc returns NULL on allocation failure, as the shown code explicitly checks at lines 8, 18, and 28.
line_length = 1 is in the admitted set of every guard on the witness path (line 13's overflow2 returns 0, line 18's NULL check passes).
limitations: line_length and windows_size are internal-helper parameters; no caller is shown, so attacker control via enclosing image-scaling code is inferred rather than demonstrated in the shown code.

The witness using the overflow branch depends on the standard semantics of overflow2; however, the identical out-of-bounds/invalid-free/hang behavior also fires on the Weights==NULL arm of line 28, which does not depend on overflow2's threshold.
If line_length == 0 the for-loop never executes and the failure branch is unreachable; the finding requires line_length >= 1, which the shown code permits.
The non-terminating loop (CWE-835) and invalid free (CWE-590) consequences share the same unsigned-underflow root cause as the CWE-125 out-of-bounds read and are not reported as separate CWEs.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in readconf_main: a config-file-list item is copied into big_buffer (capacity big_buffer_size, line 10), then suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename) (line 16) is used as the target of unbounded sprintf appends (lines 25/30/41) of euid and nodename; a filename of length big_buffer_size-1 makes the append extend past the buffer by up to 268 bytes (confirmed witness: 5 bytes written at offset big_buffer_size-1, 4 bytes past the end), corrupting the heap during privileged config processing. Secondary: line 391 dereferences the unchecked expand_string(host_number_string) result, crashing on an expansion failure for any non-NULL configured value.

evidence.reason: suffix (line 16) = filename + Ustrlen(filename) with filename length in [0, big_buffer_size-1] (residual range from the copy cap imposed by string_nextinlist's buffer/size arguments at line 10). The loop guard (10-11) admits any non-NULL item and the uname guard (22) admits return 0, so a witness of a big_buffer_size-1 char item with euid=0 and nodename="x" passes both guards; this sprintf then writes 5 bytes at offset big_buffer_size-1, i.e., 4 bytes past the big_buffer_size-byte big_buffer (CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write); no remaining-capacity check exists before the call.

Same sink derivation as line 25: suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename) (line 16) points at the end of a big_buffer_size-1 char item (admitted by guard 10-11 and, for this branch, guard 22 admitting uname()==0); writing "." + nodename + NUL is at minimum 3 bytes at offset big_buffer_size-1, 2 bytes past the buffer (CWE-787). No capacity check is present.

suffix (line 16) targets the end of a big_buffer_size-1 char item; the only guard on this path, config_file == NULL (line 39), is satisfiable (first item or failed prior open) and does not bound the filename length. Writing "." + euid + NUL is at minimum 3 bytes at offset big_buffer_size-1, 2 bytes past the buffer (CWE-787).

expand_string (line 390) is called on host_number_string (guard at line 387 admits any non-NULL string) and its return is used unguarded; the same helper's NULL-on-failure is evidenced inside the shown code by the panic checks at lines 236, 250, and 310. An expansion failure (e.g., a malformed ${... construct) yields s == NULL, and this Ustrtol dereferences it, causing a NULL-pointer read (CWE-476).

assumptions: big_buffer's capacity is exactly big_buffer_size, implied by passing buffer+size to string_nextinlist (line 10), whose copy is NUL-terminated and capped at big_buffer_size-1 characters.

limitations: The OOB write requires a build with CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE and/or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID; in the plain #else branch (line 57) no append occurs.

A trigger requires an unusually long entry (>= big_buffer_size-269 bytes) in config_main_filelist; per the role classification it is treated as entry-point input with residual length up to big_buffer_size-1, but its concrete external origin (e.g., a -C argument or build-time CONFIGURE_FILE) is outside the shown code, so remote attacker control is not established here.
The CWE-476 witness relies on expand_string's NULL-on-failure contract, evidenced only indirectly by the three guarded expand_string calls at lines 236, 250, and 310.
Robustness concerns without a security sink in the shown code (e.g., accepting a negative localhost_number) are not reported as findings.

verdict.summary: Balloc dereferences the result of MALLOC without a NULL check: with unvalidated k driving line 11's size to ~8 GiB (k=30), MALLOC can return NULL and rv->k = k at line 12 dereferences it, and line 16 dereferences it again unconditionally, crashing the process (CWE-476).

evidence.reason: k is unconstrained in the shown code (residual range: full int, no guard on it). k=30 is admitted by every conditional: line 10 yields x=1<<30, line 11 derives the ~8 GiB MALLOC size, and the standard allocator returning NULL makes rv NULL; line 12 then dereferences rv. The line 7 guard only tests freelist[k] for NULL and never checks k; no NULL check exists between line 11 and line 12. Primary mechanism: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476).

On the same unchecked-MALLOC path, when the line 11 allocation fails for an admitted large k, rv is NULL and this unconditional statement dereferences rv after the unlock, regardless of which branch was taken — a second distinct NULL-dereference sink for the same CWE-476 root cause.

assumptions: int is 32-bit and size_t/Long are 64-bit/8 bytes for the quantitative witness; the C standard leaves these implementation-defined, but the NULL-dereference mechanism does not depend on them.
The caller-side range of k is not shown; per the internal-helper rule, the residual range is bounded only by the guards present in the shown code, which is none.
limitations: freelist[k] out-of-bounds read/write for negative or oversized k (lines 7-8) is not confirmed because freelist's declared type and capacity (e.g., Kmax) do not appear in the shown code, so the exact OOB boundary cannot be bound.
x = 1 << k is UB for k<0 or k>=31, so no determinate value or independent integer-overflow finding (CWE-190/682) can be confirmed from that path.

The NULL dereference requires MALLOC to actually fail; the ~8 GiB request for k=30 makes failure realistic but environment-dependent, and attacker influence over k through callers is outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: FSCTL_GET_SHADOW_COPY_DATA computes labels_data_count with 32-bit arithmetic: for a helper-reported num_volumes of 2^31, num_volumes*2 wraps to 0, labels_data_count truncates to 2, and *out_len becomes 18 (line 134). After the max_out_len>=18 guard passes, an 18-byte buffer is allocated (line 144) and the loop over num_volumes writes up to 2*sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL) bytes per iteration at cur_pdata (lines 168-173), overflowing the heap object.

This truncated value drives the reply-size derivation and the allocation of the output object, anchoring the CWE-190 wrap.

The output object is allocated with the wrapped size *out_len=18 bytes, fixing its capacity in the shown code immediately before the label loop writes into it.

Primary CWE-787 sink: the loop bound is the unconstrained num_volumes (2^31 iterations when num_volumes=2^31), and each iteration writes up to 2*sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL) bytes at cur_pdata starting at offset 12 of the 18-byte allocation, so the first iteration already writes past the object's capacity; no guard in the shown code bounds num_volumes.

C usual arithmetic conversions: num_volumes * 2 is evaluated in uint32_t and assignment to uint32 labels_data_count truncates modulo 2^32.

FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID returns a 64-byte non-zeroed talloc_array buffer with bytes 48-63 uninitialized while *out_len may be 64 (lines 47, 49, 55-57); the security-relevant read occurs in the caller, which is not shown, so an uninitialized-memory disclosure cannot be confirmed here.

No claim is made about the sizeof(SHADOW_COPY_LABEL) value; the wrap witness num_volumes=2^31 is valid for any sizeof >= 1.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in string_number_format: the separator-space product thousand_sep.size()*((integral-1)/3) is computed in 32-bit int (line 62) and, for d=1e304 (dec=0, integral=305) with a 42,524,433-byte thousand separator, wraps to a small positive value (101*42,524,433 = 4,294,967,733 mod 2^32 = 437), so the line 62 overflow guard silently admits the value; line 67 then sizes resstr to only 742 bytes (lines 70, 88) while the copy loop (lines 123-131) writes 4,294,968,038 bytes, so the first separator memcpy (lines 126-128) writes ~42.5 MB below the heap object (CWE-787), caused by the 32-bit integer wrap (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: Sink of the confirmed heap underflow: thousand_sep (entry-point input, residual range any non-empty string of size up to INT_MAX, admitted by the guard at line 61) is used via its int size. With d=1e304, dec=0, integral=305 (line 57) and thousand_sep.size()=42,524,433, the product at line 62 wraps in 32-bit int: 101*42,524,433=4,294,967,733 ≡ 437 (mod 2^32); the guard compares 305+437=742 < 305, which is false, so it admits the wrapped value, line 67 sets integral=742, and line 88 allocates a 742-byte resbuf. At the first insertion t=resbuf+738, so this memcpy writes 42,524,433 bytes starting at resbuf-42,523,694, i.e., ~42.5 MB before the heap object start; the loop repeats it 101 times. Primary mechanism: CWE-787 out-of-bounds write.

Secondary sink of the same confirmed finding: the byte-copy pointer walk t (started at resbuf+reslen-1 with reslen=742, line 92) writes the 305 integral digits and, combined with the 101 separator memcpys (lines 126-128), advances t far below resbuf. Total writes 305 + 101*42,524,433 = 4,294,968,038 bytes against the 742-byte allocation sized from the line 62 wrap-bypassed integral; every preceding guard (lines 12, 17, 28, 29, 33/39, 46/49, 61, 62) admits the witness path. Mechanism: CWE-787 out-of-bounds write driven by the CWE-190 int wrap.

assumptions: String::size() and the size arithmetic used in the shown code are 32-bit int (the code declares integral/tmplen/reslen/count as int and its own overflow guards at lines 62 and 76 are written for int wrap).

snprintf returns the would-be length and prints %.0F of 1e304 as 305 characters; the two-phase format (lines 24-37) yields exactly tmplen characters, and String(n, ReserveString) provides n+1 usable bytes per the 63+1 convention stated at lines 20-22.

limitations: If String::size() were 64-bit, the line 62 product would not wrap and this witness would not under-allocate; the finding is contingent on the 32-bit int size semantics stated in assumptions.
C++ signed integer overflow at line 62 is undefined behavior; the wrap-based witness relies on the two's-complement behavior of mainstream compilers.

DoS via attacker-controlled dec near INT_MAX (multi-GB allocations at lines 35/88 and O(dec) formatting work, plus the tmplen+1 wrap at line 37 when tmplen==INT_MAX) is plausible but environment/libc-dependent and not confirmed from the shown code.
A locale whose decimal separator is neither '.' nor ',' makes strpbrk (line 47) miss the point so dp==nullptr with dec>0, causing mis-formatting only; no memory-safety impact demonstrated.
isdigit((int)tmpbuf[0]) (lines 29, 39) with a negative char value is technically UB; no security impact demonstrated.
Resource exhaustion (CWE-400) via attacker-controlled dec/thousand_sep sizes is not added as a separate confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: luaG_runerror is a standard Lua error-reporting helper: it formats a message via Lua's internal string formatter (line 7), optionally appends source:line info under the isLua(ci) guard (lines 9-13), and never returns (line 14). The dangerous-looking operations (format-string call, stack index L->top - 2, ci dereference) each depend on callee contracts or VM invariants that are not present in the shown code, and no attacker-controlled path, identifiable object capacity, or in-path NULL production can be established. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: L is a valid lua_State whose L->ci points to a valid current CallInfo and whose stack has capacity for the slots used below L->top (VM invariant, not shown).

luaO_pushvfstring (line 7) leaves the formatted message anchored at L->top - 1 and returns a pointer to it; luaG_addinfo (line 10) pushes exactly one more string, so L->top - 2 and L->top - 1 are the two message slots (as the line 11 comment 'remove msg from the stack' implies).
luaO_pushvfstring is Lua's own string formatter, not the C printf family, and raises on OOM rather than returning NULL.
fmt is supplied by internal call sites as a static format string matched to the varargs (caller contract not visible in the shown code).
luaG_errormsg (line 14) never returns, consistent with l_noret on line 1.
limitations: Format-string content of fmt is unconstrained in the shown code (line 7), but its provenance is an internal-helper parameter with no shown attacker path, and the callee luaO_pushvfstring is not printf-family; a format-string injection finding cannot be confirmed from the shown code (CWE-134 unconfirmed).

setobjs2s(L, L->top - 2, L->top - 1) at line 11: the capacity of the target stack buffer (L->stack / stacksize) is not identifiable from the shown code, so any out-of-bounds read/write claim is unconfirmable per the capacity rule.

Behavior of Lua's formatter, luaG_addinfo internals, GC/longjmp failure paths of luaC_checkGC / luaO_pushvfstring / luaG_errormsg, and memory exhaustion during error-message construction all reside in unshown callee bodies and are out of scope for confirmation.

Remaining concerns (unchecked r_list_newf result, count/list mismatch on early break, attr->size exceeding sz, ut64 wrap of buf_offset+offset) are robustness/downstream issues, not confirmed vulnerabilities in the shown code.

limitations: No confirmed vulnerability: the only direct buffer read (line 13) and the callee invocation (line 21) are preceded by effective guards (lines 9 and 18) whose admitted sets exclude every failing value; a not-vulnerable verdict rests on these guards and on the standard size-bounded semantics of the callee.

If r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new can return non-NULL with size 0 (callee body not shown), offset stalls and the same data is re-parsed up to 65535 times — a bounded robustness/DoS-hardening concern, not a hang or OOB in the shown code.

Any OOB inside r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new itself would be a callee-internal defect; the shown call site passes in-domain arguments and is not itself a confirmed out-of-domain derivation.

limitations: Log injection (CWE-117) into stderr via newline/control characters in data->backing or data->expect reaching fprintf %s (lines 23-24, 35-38) is reachable but has no established security mechanism: the sink is a unit-test stderr print with no machine-parsed log or log-based control flow in the shown code.
