verdict.summary: The inode pointer returned by read_inode (line 16) is stored in *i and dereferenced at line 24 with no NULL check; when a crafted/corrupt squashfs image makes read_inode fail, the returned NULL pointer is dereferenced (lines 24-28, 31, 40-42), crashing unsquashfs. Primary mechanism: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476) with DoS impact.

evidence.reason: read_inode(block_start, offset) at line 16 fills *i from attacker-controlled image data with no validation; the shown code imposes no NULL check before line 24 dereferences (*i)->mode (followed by lines 25-28, 31, 40-42). The residual range of the return value therefore includes NULL, and a crafted image that makes read_inode fail yields *i == NULL, a member of the admitted set of every (absent) guard on the path, causing a NULL-pointer dereference crash at line 24 (primary mechanism CWE-476).

assumptions: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN is 256 and SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT is 256 (the boundary math in guards at lines 57 and 72 also holds for any value pair since buffer capacity is derived from SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN).
struct squashfs_dir_entry places name immediately after its fixed members, so dire->name starts at offset sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry) within buffer.
dire->size and dirh.count are small on-disk (16-bit) values promoted to int without loss.
read_inode returns NULL on failure (callee contract not visible in the shown code); the shown code then dereferences the result without a check.
The squashfs image data consumed by read_inode/read_directory_data is untrusted attacker-controlled input.
limitations: The exact image contents that make read_inode return NULL are produced in callee code not shown, so the trigger is a range-based confirmation (confidence 0.6) rather than a value demonstrated entirely within the shown code.

bytes (int) accumulation at lines 54/69/109 can overflow only with a directory table exceeding roughly 2^31 counted bytes (~8.4M entries); it does not cause an OOB memory access because every read goes through read_directory_data, which returns FALSE at the end of the decompressed table; impact would be limited to pathological parsing/DoS at extreme image sizes, so it is not reported with a CWE.
size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3 (line 42) underflows when unsigned data < 3, but the int truncation makes the outer loop condition false (negative size), so no memory sink is reached.
strdup(dire->name) at line 98 is unchecked; a NULL result requires OOM of a constant-size allocation and is not attacker-sized as a single allocation, so it is recorded here rather than as a finding.

verdict.summary: virtbt_rx_handle reads skb->data[0] (line 5) and calls skb_pull(skb, 1) (line 6) with no skb->len >= 1 guard. An empty skb (skb->len == 0, a value wholly unconstrained by the shown code) causes a 1-byte out-of-bounds read and wraps the unsigned skb->len to 0xFFFFFFFF; when the read byte is one of {0x02..0x05} the corrupted skb is passed to hci_recv_frame (line 14) as an out-of-domain frame length, enabling out-of-bounds processing (CWE-125). Independently, pkt_type values outside {0x02..0x05} fall out of the switch with no kfree_skb, leaking each such skb (CWE-772).

evidence.reason: skb is an internal-helper parameter whose skb->len is left entirely unconstrained by the shown code (no length check appears before this load), so the residual range admits skb->len == 0. The sk_buff API invariant gives the valid payload capacity as [skb->data, skb->data + skb->len); with len == 0 the load at index 0 exceeds that capacity by 1 byte — a confirmed 1-byte out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The switch that follows guards only dispatch and cannot protect this read.

Same unconstrained input (skb->len == 0 is a member of every admitted set on the path — there are no guards before line 6). skb_pull decrements the unsigned skb->len by 1, wrapping 0 to 0xFFFFFFFF, and advances skb->data 1 byte past the end, corrupting the skb's length field to an out-of-domain value; this is the root mechanism that turns the empty-buffer input into a memory-safety failure (CWE-125; unsigned-wrap aspect CWE-191-style, not counted separately).

When the byte read at line 5 equals one of {0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x05} (the switch's admitted set; the byte is unconstrained, so these values are reachable), the skb whose skb->len wrapped to 0xFFFFFFFF at line 6 is passed to hci_recv_frame, a name-implied consumer of skb->len as the frame length. The shown code thus forwards a length that is out of the domain the consumer requires, enabling length-driven out-of-bounds reads in the HCI stack (CWE-125).

pkt_type has the __u8 residual range 0..255; the switch admits only {0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x05} and has no default branch, so any of the remaining 252 values (e.g., 0x00) exits the function with skb neither freed nor forwarded — the shown code provides no release on this path. Each such device-supplied packet leaks one skb, and the volume is attacker-controlled, yielding unbounded kernel memory exhaustion (CWE-772).

assumptions: sk_buff API invariant used as the capacity source: valid payload bytes are [skb->data, skb->data + skb->len), and skb->len is an unsigned field so the one-byte decrement at line 6 wraps for len == 0.

Ownership contract (caller, not shown): virtbt_rx_done transfers ownership of each dequeued virtio buffer to this handler and does not separately release skbs the handler neither frees nor passes to hci_recv_frame; the CWE-772 conclusion depends on that contract.
skb is assumed non-NULL on entry because the shown code performs no NULL check; a caller-supplied NULL is treated as out of scope.
limitations: Reachability of skb->len == 0 depends on the unshown caller/virtio-backend behavior: if some invariant outside the shown code guarantees skb->len >= 1 for every queued buffer, the line-5 OOB read and line-6 wrap cannot trigger; no such invariant is visible in the shown code, so the residual range keeps len == 0 admitted.

The precise out-of-bounds offsets read inside hci_recv_frame (or its sub-parsers) after skb->len wraps to 0xFFFFFFFF are not enumerated because the callee bodies are not shown; the finding anchors at the call site forwarding an out-of-domain length to a name-implied length consumer.

If skb->head was allocated with at least 1 byte of headroom, the line-5 read with len == 0 may remain inside the underlying allocation and read only stale bytes; the confirmed violation is against the API-defined valid-data boundary, with the primary memory-safety impact flowing through the line-6 length wrap.
The int return value of hci_recv_frame (line 14) is discarded; a failed receive then leaving exploitable state is not confirmable from the shown code (possible CWE-390/754, not confirmed).

For the downstream hci_recv_frame branch in the len == 0 case, pkt_type must equal one of {0x02..0x05}, which requires the stale byte at skb->data to take one of those values; the OOB read itself does not depend on the byte value.

verdict.summary: In sctp_make_strreset_req, stream_num is unconstrained (__u16, 0..65535). For stream_num=32760 (out path) or 32764 (in path), stream_len is 65520/65528 bytes while `(sizeof + stream_len)` wraps mod 65536 so outlen/inlen become 2; sctp_make_reconf then requests only 2 payload bytes (line 15) and the sctp_addto_chunk calls (lines 26/29 and 37/40) append 65538 bytes, producing an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787) caused by the __u16 size wraparound (CWE-190 secondary).

evidence.reason: With stream_num=32760 (admitted: no guard restricts stream_num), stream_len=65520 (line 6) and outlen=(18+65520) mod 65536 = 2 (line 12, __u16 wrap), so the chunk was requested with 2 payload bytes at line 15. Guard `if (outlen)` at line 19 admits outlen=2; this call then appends sizeof(outreq)=18 bytes (plus 65520 more at line 29), i.e. 65538 bytes total into a 2-byte payload chunk — out-of-domain length at the sctp_addto_chunk call site, CWE-787 heap OOB write; the wraparound corrupting the size is CWE-190.

stream_len=65520 is derived entirely from stream_num=32760 at line 6 (2*32760, no truncation at this step); outlen wrapped to 2 at line 12, so payload capacity requested at line 15 is 2 bytes. Guard `if (stream_len)` at line 28 admits 65520 (it only tests nonzero), so this call appends 65520 bytes — exceeding the identifiable 2-byte payload capacity by 65518+ bytes, CWE-787 OOB write; size wraparound is CWE-190.

With stream_num=32764, in=1, out=0: stream_len=65528 (line 6) and inlen=(10+65528) mod 65536 = 2 (line 13, __u16 wrap), so the chunk was requested with 2 payload bytes at line 15. Guard `if (inlen)` at line 32 admits 2; this call appends sizeof(inreq)=10 bytes (plus 65528 more at line 40), 65538 bytes total into a 2-byte payload chunk — CWE-787 OOB write; secondary CWE-190.

stream_len=65528 is derived from stream_num=32764 at line 6; inlen wrapped to 2 at line 13, so payload capacity requested at line 15 is 2 bytes. Guard `if (stream_len)` at line 39 admits 65528 (tests only nonzero), so this call appends 65528 bytes — exceeding the 2-byte payload capacity by 65526+ bytes, CWE-787 OOB heap write; secondary CWE-190.

assumptions: sizeof(struct sctp_strreset_outreq)=18 and sizeof(struct sctp_strreset_inreq)=10 (standard kernel struct definitions); the overflow shown at lines 29/40 does not depend on these constants because stream_len itself exceeds the line-15 capacity.

sctp_make_reconf(asoc, length) constructs a reconf control chunk sized for `length` payload bytes (plus only fixed header overhead), and sctp_addto_chunk(chunk, len, data) appends `len` bytes into that chunk — name-implied standard semantics.
stream_num is the count of __be16 stream-list entries, so the caller provides at least 2*stream_num bytes at stream_list.
limitations: End-to-end provenance of stream_num (e.g., a userspace SCTP_RESET_STREAMS setsockopt) is outside the shown code; it is classified as an internal-helper parameter with unconstrained residual range [0,65535].
A NULL stream_list with stream_len != 0 would fault inside the callee, but the shown code cannot produce NULL, so it is not reported as a finding.

The wire parameter lengths written by htons(outlen)/htons(inlen) (lines 21/34) under-report the chunk in the wrapped case; this is a protocol-integrity consequence of the same truncation, not an independent root cause.
asoc->strreset_inseq - 1 and asoc->next_tsn - 1 (lines 23-24) can wrap in value space for sequence 0, but they reach no security-relevant sink in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in the MNG DEFI chunk handler: object_id is decoded from two attacker-controlled file bytes (0..65535) and the guard `object_id > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS` admits object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, so `mng_info->exists[object_id]=MagickTrue` writes one element past the object arrays whose valid index domain the shown code itself fixes at 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1 (lines 114-118, 326-327, 813, 895). A DEFI chunk with payload 0x01 0x00 (object_id 256 when MNG_MAX_OBJECTS==256) triggers the write at line 406 and preceding out-of-range reads at lines 395-396; the same index is reused on the IHDR path (1295-1296, 1466-1467, 2062-2068).

evidence.reason: CWE-787 heap OOB write. object_id derives from chunk bytes p[0]<<8|p[1] at line 377 (residual 0..65535); after the line-384 guard `object_id > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS` and line-392 clamp, the admitted set is 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, which includes object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS. The shown code's own exclusive-bound uses (i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS at 114-118/326-327; i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS -> continue at 813/895) establish the valid range as 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1, so the index at this write exceeds capacity by exactly one element. Witness: DEFI chunk with length 2 and payload 0x01 0x00 (object_id 256) passes line 370 and 384 and reaches this sink.

OOB read with the same out-of-domain index object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS admitted by the line-384 guard (same root cause as the CWE-787 write at line 406): these are the first uses of the index one step after the clamp, reading one element past the exists/frozen arrays whose valid range is 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1 per lines 114-118/326-327/813/895.

assumptions: MNG_MAX_OBJECTS is the element count of the MngInfo object arrays (exists, frozen, invisible, viewable, x_off, y_off, object_clip): the shown code always uses it as an exclusive upper bound (lines 114-118, 326-327, 813, 895), so index == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS is out of the arrays' valid range by one element.
Only the MNG path (image_info->magick == "MNG") is analyzed; the chunk-parsing path is the only one that initializes type/length in the shown code.

Compile-time options (MNG_INSERT_LAYERS, MNG_LOOSE, MNG_OBJECT_BUFFERS, MNG_BASI_SUPPORTED, MNG_COALESCE_LAYERS) are treated as not defining the primary finding; none of them changes the DEFI object_id analysis.
limitations: LOOP/ENDL use a chunk byte as loop_level (0..255) to index loop_active/loop_count/loop_jump/loop_iteration (lines 926, 941-945, 965, 971-1005); the capacities of those arrays are not identifiable from the shown code, so the out-of-bounds claim is unconfirmable.
DISC/SEEK (lines 866-869) forward 16-bit object ids (up to 65535) to MngInfoDiscardObject with no visible bounds check; the callee is not shown, so the impact is unconfirmed.

PLTE (lines 500-508) dereferences global_plte when the fixed-size (256-entry) allocation fails, and SetImageBackgroundColor/CopyMagickMemory return values are discarded (1705/1732, 781/1367/1416/1664/1669/2127/2214); these need an unchecked allocation failure with no attacker-controlled size, so they are not findings.
MNG_LOOSE branches (lines 513-523, 539-542) can use an uninitialized i and a NULL global_plte, but only under a build flag not present in the shown code.

FRAM/TERM chunk parsing can over-read up to p-chunk == length+23 (lines 653-668, 672-714) but the allocation capacity is length+MagickPathExtent (lines 185-186), so reads stay inside the malloc'd object; no CWE-125.

MAGN arithmetic (lines 1537-1552, 1563-1579) can wrap in png_uint_32 and the magnified dimensions are attacker-influenced via image->columns/rows from ReadOnePNGImage, but no consuming allocation/size sink and its capacity are identifiable in the shown code, so an overflow/OOB consequence is unconfirmed.

LOOP/ENDL seek-back loops (lines 920-1018) are finite per level (loop_iters is 32-bit and chunk count is bounded by file size), so no non-termination finding; only algorithmic amplification potential is noted.
For non-MNG magick the loop body uses uninitialized type/length (lines 147-161 gated by line 150); the caller contract for this function is not shown, so it is not analyzed.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The frag-descriptor write sink (__skb_fill_page_desc, lines 50-51) is protected by the guard at lines 24-25, which admits only nr_frags in [0, MAX_SKB_FRAGS-1] and excludes the out-of-bounds index MAX_SKB_FRAGS; the same value read at line 48 is used as the index with no intervening modification. The pskb_put sink (line 81) is bounded by tailen <= skb_tailroom (line 18) on the skip_cow path and by skb_cow_data's tailroom guarantee on the cow path. Every path to the return at line 84 initializes nfrags, and both encap and skb_cow_data failures propagate correctly (lines 13-14, 73-75). Residual concerns (negative esp->tailen admitted into the page-frag path by the signed/unsigned comparison at line 18; esp_output_fill_trailer write size vs tailen; the +2 return convention in the page-frag path) depend on caller-side invariants or caller use not present in the shown code, so they are unconfirmed.

assumptions: MAX_SKB_FRAGS is the capacity of skb_shared_info.frags[], which is name-implied by the guard using the same constant at line 24.

skb_cow_data(skb, tailen, &trailer) (line 73) guarantees at least tailen bytes of tailroom in the returned trailer, which is the documented contract of the API; the shown code uses it in the standard pskb_put(skb, trailer, tailen) pattern (line 81).
limitations: esp->tailen is an internal-helper input with no range check in the shown code. Because line 18 compares the int tailen against the unsigned skb_tailroom(), a negative tailen is converted to a huge unsigned value, is excluded from the tailroom branch, and is still admitted into the page-frag branch (lines 24-25 do not involve tailen), reaching the size argument of __skb_fill_page_desc (lines 50-51) and pskb_put (line 81) as a negative/underflowed length. Attacker control of esp->tailen cannot be established from the shown code (its derivation is in caller code), so this is an unconfirmed hardening concern, not a finding.

The write size of esp_output_fill_trailer (esp->plen/esp->tfclen, lines 46 and 80) is not bounded by tailen or allocsize within the shown code; an inconsistent esp state would overrun the page-frag or tailroom region, but the consistency invariant is established outside the shown code.

The page-frag path returns nfrags = old_nr_frags + 2 (lines 48-58), one more than the resulting fragment count; whether the caller consumes this as an exact index bound and over-reads frags[] cannot be verified from the shown code.

The known OOB-write bug class of this function family (missing nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS check before __skb_fill_page_desc) is not present: the guard at lines 24-25 is exactly the protective check and fully excludes the OOB index.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The directory-entry name read/write (lines 90-96) is bounded by the guard at line 85 (dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN), which admits only sizes 0..255 and therefore keeps the length-256 write and NUL-termination index 256 inside the 257-byte name region of buffer; the entry-count loop at line 68 is capped at SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT by line 63; all read_directory_data calls are failure-checked, bounding iteration at file EOF. The unchecked read_inode result (line 17) and unchecked strdup (line 112) are NULL-dereference candidates whose NULL production is not demonstrated in the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN is 256 and SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT is 256, so the buffer's trailing name region is SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN+1 = 257 bytes and the dir_count check admits at most 256 entries.
squashfs_dir_entry_3 contains the fixed on-disk fields followed by a flexible/zero-length name member at offset sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3), so dire->name points into buffer with 257 usable bytes.
FALSE is 0 and read_directory_data returns FALSE on a failed/short read, which is what the res checks at lines 54-55, 79-80, and 93-94 rely on.
On-disk directory-data length is bounded by the actual supplied file, so successful reads cannot continue past the end of the file and the outer loop terminates on attacker-chosen input.
limitations: Line 17 stores read_inode(block_start, offset) into *i and lines 25-30, 32, 41-43 dereference it without a NULL check; whether read_inode can return NULL for attacker-controlled block_start/offset is not demonstrable from the shown code because its body is not shown (potential CWE-476, unconfirmed).
Line 112 ignores the return of strdup; a NULL ent->name would only arise from OOM of a <=256-byte allocation, and the dereference sites are outside the shown code (no confirmed impact).

bytes and size are signed int; bytes could in principle exceed 2^31-1 only for a directory stream larger than 2GB, which the shown code cannot demonstrate and whose only effect would be non-security-relevant arithmetic behavior.

The size-consistency gap (bytes is not revalidated against size after each entry inside one header) is a corruption-detection robustness issue only; it cannot reach a memory-safety sink because every per-entry read is length-bounded and EOF-checked.
The dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT check is effectively dead code for an 8-bit count field, but the inner loop is still bounded at 256 iterations, so no vulnerability results.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The directory-entry name path (read_directory_data(dire->name, ..., dire->size + 1) and dire->name[dire->size + 1] = '\0') is contained: the guard at the filename-length check admits only sizes < SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, and the declared buffer reserves sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 bytes, so the maximum reachable byte index (the terminator for size == SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN-1) is the buffer's last valid index. Loop bounds are enforced by successful reads plus a strictly increasing byte counter, so the parsing terminates on finite input. Remaining concerns (unchecked read_inode result dereferenced, dead guards, int overflow in bytes/size) are not confirmable from the shown code and have no demonstrated security impact.

assumptions: SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN is 256, consistent with the buffer expression sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 and with the guard comparison on dire->size.

squashfs_dir_entry_3 layout has the flexible name member immediately after the 4-byte bitfield unit, so offsetof(name) == sizeof(squashfs_dir_entry_3) == 4; the buffer expression directly encodes this accommodation.
read_directory_data advances *start/*offset and returns FALSE at end of available data, as its use in this function implies.
MEM_ERROR() terminates the process (conventional); if it returned, the malloc(NULL) result would be dereferenced at line 23.
dirh.count and dire->size are unsigned bitfields of width 8 per the v3 format implied by the guard comments; the safety conclusion holds even if they are wider.
limitations: read_inode (line 17) is a parse call whose result is dereferenced unguarded at lines 25-29; if it can return NULL on a corrupted image this is a NULL-dereference DoS (CWE-476), but the shown code does not demonstrate that NULL outcome, so it is not confirmed.

The guard at line 85 (and line 63) may be dead if dire->size (dirh.count) is an 8-bit field, since 255/256 can never trip the >= / > comparisons; this is defense-in-depth hardening only, with no memory impact because the buffer sizing covers the admitted maximum.

32-bit int arithmetic on bytes/size (lines 43, 60, 82, 123) could wrap for directories larger than ~2 GiB; no memory index is derived from bytes in the shown code and reads fail at EOF, so no security-relevant sink is reachable.

Unchecked strdup (line 112) and per-entry malloc (line 108) scale with attacker-controlled entry count; impact is memory exhaustion proportional to the image size, which is inherent to the extraction tool and not separately confirmed.
Bounds claims rely on the declared buffer capacity and standard flexible-array semantics; capacities of read_directory_data/check_name/check_directory internals are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The guards (IS_MNT_UNBINDABLE, check_mnt, has_locked_children at lines 7-14) bound old_mnt to a non-unbindable, current-namespace mount with no locked children before clone_mnt (line 16); IS_ERR (line 19) bounds new_mnt to a non-error pointer before the mnt_ns write (line 23); and namespace_sem is balanced on every return path (lines 6, 17, 28). Remaining concerns (raw NULL from clone_mnt, invalid caller-supplied path, post-unlock visibility) are not confirmable from the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: path, path->mnt, and path->dentry are non-NULL valid pointers supplied by an internal kernel caller; the shown code performs no NULL validation, so NULL-supply is a caller precondition, not a reachable defect in the shown code.
real_mount implements the standard container_of-style conversion and cannot return NULL for a valid path->mnt.
clone_mnt follows kernel convention and reports allocation/lookup failure via ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM)-style error pointers rather than raw NULL.
namespace_sem excludes concurrent namespace mutation between check_mnt (line 10) and clone_mnt (line 16).
limitations: A NULL dereference of new_mnt at line 23 if clone_mnt returned raw NULL cannot be confirmed: IS_ERR(NULL) is false, but no value inside the shown code can produce NULL from clone_mnt (line 16).
NULL dereference of path/path->mnt/path->dentry at lines 3, 13, and 16 depends on an out-of-scope caller and is not producible inside the shown code.

Concurrent visibility of the CL_PRIVATE clone while new_mnt->mnt_ns is written (line 23) after up_read (line 17) depends on clone_mnt's unshown publication internals and on MNT_NS_INTERNAL/MNT_NS semantics outside this snippet; unconfirmed.
has_locked_children (line 13) may contain loops internally, but its body is not shown, so no iteration-bound or read-position invariant can be derived from the shown code.
No memory-safety arithmetic, string/path construction, crypto, or injection sinks exist in the shown code, so those vulnerability classes are inapplicable to this snippet.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The size arithmetic feeding snd_pcm_format_set_silence (lines 30-33 and 41-44) and snd_pcm_oss_sync1 (lines 34 and 45) can underflow only if buffer_used or period_ptr exceeds period_bytes, and the OOB impact cannot be established because the capacity of runtime->oss.buffer and those bounding invariants are maintained outside this function; the divide-by-zero risks at lines 30/44 (width) and 53 (period_size) likewise depend on callee/state invariants not present here. The only shown-code-visible status gap is the discarded return values of snd_pcm_lib_write and snd_pcm_lib_writev (lines 57 and 59), which can mask a failed fill and return success (line 95), but it breaks no security mechanism and is recorded as a robustness limitation.

assumptions: substream->runtime and pcm_oss_file are guaranteed non-NULL by the ALSA core layer that invokes this ioctl handler; the shown code cannot produce NULL for them.

The OSS emulation layer outside this function maintains buffer_used <= period_bytes and period_ptr <= period_bytes by resetting them at period boundaries, and hw_params guarantees period_size > 0 by the time sync runs after snd_pcm_oss_make_ready (line 16).

runtime->oss.format is validated at the SNDCTL_DSP_SETFMT path so that snd_pcm_format_physical_width returns a real non-zero width; on an unknown value it would return a negative error widened to a huge unsigned long, not zero.
limitations: Unsigned-underflow-driven oversized write: if buffer_used > period_bytes (e.g. buffer_used = period_bytes+1, period_bytes = 4096, width = 16), the size_t subtraction at line 30 wraps and size becomes ~2^60 samples, giving an ~2^61-byte write at line 33 via buffer+buffer_used; the guard at line 26 (buffer_used > 0) admits such values, but the capacity of runtime->oss.buffer and the invariant bounding buffer_used are not present in the shown code, so the OOB claim is unconfirmable (no CWE attached).

Same structure for the else branch: period_ptr > period_bytes wraps the subtraction at line 41, feeding a huge count to snd_pcm_format_set_silence (line 44) and snd_pcm_oss_sync1 (line 45); guard line 37 (period_ptr > 0) does not bound it, but the same missing-capacity/invariant problem applies.

Division by zero at lines 30 and 44 requires width == 0, but the shown code never checks width and the helper semantics of snd_pcm_format_physical_width are not shown; such a zero value is not demonstrable from the shown code.

Modulo by zero at line 53 (runtime->control->appl_ptr % runtime->period_size) if period_size == 0; the shown code has no period_size > 0 guard, but a zero period_size cannot be produced by anything in the shown code and is excluded by the surrounding ALSA hw_params flow.

Discarded return values of snd_pcm_lib_write (line 57) and snd_pcm_lib_writev (line 59): a negative error (e.g. -EAGAIN or an xrun recovery failure) is silently dropped and the function proceeds to DRAIN (line 72) and returns success (line 95), potentially reporting a successful SYNC with only partially filled trailing silence; this is a robustness/status-handling gap with no demonstrated security impact.

NULL dereference of substream->runtime (lines 24-26, 53, 62-63, 76-77, 90-93) is not producible on any in-scope path; it would require a NULL runtime supplied by the ALSA core, an invariant violation outside the shown code.

32-bit wrap of 8*(period_bytes - buffer_used) and size*8 at lines 30 and 44 would require period_bytes or size >= 2^29 bytes, a magnitude not derivable from any bound the shown code establishes, and on LP64 these expressions do not wrap for realistic OSS period sizes.
The mmap path (goto __direct, line 15) skips the params_lock-held flush section but does not bypass a held lock or skip any required unlock, so no double-lock/unlock or lost-dec flaw is confirmed.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in sixpack_close. The function serializes teardown to a single owner by clearing tty->disc_data under disc_data_lock (lines 5-8, re-entry returns at line 10), and drains in-flight users via refcount_dec_and_test plus wait_for_completion (lines 16-17) before the free sites (lines 31, 32, 34). The only remaining UAF possibility would require an accessor that uses sp without holding a reference, which is code not shown here.

assumptions: tty is a valid pointer when sixpack_close is invoked (caller contract, not established in the shown code).

Other driver paths (e.g., sp_xmit/sixpack_receive_buf) take and release refcount references while using sp, and sp->dead is completed when the last external reference is dropped; these invariants live outside the shown code.
sp is assumed to be netdev private data whose memory is released by free_netdev(sp->dev) at line 34; no use of sp follows that line in the shown function.
limitations: A use-after-free would be confirmed only if some accessor used sp (via tty->disc_data or sp->dev) without holding a refcount while teardown ran; such accessors are not present in the shown code, so the claim is unconfirmed (CWE-416 candidate, no evidence).

wait_for_completion(&sp->dead) at line 17 has no timeout and can hang if the external signaler never fires; the condition is not producible from the shown code (CWE-400/deadlock candidate, no evidence).
The safety of the skip-wait path (refcount_dec_and_test returning true at line 16) depends entirely on the refcount discipline of other functions, which cannot be verified from the shown code.
If sp->refcnt were already zero on entry due to mis-accounting elsewhere, line 16 would perform an invalid decrement; no path in the shown code can produce that state.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only security-sensitive operations are guarded by shown checks: line 8 admits only non-NULL files whose f_mode carries the requested access bit and returns -EBADF otherwise; line 29 gates the file->f_op->iopoll dereference behind the IOCB_DIRECT test via short-circuit || and rejects non-direct files with -EOPNOTSUPP; line 37 rejects IOCB_HIPRI outside IOPOLL; and the kiocb_set_rw_flags return (line 15) is checked and propagated (lines 16-17). Attacker-driven resource exhaustion: a huge (*i)->data (up to 2^31+2) with a crafted stream that keeps read_directory_data succeeding (e.g., a nominal >2GB archive/sparse file) permits ~1.6e8 loop iterations and matching per-entry malloc/strdup (GB-scale memory) — noted as a DoS/robustness concern, not reported as the primary finding.
strdup() at line 113 is unchecked; an OOM there leaves ent->name NULL — OOM-only with no attacker control over the failing allocation.
TRACE() at lines 14 and 105-107 pass unsigned ints to %d (benign mismatch); all format strings are literals, so no format-string or log injection was confirmed.
SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_ENTRY_3 / read_directory_data internals (byte-swap copy sizes, metadata-block boundary handling) are not shown and were not used to assert any vulnerability.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in em28xx_usb_probe. All attacker-influenced USB counts feed strict-inequality loops over framework-guaranteed array capacities; all allocations are NULL-checked; every error path initializes retval before returning; and no attacker-derived size/index reaches an operation with an identifiable capacity in the shown code. Candidate concerns (card[nr] capacity, device-string content in dev_info, discarded return values) lack an identifiable capacity, reachable failure, or security mechanism in the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: USB core guarantees intf->altsetting has exactly intf->num_altsetting entries and each altsetting has bNumEndpoints endpoint entries, so the nested loops at lines 58-69 index within capacity.
At probe time udev->config is the active configuration and config->interface[0..bNumInterfaces-1] are valid, non-NULL entries, so the loop at lines 131-142 is in-bounds.
em28xx_duplicate_dev(dev) returning 0 is a success contract that leaves dev->dev_next set; the helper's callee body is outside the shown code.

dev->name is at least 28 bytes (implied by snprintf(dev->name, 28, ...) at line 122), and em28xx_init_dev/em28xx_check_usb_descriptor initialize dev->board, dev->tuner_type, dev->em28xx_sensor, dev->is_webcam, endpoint flags, and dev->media_dev before the shown code reads them.
limitations: card[nr] at lines 157-158 is an OOB-read candidate (CWE-125 shape): nr is bounded to [0, EM28XX_MAXBOARDS) by lines 16-25, but the element count of card[] is not declared in the shown code, so the boundary/excess claim is unconfirmable.

udev->manufacturer and udev->product (lines 93-94) flow unconstrained into dev_info '%s' at lines 91-99; newline bytes could split kernel log lines (CWE-117 shape), but dmesg is not a security boundary and no security mechanism is bypassed, so this is not a confirmed finding.

Return values of em28xx_write_reg (lines 257, 259, 263, 265) and media_device_register (line 282, overridden by the unconditional return 0 at line 285) are discarded (CWE-754 shape); failure of these steps has no demonstrable memory, injection, or access-control impact within the shown code.

On failure of em28xx_init_dev(dev->dev_next, ...) (lines 223-226) the err_free path (lines 287-289) frees dev but not dev->dev_next — a single-shot leak whose volume compounding depends on unshown callee behavior and replug rate, not attacker-scalable from the shown code.

The possibly-dangling intf->dev_data left by usb_set_intfdata(intf, dev) (line 161) followed by kfree(dev) on err_free is not exploitable in the shown code: USB core does not invoke disconnect for a probe that returned an error.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. Dangerous-looking operations (multibyte byte compares in MULTIBYTECODE, rex.input advances on failed compares, backpos/regstack growth and writes, previous-char reads in EOW/BOW) are each bounded by identifiable guards: the byte loop breaks at the first mismatch and can never read past the line's terminating NUL; advances on RA_NOMATCH are always followed by reg_restore (or immediate return) before any rex.input use; BACK writes bp[i] only after ga_grow(&backpos,1) succeeds; EOW guards rex.input==rex.line before reading input[-1]. Candidates requiring caller-supplied pattern/text provenance (ReDoS), an unverifiable reg_getline NULL, or unshown helper semantics (cstrncmp *n update, regstack_push growth) fail the three-part confirmation and are recorded as limitations with no CWE.

assumptions: regstack.ga_len is used as a byte count and regstack.ga_data+ga_len addresses the next regitem_T; the shown code's own arithmetic ((char*)regstack.ga_data + regstack.ga_len, regstack.ga_len += sizeof(regstar_T)) is consistent only with byte-count semantics, and regstack_push is assumed to reserve sizeof(regitem_T) bytes (helper body not shown).
cstrncmp updates *n to the number of bytes consumed on a successful compare; the shown code relies on this for rex.input += len (lines 478, 776, 803).
Input lines are NUL-terminated within their allocated storage; the shown code itself depends on this via *rex.input and STRLEN (lines 100-103, 1412).
rex.reg_startpos/reg_endpos/reg_startp/reg_endp have NSUBEXP entries so op ranges MOPEN+0..9 / MCLOSE+0..9 / BACKREF+1..9 index within bounds.
backpos.ga_len counts backpos_T entries, consistent with the manual ++backpos.ga_len and ga_grow(&backpos, 1).
limitations: MULTIBYTECODE byte loop (lines 534-539): an OOB read would require a read index > STRLEN(rex.input); the loop breaks on the first byte mismatch, and a validated multibyte operand (line 503, len >= 2) contains no NUL, so the largest readable index is the line's terminating NUL inside the line storage; no out-of-domain index is derivable from the shown code.

rex.input += len executed on RA_NOMATCH (lines 540, 776): the corrupted pointer is never dereferenced, because status != RA_CONT forces the inner break (1080) and all stack-state handlers that read rex.input first restore it (reg_restore at 1145, 1168, 1179, 1193, 1212, 1247, 1334) or the function returns at 1468-1480 when the stack is empty.

RE_MARK NULL deref via reg_getline (lines 158-159): producing NULL requires pos->lnum - rex.reg_firstlnum outside the reachable line range; the shown code only establishes pos->lnum > 0 (line 150) and cannot derive such a witness, so this is unconfirmed.

ReDoS/exponential backtracking (regrepeat at 959, RS_STAR_LONG loop 1387-1444): pathologically long matching is possible for adversarially chosen patterns and text, but both the program (scan) and the text (rex) are internal-helper/framework state for this function; no attacker-controlled entry input flows into the loops in the shown code, and maxmempattern caps (971, 1016), interrupt (40) and optional timeout (47-57) controls are visible, so a CWE-1333 claim cannot be confirmed here.

BACKREF len derivations (lines 733, 752): a negative len would require saved end-before-start submatch state that cannot be produced by the shown code's own save/restore logic; cstrncmp's behavior for negative *n is not visible, so this is unconfirmed.

regstack growth at push sites other than STAR/BEHIND is not bounded by the p_mmp check, but per-program-node pushes are finite and a resource-exhaustion impact cannot be confirmed without caller context.
Only constant-format messages and printf("Illegal op code %d\n", op) (line 1072) with an int argument are used; no format-string injection is possible.

verdict.summary: In handleLWPolylineData, the allocation size 4*maxVertices is computed in 32-bit int arithmetic: for maxVertices >= 2^30 the product wraps (e.g. 1073741824 gives 0), so new double[0] (or a tiny buffer) is allocated while the initialization loop writes vertices[i*4+3] with indices up to 4*maxVertices-1, causing a heap out-of-bounds write controllable via the DXF file's group code 90 value.

evidence.reason: maxVertices derives from entry-point input groupValue via toInt (line 4) and the only guard, maxVertices>0 (line 5), admits [1, INT_MAX]. For maxVertices=1073741824, the int expression 4*maxVertices wraps to 0, allocating a zero-capacity object; the subsequent write loop then corrupts the heap (CWE-190 wrap feeding CWE-787).

With maxVertices=1073741824 admitted by the line-5 guard, line 9 wraps the allocation size to 0 (capacity 0 doubles) and i=0 here writes vertices[0], already out of bounds — heap OOB write from DXF-controlled count.

Largest loop index is 4*maxVertices-1 for i<maxVertices (lines 10-14); with the overflowed allocation (capacity 0 for maxVertices=2^30, or capacity 4 for maxVertices=2^30+1) line 14 writes element 4294967295 (or 4294967299), an excess of billions of doubles over the wrapped capacity — CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write with CWE-190 as the enabling wrap.

assumptions: int is 32-bit, so 4*maxVertices wraps modulo 2^32; maxVertices is an int member (used with int i and int vertexIndex).
toInt behaves like atoi/strtol for the decimal string literal '1073741824', returning exactly that value, which fits in int.
new double[0] returns a valid non-null pointer with capacity 0 per standard new[] semantics, making the first write already out of bounds.
groupValue (DXF group code value) and groupCode are set by the surrounding parser from file contents; the shown code itself consumes them as entry-point data.
limitations: Wrap-to-negative variants (e.g. maxVertices=2^29) convert to a huge size_t and cause bad_alloc; this is a DoS-only consequence subsumed by the confirmed OOB-write finding (and depends on the exception policy of the caller, which is not shown).
If int were 64-bit, 4*maxVertices would not wrap for the stated witness and the failure would reduce to a large-allocation DoS rather than OOB write.
The vertex processing path (lines 25-35) stays within capacity for unwrapped allocations (max index 4*maxVertices-1) and is not an independent finding.

verdict.summary: The only array access, id->name[i] on line 12, is guarded by i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN with && short-circuiting, so the maximum evaluated index is MAXLEN-1 regardless of NUL termination; field values feed only an unsigned-long hash accumulator that is masked with LONG_MAX, and no index, size, length, pointer, or formatting value derived from input reaches any sink in the shown code.

assumptions: SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN is the capacity of id->name under the standard ALSA ABI (name[SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN]); the loop's strict < bound and short-circuit && keep the evaluated index at MAXLEN-1.
MULTIPLIER is a positive integer constant; unsigned long multiply-add wraps by definition and is used only for hash mixing before the LONG_MAX mask.
limitations: The definition of struct snd_ctl_elem_id and the values of SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN, MULTIPLIER, and LONG_MAX are not declared in the shown code; exact field types are inferred from the standard ALSA ABI.
A NULL id cannot be produced inside the shown code (no allocation, lookup, or derivation), so a NULL-dereference claim would depend on an out-of-scope caller.

Hash-collision/algorithmic-complexity concerns for the non-cryptographic polynomial hash are not confirmable here: the hash table, bucket size, and attacker-reachable control-ID creation all live outside the shown code.

Unsigned wraparound in MULTIPLIER * h + field is defined behavior and reaches no allocation-size, index, length, or pointer-arithmetic sink in the shown code; only the returned hash value is produced.
Signed-char sign extension of name bytes (when char is signed) affects only the hash value, never an index or size.

verdict.summary: protocol_client_msg validates incoming VNC message lengths with equality checks (`len == 1`, `len == 4`, `len == 8`) instead of range checks, so a remote client sending a partial message of length 2..(required-1) passes every guard and the handler reads (SET_PIXEL_FORMAT indices up to 16, SET_ENCODINGS loop up to index 262143, CUT_TEXT an unbounded 4 GB copy) past the `len` valid bytes, causing out-of-bounds heap reads, uninitialized-data disclosure, and denial of service.

evidence.snippet:
set_pixel_format(vs, read_u8(data, 4), read_u8(data, 5),
                            read_u8(data, 6), read_u8(data, 7),
                            read_u16(data, 8), read_u16(data, 10),
                            read_u16(data, 12), read_u8(data, 14),
                            read_u8(data, 15), read_u8(data, 16));
evidence.reason: Entry-point `len` (size_t) is only constrained by the equality guard `if (len == 1) return 20;` at line 13, whose admitted set is `len != 1`, i.e. {2..SIZE_MAX}. The sink reads bytes at indices 4..16 (max index 16 at line 20) which require `len >= 17`; the intersection of admitted set and failure set {2..16} is non-empty. Witness: `len = 3` (buffer capacity = 3 valid bytes per the data/len contract) passes the guard and reads 13 bytes past the valid region. Remote-triggerable OOB heap read (CWE-125) causing crash/info disclosure.

With `len = 5` (admitted by guards at lines 23 and 26 since 5 != 1 and 5 != 4) the attacker-controlled `limit = read_u16(data, 2)` (line 31) can be 0xFFFF; the loop `for (i = 0; i < limit; i++)` (line 33) admits i=0..65534, and `read_s32(data, 4 + (i*4))` reads bytes 4..7 while only bytes 0..4 are valid — a 3-byte OOB read on iteration i=0, extending to index 262143 in later iterations. CWE-125 OOB read from entry-point data/len with attacker-chosen length.

With `len = 9` (admitted by guards at lines 61 and 64, since 9 != 1 and 9 != 8), `dlen = read_u32(data, 4)` is attacker-chosen without the 1 MB bound of line 66 (that bound only runs on the `len == 8` path). A value `dlen = 0xFFFFFFFF` makes client_cut_text copy ~4 GB from `data + 8` while only byte 8 is valid, an unbounded OOB read. For `len` in {2..7}, the `read_u32(data, 4)` itself exceeds the valid region. CWE-125.

assumptions: The `data`/`len` parameter pair means exactly `len` valid bytes are available at `data`; any index >= len is out of bounds.

The caller re-invokes the handler with the currently buffered byte count between 1 and the previously returned expected total, consistent with the `return N`/`vnc_read_when(...,1)` re-arm protocol at lines 14..145.
The `read_u8/read_u16/read_u32/read_s32` helpers read the wire (big-endian) value at the given offset without bounds checks; `client_cut_text` copies the given length from the given pointer.
limitations: The `memcpy(data + 4 + (i * 4), &val, sizeof(val))` write at line 35 (potential CWE-787) cannot be confirmed because the destination buffer's allocated capacity is not identifiable from the shown code — only the `len`-valid region is; the loop's OOB read at line 34 is the confirmed mechanism.

The same equality-guard root cause recurs at the FRAMEBUFFER_UPDATE_REQUEST (lines 41-46), KEY_EVENT (49-52), POINTER_EVENT (55-58), and QEMU ext/audio (80-124) cases; they are covered by the confirmed CWE-125 mechanism but not separately evidenced.
A zero-length invocation would read `data[0]` before any check, but the shown code's own re-arm at line 145 implies the caller guarantees `len >= 1`, so this is not independently confirmable.
The `(int32_t *)(data + 4)` cast at line 38 may cause unaligned access on strict architectures; no security boundary breached in the shown code, so not a finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed security vulnerability in the shown code. The file-controlled lengths n1/n2 are bounded by UT32_ADD_OVFCHK guards (lines 17, 38) that exclude 0xFFFFFFFF, the only value that would overflow n+1 or make s1[n1]/s2[n2] out-of-bounds; short rz_buf_read results are exactly compared and cleaned up; the %s arguments to rz_str_newf are NUL-terminated data, not format text. Identified weaknesses (memory leaks on OOM/truncated-input paths at lines 23/39/43, and allocations of up to ~4GB directly sized by input at lines 21/41) are robustness/DoS concerns and are excluded as findings per the analysis rules.

assumptions: get_ut8/get_st32 set *error on short or EOF reads (their bodies are not shown; this is the name-implied behavior used by the caller).
The caller aborts the pyc parse when get_complex_object returns NULL, so the error/OOM leaks are single-shot per parse.
UT32_ADD_OVFCHK(a, b) is true exactly when a+b would overflow ut32, i.e. b > UT32_MAX - a.
limitations: Error/OOM paths leak memory: malloc failure at line 21 returns NULL without freeing ret (line 23); a second-read error or overflow at line 38 returns NULL without freeing s1 and ret (line 39); malloc failure at line 41 returns NULL without freeing s1 and ret (line 43). These are attacker-reachable via a truncated file or a forced allocation failure, but they are single-shot, non-compounding leaks, so they are not reported as findings.

malloc(n1+1)/malloc(n2+1) (lines 21, 41) are sized directly by file-controlled values in 0..0xFFFFFFFE (witness: n1 = 0xFFFFFFFE, file bytes FE FF FF FF, passes line 17 and reaches malloc(0xFFFFFFFF) at line 21). Failure is handled, success is transient and freed, and no reachable loop in the shown code scales the volume, so resource exhaustion is not a confirmed finding.
The claim that no OOB occurs relies on the standard semantics of rz_buf_read (bounded read, returns bytes actually read) and rz_str_newf (%s stops at NUL); callee bodies are not shown.
Silent truncation of number strings containing embedded NULs by %s copying has no security impact.

verdict.summary: The EDITOR/VISUAL environment string is concatenated into a shell command and executed via system() when it contains a space; shell metacharacters like ';' are not filtered, enabling arbitrary command execution by a crafted environment value.

evidence.reason: The environment-derived editor string flows from getenv at lines 20–22 through omStrDup (line25) and the space-only guard at line50 into the sprintf command construction at line58, then to sink line59. The guard admits any string containing a space; a witness like "vi; touch /tmp/pwned" passes that guard and the shell metacharacters survive because no quoting/filtering is applied before system(), yielding arbitrary command execution (CWE-78).

assumptions: The editor string comes from an environment variable that an attacker can influence (e.g., via a controlled process environment or a wrapper/service boundary).
`omStrDup`/`omAlloc` are assumed to track NUL-terminated string sizes per standard strdup/allocation semantics; the `omStrDup("/tmp/sd000000")` allocation has capacity 14 bytes incl. NUL.
limitations: Secondary confirmed concern: the predictable `/tmp/sd<pid>` temp file (lines 3–5, 68) is opened with `fopen(...,"w")`, following a pre-planted symlink and allowing arbitrary-file truncation/write if the target process can writethe victim file (CWE-377/59); it is not reported as an extra CWE to keep the verdict focused.

Line4 `sprintf(filename+7,"%d",getpid())` can heap-overflow by one byte for a PID any ≥1,000,000 (7 digits, e.g., Linux `pid_max` near 4,194,304), becauseno width/length check exists; triggering depends on OS PID allocation.

Line80 `omAlloc((int)len+1)` truncates the `long` `ftell` result to `int`; for a procedure body/file larger than `INT_MAX`, the allocation length can wrap and the subsequent `myfread`/`body[len]=0` can overflow/underflow. The required enormous body length makes this a robustness/extreme-size concern here.

Ignored returns such as `fwrite`/`fclose`/`system`/`myfread` could cause stale/empty body or failed editor execution but have no demonstrated attacker-controlled security impact beyond the above findings.

verdict.summary: In the LWPolyline vertex handler, the group-code-42 branch guards the element write only with `vertexIndex < maxVertices` (line 33) and omits the `vertexIndex >= 0` lower bound that the 10/20/30 branch enforces (line 30). Every group-code-90 record resets `vertexIndex` to -1 (line 17), so a crafted DXF that emits code 42 before any code 10 makes line 34 compute index 4*(-1)+3 == -1 and write 8 bytes of attacker-controlled data before the heap array allocated at line 9 (heap out-of-bounds write, CWE-787).

evidence.reason: vertexIndex is set to -1 by the group-code-90 path (line 17) and can remain -1 when a group-code-42 record is processed before any code-10 record. The guard at line 33 (`groupCode==42 && vertexIndex<maxVertices`) admits every vertexIndex < maxVertices with no lower bound, so -1 is a member of the admitted set; line 34 then derives index 4*(-1)+3 == -1, outside the domain [0, 4*maxVertices-1] of the array allocated at line 9. This is a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) of 8 bytes before the allocation, with an attacker-chosen double value from groupValue.

assumptions: groupCode/groupValue are supplied by the DXF decoder from the parsed file before this handler runs; the shown code consumes them as externally supplied group data.
toInt/toReal are the library's standard numeric conversions returning int/double; their exact parse-error behavior is outside the shown code.
vertices is allocated with capacity 4*maxVertices doubles whenever maxVertices > 0.
limitations: `4*maxVertices` overflows signed int for maxVertices >= 536870912 (undefined behavior): a wrapped-to-tiny size would let the init loop (lines 10-15) overflow the heap, and a huge size would make `new double[]` throw an uncaught std::bad_alloc. Because the wrapped value is undefined behavior rather than a defined value in the shown types, this is not a confirmed corruption path and carries no CWE.
For maxVertices == 0 with vertices still nullptr from prior state, the line-34 write would target a near-null address; the member's initial value is not shown, so that variant is unconfirmed.
The `vertices != NULL` pre-check (line 6) cannot detect allocation failure because `new double[]` throws; not attacker-triggerable without OOM.

verdict.summary: The EDITOR/VISUAL environment variable is concatenated verbatim with the temp filename and passed to system() whenever it contains a space (system() branch at lines 54-59). Shell metacharacters such as ';', '&&', '|', backticks, or $() are neither escaped nor filtered, so a value like "vi ; touch /tmp/pwned" executes an injected command as the invoking user.

evidence.reason: Command injection (CWE-78). Taint: getenv("EDITOR") at line 19 (entry-point environment input, residual range: any string containing at least one space after the NULL checks at lines 20-23 and the omStrDup at line 24) flows verbatim through sprintf at line 57 into p and into system at line 58. The branch guard at line 49 admits exactly the dangerous set for this path: when strchr(editor,' ') is non-NULL (editor contains a space) the code takes the system() branch, and it removes no characters — unsafe metacharacters like ';' survive. Witness: EDITOR="vi ; touch /tmp/pwned" contains spaces, passes the line 49 guard, and system() executes the injected command after the shell separator. The shell-parsing semantics of system() are standard/name-implied, so the call site at line 58 is the confirmed sink.

assumptions: omStrDup/omAlloc succeed and return valid pointers (no failure check exists in the shown code).
pi->data.s.body is NUL-terminated so strlen at line 39 is in-bounds; the shown code does not establish this invariant.
getenv returns NUL-terminated strings per OS semantics.
limitations: Temp-file re-open TOCTOU (lines 40/67/85): the mkstemp fd is closed and the 0600 random-suffix file in a world-writable tmp dir is reopened by name; exploitation requires an external actor able to remove/replace the file between close and fopen, which depends on OS invariants (sticky-bit unlink rules, protected hardlinks, guessing the ~6-character random suffix) — no in-code witness triggers it.

(int)len narrowing at line 79 plus read length len at line 80 would only overflow the buffer for len > INT_MAX (>2 GiB file); the file size is strlen(pi->data.s.body) at line 39, and no shown-code path produces such a body, so no concrete witness exists.

fork()==-1 is admitted by 'if (pid!=0)' at line 43 and sent to si_wait(&pid) with pid=-1, making the 'cannot fork' else at lines 62-65 dead code; trigger requires process exhaustion, not attacker-selected input.

Unchecked statuses: write (line 39) partial writes, myfread (line 80) short-read leaving uninitialized bytes, and fseek/ftell (lines 74-76) failures have no attacker-controlled failure mode demonstrated in the shown code.
f=NULL at line 15 assigns 0 to an int after close(f), but no later code reuses the fd on that path (non-security code smell).
The sprintf at line 57 is exactly sized by the allocation at line 56 and is not an overflow.
The execlp path at line 51 is shell-free; metacharacters without a space are inert there.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only memory-sensitive operation is strscpy at line 12 with size nbytes+1. The guard at line 9 constrains nbytes to [0, MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1], so the size reaches at most MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN, exactly the declared capacity of drc_name (line 5); strscpy writes at most that many bytes and always NUL-terminates, keeping the write in bounds and all later consumers (strchr at line 14, dlpar_remove_slot at line 18) on a valid C string. strchr and dlpar_remove_slot returns are properly checked, and the discarded strscpy return is benign because -E2BIG still leaves a fully populated, NUL-terminated destination.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is a positive compile-time constant and is the same named constant used both as the declaration capacity of drc_name (line 5) and as the guard bound (line 9), so the bound identity holds for any positive numeric value.
strscpy has standard kernel semantics: it writes at most count bytes total (count-1 copied characters plus a NUL terminator) and always terminates the destination within count bytes.

The sysfs/kernfs framework supplies a buf holding at least nbytes readable bytes; the shown code never reads more than nbytes bytes (strscpy reads at most size-1 = nbytes), so a missing NUL in buf is safe.
drc_name is guaranteed NUL-terminated by strscpy regardless of buf contents, making the strchr/end processing at lines 14-16 safe.
limitations: The numeric value of MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is not visible in the shown code; all bounds are symbolic, but the identity of the constant as both capacity and guard bound makes the safety conclusion independent of that value.
The callee dlpar_remove_slot is not shown; its processing of the (always NUL-terminated, bounded) DRC name is outside the shown code, so no claim is made about it.
nbytes == 0 passes the guard and calls dlpar_remove_slot("") — whether an empty name is mishandled depends on the unshown callee and has no security impact demonstrable in the shown code.
Returning 0 rather than a negative error for oversized input (line 10) is a behavioral/UX choice with no security impact.

verdict.summary: get_complex_object computes malloc(n1 + 1) and malloc(n2 + 1) in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic from attacker-controlled length fields read via get_st32 (lines 16/38, residual range 0..0xFFFFFFFF with no shown cap). When a length is 0xFFFFFFFF the size wraps to 0 (lines 22/42, CWE-190), under-allocating s1/s2 to capacity 0, after which rz_buf_read (lines 27/47) can write up to the full length into the tiny object and the terminator stores s1[n1] = '\0' / s2[n2] = '\0' (lines 33/54) write at offset 0xFFFFFFFF, yielding a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: n1 is a ut32 from get_st32 at line 16 with attacker-controlled residual range 0..0xFFFFFFFF and no shown upper-bound check. `n1 + 1` is 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so for n1 == 0xFFFFFFFF the size wraps to 0 (CWE-190); the caller then treats s1 as an n1+1-byte buffer and accesses n1 bytes at lines 27 and 33, making the wrap the root cause of the CWE-787 heap OOB write.

The length argument n1 (residual range 0..0xFFFFFFFF from get_st32, line 16) is passed to rz_buf_read, which writes the bytes it reads into s1, allocated with wrapped capacity 0 at line 22 for n1 == 0xFFFFFFFF. The subsequent check `size != n1` (line 28) admits size == n1, so when the attacker-controlled buffer tail holds >= 0xFFFFFFFF bytes, a read of up to 0xFFFFFFFF bytes overflows the capacity-0 allocation (CWE-787; CWE-190 wrap derives the size).

Index n1 retains its full residual range 0..0xFFFFFFFF (line 16). For n1 == 0xFFFFFFFF the object allocated at line 22 has capacity (n1+1) mod 2^32 == 0, and the guard `size != n1` (line 28) admits exactly size == n1, so this 1-byte write lands at offset 0xFFFFFFFF — a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) enabled by the size wrap (CWE-190).

verdict.summary: openssl_decrypt decrypts with an unvalidated, attacker-supplied IV: the length returned by php_openssl_validate_iv is used only to decide efree(iv), never to abort decryption, so a short IV (e.g., 1 byte with aes-128-cbc) reaches EVP_DecryptInit_ex, which reads EVP_CIPHER_iv_length (16) bytes, an out-of-bounds read that leaks heap bytes into the cipher IV (recoverable via the returned CBC plaintext). Secondarily, data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size wraps in int and the wrapped value is passed to emalloc(outlen + 1), causing a request-fatal allocation failure for attacker-chosen input lengths.

evidence.reason: CWE-125: iv/iv_len are entry-point inputs with residual range iv_len in [0, INT_MAX] (zend_parse_parameters, line 14) and the shown code imposes no iv_len == EVP_CIPHER_iv_length check; the validation result (line 44) is consumed only by the efree decision at line 67, never as an abort guard. A 1-byte IV with aes-128-cbc passes every shown guard (method_len>0 at 18, cipher_type non-NULL at 24, raw_input unconstrained), and by the free_iv ownership contract a return of 0 leaves the pointer unchanged, so OpenSSL reads 16 bytes from the 1-byte string at this call — a 15-byte out-of-bounds read whose bytes are XORed into the first returned CBC plaintext block and are recoverable with chosen ciphertext.

CWE-190: data_len is an entry-point int with residual range [0, INT_MAX] (no length cap in the shown code). For data_len = INT_MAX and block size 16, the int addition wraps to INT_MIN + 15, and outlen + 1 = INT_MIN + 16 sign-extends to a size_t around 1.8e19 at the emalloc allocation-size sink, causing a request-fatal allocation failure (DoS) with attacker-chosen input size; the wrap occurs in the shown types and the corrupted value is consumed at the allocation.

assumptions: OpenSSL standard semantics: EVP_DecryptInit_ex reads EVP_CIPHER_iv_length(cipher) bytes from the iv pointer; EVP_DecryptUpdate writes at most data_len bytes and EVP_DecryptFinal at most one block, so the non-wrapped allocation outbuf of data_len + block + 1 suffices and outbuf[outlen]='\0' stays in bounds.

php_openssl_validate_iv returns zend_bool used only for ownership: an allocated replacement implies free_iv = 1 (otherwise the caller would leak), so free_iv = 0 implies the original attacker iv pointer is passed through.
PHP string lengths are int, so data_len/password_len are at most INT_MAX; emalloc aborts the request on allocation failure.
limitations: NULL data after a failed php_base64_decode (lines 30-32) is unchecked before EVP_DecryptUpdate (line 54): a NULL plus nonzero decoded length would be a NULL dereference, but the non-strict callee semantics are not shown and the callee is not demonstrated to return NULL with a nonzero length here.

EVP_CIPHER_CTX cipher_ctx (line 7) is used by EVP_DecryptInit (line 49) without prior initialization: uninitialized-use crash depends on stack contents, so no concrete attacker-managed witness is provable from the shown code.

Returns of EVP_DecryptInit, EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length, EVP_DecryptInit_ex and EVP_DecryptUpdate (lines 49-54) are discarded; on an update failure, i and outlen could be uninitialized and reach outbuf + i (line 56), but reaching that callee failure requires internal error behavior not demonstrated for attacker input.

Reaching the CWE-190 witness requires a roughly 2 GB string argument, which is only feasible under raised memory limits; this is factored into severity and confidence.
