assumptions: struct sctp_authkey uses the standard UAPI layout: fixed header (sca_assoc_id, sca_keynumber, sca_keylength; sizeof == 8) followed by flexible array sca_key[], so key bytes start at offset sizeof(struct sctp_authkey).
sctp_auth_set_key consumes authkey->sca_keylength bytes from authkey->sca_key, as implied by the parameter name and the length checked in this function; its body is not shown.
sca_keylength is a 16-bit unsigned field (max 65535); the confirmed witness uses the value 16, so the finding does not depend on that bound.
limitations: The exact over-read extent (up to sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) bytes) depends on the struct layout, which is not literally declared in the shown code; for any nonzero header the over-read still follows from the shown arithmetic (sca_keylength up to optlen vs. key capacity optlen - sizeof).

The line 30 guard admits asoc == NULL when sca_assoc_id == 0 or on non-UDP-style sockets; whether NULL asoc passed to sctp_auth_set_key is a NULL dereference cannot be confirmed because the callee body is not shown.
No loops exist in the shown code, so no loop-bound or sentinel-termination analysis is applicable.
For very large optlen, kmalloc(optlen) fails and returns -ENOMEM (handled at lines 16-17); no allocation-size overflow is confirmed.

verdict.summary: No confirmable vulnerability: every index/size consumed by the shown sinks (strncasecmp n, input[len-2]/[len-1], sscanf region, memcpy length and errormsg[copy_len-1]) is guarded by a check in the shown code that keeps the value strictly inside the deliverable buffer (capacity = size*nmemb) and inside sizeof(url->errormsg). Candidate issues (NULL derefs, size*nmemb wrap, loose auth-header prefix match, oversized timelimit, unsanitized errormsg) fail taint/reachability within the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The callback ABI delivers size*nmemb contiguous bytes at ptr (index domain [0, len-1]); len can therefore never exceed the physical buffer, so a mathematically wrapped size*nmemb only under-approximates capacity.
client->auth, auth->state (url), client->con and url->errormsg are considered live, valid objects for the callback duration (internal invariants set outside the shown code).
url->auth_header_len / url->timelimit_header_len are treated as in-bounds lengths matching the configured header strings (set outside the shown code).
limitations: NULL dereference of client->auth (line 8), auth->state/url (line 9), client->con (line 22) and unvalidated stream/auth_user (lines 3, 5) is not producible by any path inside the shown code, so it cannot be confirmed.

Integer overflow of size * nmemb (line 4) cannot drive an out-of-bounds access: a wrapped len is less than the true byte count, and every sink is checked against len; a buffer large enough to make the product wrap is not realizable.

The auth-header check (lines 11-12) authenticates on a case-insensitive prefix match with no delimiter or CRLF validation; exploiting it requires attacker control of the backend response, which the shown code does not establish — hardening concern only.

sscanf %u on an over-long digit run is UB per the C standard but is clamped/ignored in practice; worst case (limit = UINT_MAX) only pushes discon_time ~136 years into the future on 64-bit time_t, with impact conditioned on response control.
errormsg is copied verbatim (only the trailing CR is NUL-overwritten) with no sanitization; any downstream log/HTML injection sink is outside the shown code, so no injection is confirmable here.

The loose semantic of sscanf's "\r\n" directive (matches any whitespace run) and the len > tlh vs len >= auth_header_len asymmetry are parsing quirks with no memory-safety or authz impact demonstrated in this function.

verdict.summary: hfsplus_find_cat copies an attacker-controlled, possibly very short catalog thread record into the stack union tmp (line 9) and validates only tmp.type (lines 14-17). When the record length R is small (e.g., R=2 with type=HFSPLUS_FOLDER_THREAD), tmp.thread.parentID and tmp.thread.nodeName — including the u16 nodeName.length consumed as a copy length by hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni — remain uninitialized stack bytes; they flow into the search key (lines 19-20) and into the b-tree key comparison at hfs_brec_find (line 21), i.e., use of uninitialized value (CWE-457).

evidence.reason: hfs_brec_read at line 9 initializes only the first R bytes of the stack union tmp (R attacker-controlled, residual 0..sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry)); the branch at lines 14-17 admits any record whose type is HFSPLUS_FOLDER_THREAD or HFSPLUS_FILE_THREAD and constrains only bytes 0-1. For a witness record R=2 with type=HFSPLUS_FOLDER_THREAD, bytes 2+ stay uninitialized: parentID is any u32 and nodeName.length any u16 in 0..65535. The shown code passes &tmp.thread.nodeName as a length-prefixed string to hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni, which consumes nodeName.length as the copy length and nodeName.unicode as the source; uninitialized stack data therefore drives the key copy. Primary mechanism: CWE-457 use of uninitialized value.

The search key built at lines 19-20 contains uninitialized parentID/name-length/unicode bytes (residual ranges above, reachable via a short thread record passing the type guard at line 14). hfs_brec_find compares that key against b-tree keys, so uninitialized stack bytes are consumed in a security-relevant key comparison/decision, completing the CWE-457 chain from line 9 through lines 19-20.

assumptions: hfs_brec_read(fd, &tmp, sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry)) initializes at most sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry) bytes and typically fewer (the on-disk record length R); it cannot initialize fields beyond the record bytes.
hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni treats its third parameter as a length-prefixed unicode string (length consumed as the copy size), and hfs_brec_find performs key comparison on the constructed key.
The catalog/btree record content and record length originate from the mounted filesystem image, i.e., attacker-controlled in a malicious-image scenario.
limitations: CWE-125 out-of-bounds read past tmp and CWE-787 out-of-bounds write into fd->search_key are not claimed: the clamping behavior of hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni and the exact capacity of fd->search_key are not visible in the shown code.
An oversized on-disk record (R > sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry)) writing past tmp would depend on hfs_brec_read ignoring its size argument, i.e., unchecked callee behavior not shown.
The stale value of nodeName.length can only be certified as the residual range 0..65535, not as a single demonstrated constant, which bounds confidence to the 0.5-0.7 band.
The shown code contains no loops, so iteration-bound and parser-loop claims are out of scope.

verdict.summary: TGS-REQs carrying the user-to-user option (enc_tkt_in_skey) leak the heap string allocated for tpn at line 94: the unconditional `tpn = cpn;` at line 550 drops the only reference, and the cleanup guard at line 1013 (`free` only when tpn != cpn) cannot reach it afterward. The same overwrite pattern leaks the S4U2Self tpn when a S4U2Self request also satisfies the constrained-delegation guard and line 804 re-allocates into tpn. Each request leaks heap memory without any per-request cap, so an attacker able to present valid TGTs can drive KDC memory exhaustion (CWE-401); no more severe memory-safety, injection, or crypto defect is confirmed in the shown code.

evidence.reason: CWE-401: in the U2U branch (enc_tkt_in_skey set by the attacker and a valid second TGT present), krb5_unparse_name(context, p, &tpn) at line 94 allocates a caller-owned heap string T; this unconditional assignment at line 550 overwrites tpn with cpn (priv->cname) and drops the only reference to T. The out: cleanup at line 1013 (`if (tpn != cpn) free(tpn);`) admits only the current allocation; T is in the excluded set (tpn == cpn) and is never freed on any path of the shown code. Each successful U2U request leaks one heap string with attacker-controlled volume, enabling slow KDC memory exhaustion.

CWE-401: when a request with S4U2Self padata (line 556) also satisfies the constrained-delegation guard at lines 753-757 (client != NULL, additional_tickets->len != 0, cname_in_addl_tkt, enc_tkt_in_skey == 0), the S4U2Self allocation made into tpn at line 646 is overwritten here by a fresh krb5_unparse_name allocation; the line-646 string becomes unreachable. The out: cleanup at line 1013 frees only the current tpn (the line-804 string), so the S4U2Self allocation leaks per such request, compounding with attacker-controlled request volume.

assumptions: krb5_unparse_name allocates a caller-owned heap string (confirmed by the shown code itself freeing such strings at lines 1013-1014).
The function runs only after the caller has validated the presented TGT (ticket is decrypted/valid before this function consumes tgt).
An attacker can obtain a valid second TGT for the U2U path and principal names of arbitrary content/length for sname/realm.
Line numbers were counted from the pasted source; they are internally consistent with the quoted snippets.
limitations: krb5_make_principal results are unchecked at lines 233-236 and 251-254, and strdup(realms[0]) at line 263 is unchecked; triggering these requires OOM only, with no confirmed crash path in the shown code (CWE-252/754 concern only).

The dereference server->entry.principal->realm on HDB_ERR_WRONG_REALM (lines 177-180) would be a NULL deref only if _kdc_db_fetch does not populate server on that error; that contract is not visible in the shown code.

spp (lines 527-533, passed to tgs_make_reply at line 1008) and the first _kdc_get_preferred_key result overwritten at lines 442-443 are not freed in the shown out: block; whether the callees take ownership is not visible, so these are unconfirmed leaks.
realms[0] is dereferenced at lines 247/251/266 without a shown length check on the need_referral output; the function's contract is outside the shown code.

The return value of _krb5_principalname2krb5_principal is discarded at lines 90/144/149; uninitialized-principal use would require that callee to fail and leave its output unset, which is not demonstrable from the shown code.

kdc_log lines 155-163 pass attacker-derived principal names as %s arguments; newline-based log forgery (CWE-117) is unconfirmed because newline survival through krb5_unparse_name and kdc_log internals is not visible in the shown code.
The kdc_log format strings are all literals; no format-string injection (CWE-134) was found.

The server_lookup re-iteration driven by WRONG_REALM/need_referral (lines 175-269) is not provably terminating from the shown code because it depends on HDB and need_referral behavior; the capath path (line 221) is strictly bounded by num_capath.

verdict.summary: The STUN ERROR-CODE attribute decoder trusts the attacker-controlled attribute length field without bounds validation. It unconditionally reads buf[6]/buf[7] (line 15) before verifying that the declared value length is >= 4, and it feeds hdr.length - 4 (residual range 0..65531) as the copy length into pj_strdup (line 25) with no upper-bound check against the actual message size — msghdr is discarded at line 9. A crafted or truncated message therefore causes an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) at either sink.

evidence.reason: Unconditional reads at payload offsets 2 and 3 of the attribute value before any check that the attacker-controlled length field (read into attr->hdr.length at line 13) is >= 4. For a length field value of 0..3 the bytes buf[6]/buf[7] lie 4-hdr.length bytes beyond the attribute's declared value end (buf + ATTR_HDR_LEN + hdr.length); the only length guard in the function (lines 21-22) runs after this read and protects only the reason-string length, so its admitted set ({slen>=0}) does not cover this access. OOB read, primary CWE-125.

The copy length value.slen = attr->hdr.length - 4 (line 19) has residual range [0, 65531] after the line 21-22 clamp, derived entirely from attacker-controlled message bytes (line 13). pj_strdup reads that many bytes from value.ptr = buf + 8 (line 18), but the shown code never bounds slen against the actual message/buffer size and explicitly discards msghdr (line 9), the only bracketing length source. A length field of 65535 (slen 65531; member of the admitted set of the sole guard, which excludes only negatives) on a truncated message drives a read of up to 65531 bytes past the valid data. OOB read, primary CWE-125.

assumptions: GETATTRHDR reads the 4-byte STUN attribute header at buf (type at buf[0..1], length at buf[2..3]) per pj_stun_attr_hdr semantics.
The platform uses a 32-bit int, so the uint16 length promotes to signed int in 'attr->hdr.length - 4', making the negative clamp at lines 21-22 functional; no unsigned wrap occurs on this platform.
value.slen (pj_ssize_t) is signed, matching the clamp's intent.
The buffer passed as buf contains attacker-controlled STUN message bytes, and the length field is part of that input.
limitations: The physical capacity of buf (the STUN message/receive buffer) is not identifiable from the shown code: the function has no size parameter and discards msghdr, so the exact OOB excess against the real allocation cannot be pinned; if the enclosing decoder first validates that each attribute (hdr.length bytes) fits inside the received message, the pj_strdup read stays within the message and only the fixed-offset reads at line 15 (short length, no padding) remain.

Unchecked result of PJ_POOL_ZALLOC_T (line 12) dereferenced at line 13 is a NULL-deref candidate only on pool exhaustion; the allocation size is fixed, so it is out of scope per the allocation-failure rule.

The discarded pj_strdup return status (line 25) with a still-successful return (line 30) is an error-handling flaw only when pj_strdup fails (PJ_ENOMEM) and its downstream effect on attr->reason is consumed outside the shown code; not independently confirmed (no CWE attached).

The attacker-influenced allocation of slen+1 (~64 KB per attribute, bounded by the 16-bit length field) stays within normal STUN message size and creates no unbounded volume loop in the shown code; no separate resource-exhaustion finding.
Any 16-bit-int platform underflow of 'length - 4' is outside this codebase's platform model and was not treated as a finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability is demonstrable from the shown code. Every read and write whose argument arithmetic is fully visible is bounded by section-geometry checks computed from the same variables (left >= 4/8 at lines 47/55; o4+4 <= left and o4+l <= left at lines 110/115; section bounds at lines 16/24/39; p < e at line 39) and by the CDF_PROP_LIMIT cap on sh_properties (line 30). Array writes to inp[i] stay inside the capacity produced by cdf_grow_info, whose NULL result is always handled (lines 32-34, 98-100). The remaining suspicious reads (CDF_GETUINT32(p, i << 1) at line 45, the cdf_grow_info(nelements) call at line 98, and the o4 = slen*4 recomputation at line 131) each depend on un-shown helper bodies, debug-only DPRINTF, or a 32-bit+unshown-CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT condition, so they fail the three-part confirmation and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: cdf_get_property_info_pos returns either a valid pointer satisfying q >= p and q <= e (and readable q+4 <= e for admitted entries) or NULL (name-implied contract); the shown code only checks NULL.
cdf_grow_info honors its increment by resizing *info/*maxcount by the passed incr and returns NULL on failure (shown code relies on the NULL return at lines 33 and 99).
cdf_copy_info validates its value+len against the e bound it receives (lines 77/84/91 pass e for exactly that purpose).
size_t is 64-bit for the o4 == slen*4 conservation analysis; 32-bit wrap scenarios are treated as limitations.
DPRINTF is a debug-only macro that is empty in production builds.
limitations: Line 45 (inp[i].pi_id = CDF_GETUINT32(p, i << 1)) could be an OOB heap read only if cdf_get_property_info_pos admitted an entry whose 8-byte header exceeds the section; that behavior is in the un-shown helper, so a concrete witness cannot be constructed from the shown code (C1).

Line 98 passes nelements (residual range [1, UINT32_MAX]) unchanged to cdf_grow_info; a *maxcount + nelements wrap / undersized allocation would occur inside the un-shown helper (32-bit only), and on 64-bit an oversized growth fails cleanly and is handled at lines 99-100 — a pass-through of the value, not a derivation in the shown code (C2).

Lines 130-131 (slen += l >> 1; o4 = slen * sizeof(uint32_t)) can wrap only for 32-bit size_t with l ~ 2^31 and left ~ 4 GB, which requires CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT >= ~2^30; that constant's value is not in the shown code, so the boundary is unconfirmable (C3).
Line 46 (left = (size_t)(e - q)) would underflow only if the helper returned q > e, violating its position-return contract; not demonstrable from the shown code (C4).

Line 124 prints inp[i].pi_str.s_buf with %s even though no NUL termination is guaranteed; this is a debug-only DPRINTF macro, not reachable in a production build from the shown code, and consumers of s_buf/s_len are outside the analyzed function (C5).
cdf_copy_info (lines 77/84/91) bounds checks against e are not visible; failure is handled gracefully via goto unknown, and no out-of-domain argument is derivable in the shown code.

Vector string expansion advances *count by sh.sh_properties only (line 36) while writing nelements-1 extra entries (lines 96-102); this undercounts reported entries but is memory-safe because cdf_grow_info grows capacity by nelements, so it is a robustness/correctness note, not a finding (C7).

verdict.summary: In ex_substitute, the temporary substitution buffer size is computed in 32-bit int (needed_len, len; declared at line 346). When a single line plus substitution output exceeds INT_MAX bytes (line content and sub length are unconstrained by the shown code), needed_len wraps negative at lines 797-798 and 819-820, the grow guard at line 821 admits the wrapped value and skips reallocation, and the subsequent writes — mch_memmove at line 839, vim_regsub_multi at lines 842-844, and STRCAT at line 984 — write past the under-sized new_start heap allocation (CWE-122, root cause CWE-190).

evidence.reason: needed_len is int (line 346); the operands copy_len, STRLEN(p1)-endpos.col, and sublen derive from unconstrained buffer text and substitution input (Phase 1 residual range), so the signed 32-bit sum wraps negative when the true requirement reaches 2^31. The wrapped value is consumed by the allocation-size computation at lines 806/823 and the grow guard at line 821, producing the CWE-122 under-allocation.

len truncates STRLEN (size_t) to unsigned then stores into int, and needed_len += len is 32-bit int addition: once the accumulated output exceeds INT_MAX both wrap. The guard at line 821 has admitted set needed_len <= new_start_len after the wrap, so a negative wrapped needed_len skips reallocation exactly when the true size exceeds capacity; a witness range is a line of ~2^31 bytes with two or more matches and small sublen, which no guard in the shown code excludes.

Writes copy_len bytes at new_end inside the heap buffer whose size new_start_len was computed from the wrapped int values (whether grown at 823 or, on the wrap path at 821-833, left undersized). The write extent plus the subsequent vim_regsub_multi write at 842-844 and STRCAT at 984 exceeds the allocation capacity, causing the confirmed CWE-122 heap out-of-bounds write.

STRCAT appends the unmatched line remainder to new_start without a capacity re-check; the buffer was sized only by the wrapped needed_len/len values from lines 797-798 and 819-820, so on the overflow path the appended bytes (up to a line of ~2^31 bytes) land past new_start_len, the same CWE-122 heap overflow as line 839.

assumptions: Line content length is bounded only by memory and buffer/column arithmetic; the shown code imposes no cap on line or substitution length, so sums in the int variables needed_len/len can reach 2^31.
The regex engine's reported match columns are assumed consistent with line bounds; only nmatch is clamped by the shown code (lines 757-761).
limitations: The confirmed overflow relies on residual-range analysis (values >= 2^31 for the accumulated length), not a single literal input value, because the magnitudes originate in buffer contents and helper return values not instantiable from the shown code alone; confidence calibrated to 0.55.
Unsigned underflow of (unsigned)STRLEN(p1) - regmatch.endpos[0].col would require endpos.col > line length from the regex engine; not confirmable from the shown code.
Signed overflow of eap->line2 += i - 1 (line 263) from a huge trailing count was not tied to a corrupting sink; a wrapped line2 only ends/narrows the outer loop.

Unchecked vim_strsave results at lines 858 and 874 could produce a NULL dereference at sub_firstline[matchcol] (line 955), but only under allocation failure (OOM), which is not attacker-volume-controlled.
Discarded ml_append status (line 910) and a potential count-vs-write divergence of vim_regsub_multi depend on callee-internal behavior not visible in the shown code.

verdict.summary: io_read frees 'iovec' without verifying ownership: io_import_iovec can leave *iovec pointing at the stack array 'inline_vecs' (vectored requests with 2..UIO_FASTIOV segments), and the failure/completion paths then call kfree(iovec), freeing a stack address (CWE-590, invalid free) and crashing the kernel. Triggerable with a 2-segment READV via rw_verify_area failure (request offset >= 2^63), an -EIOCBQUEUED read, or a blocking-issue read that reaches the done/out_free merge.

evidence.reason: iovec's residual range after io_import_iovec (L14) includes the stack object inline_vecs declared at L3 for a request with 2..UIO_FASTIOV segments (standard fast-segs import contract; segment count is entry-point input with no shown-code constraint). rw_verify_area's failure set (L34) is admitted by a request with offset >= 2^63 making ki_pos negative, or an out-of-range count, and none of it excludes iovec == inline_vecs; the kfree at L35 then releases a stack pointer (CWE-590), causing an invalid-free kernel fault / DoS.

out_free is reached from -EIOCBQUEUED (L52-53) and from every read satisfying ret<=0, ret==io_size, or !force_nonblock (L54-57), including a normal blocking 2-segment READV that fully succeeds. The L94 guard admits all non-NULL iovec, but iovec may still be the stack array inline_vecs (L3/L14), so this sink performs invalid kfree of stack memory (CWE-590); the shown code contains no check that iovec != inline_vecs before freeing.

assumptions: Line numbers are relative to the supplied snippet only (no file present in the workspace).

UIO_FASTIOV == 8 and io_import_iovec follows the kernel's standard import_iovec fast-segments contract: the caller-supplied inline_vecs array is used when segment count <= UIO_FASTIOV, a kmalloc'd array is used above that, and the single buffer/len path yields iovec == NULL; iovec counts and offsets derive from userspace io_uring SQEs.
Kiocb position is a loff_t, so a request offset >= 2^63 becomes negative through io_kiocb_ppos and makes rw_verify_area fail with -EINVAL (admitted set of L33-34).
limitations: Double-free variant of the same kfree (heap iovec also freed later by request cleanup via REQ_F_NEED_CLEANUP) depends on the request-completion path outside the shown code - unconfirmed here, no CWE attached.

Use-after-return of a stack iovec persisted into req->async_data by io_setup_async_rw (L29/L60) and read after io_read returns (L30/L62/L75/L86) cannot be fully traced: the later dereference happens in callers not shown, and whether the callee copies the iovec off the stack is callee-internal - unconfirmed, no CWE attached.
iovec leak when io_setup_async_rw fails (L61-62 return ret2) requires that internal allocation to fail and is therefore treated as a robustness concern, not a finding.
io_size -> req->result truncation (L19) cannot be confirmed because req->result's type and its consumers are not shown.
iov_iter_revert over-revert (L50) when REQ_F_REISSUE is set with a non--EAGAIN ret is unreachable from the shown code since nothing here sets REQ_F_REISSUE.
Loop termination is guaranteed (io_size strictly decreases by ret >= 1 while ret < io_size); no OOB within the user-declared segments is derivable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: get_lisp_indent contains no attacker-reachable vulnerability confirmable from the shown code. Every character-scan loop is bounded by NUL checks and advancing-only pointer updates (L37-74, L97-101, L121-125, L143-165, L167-172), and the backward line-search loop at L33 cannot feed a line below pos->lnum into linewhite/ml_get_curline whenever the (unshown) findmatch contract pos->lnum >= 1 holds; the boundary value 0 fails the >= guard. The string scan (L51-69) breaks the enclosing for-loop on end-of-line inside a string (L67-68), so that never advances past the NUL. Remaining concerns (pos->lnum <= 0 from findmatch, lisp_match reading past a trailing NUL, int overflow of amount) depend on callee behavior or capacities not visible in the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated line buffer, so loops bounded by *that != NUL and *(that+1) != NUL cannot read past the line.
findmatch() returns a valid position in the current buffer with lnum >= 1 and col within the line; this invariant is not stated inside the shown code.
curwin->w_cursor.lnum >= 1 and curwin->w_cursor.col >= 0 at entry.
linenr_T is a signed long and colnr_T is int, as in Vim's standard types.
limitations: If the unshown callee findmatch() could return pos->lnum <= 0, the L33 guard (--curwin->w_cursor.lnum >= pos->lnum) would admit lnum <= 0 into linewhite() (L35) and ml_get_curline() (L37); that witness cannot be derived from the shown code, so it is unconfirmed with no CWE.

lisp_match(that + 1) at L110 can receive a pointer to the line's trailing NUL when '(' or '[' is the last character; whether the unshown lisp_match reads past the NUL cannot be confirmed from the shown code.

int amount accumulation across many lbr_chartabsize_adv/lbr_chartabsize additions (L99, L123, L162-164, L169) could wrap on multi-GB display-width lines; the capacity and reachability are not demonstrable from the shown code.
parencount is cumulative across scanned lines and can go negative (L73, L160); this only affects indentation results, not memory safety.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in the skip-loop bounds: for a keyword with len = 357,913,942, the int products 12*len (line 26) and 11*len (line 28) wrap, making size > 12*len true for size = 500,000,000 and computing ep = text + 857,913,934, well past the end of the 500,000,000-byte buffer; the loop then reads text out of bounds via d1[U(tp[-1])] (e.g. line 32), causing an OOB read of up to ~357 MB (CWE-190 -> CWE-125).

evidence.snippet: for (ep = text + size - 11 * len; tp <= ep; )
evidence.reason: 11 * len is an int product; with len = 357,913,942 it wraps to -357,913,934 (residual range 1..INT_MAX admitted by the lines 11/13 guards), so as size_t the offset becomes 2^64 - 357,913,934 and ep = text + (500,000,000 + 357,913,934) = text + 857,913,934, i.e. 357,913,934 bytes beyond the text+size capacity. The loop test tp <= ep then admits a start index (357,913,942) that is valid but permits the loop body to advance tp past the object; this corrupted bound is the root cause consumed at the pointer-arithmetic sink, primary-relevant CWE-190.

With the line-28 overflow, the line-26 guard (size 500,000,000 > wrapped 12*len = 8) is true, the loop body is entered, and a text filled with 0x0B (d1[0x0B] = 255 by a pattern-constructed delta-table value in the admitted helper-input range) advances tp by 255 per read. In body 55,721 tp becomes text + 500,000,197, so this statement reads text + 500,000,196, which is 197 bytes past the last valid byte text + 499,999,999; the loop keeps performing such reads until tp > ep (~357 MB past the buffer). This is a confirmed out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose index derives from the entry-point buffer size and the attacker/text byte plus the wrapped ep bound.

assumptions: Signed int overflow wraps two's-complement (implementation behavior), as assumed for all mainstream compilers; the C standard declares 12*len and 11*len UB at these magnitudes.

The delta table d1 is a Boyer-Moore delta-1 table of unsigned char entries (d in [0,255] by the declared pointer type), with pattern-constructed values selectable within the helper input's admitted residual range (e.g. d1[0x0B] = 255 when the rightmost 0x0B in the keyword is at position len-256).
bm_delta2_search and memchr_kwset behave per their standard/name semantics: delta2 keeps tp bounded by ep and advances tp; memchr_kwset scans at most its length argument.
kwset->mind fits in int for the demonstrated witness (357,913,942 < INT_MAX); no size_t-to-int truncation is involved in the finding.
limitations: Exploitability requires an unusually large keyword (~358 MB) and a buffer of at least that size; impact is OOB read (crash/DoS, potential influence on the returned match offset), so severity is rated low.

The length underflow at memchr_kwset (line 54), text + size - tp wrapping huge when tp > text + size, is not reached on the deterministic witness (the goto big_advance path at lines 51-52 skips it); reaching it needs unpredictable byte values in out-of-bounds memory, so it is not a separate confirmed finding.

All conclusions of safety rely on the invariants listed in assumptions; none of them is established by the shown code itself.

No shown check rejects symlinks or verifies that the resolved path stays under destination.

This is the enabling sink whose created object is later reopened by the write path.

evidence.reason: Sink of the CWE-59 overwrite: for an AE_IFREG entry whose pathname equals a symlink created by an earlier iteration (line 206), file resolves to that symlink and g_file_replace opens/truncates through it (standard open-with-replace semantics), so attacker data lands at the attacker-chosen external target such as /home/victim/.bashrc. The only guard on this path (line 48) is skipped when overwrite=TRUE and skip_older=FALSE, and no shown check inspects the file type or symlink resolution before this call.

Payload-delivery sink: attacker-controlled archive data (buffer/buffer_size from archive_read_data_block, line 192) is streamed into the stream opened at line 188, completing the arbitrary overwrite of the file the symlink points to.

assumptions: Archive container bytes (entry pathnames, symlink targets, hardlinks, content) are attacker-controlled; no shown code constrains them.
g_file_replace follows symlinks like open(O_CREAT|O_TRUNC) and g_file_make_symbolic_link creates the entry with the target string verbatim; these are standard GLib/POSIX semantics.
_g_path_get_relative_basename is relied on only to reproduce the same relative name 'z' for both entries of the witness; its body is not needed for the symlink-reuse attack.
limitations: Plain '..' / absolute-path traversal outside destination is unconfirmed because the only filter, _g_path_get_relative_basename (lines 44 and 135), is not part of the shown code; a hardlink escape via link() (line 140) shares the same unconfirmed dependency.

Minor error-handling flaw: after a g_output_stream_write failure the specific G_IO_ERROR is replaced by a generic FR_ERROR at lines 199-200; the error is still propagated, so no security impact is confirmed.
Volume-based resource exhaustion and single-shot leaks were not assessed; no unbounded attacker-controlled loop was identified in the shown code.

verdict.summary: In warnf, vsnprintf's return value len is the full would-be formatted length, not the 255 characters actually stored in print_buffer[256] (line 11 vs line 7). When a warning message's formatted length exceeds 255, len > 255 drives the wrap loop, which consumes characters with ptr advanced by cut+1 (line 31) while len is decremented by only cut (line 32). For a sufficiently long message the loop continues reading past the 256-byte buffer: ISSPACE(ptr[cut]) at line 21, fwrite(ptr, cut+1, ...) at line 29, and fputs(ptr, ...) at line 35 all read at indices >= 256, causing a stack out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose bytes are written to config->errors. For example, with WARN_TEXTWIDTH=79 and a would-be length of 314, the fourth wrap reads index 237+78=315. The exact first-OOB threshold depends on the unseen WARN_TEXTWIDTH value, but the shown code imposes no upper bound on len, so an OOB read is reachable for any plausible WARN_TEXTWIDTH >= 2.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read sink (CWE-125): ptr is advanced by cut+1 each wrap iteration (line 31) while len (the unbounded vsnprintf would-be length from line 11) decreases by only cut (line 32), so after processing a message longer than 255 stored characters, ptr[cut] is read at offset+cut >= 256, past the declared char print_buffer[256] (line 7). The guards at lines 15 and 18 admit any len >= WARN_TEXTWIDTH+1 and never bound ptr or the remaining buffer data; for WARN_TEXTWIDTH=79 a would-be length of 314 reaches read index 315 in the fourth wrap.

Out-of-bounds read sink (CWE-125): fwrite copies cut+1 bytes from ptr, where cut is at most WARN_TEXTWIDTH-1 and ptr's offset is the unbounded cumulative advance (line 31) driven by len from line 11. When the formatted message exceeds the 255 stored characters and the wrap walk passes index 255, this call reads bytes at indices >= 256 of print_buffer and writes them to config->errors, disclosing adjacent stack memory. For WARN_TEXTWIDTH=79 and would-be length 314, the fourth wrap's fwrite reads indices 237..315.

Out-of-bounds read sink (CWE-125): in the else branch, fputs reads from ptr until a NUL. ptr's offset is the unbounded cumulative advance (line 31) sized by the vsnprintf would-be length len (line 11); once ptr points past index 255, the buffer's NUL at index min(len,255) is behind ptr, so fputs walks uninitialized/adjacent stack bytes with no shown bound. This occurs whenever remaining len <= WARN_TEXTWIDTH but ptr is already beyond the stored data.

assumptions: WARN_TEXTWIDTH is a small positive text-width constant (>= 2) as implied by its name and use as a wrap width; its exact value is not in the shown code.
vsnprintf follows standard C semantics: it NUL-terminates when size > 0 and returns the full length that would have been written, which is the basis for len exceeding the buffer content.
config and config->errors are valid non-NULL objects as supplied by callers; no check exists in the shown code.
limitations: The exact first-OOB threshold depends on the unseen WARN_TEXTWIDTH value (for WARN_TEXTWIDTH=79 it triggers at would-be length 314); the finding is confirmed via residual-range analysis (len is unbounded by the shown code) rather than a single WARN_TEXTWIDTH-independent witness value.

Attacker-controllability of fmt/args is not visible in the shown code: the function is an internal-helper parameter with unknown provenance, so reachability of a hostile >255-character message by an attacker is assumed but not proven by the shown code alone.

Double va_start at lines 9-10 without an intervening va_end is undefined behavior (C 7.16.1.4) but has no demonstrable attacker-visible impact on mainstream ABIs; treated as a hardening concern, not a finding.

If WARN_TEXTWIDTH were 1, cut would always be 0 and line 32 would never decrease len, causing an infinite loop; this value is not in the shown code and is implausible, so it is not reported as a confirmed hang.
NULL config or config->errors dereference would require out-of-scope caller misuse; no shown path produces NULL.

Demoted concerns: unchecked dquot_initialize return (line 8), unguarded bmap dereference (line 35), BUG_ON panic gate (line 31), and possible evict/umount lifetime races.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The teardown path is guarded: tty->disc_data is detached under disc_data_lock (lines 5-7), the NULL guard (lines 10-11) bounds every teardown sink and prevents double-close double-free, and lines 17-18 block until the refcount reaches zero before netif_stop_queue/unregister_netdev/kfree/free_netdev (lines 23-33) execute. The shown code contains no arithmetic, index, or size derivation, so no tainted memory-safety or injection sink exists. The only remaining concerns (concurrent-user UAF, NULL ax->dev, wait_for_completion hang, irq-state handling) all depend on invariants or callers outside the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: Every path that uses ax after retrieving it from tty->disc_data holds an increment of ax->refcnt and the final release completes ax->dead; this get/put contract is what makes line 18 a wait-until-no-users barrier, and its complete() producer is outside the shown code.
tty is a valid struct tty_struct * when the line-discipline close callback runs (tty-core contract, not shown).
disc_data_lock also guards every other retrieval of tty->disc_data in the discipline, so clearing it at line 7 is atomic with respect to new users.
The mkiss fields used at lines 23-33 (dev, rbuff, xbuff) were fully initialized by a successful open; the shown code never creates a NULL dev.
limitations: A concurrent-use use-after-free would require a socket receive/transmit path touching ax without a refcount; that path is not in the shown code, and lines 17-18 already block close until the refcount is zero, so no witness can be constructed inside the shown code.
A NULL ax->dev at lines 23/25/33 is not producible by any expression in the shown code, so the unguarded dereferences are not a confirmable CWE-476 finding from this snippet alone.

If a reference to ax were leaked elsewhere, wait_for_completion(&ax->dead) (line 18) would block indefinitely; the leak and the complete() producer are outside the shown code, making this a hang hypothesis rather than a confirmed finding.

write_lock_irq (line 5) restores the IRQ-enabled state rather than the pre-lock state and would corrupt interrupt state if mkiss_close were ever invoked with IRQs already disabled; no such caller or context is shown.
Teardown safety additionally relies on standard kernel-API semantics of netif_stop_queue, unregister_netdev, and free_netdev, which are outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The refresh loop at lines 10-11 is bounded by the visible guard i < *nmdev_types, and every state the shown code writes keeps *mdev_types consistent with *nmdev_types (NULL paired with count 0 at line 13 / lines 18-19, array paired with its count at lines 18-19). verdict.summary: remove_slot_store copies attacker-supplied sysfs data into the stack array drc_name (line 12) without writing a NUL terminator, then passes the unterminated array to strchr (line 14). Because nbytes is only bounded below MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN and the input content is unconstrained, an input containing no '\n' byte lets strchr's scan read past the end of drc_name (OOB stack read, CWE-125); the resulting pointer can also make the subsequent '*end = '\0'' (line 17) an out-of-bounds one-byte stack write. The line 17 write is the same root cause reaching a second sink, not an independent CWE.

evidence.reason: drc_name is a char[MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN] stack buffer (line 5); line 12 copies nbytes attacker-controlled bytes into it. The guard at line 9 admits nbytes in [0, MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1] but neither it nor any later statement imposes a content constraint or NUL-terminates the array, so drc_name is an unterminated string passed to strchr, which scans until '\n' or '\0'. With nbytes=5 and buf='abcde' (no '\n'; a member of the line 9 guard's admitted set and of the unconstrained content residual range), the scan must read index >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN unless uninitialized stack bytes happen to contain a terminator, making this an out-of-bounds stack read (primary CWE-125, missing termination).

end receives the result of the unbounded strchr scan at line 14. When that scan crosses the array boundary (same witness: input without '\n', no terminator inside drc_name), end points at or past &drc_name[MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN] and this statement writes a NUL byte out of bounds on the stack — the downstream write sink (CWE-787 mechanism) of the same missing-termination root cause, reported here as part of the primary CWE-125 finding rather than as an independent CWE.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is the compile-time capacity of drc_name as declared at line 5; the shown code uses it as the array bound in both the declaration and the guard at line 9, so the capacity is identifiable from the shown code.
buf points to nbytes readable bytes (standard memcpy domain), so the copy at line 12 is in-bounds once the line 9 guard passes.
No NUL-termination of buf's copied region or of drc_name is guaranteed by the shown code; line 17 is the only termination write and it occurs after strchr.
limitations: The exact position where strchr stops, and therefore whether the line 14 read and the line 17 write actually cross index MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1, depends on uninitialized stack contents in drc_name[nbytes..MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1] and beyond, which are not visible in the shown code; the witness is a residual-range demonstration rather than a single fully deterministic value, capping confidence at 0.7.
The one-byte OOB write at line 17 is not reported as an independent CWE because it shares the identical trigger and root cause with the OOB read.
dlpar_remove_slot's body is not shown, so no command-injection or TOCTOU claim is made against it.

verdict.summary: The warning wrapper's wrap loop desynchronizes its length bookkeeping from its pointer advance: ptr advances cut+1 per wrap (line 27) while len decreases by only cut (line 28), and cut can be 0 for all-non-space text, leaving len unchanged so the while(len > 0) loop never terminates. A message of 300+ non-space characters (in the unconstrained residual range of the variadic arguments) drives ptr past the 256-byte print_buffer, causing a deterministic out-of-bounds read at ISSPACE(ptr[cut]) (line 21) and fwrite(ptr, cut+1, ...) (line 25), with the loop also hanging thereafter (non-termination from the same root cause, not a separate CWE).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) of the 256-byte print_buffer (declared line 7): content from the variadic-argument residual range (any text, unconstrained by the shown code) is formatted into the buffer at line 11, giving len=300 for a 300-char non-space message, admitted by while(len > 0) (line 15) and if(len > (int)WARN_TEXTWIDTH) (line 18). The inner loop admits cut=0 because all bytes up to index 255 are non-space, so each wrap executes ptr += cut+1 (line 27) while len -= cut (line 28) leaves len unchanged; the loop therefore never terminates and ptr advances unboundedly. On wrap 178, ptr == print_buffer+178 and the first probe ptr[cut] with cut=WARN_TEXTWIDTH-1=78 reads index 256, exactly one past the 256-element array's capacity (indices 0..255) — a confirmed index==capacity OOB read with no protective bound on ptr+WARN_TEXTWIDTH-1 anywhere in the shown code.

Second OOB-read sink (CWE-125), same root cause as the ISSPACE probe: with an all-non-space 300-char payload, cut=0 keeps len at 300 forever (line 28), so the loop advances ptr by 1 per wrap (line 27) and never exits; once ptr reaches print_buffer+256, fwrite(ptr, cut+1, ...) reads ptr[0], i.e., byte index 256, outside the 256-byte stack array, and copies out-of-bounds bytes to config->errors. The unsafe pointer/value flow is derived entirely in the shown code (lines 14, 21, 27, 28); no guard bounds ptr or cut against the buffer capacity.

assumptions: WARN_TEXTWIDTH is a positive integer (typical value 79); its exact definition is not in the shown code, so the iteration counters in the evidence assume 79. The walk-off/OOB mechanism holds for any positive width <= 255, and a longer payload covers larger widths (for width > 255, the first wrap reads ptr[WARN_TEXTWIDTH-1] at index >= 256 immediately).
ISSPACE is the standard ctype macro: false for 'a' and for '\0', so NUL bytes do not stop the cut search.
config->errors is a valid FILE*; failures of fputs/fwrite are only discarded on a diagnostic stream.
limitations: fmt and the variadic arguments are internal-helper parameters; attacker control of the warning content is not independently established by the shown code (format-string/%n misuse via fmt is therefore unconfirmed).
The double va_start at lines 9-10 is formally undefined behavior but on typical ABIs merely re-initializes ap to the same position and has no observable security effect.
A negative vsnprintf return (line 11) silently drops the warning; robustness only.
Between the written string's NUL and the end of the array, the wrap logic may read uninitialized stack bytes into the error stream before the walk-off; not separately confirmed as a security impact.
The non-termination (hang) of the while(len > 0) loop shares the same root cause as the OOB read and is not reported as a separate CWE.

verdict.summary: When getsistring receives len == 1, the loop at line 18 exits with i == 2 and the terminator write name[i/2]='\0' at line 19 writes to name[1], one byte past the 1-byte buffer from cli_malloc(1) (line 7) — a heap out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: len is a uint32_t internal-helper parameter; the guards at lines 5-6 (len != 0, then clamp to <= 400) leave residual admitted range 1..400, so len == 1 is admitted. With len == 1, cli_malloc(1) at line 7 produces a buffer of capacity 1 (indices 0..0) and fread at line 13 succeeds on a non-empty stream. The loop at line 18 then terminates with i == 2, so line 19 writes name[1] = '\0', exceeding the identifiable capacity by one byte. With n_slide_infos[0]=n_slide_infos[1]=0x80000001 the true sum is 0x100000002 but total_slide_infos becomes 2; the guard at line 20 admits 2 (the excluded set is only {0}), so line 24 allocates 2 elements while the line 47 loop admits j up to n_slide_infos[i]-1 and k increments on every entry passing line 54. Writes at k=2 (== capacity, excess one RzDyldRebaseInfosEntry) and beyond corrupt adjacent heap memory; the wrap corrupts the allocation size, making CWE-190 the secondary root cause.

verdict.summary: Double free of the TX skb in the xmit-failure path: after can_put_echo_skb() (line 50) stores the skb in echo_skb[ctx->ndx], a nonzero err from mcba_usb_xmit (line 52) sends control to xmit_failed, where can_free_echo_skb(..., ctx->ndx, ...) (line 59) frees that same skb and dev_kfree_skb(skb) (line 61) frees it a second time, producing a kernel use-after-free/double free.

Second free of the same object: line 59 already freed the skb stored in the echo slot, then dev_kfree_skb(skb) frees the identical pointer again — double free (CWE-415) leading to kernel use-after-free.

assumptions: can_dropped_invalid_skb() (line 14) enforces CAN-frame validity, in particular cf->len <= CAN_MAX_DLEN (8), per its standard kernel semantics; the shown code imposes no other bound on cf->len.

can_put_echo_skb() stores the passed skb in priv->echo_skb[ctx->ndx] and can_free_echo_skb() frees the skb stored in that slot, per the CAN driver helper semantics this code is written against. If a kernel variant clones the skb inside can_put_echo_skb, the pairing would no longer be a double free; the shown code originates from kernels where the skb itself is queued.

The return value of can_put_echo_skb (line 50) is discarded; on -EBUSY/-ENOMEM the driver still reports NETDEV_TX_OK, which can cause echo-accounting drift or an skb leak, but the trigger depends on device-paced state not controlled by attacker input in the shown code.

verdict.summary: atusb_disconnect dereferences the unguarded result of usb_get_intfdata(interface) at line 5 (dev_dbg) and line 7 (atusb->shutdown = 1). usb_get_intfdata returns NULL whenever no driver data is set, and the shown code imposes no NULL check before using the pointer across the whole teardown chain (lines 5-19), so a disconnect entry with unset/cleared interface data causes a NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476) and kernel oops/DoS. The same root cause also delays usb_set_intfdata(interface, NULL) until line 21, after all atusb dereferences.

evidence.reason: NULL-deref sink (CWE-476): `atusb` is assigned from `usb_get_intfdata(interface)` at line 3 with residual range {NULL, valid pointer} because the shown code applies no constraint; the API returns NULL when driver data is unset, and the driver itself stores NULL into that field at line 21. There is no `if (!atusb)` guard between line 3 and this dereference of `atusb` and `atusb->usb_dev`, so the witness atusb == NULL is a member of the (empty) admitted guard set and reaches this dereference.

First unconditionally-executing dereference of the same unguarded `atusb` value from line 3 (CWE-476). `usb_get_intfdata` can return NULL (residual range unconstrained by the shown code, which only stores NULL into the field at line 21), and every guard along the path is absent, so atusb == NULL is admitted and the write-through at line 7 faults in every build regardless of debug-macro evaluation of line 5.

assumptions: `usb_get_intfdata` follows the standard kernel driver-core semantics: it returns the last value stored via `usb_set_intfdata`, or NULL if none was stored.
`disconnect` is the USB-core unbind callback, invoked in response to attacker-controllable device plug/unplug, with the interface pointer supplied by the core.
`ieee802154_free_hw(atusb->hw)` frees the hardware state whose private region contains the `atusb` object, making `atusb` dangling after line 19.
limitations: The exact kernel state that produces `usb_get_intfdata(interface) == NULL` at disconnect entry (e.g., probe failure/unbound-interface timing) is established outside the shown function; the shown code only demonstrates that NULL is a legal value of this field by storing it at line 21.
Use-after-free/double-free of `tx_urb` at lines 12-13 would occur if `atusb_free_urbs` (line 11) also frees `tx_urb`; the helper body is not shown, so the claim is unconfirmable and has no CWE.

A re-entrant or second disconnect call after line 19 (where `atusb` is freed) while intfdata is still set until line 21 could cause a use-after-free, but no re-entry mechanism is visible in the shown code; unconfirmed.
`&atusb->usb_dev->dev` at line 5 also requires `atusb->usb_dev` to be non-NULL; that invariant is not established in the shown code, but the primary NULL fault on `atusb` alone is sufficient.
No OOB, integer-overflow, injection, weak-crypto, or authorization surface exists in this function because it performs no arithmetic, no buffer access, no string building, and no permission checks.
Impact is kernel oops/denial-of-service; no privilege escalation or data corruption was confirmed.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code alone.
