NULL dereferences of auth_user (line 5), client->auth (line 9), auth->state (line 10), and client->con (line 17) are not producible on any shown path and would require out-of-scope caller state.
size*nmemb overflow at line 4 is not attacker-reachable because the callback counts are libcurl-internal lengths.

verdict.summary: In jp2_decode, when the input file supplies a CMAP box together with a PCLR box but no CDEF box, dec->cdef remains NULL (set only in the box loop at lines 83-88, zeroed at line 30); the else branch entered at line 265 then evaluates &dec->cdef->data.cdef at line 268, a NULL-pointer dereference reachable from a crafted JP2 file. Every guard before the sink (IHDR/numcmpts/comptype/COLR presence, CMAP sanity checks, CMAP-PCLR pairing) admits the witness box set, so the NULL deref is attacker-triggerable undefined behavior / crash (CWE-476, denial of service).

evidence.reason: dec->cdef is attacker-controlled box presence: it is zero-initialized by jp2_dec_create (line 30) and assigned only when a JP2_BOX_CDEF box is parsed (lines 83-88). A crafted stream with CMAP (numchans=1, ent map=DIRECT/pcol=0/cmptno=0) and PCLR (numchans=1) but no CDEF passes every prior guard (line 218 retains cmap because pclr is present; lines 240-241 admit cmptno=0<1; lines 246-247 admit pcol=0<1), so the else branch at line 265 is taken with dec->cdef == NULL and line 268 dereferences it via &dec->cdef->data.cdef. That is a NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476): undefined behavior and, unless the dead store is optimized away, a SIGSEGV / UBSan fault, i.e., attacker-triggerable denial of service. Confidence is capped by the fact that cdefd is used only inside #if 0, so compilers may eliminate the computation.

assumptions: jp2_dec_create() zero-initializes dec so dec->cdef is NULL unless a CDEF box is parsed (lines 30, 83-88).
Component-number validity follows the domain [0, jas_image_numcmpts(image)) that the shown code itself enforces for cmptno at lines 240-241.
A JP2C codestream with at least one component can be embedded in the file, satisfying jpc_decode and the checks at lines 122, 141.
limitations: The NULL dereference at line 268 may be eliminated by dead-code elimination because cdefd is only used inside #if 0 (lines 285-293); observable impact depends on build/optimization, which is why severity is medium and confidence 0.7 rather than higher.

The lutdata read at line 276 (index cmapent->pcol + i*pclrd->numchans) is bounded by the guard at 246-247 (pcol < pclr.numchans) and the loop at 275 (i < numlutents); under the format-implied capacity of numlutents*numchans the maximal index equals capacity-1, so it is in-domain, but that capacity is fixed by the box parser outside the shown code, and 32-bit wrap of i*numchans would require capacities not shown — OOB here is unconfirmable.

Entries arrays (cmap.ents, cdef.ents) and bpcc.bpcs are indexed by input-derived counts (lines 179-182, 238-251, 307-318) whose allocated capacity is established by jp2_box_get parsing, not visible in the shown code; boundary claims against them are unconfirmable.

A DIRECT CMAP channel with numchans > numcmpts stores chantocmptlut[channo] = channo (line 272) without a numcmpts cap, so lines 313-317 / 321-322 can pass a component index >= numcmpts to jas_image_setcmpttype; the OOB write (CWE-787) would occur only if that callee indexes without internal bounds checking, which is not shown, and its return value is discarded at 313/321 — not confirmed, so kept as a limitation.

lutents = jas_alloc2(...) at line 274 is not NULL-checked before lutents[i] at line 276; NULL requires failure of the attacker-sized allocation (DoS-only, no attacker-controlled corruption), so it is a limitation, not a confirmed finding.

assert(dec->image->cmprof_) at line 212 can abort on a crafted ICC profile if jas_cmprof_createfromiccprof returns NULL, but only in assert-enabled builds (NDEBUG removes it); debug-only robustness concern.

jas_image_numcmpts returning a value that exceeds the actual component array would be a library invariant issue not established by the shown code; the shown checks (141, 327-337) use the returned count consistently.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds read in get_lisp_indent(): when a multi-byte character precedes a '(' that is the last character of the found-paren line, the column loop at lines 97-101 advances `that` past the paren onto the line's NUL, line 114 then moves it past the NUL, and line 118 dereferences it in VIM_ISWHITE(*that) (plus further reads via lbr_chartabsize at line 120 and the block at lines 124-171). Reachable from attacker-chosen buffer text on the 'no same-level line found' path (amount == -1).

evidence.reason: Sink: first read past the line buffer. `that` derives entirely within the shown code: `col = pos->col` (line 86, byte offset of the '('), the loop at 97-101 advances `that` by one full character per iteration while `col` counts iterations (line 100), so a multi-byte char before the paren overshoots onto the NUL (witness: line `é(` with pos->col=2); line 109 admits the NUL into the else, and line 114's `that++` moves past the NUL; VIM_ISWHITE(*that) then dereferences NUL+1. No guard in the shown code bounds this deref (line 97 limits iteration count, line 109 tests only paren chars). The paren at end of line and amount==-1 path (lines 33-82) make the witness reachable; capacity is the NUL-terminated `ml_get_curline()` line, so pointer = end+1 is out of bounds. Primary CWE-125.

Sink: second read on the same OOB pointer. If the out-of-bounds byte after `that++` (line 114) is whitespace, the loop at 118-122 walks further past the line buffer and lbr_chartabsize() (line 120) reads from the out-of-bounds `that` repeatedly, extending the heap over-read; same CWE-125 mechanism and same taint (buffer text, entry-point) as the line-118 deref.

assumptions: findmatch() returns pos->col as the byte offset of the found paren in its line (implied by lines 85-86 and the loop at 97-101, which uses col to position `that` on the paren).
lbr_chartabsize_adv() advances `that` past one full character (byte length >= 1 for a multi-byte char) — its name-implied advance semantics.
ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated line, making the NUL position identifiable as the line buffer's final readable byte.
limitations: Integer-overflow candidates for `parencount` (lines 31/71/73/131/153/156) and `amount` (lines 99, 120, 158-161) require ~2^31 parens or columns on one line and have no concrete realistic witness; not reported as findings.

The exact internals of findmatch()/lbr_chartabsize_adv() are not in the shown code; the OOB derivation relies only on their name/use-implied semantics (byte-based paren column; character-wise pointer advance), so the witness value is confirmed to that standard but not to callee implementation details.
Single-byte lines cannot trigger the overshoot (the loop lands exactly on the paren), so the vulnerability requires valid multi-byte UTF-8 text before a line-final '('.
Impact is read-only (crash/DoS, potential disclosure); no write, injection, crypto, or authz sink exists in this function.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The destination write is fully bounded: line 6 asserts sizeof(release_agent_path) >= PATH_MAX and line 13 passes that sizeof to strlcpy, so at most sizeof-1 bytes plus a NUL are written into the path array. The sole residual concern is source-side: strstrip(buf) and the strlcpy source scan (lines 12-13) require a NUL terminator inside buf, which the shown code neither writes nor validates and which it never bounds by nbytes; however, the capacity of buf and the caller's buffer semantics are not identifiable from the shown code, so no concrete overread (index, excess, or impact path) can be demonstrated. The unconditional 'return nbytes' (line 16) can report success after silent truncation of an over-long input, but that is silent truncation with no security impact.

assumptions: cgroup_kn_lock_live() returns either NULL or a live cgroup; the non-NULL continuation path (lines 11-16) is the only path that dereferences cgrp->root.
strstrip() and strlcpy() have standard kernel semantics: both scan the source for a NUL terminator; strlcpy writes at most size-1 bytes plus a NUL and never fails.
The storage backing buf and its termination/lifetime semantics are managed by the kernfs caller outside the shown code.
Authorization to reach this write callback (e.g., file permissions on the kernfs node) is enforced outside the shown code.
limitations: Source-side overread hypothesis: strstrip(buf) and the strlcpy source scan (lines 12-13) terminate only at a NUL inside buf; a full-length, newline-less write with no NUL byte could drive the internal strlen past the writer-provided data. This is not a confirmed finding because the shown code neither identifies buf's capacity nor guarantees termination, so no exact excess index or target-object capacity can be derived from the shown code alone.
Silent truncation: line 16 returns nbytes even when nbytes > PATH_MAX-1 and line 12 truncates the stored path; the strlcpy return is discarded. Silent truncation with no demonstrated security impact.

release_agent_path content is not validated in the shown code (relative paths, control characters, non-path data); any consequence would occur in code not shown (agent execution/display paths), so it is unconfirmed.
No authorization check is visible in this function; whether an unprivileged caller can open the file is decided by kernfs permissions outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: jp2_decode has three attacker-reachable flaws from crafted JP2 input: a heap out-of-bounds read in the BPCC loop (line 182) because the loop bound is the code-stream component count N while bpcs[] has only bpcc->numcmpts entries and the mismatch at lines 172-175 is warning-only; a second heap OOB read in the CDEF loop (lines 307-318) because dec->numchans bounds the loop while ents[] has only cdef->numents entries with no cross-check; and a NULL pointer dereference at line 268 when a CMAP box is present without a CDEF box. Primary CWE-125; secondary CWE-476.

evidence.reason: The loop at lines 179-180 admits i in [0, jas_image_numcmpts(dec->image)-1] (file-controlled N), while bpcs[] has only bpcc->numcmpts entries (file-controlled M). The mismatch check at lines 172-175 only prints a warning and does not clamp or reject. Witness: code stream with 3 components of differing bit depth (samedtype==false, admitted by line 178) and a BPCC box declaring numcmpts==1; i=1 and i=2 pass the guard at line 179 and read bpcs[1]/bpcs[2] past the 1-element array — heap OOB read (CWE-125).

The CDEF loop at line 307 bounds i by dec->numchans (set from CMAP numchans or image component count at lines 233-234), but ents[] has only cdef->numents entries, and the shown code never compares numents with numchans. Witness: image with 4 components, no CMAP (dec->numchans==4), CDEF box with numents==1; i=1,2,3 are admitted by the loop, so ents[1].channo (and .type/.assoc at lines 316-317) are read 1-3 elements past the 1-element array — heap OOB read (CWE-125); the channo-vs-numchans test at line 309 only guards the subsequent LUT index, not i against numents.

dec->cdef is set only when a CDEF box is parsed (lines 84-86) and line 306 proves CDEF is optional (NULL is an admitted value). Witness: file containing a valid CMAP box plus its required PCLR box and no CDEF box: the cmap/pclr guards at 218-229 leave dec->cmap non-NULL, the CMAP sanity loop at 238-251 passes, the else branch of `if (!dec->cmap)` at line 261 is taken, and line 268 dereferences dec->cdef while it is NULL — NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), deterministic crash.

assumptions: jp2_dec_create zero-initializes the decoder fields; this is grounded in the shown control flow, which assigns dec->ihdr/bpcc/cdef/pclr/cmap/colr only conditionally (lines 72-106) and later tests them with if (!dec->...) at lines 128/169/192/218/306.

jp2_box_get allocates each box's variable-length arrays (bpcs, ents, lutdata) with exactly the element count declared by that box (bpcc->numcmpts, cdef->numents, pclr numlutents*numchans) per JP2 box semantics referenced by the shown fields.
jas_image_numcmpts/jas_image_cmptdtype reflect the attacker-controlled component count and per-component bit depths from the decoded code stream.
limitations: The unchecked jas_alloc2 at line 274 would only yield a NULL deref at line 276 if allocation fails; that is nondeterministic OOM with DoS-only impact and is not counted as a confirmed finding.
The discarded return of jas_image_depalettize (line 279) allows later use of newcmptno even if the depalettize failed; a concrete out-of-bounds effect depends on the unshown callee's error behavior.
assert(dec->image->cmprof_) at line 212 aborts only in debug builds (assert-based DoS).

When CMAP numchans exceeds the image component count, channel numbers >= N stored in chantocmptlut are passed to jas_image_setcmpttype at lines 314 and 321; the callee's bounds checking is not visible, so no confirmed OOB is derived.
pclr.lutdata[pcol + i * pclrd->numchans] (line 276) cannot overflow 32-bit arithmetic within the shown code; absent overflow, the pcol check at lines 246-247 keeps every index within lutdata.
The exact heap-contiguous extent of the BPCC/CDEF overreads depends on jp2_box_get's allocation internals; the declared box counts suffice to establish the CWE-125 out-of-bounds index.

verdict.summary: LoaderXM::load trusts multiple file-supplied sizes. (1) The instrument-size guard `instr[y].size - 33 > 230` is a signed comparison: sizes <= 32 pass it, and the resulting negative length is converted to a huge unsigned count passed to f.read into the 230-byte stack array insData (and a 29-byte local), giving a stack buffer overflow from a crafted XM (CWE-121/195). (2) The MODPLUG 'text' extension wraps len+1 to 0 for len=0xFFFFFFFF and then f.reads up to len bytes past the message buffer (CWE-122/190). (3) Pattern decompression and sample remap read out of bounds (buffer[pc], smpReloc[nbu[sc]], CWE-125). (4) The header-size word can underflow to force an ~4 GiB allocation/memset (CWE-770).

evidence.reason: instr[y].size comes from f.readDwords (line 81) and keeps its full mp_sint32 range; the guard at 104 (`if (instr[y].size - 33 > 230)`) is a signed comparison that admits every size with size-33 <= 230, including size=32 (witness: 32-33=-1). The negative value is promoted to an unsigned f.read length 0xFFFFFFFF while insData has capacity 230 (declared line 3); a file supplying >= 231 bytes at this offset overflows the stack buffer. Primary CWE-121 (stack buffer overflow by unbounded copy over visible size), secondary CWE-195 (negative signed value converted into a huge unsigned length).

instr[y].size (read at 404) is attacker-controlled; the guard at 406 `if (instr[y].size < 29)` admits size=0 (witness), so size-4 = -4 is converted to unsigned 0xFFFFFFFC and f.read writes available file bytes into the 29-byte local buffer[29] (line 408). Excess >= 1 byte once the file supplies 29 or more bytes. CWE-121 primary, CWE-195 secondary.

Sizes 30..32 are admitted by the guarded sequence: line 426 excludes size <= 29 and the signed check at 442 admits them (witness size=31 -> size-33=-2). The negative count converts to unsigned 0xFFFFFFFE and overflows insData[230] (line 3) with >= 231 supplied bytes. CWE-121 primary, CWE-195 secondary.

len is an attacker-controlled mp_uint32 dword (line 769). For len = 0xFFFFFFFF, len+1 wraps to 0 in mp_uint32 arithmetic at lines 770/772, so module->message holds 0 bytes (capacity implied by memset(module->message, 0, len+1) at 772) while this f.read with length 0xFFFFFFFF writes any appended payload (>= 1 byte) past the buffer. Primary CWE-122 (heap overflow), secondary CWE-190 (wrap corrupting the allocation size).

buffer is allocated with patdata bytes (line 289); rows/channum/patdata are attacker words. pc is incremented at least once per cell (311 and 315-336) with no pc < patdata check anywhere in the loop; with patdata=1, rows=256, channum=2 (0x102 path, rows=readByte()+1 at 271), pc reaches index == capacity (>= patdata), reading out of bounds. CWE-125 heap over-read.

For an unpacked cell the code copies 5 bytes from buffer+pc; with patdata=1, rows=1, channum=1 and buffer[0]=0x00, this reads indices 0..4 from a 1-byte allocation (capacity patdata, line 289), an excess of 4 bytes. pc is not bounded by patdata anywhere in the shown loop. CWE-125 heap over-read.

nbu[] is filled with attacker bytes via memcpy(nbu, insDataPtr, MP_MAXINSSAMPS) at 112 (file data when size-33 >= 96, e.g. size=129). nbu[sc] ranges over full bytes 0..255 while smpReloc has MP_MAXINSSAMPS entries (declared line 4); nbu[sc]=200 (0xC8) reads smpReloc[200] out of bounds (index >= capacity). CWE-125 out-of-bounds read feeding sample relocation.

Duplicate of the smpReloc out-of-bounds read in the 0x104 path: nbu is copied from file-controlled insData at 464, and nbu[sc] (byte, 0..255) indexes smpReloc[MP_MAXINSSAMPS] (line 4) without bounds; a byte value >= MP_MAXINSSAMPS, e.g. 200, is out of domain. CWE-125.

hdrSize is derived from attacker hdrsize dword (34): mp_uint32 subtraction at 36 wraps hdrsize=0 to 0xFFFFFFFC, and the max at 39-40 admits that value, so this new[] requests ~4 GiB and memset at 43 touches it, terminating the process via bad_alloc/OOM. CWE-770 uncontrolled resource consumption (integer wrap corrupts the allocation-size expression at the sink).

assumptions: f.read(void*, size, count) writes up to count bytes into the destination, bounded by remaining file bytes (standard read semantics); readByte/read* return the values read from the file.
mp_uint32 is 32-bit unsigned, mp_sint32 is 32-bit signed, mp_uword is 16-bit; signed/unsigned conversions of negative counts to f.read lengths follow C++ implicit conversion.
module->message capacity is exactly len+1 as implied by memset(module->message, 0, len+1) at 772.
MP_MAXINSSAMPS is the XM instrument sample count (used as smpReloc/nbu capacity at lines 4-5 and as the numSamples cap); its numeric value is smaller than the full byte range 0..255 used in nbu[].
new[] uses the default throwing allocation; module->smp capacity is the named constant MP_MAXSAMPLES used as the guard at 616/668.
limitations: Old-version (0x102/0x103) instrument loop writes smp[g+s] with the cumulative s incremented at 247 and, unlike the 0x104 branch (616-617) and the 0x102 sample-load loop (668-669), contains no s >= MP_MAXSAMPLES check; the named constant MP_MAXSAMPLES bounds the array but its numeric value is not shown, so the exact excess cannot be stated from the shown code.

phead[y].rows*header->channum*6 (278/286) and the patnum-driven phead indexing (258, 741-760) involve attacker words but the phead capacity constant and the concrete 32-bit wrap result are not shown; no clean witness was derived.
Discarded return values of f.read* and allocateSongMessage (770) are robustness/error-handling concerns; the confirmed overflows are independent of them.

VERBOSE-only printf("%s", instr[y].name) (198, 442) may read past a non-NUL-terminated 22-byte name field; the field's NUL behavior is not established in the shown code and the call is build-conditional.
Huge-but-non-wrapping allocations (e.g. hdrSize near 4 GiB without underflow, pattern sizes up to 65535*65535*6) are additional DoS vectors but are subsumed by the confirmed 4 GiB hdrSize case.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Every attacker-derived length (w_length, w_value, w_index) is constrained by shown guards before reaching a sink: w_length is clamped to USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ for IN requests (lines 14-20, 20) and re-clamped to USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ on the OS-descriptor path (line 286); each descriptor/setup branch further caps reply lengths with min()/min_t() (lines 70, 78-79, 89, 95, 101, 126, 156, 202, 303, 322); interface[] lookups are gated by intf >= MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES (lines 163, 192, 228, 251, 356); and req->length is assigned only when value >= 0 (line 403). Unconfirmable concerns (OTG empty-configs deref, test_bit() bitmap capacity, helper-internal write bounds, error-to-success conversions) are recorded in limitations without CWE.

assumptions: cdev->req->buf capacity equals the named constant USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ used as the shown clamp bound at lines 14/20; cdev->os_desc_req->buf capacity equals USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ used at line 286.
cdev->config->interface[] is an array of MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES entries, matching the guard at lines 163/192/228/251/356.
f->endpoints bitmap covers bit indices 0..31 used by test_bit() at line 366.

Gadget-side state (cdev->configs non-empty on the USB_DT_OTG path, callbacks such as set_alt/get_alt/func_suspend returning status values, get_string/fill_ext_*/config_desc/bos_desc/device_qual respecting the EP0 buffer size) is setup by the composite/function drivers.
limitations: USB_DT_OTG path: at lines 112-116 list_first_entry() can never produce NULL, so the if (!config) guard is dead; on an empty cdev->configs the code would dereference a non-NULL in-struct pointer at config->descriptors[0] (line 127). The state is device-side configuration, not attacker-derived in the shown code, and the resulting pointer is garbage rather than NULL, so the NULL-deref rule does not apply; treated as out-of-scope/robustness.

Capacity of config->descriptors[0] is not identifiable from the shown code, so the memcpy read bound at line 127 cannot be independently confirmed; the written value is bounded by w_length <= EP0_BUFSIZ and a compile-time descriptor-struct size.
Capacity of f->endpoints bitmap is not shown in the code, so test_bit(endp, f->endpoints) at line 366 cannot be confirmed in-bounds for all endp in [0,31].

OS-descriptor header stores at buf[5]/buf[6]/buf[8]/buf+0/buf+8 occur even when w_length < 9 (lines 288, 293, 296, 299, 310, 313, 316); they are only provably in-bounds if USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ >= 16, whose numeric value is not shown.

Error-return handling: get_status() failure yields a successful 2-byte zero reply (lines 233-235 with value=2 set at 226-227), and a negative fill_ext_compat() return is converted via min_t(u16, ...) into a success reply (lines 302-303); outcomes are zeroed buffers with no disclosure or OOB, so this is protocol/robustness behavior, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Integer arithmetic count *= 24, count += 16 (lines 297-298) could in theory wrap if count_ext_compat() returned an extreme value, but the count's provenance is a gadget-side interface enumeration, no attacker magnitude is derivable in the shown code, and the result feeds only a fixed 4-byte put_unaligned_le32() and reply content, never a size or index sink.

Write bounds of the helper calls whose buffer argument is req->buf (get_string line 92, config_desc 87, bos_desc 100, device_qual 77, fill_ext_compat 302, fill_ext_prop 319) are not visible in the shown code; only the reply lengths are capped here.

verdict.summary: Double free of the ssh_buffer and ssh_string in sftp_mkdir: if any of buffer_add_u32/buffer_add_ssh_string/buffer_add_attributes/sftp_packet_write at lines 28-31 returns <0, the branch frees buffer and path at lines 32-33 but does not return, so the unconditional frees at lines 35-36 free the same heap handles a second time, corrupting the heap. The failure is reachable for entry-point input: an uncapped `directory` can force buffer growth failure in buffer_add_ssh_string (line 29), and a peer transport failure makes sftp_packet_write (line 31) fail.

evidence.reason: Second free of the same heap object: the guard at lines 28-31 admits any failure return (<0) of buffer_add_u32/buffer_add_ssh_string/buffer_add_attributes/sftp_packet_write, including an uncapped entry-point `directory`-derived path causing buffer_add_ssh_string (line 29) to fail or a peer transport failure in sftp_packet_write (line 31); line 32 already freed `buffer` and the branch contains no return, so this line frees the identical pointer again (double free, CWE-415).

Second free of the same heap object: `path` was allocated from the uncapped entry-point string `directory` at line 16 and freed once at line 33 inside the failure branch (guard at lines 28-31, admitted set = any call returning <0); since the branch does not return, this unconditional line frees the identical `path` pointer a second time (double free, CWE-415).

assumptions: Line numbers are assigned by counting the verbatim snippet supplied in the prompt (no file/line metadata was available; the workspace is empty).

ssh_buffer_free, ssh_string_free, ssh_string_from_char, buffer_add_*, sftp_packet_write, sftp_read_and_dispatch, sftp_dequeue, and parse_status_msg behave as the standard libssh helpers: pointer-valued frees that do not clear the caller's copy, allocation/failure returns as stated, and <0 on failure.
limitations: Whether the L28-31 failure fires depends on peer/transport behavior or buffer-growth/OOM conditions rather than being deterministic per input; the double free itself, once the branch is entered, is unconditional and confirmed (confidence 0.8).

The `while (msg == NULL)` loop (L38-43) has no guaranteed termination against a malicious server that keeps the transport open, but it is I/O-bound with no CPU-spin in the shown code; treated as a robustness limitation, not a confirmed hang.
status->errormsg (L78) is not proven non-NULL by the shown code; the failure mode is library-dependent only, so no CWE is attached.
`sftp` (L12/L18/L77) could be NULL only if an out-of-scope caller supplies it; no path in the shown code produces NULL.
The L60 sftp_lstat re-check of `directory` is read-only and serves only to synthesize EEXIST; no authz or write decision in the shown code makes it a TOCTOU finding.
No format-string control is possible: L77-78 and L82-84 use literal formats with attacker text passed as arguments (safe %s/%d use).

verdict.summary: mobi_buffer_move calls memmove (line 19) with a caller-supplied length and source pointer that the shown bounds checks fail to bound. On the negative-offset path the only guard (line 12) checks the copy start but never validates len, so any len > maxlen - buf->offset writes past buf->data + buf->maxlen (heap OOB write, CWE-787). On the positive-offset path the line 5 guard sums size_t values modulo 2^64, so buf->offset=2, offset=0, len=SIZE_MAX wraps the sum to 1 and passes the check while memmove copies ~2^64 bytes (CWE-787 with the wrapped bounds computation as secondary root cause CWE-190).

evidence.reason: Negative branch (lines 11-18): len retains its full Phase-1 residual range [0, SIZE_MAX] because the only guard on this path, line 12 ('buf->offset < aoffset'), bounds merely the copy start and not the copy end. Witness with maxlen=64, buf->offset=8, offset=-4 (aoffset=4; line 12 admitted, 8>=4): line 17 sets source=data+4 and line 19 copies len=57 bytes to data+8, writing index 64 which equals the code's own end-of-buffer bound data+maxlen (excess 1 byte; len=256 exceeds by 200 and also reads past the end). The positive branch would reject the same length at line 5 (8+4+57=69>64), confirming the branch asymmetry. Primary CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write at the line 19 sink.

Positive branch (lines 4-10): line 5 computes buf->offset + aoffset + len in unsigned size_t, wrapping modulo 2^64 (len and aoffset are size_t; any narrower offset field is promoted to size_t). Witness: buf->offset=2, offset=0 (line 4 admitted, aoffset=0), len=SIZE_MAX, maxlen=64: the computed sum is (2 + 2^64 - 1) mod 2^64 = 1, so guard '1 > 64' is false and the huge len is admitted, while the true sum is 2^64+1. Line 19 then executes memmove(data+2, data+2, 2^64-1), writing/reading ~2^64 bytes far beyond [data, data+maxlen); line 20 also wraps buf->offset. Primary CWE-787 OOB write with the wrapped line-5 bounds computation as the independent root cause (secondary CWE-190).

assumptions: size_t is 64-bit unsigned on the analyzed platform; the same wrap exists on 32-bit builds with SIZE_MAX=2^32-1.
The shown code's own guard at line 5 ('End of buffer') identifies the buffer extent as [buf->data, buf->data + buf->maxlen), so maxlen is the capacity used for the boundary claims.
memmove has its standard semantics: it copies len bytes between the two given addresses and is overlap-safe.
limitations: len and offset are internal-helper parameters (role b), so attacker reachability depends on callers not shown; the analysis targets the residual range the shown guards leave unconstrained, as required by the role classification.
abs(INT_MIN) at line 2 is undefined behavior, but the resulting huge aoffset is rejected on the negative path by line 12 for any plausible buf->offset, so it is not a confirmed exploit.
A NULL buf or buf->data dereference is caller-dependent and not producible inside the shown code, so it is not confirmed.
The shown error handling is not flawed: both guarded failure paths set buf->error (lines 7, 14) before returning (lines 8, 15).

verdict.summary: simplestring_addn has an integer-overflow guard hole: with target->len == 0 and add_len == SIZE_MAX, the check (SIZE_MAX - add_len - 1) < target->len underflows to SIZE_MAX < 0 (false) at line 8, admitting the pair. The needed-size expression target->len + add_len + 1 wraps to 0 at line 13, so no reallocation occurs, and line 33 executes memcpy(target->str, source, SIZE_MAX) into a buffer of capacity target->size, a confirmed heap out-of-bounds write (with a parallel out-of-bounds read from source), followed by an out-of-bounds null write at index SIZE_MAX on line 36. Primary CWE-787; the integer wrap in the guard and size arithmetic is the independently confirmed root cause (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: add_len's residual range is [0, SIZE_MAX] (internal-helper parameter, no shown constraint excludes the maximum). Witness len=0, add_len=SIZE_MAX passes the L8 guard because (SIZE_MAX - add_len - 1) underflows to SIZE_MAX and SIZE_MAX < 0 is false; then target->len + add_len + 1 wraps to 0 at L13, so the grow branch is skipped and the memcpy length SIZE_MAX exceeds the destination capacity target->size (maintained at L26/L28) by SIZE_MAX - size, an out-of-domain length for memcpy causing a heap OOB write (CWE-787) and an OOB read of source of the same length.

On the same witness path (len=0, add_len=SIZE_MAX), L35 increments target->len to SIZE_MAX and this statement writes a null byte at index SIZE_MAX, exceeding the capacity target->size by SIZE_MAX - size bytes (at least one byte past the end), a second confirmed heap OOB write of the same CWE-787 finding.

assumptions: size_t is unsigned with SIZE_MAX = 2^64-1 on 64-bit (equivalently 2^32-1 on 32-bit); the underflow analysis holds identically on both.
simplestring_init_str (L5) succeeds and leaves target->str non-NULL for a fresh target; alternatively target arrives with str != NULL and len == 0 from prior use.
source points to readable memory long enough for at least part of the oversized copy, so the OOB write begins; the out-of-domain length argument alone is the confirmed defect regardless.
limitations: Line 2 reads target->size before the NULL check at line 3; a NULL target would crash, but NULL is not produced anywhere in the shown code, so CWE-476 is not confirmed.
The actually observed extent of the L33 overflow is bounded by when memcpy's read from source faults; the derived out-of-domain length (SIZE_MAX > capacity) is the confirmed defect.

On realloc failure (L26) the function silently does nothing (void return, size set to 0 via L28 and the copy skipped at L31): silent data loss without a deterministic attacker-controlled trigger, not a confirmed memory-safety or status-handling security flaw.
The exact initial capacity after simplestring_init_str is not shown; the finding uses capacity = target->size, which the shown code itself maintains at L26/L28.

verdict.summary: In the ASCII read path, GmfOpenMesh reads whitespace-delimited tokens from the mesh file with fscanf(msh->hdl, "%s", str) and no field width, writing an attacker-controlled token plus NUL into the stack buffer char str[GmfStrSiz]. A token of length >= GmfStrSiz overflows the buffer (excess token_len + 1 - GmfStrSiz), enabling unbounded stack corruption from a malicious .mesh/.sol file.

evidence.reason: File contents are entry-point input with no length constraint imposed by the shown code: the only length guard (line 39) bounds FilNam, not file tokens, and no field width is given to this fscanf. A whitespace-delimited token of length GmfStrSiz (admitted by the loop condition at line 128, which only requires res != EOF) writes GmfStrSiz + 1 bytes into char str[GmfStrSiz] declared at line 5, overflowing by at least 1 byte with unbounded growth as token length increases. This is a stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121) reachable with mod == GmfRead and a filename passing the line 53 extension check.

Same unbounded %s sink as line 127, reachable after the MeshVersionFormatted scan succeeds: a token of length >= GmfStrSiz in the Dimension scan overflows char str[GmfStrSiz] (declared at line 5) by token_len + 1 - GmfStrSiz bytes. The loop condition at line 141 admits any successful read (res != EOF), and no width cap or length check exists anywhere between fopen (line 122) and this call, so the OOB write is confirmed at this second distinct sink statement (CWE-121).

assumptions: GmfStrSiz is a positive constant equal to the declared array bound of str (line 5) and, per the +7 reserve at lines 39-42, the intended capacity of msh->FilNam.
GmfRead/GmfWrite and GmfDimension/GmfVersionFormatted are the library's constants.
fscanf("%s", buf) has standard C semantics: it writes the token bytes plus a terminating NUL with no width limit.
limitations: The numeric value of GmfStrSiz is not shown; the overflow boundary and excess are expressed relative to the declared GmfStrSiz-element capacity of str.
The capacity of msh->FilNam is not visible in the shown code; the strcpy at line 42 is treated as safe only under the GmfStrSiz-capacity assumption, and any contrary claim would be unconfirmable.
NULL or wrong-arity varargs usage for PtrVer/PtrDim (lines 71-72, 152-153) is a caller-contract issue; the shown code cannot produce NULL on that path.
Bodies of safe_fread/safe_fscanf/ScaWrd/RecWrd/ScaKwdTab are not shown; their internal behavior was not assessed.
Path/symlink semantics of fopen/open with FilNam are out of scope; no sandbox or privilege context exists in the shown code.
The pointer-to-int64 handle cast (line 16) is not used for arithmetic or indexing in the shown code.

verdict.summary: In the non-auth path the loop calls uni_utf8_get_char_n with max_len = (size_t)(p - parser->end); since the loop only executes while p < parser->end, the pointer difference is negative and the cast underflows to a huge size_t (e.g. 2^64-1 for the final byte), so a truncated UTF-8 sequence at the end of the buffer is decoded across the boundary, reading 1-3 bytes past parser->end (heap overread when the line buffer is exactly sized).

evidence.reason: Entry-point byte input with residual range [0x00,0xFF] per byte (no shown constraint) reaches this sink. The loop guard at line 9 (p < parser->end) admits p = end-1 with (p - parser->end) = -1, and the cast to size_t underflows to 2^64-1, which uni_utf8_get_char_n consumes as its byte-length bound; with a truncated multi-byte lead (e.g. 0xC2 as the last byte) the decoder then reads the missing continuation byte(s) at end[0]..end[2], i.e. past the parseable region [parser->cur, parser->end) — a CWE-125 overread whose root cause is the signed-to-unsigned underflowed length argument derived entirely in the shown code.

assumptions: parser->cur, parser->state.poff and parser->end are in-bounds and consistent at function entry (poff <= end - cur and p < end admitted by line 9).
uni_utf8_get_char_n(p, max_len, &out) consumes the second argument as the maximum number of source bytes it may consider, matching its name and the 'nch < 0' short-input path used in the shown code.
limitations: Whether the 1-3 byte overread crosses an allocation boundary (heap overread vs. read of padding past the logical data) depends on the caller's buffer allocation, which is not shown; severity and crash/exfiltration impact scale with that layout.
If uni_utf8_get_char_n internally refuses to peek at continuation bytes for a truncated sequence, the defect manifests as wrong-input acceptance/parse-error denial rather than memory corruption.
With max_size == 0 the length check at line 22 is disabled for the shown code (unbounded parameter length up to the buffer).
Validity of state.poff at entry and the buffer lifecycle are enforced by callers, not shown here.

verdict.summary: The only confirmed weakness is low-severity log injection (CWE-117): the externally supplied url/title/description/feed_title are never validated or newline-escaped, and after `utils::replace_all` removes only the single-quote character (lines 12-15) the raw values flow into the DEBUG log at line 17, so a value such as title="x\nFAKE-EVENT\n" splits the log record and forges log content. The `/bin/sh -c` execution paths (lines 22 and 26-31) are not command-injectable: the program supplies the only single quotes and deletes the one character that can terminate a POSIX-sh single-quoted literal, so `;`, `|`, `$()`, backticks and newlines in the fields remain literal.

evidence.reason:
url/title/description/feed_title are consumed with no validation, so their residual range (Phase 1) includes newline and control characters; `utils::replace_all` at lines 12-15 removes only single quotes, preserving `

FAKE-EVENT

`utils::run_program` and `utils::run_interactively` execute the constructed command with standard exec-family semantics under `/bin/sh` and do not modify the argv strings; POSIX sh terminates a single-quoted string only at a `'` character.
`strprintf::fmt` and `LOG` use printf-style semantics where the literal strings are the formats and the supplied values are arguments.
Values returned by `cfg.get_configvalue`/`cfg.get_configvalue_as_bool` are trusted application configuration; the shown code establishes no attacker-controlled path into them.
`cmdline.c_str()` (line 29) stays valid for the duration of the `run_program` call because `cmdline` is not modified or destroyed until after the call.
limitations: Command injection via the unquoted `bookmark_cmd` prefix (line 10) is not confirmed: its provenance is configuration rather than attacker input in the shown code. If configuration were ever attacker-influenced, line 31 would become a CWE-78 sink.

`utils::run_interactively`'s return value is discarded (line 22), but no security-relevant operation consumes a failure state afterward, so no CWE-390/754/703 finding is confirmed.
No fixed-size buffers, numeric casts, or attacker-derived sizes/indexes exist in the shown code, so no memory-safety candidate was formed.

verdict.summary: In the non-AUTH branch, the decoder is invoked with max_len = (size_t)(p - parser->end) (line 19). Since the call is only reached while p < parser->end, the negative pointer difference is converted to a huge size_t (e.g., SIZE_MAX with one byte remaining), giving the callee a near-unbounded read budget. When an attacker-controlled command parameter ends with a truncated multi-byte UTF-8 sequence at the buffer boundary, the decoder reads 1-3 bytes past parser->end — a heap out-of-bounds read that can crash the SMTP process (CWE-195 root cause at the length sink; CWE-125 consequence).

evidence.reason: The second argument is a read-budget length derived at the call site from reversed pointer subtraction: line 13 admits only p < parser->end, so p - parser->end is negative on every iteration and the explicit cast yields ~SIZE_MAX-(remaining), e.g. 2^64-2 when two bytes remain. uni_utf8_get_char_n consumes this as the maximum bytes it may read to decode a character; with witness buffer {0xE2, 0x82} (cur=&b[0], end=&b[2], poff=0, auth_response=0), the 3-byte sequence started by 0xE2 forces a read from b[2], 1+ bytes past end. The max_size check (line 35) and textstr check (lines 30-31) execute after the call and never constrain the argument. Primary CWE-195: negative signed difference converted to a huge unsigned size feeding a length sink; secondary CWE-125: consequent heap OOB read.

assumptions: parser->cur and parser->end delimit a contiguous input buffer, and parser->state.poff is non-negative, so p starts within [cur, end) (line 12) — the loop guard at line 13 enforces the only bound relied on for the finding.
uni_utf8_get_char_n's second parameter is a maximum-byte-count read budget, per the standard semantics implied by its name and by the callee's use of the argument.
limitations: The exact number of bytes read past parser->end depends on the unshown decoder internals, but it is at least 1 (the buffer boundary byte) whenever a 2-4-byte UTF-8 sequence is truncated at the buffer end, because the huge max_len defeats any 'sequence does not fit' check.

The failure requires attacker-influenced content such that the tail of the current transport buffer begins a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence (e.g., a chunk ending in 0xE2 0x82); if the remaining bytes are ASCII/CRLF the decoder reads only one byte and no OOB occurs.
The duplicate-space check and i_strdup_until call were reviewed and found safe in the shown code (mp is bounded below by parser->cur at lines 54-58, so the copied range is internal).

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability is confirmed in mlx5_fpga_conn_create_cq. The WQ initialization loop is bounded by the WQ entry count (i in 0..size-1 vs. size entries), the inlen arithmetic ties the pas-fill write volume exactly to the allocation size (inlen = 96 + 8*npages; pas at the header offset), and every called function's return status (mlx5_cqwq_create, kvzalloc, mlx5_vector2eqn, mlx5_core_create_cq) is checked with correct free/teardown on failure. Residual concerns (unvalidated cq_size feeding roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2, and a theoretical int overflow in inlen) cannot be demonstrated with a witness derived entirely from the shown code because npages and WQ-success limits originate in the unshown mlx5_cqwq_create.

assumptions: mlx5_cqwq_create, on success, initializes conn->cq.wq and conn->cq.wq_ctrl consistently, including buf.npages and the entry count returned by mlx5_cqwq_get_size, and mlx5_cqwq_get_wqe is valid for indices 0..size-1.
The caller supplies a cq_size for which the kernel roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2 contract holds (non-zero, power-of-two-compatible), since the shown code imposes no such constraint.
MLX5_ST_SZ_BYTES(create_cq_in) equals the byte offset of the pas array, so inlen = header + 8*npages exactly covers the fill performed by mlx5_fill_page_frag_array.
conn and fdev->conn_res.uar are non-NULL, supplied correctly by the (unshown) caller; the shown code never produces NULL for them.
limitations: Integer overflow of inlen (line 31-32) would require npages >= 2^28, which in turn requires mlx5_cqwq_create (line 21-22) to have succeeded in allocating a WQ of over a TiB; npages and the WQ allocation limits are set inside an unshown function, so no concrete witness value can be derived entirely from the shown code. Not reported as CWE-190/CWE-787.

cq_size is never validated in the shown code before roundup_pow_of_two(cq_size) (line 15) and ilog2(cq_size) (lines 16, 46); zero/negative values invoke undefined kernel-macro shifts and oversized values truncate in the int store, but all downstream sizes derive from the same value and stay mutually consistent, so no in-bounds/out-of-bounds mismatch is demonstrable. Hardening concern only.

A huge cq_size would scale WQ allocation, the initialization loop (line 26), and inlen, but reaching those sinks requires the WQ allocation itself to succeed first; no attacker-controlled volume is demonstrated inside the shown code (CWE-400 not confirmed).
NULL-pointer dereference of conn/uar (lines 3, 48, 67) depends on caller-supplied invariants not visible in the shown code; the shown code never produces NULL on any path.

Internal cleanup behavior of mlx5_cqwq_create on its own partial failure (e.g., WQ frags allocated but DB allocation failing) is not visible in the shown code, so its error path cannot be audited here.

verdict.summary: glob()'s ~user tilde expansion writes past its user-name buffer: with GLOB_TILDE and a pattern such as "~a\bc/defg/e" (literal backslash before the first '/'), the unescape loop at lines 487-504 copies the entire remainder of dirname (including the tail after end_name) into newp, whose capacity is only end_name - dirname bytes (allocation at lines 470-474). The loop has no bound tied to that capacity, producing an attacker-controlled-length out-of-bounds write (heap via malloc at line 474, or stack via the alloca path at line 471): CWE-787.

evidence.reason: Unbounded copy sink: p iterates over every byte of dirname from unescape (memchr at line 463) to the terminating NUL, including the portion after end_name, while newp has capacity exactly end_name - dirname bytes (malloc at line 474 / alloca at line 471). For the witness flag set GLOB_TILDE (GLOB_NOESCAPE clear) and pattern "~a\bc/defg/e", dirname="~a\bc/defg", end_name at index 5, unescape at index 2, capacity 5 (indices 0-4); the loop writes to indices 5,6,7 (chars 'e','f','g'), all out of bounds. Guards at lines 16, 226-228, 281, 315, 317-319, 454, 465, and 482 all admit this value; no check bounds the loop against the allocation size. Primary CWE-787 out-of-bounds write.

Second out-of-bounds write of the same finding: after the loop, *p = '\0' terminates the user_name string; with the witness above p has advanced to newp+8 while newp is only 5 bytes (end_name - dirname from lines 470-474), so this NUL lands 4 bytes past the allocation. Same taint (pattern backslash/tail via lines 463 and 487-503) and same guard admission as the loop write; CWE-787.

assumptions: POSIX (non-Windows) build: the vulnerable ~user branch is inside "#ifndef WINDOWS32".
GLOB_TILDE and GLOB_NOESCAPE are defined bits within __GLOB_FLAGS, so flags=GLOB_TILDE passes the format guard at line 16 (standard glibc flag values).
pattern is NUL-terminated (the strlen-based API contract) and pglob is a valid non-NULL glob_t set up by the caller per the documented GLOB_APPEND/GLOB_DOOFFS usage.
limitations: The exact alloca-vs-heap flavor of the overflow depends on glob_use_alloca/alloca_account, whose bodies are not shown; both branches share the identical OOB write, so only CWE-787 (the confirmed mechanism) is asserted rather than CWE-121/CWE-122.

Nested GLOB_BRACE alternatives cause recursive glob calls (lines 146-148) whose total work can be exponential in the number of brace groups; this is inherent brace-expansion design (potential CWE-400 DoS) and is not asserted as a confirmed defect.

Brace-construction buffer sizing (pattern_len = strlen(pattern)-1 at line 91 vs. copies at lines 103/144) depends on next_brace_sub's unshown semantics; all plausible parse semantics fit the buffer, so no finding is asserted there.
Error-path calls to globfree(pglob) at lines 157-158 may leave gl_pathv dangling for a subsequent caller-side globfree; the post-free state of globfree is not shown, so a double-free is unconfirmed.
The overflow is only reachable when the calling application enables GLOB_TILDE; the shown code itself imposes no additional pre-condition on the pattern contents.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. All error statuses are checked (L23-24, L34-37, L40-41, L57-58) with correct cleanup and no double-free; the CQE init loop (L26-29) uses a strict i < size bound consistent with the created queue's own size; inlen (L31-32) cannot overflow for any cq_size representable through the L15 rounding; and the PAS region (L51-52) is sized from the same npages used for the allocation. The only real concerns are the missing validation of cq_size (L15-16, L44) before roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2 and the unshown capacities of the CQ buffer and doorbell page; none reaches a security-relevant sink in the shown code, so they are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The called kernel APIs honor their documented semantics: mlx5_cqwq_get_size returns the CQ entry count and mlx5_cqwq_get_wqe(wq, i) returns CQE i of the same queue; mlx5_fill_page_frag_array writes exactly buf.npages entries; mlx5_cqwq_create allocates a buffer sized by log_cq_size and initializes wq_ctrl.buf.npages/page_shift/db consistently; the frag-buf allocator guarantees page_shift >= MLX5_ADAPTER_PAGE_SHIFT; mlx5_db_alloc guarantees a doorbell region of at least two dwords.
conn/fdev/mdev and fdev->conn_res.uar are valid for the call; validity is established only by the unshown caller (internal-helper provenance).
mlx5_cqwq_create consumes only wqp.buf_numa_node and wqp.db_numa_node, the two fields set at L18-19.
limitations: cq_size is never validated before roundup_pow_of_two(cq_size) (L15) and ilog2(cq_size) (L16, L44). For cq_size <= 0 the kernel macros exhibit undefined behavior, and for cq_size >= 2^30+1 the narrowing at L15 wraps (2^31 to INT_MIN), yielding log_cq_size = 31 and a ~2^37-byte allocation attempt that fails cleanly with -ENOMEM. No corrupted index/size/length reaches a memory or injection sink in the shown code, and attacker control of cq_size is not established (internal-helper parameter), so this is not a confirmed finding (no CWE).

The in-bounds status of the L26-29 CQE loop depends on the unshown unit consistency of mlx5_cqwq_get_size (entry count) with mlx5_cqwq_get_wqe (entry index); the CQ buffer's capacity is not identifiable from the shown code, so no OOB claim is confirmable.
inlen (L31-32) cannot overflow int for any cq_size representable through L15 (npages <= 2^25 yields inlen ~2^28), but the npages bound itself derives from unshown allocator semantics.
The doorbell stores at L61-64 write db.db[0] and db.db[1] and rely on the unshown >=2-dword slot invariant of mlx5_db_alloc.
